ee ee) My Lord, Constantinople, May 20, 1890. 
| A QUESTION likely to be attended with much discussion and excitement 
| is on the point of being raised between the conflicting interests of the Latin and 
| Greek churches in this country. The immediate point of difference 1s the right 
| of possession to certain portions of the Chureh of the Holy Sepulchre at 
| Jerusalem. ‘The Greeks are aceused of having usurped property which belongs 
: of right to the Roman Catholies, and of having purposely allowed the chapels, 
ty and particularly the monuments of Godefroi de Bouillon, and of Guy dle 
' Lusignan, to go into decay. The French Legation at this Court considers itself 
tt entitled by Treaty,—the Treaty, I believe, of 1740,—to take the lead in vin- 
Dy dicating the alleged rights of the Latin Church; the French Consul at Jerusalem, 
4 M. Botta, has been recently here, and returns by-and-bye to assist the cause ; 
i) ' and General Aupick, who has received ‘nstructions from Paris, and to whom i 
! am indebted for a conversational overture on this subject, has applied for a con- 
ference, with the probable intention of bringing his case at once under the notice 
of the Turkish Government. It appears that the Pope has been moved to exert 


EA | his influence in furtherance of the views adopted by Franee; and that all the 

i Catholic Powers will be engaged by His Holiness to cooperate for the same 

‘ purpose, | 

: General Aupick has assured me that the matter in dispute is a mere question 
of property, and of express treaty stipulation. But itis difficult to separate any 


fi such question from political considerations ; and a struggle of general influence, 
ha especially if Russia, as may be expected, should take up the eudgels on behalf of 
f the Greek Church, will probably grow out of the impending discussion. 

The Porte, | conceive, will do well to abstain from committing itself to 
either side without the maturest deliberation, and such is the impression which | 
have conveyed privately to Reshid Pasha. 
I have, &e

No. 5. 
Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received July 19.) 


(No, 221. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Therapia, July 9, 1850, 

1 AM not aware that any further step of an official character has been 
taken by the French Legation here concerning the holy buildings at Jerusalem 
since the note verbale delivered to Aali Pasha by General Aupick, and mentioned 
to your Lordship in one of my preceding despatches. The Porte, 1 would also 
appear, has not yet declared or taken any decision on the subject of that 
Minister's demand. 

With respect to the Catholic Representatives, from whom, on such an 
occasion, the French would naturally expect agreement and support, I learn that 
the Portuguese Chargé d' Affaires, in seconding General Aupick by means of an 
official note, acted entirely on his own responsibility ; that the Spanish Minister 
has not yet taken a step of that character; that the Austrian Chargé d’Affaires 
has recently reecived ‘nstructions to. support the Latin view of the question ; 
and that the Belgian Minister, while continuing to plead for the repar of those 
chapels in which the monuments of Godefrey de Bouillon and his kindred 

crusaders were erected, abstains from bearing any direct part in the general 
claim asserted by France. 

| have reason to believe that some animated discussions have lately passed 
between M, de Blondel and General Aupick on this subject. ‘The point at 
issue, if | am rightly informed, was not the question of right, respecting which 

little difference of opinion may be anticipated between any two Catholic Powers, 
but the manner in which the question had been arrayed, as it were, under the 
banner of France, and &x ed to the hostility of those whom a renewal of the 


old French influence in Syria could never please. It would seem that when 
General Aupick asserted the perfect simplicity of his intention, and declared 
that the matter in debate was @ mere question of right and international law, he 
was reminded of certain publications which were not easil reconcileable with 
that hypothesis; and that the grounds and mode of proceeding adopted by him 
had naturally laid him open to the very objections which he disclaimed. 

Language of this kind was not likely to prove the less unwelcome from 
being founded in reason, and expressed with a tone of conviction ; and if the 
Porte should acquiesce, a5 1 am privately assured it will, in M. de Blondel’s 
demand, and does not at the same time extend its compliance to the French 

reposition, a strong feeling of mortification, if not resentment, will probably be 

excited on the losing side. 

On the part of the Greck interest, nothing that wears the appearance of 
an angry or hostile opposition has yet been manifested ; ut no one seems to 
doubt that every nerve will be strained hy that Chureh and Nution to mamta 
their present vantage-ground, and that Russian influence, however masked, will 
be vigorously exerted, as on former occasions, to defeat the attack of the Latin 
rarty. 
: "Mindful of your Lordship’s instructions, L confine myself to the duty of 
watching from & distance any movements that may occur in the two antagonist 
camps. A Christian, having no -mmediate concern in the dispute, might reason. 
ably wish to see the removal of a gcandalous contention between the two 
Churches, which arrogate an exclusive guardianship of places ganctified by our 
common religion. But no Englishman, alive to the interests of a true European 
policy in the East, could witness without regret and anxiety the triumph of a 
political influence which would always be ready to overflow its bounds, ane 
would render this land of infidels more than ever the battle-ground of Christian 
antagonists. 

I have, &e. 

(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING.

Viscount Palmerston to Sir Stratford Canning. 
(No, 210.) 


Sir, Foreign Office, August 3, 1850. 

I HAVE to state to your Excellency in reply to your despatch No. 221, of 
the Sth of July, that you are quite rig it in not interfering in any way in the 
pending dispute between the Greek Latin Churches respecting their claims 
to the holy buildings at Jerusalem, and in contenting yourself with attentively 
watching its progress, and reporting what takes place to Her Majesty's 
Government.

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received Auqust 6.) 


(No. 225. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Therapia, July 19, 1850. 

INCLOSED herewith for your Lordship’s further information, are copies 
obtained confidentially of several notes addressed to the Porte in recommen- 
dation of the French demand respecting the chapels and monuments at 
Jerusalem. 

1 am informed that the Sardinian Minister, though he supported General 
Aupick verbally, and read to Aali Pasha an instruction from his Government, 
did not present any note to the Porte, and that no communication has yet been 
made by the Austrian tion. 

The manner in which the Austrian Government views the question brought 
forward by France appears in another document, which has been privately 
spmerisated to me by one of my colleagues, and of which a copy is transmitted 
erewith, 

Aali Pasha assured me three days ago that nothing had yet been done 
by the Porte respecting that question, and that no orders had been sent to 
Jerusalem, 

T avail myself of this opportunity to forward a transcript of all such Articles 
of the Treaty concluded between France and the Porte in 1740, as relate to the 
right claimed by France of protecting the Latins and, on their behalf, the holy 
places at Jerusalem. 

I have, &e. |

General Aupick to Aali Pasha. 


Péra, Mai 28, 1850. 

LE Général de Division, Ministre de France prés la Sublime Porte Otto- 
mane, a eu l’honneur de donner lecture § son Excellence Aali Pasha, Ministre 
des Affaires Etrangéres de Sa Majesté le Sultan, d'une dépéche par laquelle le 
Gouvernement de la République le charge de revendiquer effieacement en faveur 
des religieux Latins la possession des lieux saints que Article XXXII des 
Capitulations de 1740 leur a garantie. 

Ces lieux saints sont : 

La Grande Eglise de Bethléem. 

Le Sanctuaire de la Nativité, avec le droit d'y placer une nouvelle étoile, 
de changes la tapisserie de la grotte; d’y agir, enfin, comme les possesseurs 
exclusify. 


Le Tombeau de la Sainte Vierge. 

La Pierre de l’Onction. 

Les sept arceaux de la Sainte Vierge dans I'Eglise du Saint Sépulere. 

Le Gouvernement Francais réclame encore pour les religieux Franes le 
droit de réparer la coupole de I'Eglise du Saint Sépulere; et enfin, il demande 
que dans cette derniére église, toutes choses soient remises en |'état ot elles 
étaient avant l'incendie de 1808, Tl prouvera surabondamment que les 
sanctuatres et les droits ci-dessus énumérés appartenaient aux religieux Latins 
en 1740. 

La franchise et le courage avec lesquels la Sublime Porte est entrée dans 
des voies d’amélioration morale et de civilisation; L’adhésion qu'elle a donnée 
var sa conduite sage et mesurée aux grands principes du droit public Européen, 
fniseent au Gouvernement Francais la ferme conviction que, dans cette circon- 
stance, il ne fera pas inutilement appel-A la bonne foi ct d l’esprit déquité du 
Gouvernement de Sa Majesté Imperiale; et que celui-ci en fournira une 
nouvelle preuve par son respect pour les engagements dont la France réclame 
lexécution. ; 

Il mettra de la sorte et pour toujours un terme a des difficultés sans cesse 


,renaissantes, et 4 d'interminables récriminations qu'il n’entre certainement pas 


dans sa pensce de vouloir perpétuer.

M. le Ministre, Constantinople, le & Mai, 1850, 

D'APRES l'inyitation de votre Excellence, je viens répéter par écrit la 
demande que j'ai eu I'honneur de lui adresser verbalement, tendant & obtenir 
Vautorisation de rétablir dans |’Eglise du Saint Sépulere de Jérusalem, les 
tombeaux de Godefroy de Bouillon et de Baudouin son frére, que l'incendie du 
12 Octobre, 1808, a fait disparaitre. 

Dé@a, M, Bug. de Kerckhove a eu l’honneur d’adresser 4 votre Excellence 
une note sur cette question en date du 30 Septembre, 1848. En renouvellant 
eette démarche par ordre exprés du Gouvernement du Roi, j’ajouterai peu de 
chose. 

Quand on se borne 4 réclamer le respect pour les tombes, pour justifier sa 
réclamation il suflit de l’énoncer ; et j'ai trop de confiance dans l'équité de votre 
Excellence et du Gouvernement de Sa Majesté Impériale, pour qu'il ne me

a été prété a cette affaire une importance qu'elle n’a pas en elle-méme, et qui ne 
peut que compromettre son succés. Je crois done devoir la rétublir dang sa 
simple vérité. Il ne s'agit pas de discuter les limites entre les diverses commu. 
nions Chretiennes dans lintérieur de I'Eglise; je n’ai pas A examiner ici gi les 
religieux Francs ou Grees sont les possesseurs légitimes ou illégaux de telle ou 
telle partie du temple: toute ma mission consiste & réclamer un acte de justice 
qui ne peut étre mis en doute par personne, qui ne peut rien cotter a nue, 
qui ne peut préjuger aucun point de droit dans les questions en litige: de 
restaurer aux frais de Ia Belgique les picrres sépulcrales de deux Princes Belges, 
profanées apres ae sitcles d'existence (1099 a 1808).

plan). Les tombes étaient placées 4 l'entrée (102); mais aprés l'incendic, 
Vesealier qui conduit au Calvaire (3) fut démoli et remplacé par une double 
échelle construite ¢n BB, dont le mur de soutien a été post sur les tom- 
beaux. Toute eette partie est possédée aujourd'hui par les Grees Orientaux. 

Ce que je demande, M. le Ministre, c'est de rétablit Vancien esealier pour 


remettre les choses dans leur état primitif, ou du moins de tirer un are de B en 
B, de faeon A lnisser A découvert emplacement ott était les deux monuments 
que la Belgique entiére a le pieux désir de relever avec l'autorisation de la 
Sublime Porte Ottomane.

a cette réparation d'un acte gratuit de vandalisme exercé sur les simples tom-

Inclosure in No. 11. 
Aali Pasha to General Aupick. 


(Traduction,) 30 Decembre, 1850. 

J'AL eu Vhonneur de recevoir la note que votre Excellence m’a adressée 
sous la date du 28 Mai dernier, et qui renfermait la demande de la restitution 
aux prétres Latins des saints lieux & Jérusalem, dont la possession leur est 
assurée par l'Article XXXIU du Traité conclu entre la Sublime Porte et le 
Gouvernement Francais lan 1740 de Vere Chrétienne, ainsi que quelques 
représentations sur certains points qui se rattachent 4 cette question. 

il est certain que la Sublime Porte a constamment et de tout temps éte 
dans 'habitude d’exéeuter avec droiture et de la meilleure foi du monde ses 
'Traités avec les Puissances amies, et il n’est pas moins vrai de dire qu'un Traité 
qui n'a subi, A une époque queleonque, aucun changement, aucune modification, 
du consentement des deux Parties Contractantes, conserve toute sa vigueur dans 
toutes ses dispositions, 

Seulement, et il est superflu de le dire, comme tous les Chréetiens des 
diverses croyances ont part aux saints lieux Chretiens qui existent 4 Jérusalem, 
et qui sont visités par eux, chaque partie est en possession de plusicurs anciens 
firmans ct titres. Cela étant, la Sublime Porte ne peut pas naturellement pro- 
noncer sur cette question, qu’an préalable une Commission Mixte n’ait vu et 
médité profondément les firmans et autres pieces authentiques et valables qui 
ont été données, soit avant, soit aprés, le Traité précité; et nul doute que le 
Gouvernement Francais, qui a déji donné tant de preuves de son amour pour 
Véquité et Ia justice, n’apprécie cette excuse bien fondee et ne Vaccepte. 

Voila, M. le Ministre, ce que, par ordre de Sa Majesté le Sultan, yrai été 
chargé de vous faire savoir, et je saisis, &e.

No. 12. 
Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received February 3.) 


(No. 9) 
My Lord, Constantinople, January 6, 185). 

THE French Minister called upon me this morning, and after stating the 
substance of Aali Pasha’s note to him on the subject of Jerusalem, informed me 
that he had given in a formal protest to his Excellency against that part of the 
Turkish communication which goes to include in the pope ile sues 
firmans and other public documents as may have been promu eated subsequently 
to the ‘Treaty concluded between France and ‘Turkey in the year 1740. He is 
of opinion that they cannot be admitted as objects of discussion without invali- 
dating the principle maintained by his Government, which is, that no firman of 
a date posterior to the Treaty can be pleaded in bar of the Treaty’s execution, 
| ventured to ask, without entering at all into the merits of the question, 
whether the subsequent firmans might not be admitted, under a suitable declara- 
tion on his part, with a view to the possibility of their containing relevant clauses 
which might be shown to be not in contradiction with the terms of the Treaty. 
I infer from General Aupick’s answer that he is not at liberty to modily hiss 
present course of proceeding without fresh instructions from Paris, that he cannot 
officially lose sight of the lead of the Catholic Powers, and that his personal 
sentiments would induce him to forego that favorite abject of French policy for 
the sake of a practical arrangement calculated to remove the twofold scandal of 
religious collision and local profanation from the holy Christian buildings of 
Jerusalem. 

A message from Aali Pasha informs me that the French Minister had 
accompanied his protest with an expression of thanks to the Porte for declaring 
its readiness to execute literally the terms of its Treaty with France, and that 
the Pasha had promised to take ete pg protest into consideration. 

| have 


, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING.

No. 13. 


Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston,—( Received February 3.) 


(No. 14. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, January 7, 1851. 

I HAVE just now obtained confidentially from Aali Pasha a copy of 
General Aupick’s protest, mentioned in another despatch, and I hasten to 
forward it herewith for your Lordship’s more complete information. A Council, 
which is held to-day on the affairs of Samos, will probably be invited to take 
it into consideration, and this promptitude looks as if the result of the pending 
deliberation may perhaps prove favourable to the views of the Freneh Govern- 
ment. 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING, 


Inclosure in No. 13. 
General Aupick to Aali Pasha. 


Peéra, le 5 Janvier, 1851. 

LE Général de Division, Ministre de France prés la Sublime Porte Ottomane, 
m recu le memorandum que son Excellence Auli Pasha, Ministre des Affaires 
Etrangéres de Sa Majesté le Sultan, lui a fait 'honneur de lui adresser, en date 
‘du 17 Safer, 1267 (30 Décembre, 1850), sous le No. 12, en réponse i la note 
‘que le Ministre de France avait cu lhonneur de remettre i son Excellence le 
48 Mai, 1840, A l'eflet de revendiquer efficacement, au profit des religieux 
Latins de la Palestine, la possession des licux saints dont les Traités leur assurent 
la jouissance. 

Si est avee une vive satisfaction que le Ministre de France a vu la Sublime 
Porte reconnaitre l'existence et la pleine valeur des Traités dont la France, en 
cette circonstance, réclame Vexécution au nom de tous les Catholiques, c'est avec 
un douloureux étonnement qu'il a remarqué une deéviation manifeste de ces 
principes dans lu fin du memorandum que son Excellence le Ministre des Affaires 
Etrangéres a été chargé de lui communiquer. 

Een effet, ctendre aux actes postérieurs aux capitulations de 1740, Vexamen 
propose par son Excellence le Ministre des Affaires Etrangeres, mest-ce pas 
infirmer partiellement les Traités dont la Porte reconnait la pleine et entiere 
validité? N'est-ce pas mettre en contradiction avee cette déclaration formelle 
“auwun Traité qui n'a pas été modifié et changé du consentement des deux 
Parties Contractantes continue & étre valable ct en vigueur ?” 

Aussi, tout en considérant comme équitable la proposition de son Excellence 
Aali Pasha, en tant qu'elle ne concerne que les titres antéricurs a 1740, le

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Reeeived April 1.) 


(No. 91.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, March 18, 1851, 

AGREEABLY to your Lordship’s instructions, 1 have continued to abstain 
from taking any part in the pending dispute relative to the sacred buildings at 
Jerusalem. But I was surprised, a few days ago, by receiving a letter from the 
Guardian, or Pére Commissaire, of the Holy Sepulchre, expressing a wish that | 
should support the Latin view of the question, by way of sequel to the assistance 
afforded to it, as he alleges, by some of my predecessors in the century before 
last, I have returned a civil, and I trust a Christian, answer to his suggestion, 
without intimating any opinion as to the merits of the case. Copies of the 
correspondence are inclosed herewith for your Lordship’s information. At the 
Porte, it appears, the question remains in the same state as when I last adverted 
to it. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING.

Inclosure in No. 21. 
Aali Pasha to General Aupick, 


(Traduit du Ture.) Shaaban 1267, Juin 1851. 


LES notes que nous avons recues de la part de votre prédeécesseur, portant 
les dates du G Janvier et du 24 Fevrier derniers, en réponse a la note officielle 
qui lui avait été remise sous la date du 17 Safer, 1267 (30 Décembre, 1850), 
relutivement A certains lieux 4 Jérusalem, ont été prises en consideration. 

J'ai été peiné de voir par le contenu des dites notes que le Gouvernement 
Francais a trouvé dans celle du Gouvernement de Sa Hautesse des contradictions. 

La Sublime Porte, dont l'une des anciennes et constantes habitudes est 
aussi d'observer avec la plus grande loyauté et franchise des Traites avec les 
Puissances amies, n'hésite nullement & déclarer de nouveau que tous les 
Articles du Traité conclu l'année 1740 de V'ére Chretienne, lesquels n'ont pas 
été modifiés par un autre Traité, conservent leur foree et vigueur. 

Seulement, il y a ceci A dire: c'est que le droit d’expliquer et de déterminer, 
de commun accord, et quand cela devient. nécessaire, un Article, ou quelques 
Articles, des Traités conclus entre la Sublime Porte et des Puissances qui sont 
également amies comme la France, est un de ces droits qui appartiennent 
également 4 toutes les Puissances; et le Gouvernement Francais lui-méme 
conviendra avec ja Sublime Porte qu’aucune Gouvernement ne peut empécher 
un autre d’user de ce droit, Mais les modifications dont il est fait mention dans 
la note dela Sublime Porte, dont l'intention et le désir tendent sans cesse a 
sauvegarder les droits légitimes et bien fondés de chaque partie, et lesquelles 
sont une conséquence de ces mémes droits, ont au premier coup d’cal paru des 
contradictions au Gouvernement Francais. . 

Vu done que ces explications franches et loyales, et les nouvelles assurances 
données ici de nouveau du respect de la Sublime Porte pour les ‘Traités seront, 
on aime A eroire appréciées, par le Gouvernement Francais aussi bien que par 
votre Excellence, que tout soupyon sera dissipé, et que les deux parties sont 
réellement animées du désir de maintenir et de resserrer de plus en plus les 
relations amicales gui existent entre les deux illustres Gouvernements, il y a 
tout lieu d'espérer qu’en se concertant ensemble on pourra aviser aux moyens de 
résoudre cette question d'une maniére conforme @ la dignité et aux droits fondés 
de toutes les parties, 

Je saisis, &c. 


No. 22. 
Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palinerston.—(Received October 2.) 


(No, 282.) 
My Lord, Therapia, September 17, 1861. 
IT appears that the negotiations respecting the holy buildings at Jerusalem 
are beginning to assume a more serious aspect. The [Russian Government has 
manifested of late an increased interest in the maintenance of the Greek pratens 
sions. M. de Lavalette informs me that the Latin right is clearly established 
by the Committee of Investigation, and that his Government is fully entitled to 
‘nsist on the execution of the Treaty which records it. He gave me to under- 
stand that if the moderation of his Government, in seeking only a joint partici. 


21 


pation of the buildings in question, were not appreciated, the claim of undivided 
possession by the Latins would be urged with all the weight of a demand 
warranted by Treaty. 

Amidst these conflicting demonstrations I cannot perceive any symptom of 
concession on the side of the Porte, nor do I conceive it probable that the 
Turkish Ministers will give way, unless their hands be fairly forced; but as I 
take no part in the contest, the tendency to concession may exist without its 
falling under my immediate notice. 

I have, &e. 


(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING. 


No. 23. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to Viscount Palmerston. —(Received October 31.) 


(No. 52.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, October 21, 1851. 


IN conversing with the Chancellor I have taken occasion to allude to the 
statement to be read in Sir Stratford Canning’s despatch No. 252, inclosed in 
your Lordship’s No. 18, and while expressing my regret at the existence of any 
dispute as to rights having again arisen between the Greek aud Latin Churches, 
I thought it advisable to observe that the contest was one from which Her 
Majesty’s Ambassador had kept wholly aloof. 

Count Nesselrode said that of this fact he was fully aware. 

His Excellency proceeded to observe that the Porte, in this question of the 
right of possession at Jerusalem, had acted a somewhat insidious part, as the 
had given some encouragement to. the exaggerated pretensions of the French 
Mission in the hope of obtaining in return the assistance of the Republican 
Government in the resistance, more or less covert, which they were opposing to 
the English scheme of establishing railroad communications in Egypt. 

His Excellency said that he would tell me in confidence that overtures for 
the same purpose had been made very directly by the ‘Turkish Government to 
the Imperial Mission.

No. 28. 


Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received November 26.) 


(No. 323. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Therapia, November 4, 1851. 

THE French Envoy at this Court purposes to send M. de Reculot, the 
Principal Secretary of his Legation, to Paris, by the sieam-packet of to-morrow, 
with his conclusive report respecting the disputed sanctuaries at Jerusalem and 
Bethlehem, Aceording to his language in the conversations with which he has 
honoured me on this subject, and particularly during a visit which I received 
from him to-day, the question has assumed a character of extreme gravity. 
His several statements amount in substance to what follows :— 

France, says M. de Lavalette, is entitled by its Treaty of 1740 with the 
Porte to vindicate the right of the Latins to an exclusive occupation of all the 
sanctuaries which they possessed at that time. The conferences lately opened 
here have resulted in-a clear establishment of that right as applied to the holy 
buildings, ten, 1 believe, in number, most of which are now possessed jointly 
by the two communions, and some exclusively by the Greeks. M. de Lavalette, 
instead of pushing his right to an extreme, took upon himself the responsibility 
of declaring his readiness to extend the principle of joint possession to the 
whole number. In so doing he would have anticipated the instructions of his 
Government, and exposed himself to the animadyersion of Rome and of certain 
parties in France. An arrangement to this effect was unofficially agreed upon 
between Auli Pasha and himself, when he learnt that the Russian Envoy had 
sent ina letter from the Emperor Nicholas to the Sultan, which immediately 
altered the intentions of the Porte, and left him no choice but that of either 
accepting an inadmissible proposal or appealing to his Government. The 
proposal, which he thought it impossible to accept, was that of including in 
the principle of joint possession all the sanctuaries now possessed exclusively by 
the Latins. ‘This proposal was represented to me by the Turkish Ministers as 
embracing all the principal sects of Christianity ; but, whichever may be the 
correct version, it appears that M. de ‘Titoff was as much opposed to itas M. 
de Lavalette. The former declared to the Turkish Minister, that he and his 
Legation would immediately quit Constantinople if the status quo of the 
sanctuaries were in any degree unsettled. The Porte has, in consequence, 
substituted another proposul, namely, that it would reserve its final decision 
until after a full investigation of the quarrel on which the scveral conflicting 
pretensions, including those of the Grecks, of the Latins, and of Russia, are 
respectively founded, ‘This proposal is scarcely less distasteful to M. de 
Lavalette than the preceding one. He has acted with moderation throughout,— 
he has been eareful not to commit his Government —he has made no written 
communication except his opening note and such documents us were necessary 
for establishing the joint commission of inquiry, —he may regret that the question 
wis ever opened, and he is anxious to act with moderation to the last; but at 
the same time he thinks it impossible to submit with honour to the present 
plan of proceeding,—his Government having embarked, wisely or otherwise, in 
the question cannot, with any degree of credit or consistency, stop short under 
the dictation of Russia,—the national party in France, the Catholic party there 
and elsewhere, will press for the full assertion of right under treaty,—and, as for 
himself, he will retire rather than be made the instrument, as he conceives he 
would be in the supposed case, of his country’s humiliation; nay more, if it 
depended upon him, be would not hesitate to make use of the great naval force 
now possessed by France in the Mediterranean, and by blockading the Darda- 
nelles bring the question in debate forthwith to a satistuctory issue, 

Sich are the leading points of M. de Lavalette’s conversation with me. 
Hearing in view the purport of your Lordship's instructions, which direct me to 
preserve a neutral course in these discussions, l have expressed no opinion on 
the merits of the case. ‘To M, de Lavulette I have made such passing remarks 
us 1 thought most likely to abate any excess of heat or precipitancy in his pro- 
ceedings, aid I gave M. de Titoff a sensonable idea of the lengths to which, m 
opinion at least, our French colleague was disposed to urge his Government, 


25 


hoping that, if he were not prepared for extremes, the intimation might incline 
him to be less peremptory with the Porte. } 

The Sultan’s Ministers, though embarrassed by their position between the 
contending parties, haye not yet expressed to me any apprehension of violence, 
or coercion, as likely to proceed from either side. ‘Their object, as usual, 1s to 
temporize ; their inclination would seem to be rather towards France ; not that 
they can feel any direct concern in the question at issue, but as deeming a con- 
cession to French influence less dangerous than the triumph of Russian sympathy 
for the Greeks, whose cause, however, as that of an important section of their 
own fellow-subjects, they can hardly afford to neglect, The Sultan himself 
would gladly content Russia by leaving matters as they are, and he has shown 
come dissatisfaction with his Ministers for haying gone too far in compliance 
with the wishes of France. 

Whatever may be the immediate consequence of M. de Lavalette’s appeal 
to his Government, the subject-matter of it, if reeeived by the French President 
and his Cabinet in the spirit which appears to accompany its transmission, can 
hardly fail, sooner or later, to be productive of much annoyance, and perhaps of 
humiliation and eventual danger, to this country. That France, in her present 
condition, should at once put all to hazard for the sake of vindicating the 
alleged rights of her protected co-religionists under a Treaty which has more or 
less slumbered during a century, is not easy to be conceived. But passing 
interests might possibly coneur with other motives to recommend a demonstra- 
tion sufficiently embarrassing, not merely to the Porte, lutalso to Ter Majesty's 
Government, though its only object might be to produce a crisis capable of being 
resolved by means of arbitration, The idea of an arbitration appears to have 
occurred as well to the French Envoy as to the Turkish Ministers, M. de 
Lavalette has informed me that the Grand Vizier suggested the notion of a 
reference to Prussia, which he had rejected with the observation that England 
was the only Power to be thought of for such a purpose, though, in his opinion, 
the expedient could not be entertained except in the event of circumstances 
involving an immediate hazard of collision. 

It may be as well to add, that M. de Titoff stated fo me in conversation, 
after being apprized of the language held by M. de Lavalette, that it was impos- 
sible for him (the Russian Envoy) to act otherwise, though he did not anal 
whether that impossibility arose out of the nature of the case, or solely from the 
peremptory character of his instructions. 

In calling attention to the present complicated state of a question which, 
however injudiciously taken up, even in the judgment of those who are most 
active in pressing it to a decision, may involve consequences disproportioned to 
its intrinsic importance, I merely discharge a duty which could not be neglected 
with prudence or propriety, If remains for your Lordship to consider the 
language and circumstances reported above, in connection with such evidence of 
the real intentions of France and Russia as may reach Her Majesty's Government 
from other sources of information. 

Inclosed herewith ave three statements, which may possibly assist your 
Lordship in estimating the merits and bearings of the pending question. The 
‘first gives a list of the sanctuaries supposed to have been posseased exclusively 
By the Latins in 1740, The second isa chronological sketch of the several 
Hatti-sherifis issued by the Mahometan Sultans in favour of the Greeks. The 
third contains references to the principal Articles of the Treaties between Mussia 
and Turkey which might be cited as giving to the former a mght of interference 
on behalf of the ecclesiastical interests of the Greeks. 

i have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING,

My Lord, Therapia, November 27, 1851. 


HAVING received from M. de Lavalette an unofficial communication of 
the procés-verbaux of the Mixed Commission appointed some time ago by the 
Porte and the French Legation with & view to investigating the adverse claims of 
the Greeks and Latins to certain sanctuaries in the Holy Land, and haying his 
permission to transcribe them, I have the honour to transmit herewith a copy 
for your Lordship’s information. 

I avail myself of the opportunity to forward in copy also the last correspond- 
ence which has taken place on this subject between Aali Pasha and the French 
Envoy. I have since learnt in confidence from an authentic source that two 
days before the departure of the last steam-packet for Marseilles, M. de Lavalette 
renewed his endeavours to obtain some arrangement aceeptable to France, and 
that during his visit to Aali Pasha for that purpose he grounded his entreaties on 
the apprehensions which he entertained of measures being taken by his Govern- 
ment to compel the Porte to comply with their demands. 

I have, &c.

Fn vertu d’une décision prise entre le Gouvernement de Ja Sublime Porte 
et Ia Légation de France, une Commission Speciale a été formée pour lire et 
examiner scrupuleusement les khatti-chérifs, firmans, et autres documents 
authentiques relatifs aux licux saints situés tant a l'intérieur qu'a Vextéricur de 
Jérusalem, et qui sont l'objet de contestation entre les religieux Latins ct la 
communauté Greeque, La Sublime Porte a choisi pour ses Commissaires son 
Excellence Emin Effendy, Seercétaire Général du Ministére des Affaires Etrangercs, 
et M, Nicolas Aristarchi, Logothete de I'Bglise Patriarcale. La Légation de 
France a désigné M. Botta, Consul de France & Jérusalem, eb M, Schefer, second 
drogman de la Légation. La Commission s‘est reunie aujourd’hui, 2 Septembre, 
1851 (6 Zileaade, 1267), chez son Excellence Emin Effendy. Déji la Commis= 
sion s'était préeédemment réunie plusieurs fois et avait tenu plusicurs séances 
sang avoir pu entrer dans une ligne de conduite bien tracée. M., le Ministre 
Plénipotentiaire de France et son i’xcellence le Ministre des Affaires Etrangeres 
ont eu d ce sujet une entrevue, a la suite de laquelle il a été convenu de la 
maniére Ia plus positive que la itigsion. des Commissaires consistait seulement 
dans l’examen des titres et des documents qui se trouvent entre les mains des 
Lating et des Grecs, ct particulitrement de coux qui ont été délivrés depuis 
année 1101 (1689), jusqu’a Pannée 1153. (1740). 

Des khatti-chérifs, firmans, et autres documents néecssaires qui ont été 
donnés aux Latins, seront d’abord lus avec la plus grande attention dans ordre 
ov ils ont été délivrés. Le contenu de chaque pidce sera consigné en abrégé au 
procés-verbal, On examinera ensuite les pices qui seront produites par la 
communauté Greeque, Le sens de ces pidces sera aussi inseré en abrége au 

srocés-verbal. Apres ces explications les Commissaires ont examing en premier 
lieu le khatti-chérif déliveé par Sultan Suleyman HH, sous la date du 15 Redjeb 
de l'année 1101 (1689), et qui se trouve Aux mains des religieux Latins. 

La teneur de cet ordre est que bien que les religieux Latins aient le droit de 
tapisser et d’orner le lieu appelé le Sépulere de Jésus (sur Bu soit le salut), situe 
au inilieu de l’Eglise de Kamamé sige a Vintérieur de Jérusalem; qu’ils possédas- 
sent les deux coupoles, Pune grande et lautre petite ; qu’ils jouissent du droit 
Wétendre des tapis, de dire la messe, et de poser des chandeliers et des tentures 
au-dedans et gu-deliors du dit Sepulere et sur la place qui se trouve devant; 
qu'ils etissent la possession du petit autel qui se trouve entre les grilles de fer ay) 
sont posées comme limite devant la porte depuis ce lieu jusqwa PEglise des 
Grecs; quils efissent le droit de suspendre des lampes sous le grand arcedt qui 
se trouve au-dessus de cet emplacement, de dire la messe, de placer des flam- 
beaux et des lampes dans la moitié du Calvaire appelée lieu de la crucifixion 5 
bien entin, qu’ils jouissent de la prés¢ance sur les autres nations dans les visites 


ou) 


aux licux de dévotion ; et qu’ils efissent le droit de célebrer leurs eérémonies dans 


la partie inférieure et supérieure des sept arceaux de Ia Vierge Marie et sur la 


pierre de l'onction; cependant, les Grecs les ont violemment et abusivement 

privés de ces droits; ils ont Até les lampes des Latins et place deux chandeliers 

de pierre sous le grand arceau en face le Sépulere, mis deux flambeaux sur la 

piers de l'onction, et construit un petit autel dans le lieu appele Grotte de la 
roix. 

Ils ont de plus enlevé aux religieux Latins la clef de Ja grande église située 
a Bethléem et les clefs des deux portes de la grotte ou est né Jésus, Ils ont 
construit une porte dans le limiti¢re des Latins au midi de la grande église, une 
autre porte au midi en face la Grotte de la Nativité, et au-dessous un escalier, 
ainsi que plusieurs siéges autour de la dite grotte, au midi et au nord. Ils ont 
fermé deux ventes précédemment ouvertes en face la porte de cette grotte, élevé 
deux portes nouvelles, enlevé les anciens autels placés au nord de la grotte et 
mis en leur place des siéges ; ils ont également fermé les portes de deux jardins 
dépendants de la grotte et construit deux portes nouvelles. L'enquéte a con- 
staté que les lieux précités avaient éte ab antiquo affectés aux Latins, et que les 
Grecs s’en étaient emparés depuis quelques années au moyen de déclarations 
mensongeres, 

Il a de plus été reconnu que le Traité présenté par les Grees et attribué par 
eux au Khalife Omar, n'a ni fondement ni réalité. 

Conformément i la sentence juridique a l'attestation générale ap elée Arai 
Maghar et aux ordres des Sultans mes prédécesseurs, ordres biases sur des fetwas 
—conformément aussi au hudjet ct au khatti-chérif délivré en l'année 1045 (1635), 
par le Sultan Murad, les lieux susmentionnés sont confirmés aux Latins apres 
que les Grees en auront été expulsés. 

Que les religieux Latins se gardent bien de rien faire qui soit contraire 4 
ancien état de choses ainsi que l’avaient faits les Grecs. 

Les Commissaires ont jugé nécessaires de prendre connaissance du khatti- 
chérif délivré en 1045 (1635), par Sultan Murad; ainsi que du procés-verbal 
denquéte mentionné dans le khatti-chérif qui vient d’étre mentionné. Mais 
ces documents ne se trouvant pas entre leurs mains, ils ont dit poursuivre leur

The Marquis of Normanby to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received December 18.) 


(No. 413, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, December 17, 1851. 


PRINCE CALLIMACHI has requested me to convey to your Lordship 
his anxious desire that you should communicate to Sir Stratford Canning your 
‘natructions to do all in his power to maintain the existing ministry in Turkey, 
Prince Callimachi hopes that his former connection with your Lordship in 
England will excuse his appearing at such an important moment to travel out of 
his proper province ; but he adds that the establishment of arbitrary power by 
guch violent means, in a country like France, which has hitherto been considered 
hand-in-hand with England as the great support of liberal opmions, has evidently 
alarmed every country which has of late years made any attempt at constitu 
tional government, and that the effect of this is sure to be still more seriously 
felt in a place like Turkey, where innovation of every kind was so difficult, 

The Prince felt convinced there would be a great effort made for the over- 
throw of Reschid Pasha, as part of a general plan to the existence of which no 
ane could shut his eyes ; that if Reschid Pasha was disgraced and a reactionary 
ministry established, there would be an end of all Englist influence at Constan- 
tinople, and arbitrary measures would at once be taken, which would probably 
lead to an insurrection on the part of the Christian population, and the conse- 

uent overthrow of the Turkish empire. ar ; 
I promised Prince Callimachi to report to your Lordship his sentiments just 
as he had stated them to me, 
1 have, &c. 


(Signed) NORMANBY.

No, 39. 


Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston—(Received December 19.) 
(No. 370.) 


My Lord, Therapia, December 4, 1851. 

THE day after the arrival of the last steam-packet from Marseilles, the French 
Envoy called’ in succession on Aali Pasha and the Grand Vizier. The object 
of his visit to each of those ministers was the same. He informed them that 
although M. de Reculot had arrived at Paris before the departure of the 
courier, he had not been able to present his despatches in time to allow of their 
being answered by that opportunity. M. de Lavalette, however, added 
that he was in possession of instructions written previously, and that he was 
authorized by them to deal with the question of the disputed sanctuaries, in such 
manner as he might judge the dignity of France to require. He availed himself 
of the occasion to go over the old ground once more, and to repeat his com- 
plaints of the manner in which the Porte had acted on that subject towards him 
and his Government. It was evidently his aim to make a strong impression on the 
fears of the Porte, and to obtain thereby the appointment of an early period 
at which a final, and of course a satisfactory, answer should be given to him. 

I have reason to believe that he failed in this endeayour, and I am also 
under an impression, produced by his subsequent language to me, that he is not 
prepared to take any step calculated to commit his Government, without further 
instructions, which may be expected on the 12th instant. 

As Aali Pasha no less than M. de Lavalette related what had passed 
between them to me, | expressed myself to each of them, without entering ito 
the merits of the case, in such terms as I thought calculated to prevent 
precipitancy on either side, 1 endeavoured, in particular, to dissuade the French 
Envoy from taking any step which might suddenly and, perhaps, irrevocably 
convert a quiet diplomatic discussion into a breach of those friendly relations 
which it is so desirable to maintain between France and Turkey, and which can 
hardly be put to hazard for a question involving little more than a religious 
sentiment and the application of a Treaty permitted to lie more or less in 
abeyance for a century, without causing general surprise, and not impossibly 
some additional entanglement in the present situation of Europe, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING,

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—(Received February 1, 1852.) 
(No. 387.) 


My Lord, Therapia, December 30, 185). 

THE French Envoy has not relaxed in his efforts to obtain a satisfacto 
arrangement of the Sanctuary Question. He has had several interviews wit 
Aali Pasha since | last wrote to your Lordship on that subject, and it does not 
appear that there has been any further intimation of a threatening character 
connected with the Toulon squadron. ‘The last French steam-packet went 
away, as far as | am informed, without conveying to France any decisive answer 
from the Porte. The Turkish Commission has, in the meantime, completed its 
report, Some proposition may come out of it, though hardly sufficient to satialy 
France without offending Russia, which is naturally enough the object of the 
Porte's manceuvres. 

M. de Lavalette has, however, concluded the year by announcing his inten- 
tion to break off the negotiation, demanding, before he does so formally, an 
audience of the Sultan, which will probaby be granted with reluctance. He 
pleads the commands of his Government, and takes credit for having delayed 
their execution in the hope of a more satisfactory conclusion. 

The interference of Russia continues to be cautiously managed by M. de 
Titof. His Government appears to apprehend that even a slight departure 
from the status que would, instead of settling the question permanently, open a 
door to further pretensions in future. 


I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD CANNING.

Sir Stratford Canning to Viscount Palmerston.—( Received February 1, 1852.) 
(Private and Confidential.) 


My dear Lord, Therapia, December 31, 1851. 

I PROPOSE to state in this manner, for your own particular information, 
some points connected with the question at issue between France and Turkey, 
which I do not feel myself at liberty to commit to the ostensible correspondence, 

The report of the Turkish Commission has been communicated privately, 
and indeed personally, to me by Aali Pasha. It was printed for the exclusive 
use of the members, and | bey to request that your Lordship will consider the 
accompanying translations of it as confidential in the strictest sense of the term. 

About ten days ago Auli Pasha sent me, in the same spirit of personal confi- 
dence, a stutement relative to the true bearing of the Porte’s existing Treaties with 
France on the question of the disputed sanctuaries. A copy of this confidential 
memorandum is inclosed herewith. My opinion was requested in reply to the 

ueries with which it concludes. This request, proceeding as it did from the 

rand Vizier ag well as from Aali Pasha, I could not entirely refuse, but | was 
careful to couch my answer, a verbal one, in guarded terms, It amounted in 
substance to this: I understood the question to be whether Article XXXII of 
the Treaty of 1740 aprile to the state of possession then, or, as a mere recapitu- 
lation, to that which existed at the date of the prior Treaty; taken in that 
manner the question was a fair one, having some appearances in favour of the 
latter construction; it could only be resolved by a special examination of the 
terms in which the Treaty was expressed. 

T learn, in private, from M. de Titoff that the Emperor Nicholas entertains 
a strong religious persuasion on the subject, and maintains the status quo under 
a conviction that the smallest concession would throw the whole existing 
arrangement into confusion. 

The zeal of M. de Lavalette, excited by desire of success, and still more 
by Russian interference, has, I suspect, been further stimulated by the Catholic 
sympathies of his Belgian colleague. M. Blondeel de Coulenbruck belongs to

IN the former of the two letters referred to in my preceding despatch,

Affairs complains of the uccusation made by the French Government that he 
had deceived M, de Lavalette, by giving, in the question of the Sacred Buildings

Aali Pacha protests against ever having held any other language to M, de

Constantinople, there is but little chance of cordiality existing between the two 
Governments, and he has since had confidential intimation that M. Sabatier is 
to be ramoved to Alexandria.

No. 59. 
Colonel Rose to the Earl of Malmesbury.—(Received August 31). 


(No, 50, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Therapia, August 14, 1852, 

THE question of the Holy Places will probably ere long again become 
the subject of discussion between the Porte and the French Ambassador. 

His Excellency says, that even allowing that the Firman does not state 
that the claims of the Latins are “ injustes et mal fondées,” the whole purport 
of it goes to deny the right of the Latins, that is, France, to the Holy Places. 

M. de Lavalette states that both the President and himself were very 
anxious to get rid of this question, and that therefore he accepted, last 
February, the tenth part only of the Sanctuaries to which France has a positive 
right by the Treaty of 1740; that he was obliged, at the same time, to give in 
a nominal protest in favour of the Treaty, but assured the Porte that all appeal 
to the Treaty should be waived for five, ten years, perhaps for ever ; that the 
Porte, with a “trahison inonie,” gave, the day after he left Constantinople on 
leave, a Firman to the Greeks, which made out the ‘Treaty to be valueless ; 
that this conduct of the Porte was as treacherous as it was impolitic, as it 
forced the French Government either to reopen the question, or to allow that 
the Treaty was an untruth, aes : 

M. de Lavalette intimates that, unless the objectionable parts in the 
Firman are altered or explained by a note, France must eventually go to war 
with Turkey if she sides with Russia, or with Russia if she alone supports the 
Firman in its present form, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) HUGH ROSE.

No. 62. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Malmesbury.—( Received September 14.) 
(No. 632. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Paris, September 12, 1852. 
IN referring lately to the affairs of Turkey, M. Drouyn de Lhuys observed 
that he was very anxious to put the question of the Holy Buildings at Jerusalem 
in a state which would permit him to consider it as terminated. He admitted, 
in confidence but with much fairness, that the question ought never to have been 
raised, He attributed the raising of it to the inexperience of General La Hitte, 
while Minister for Foreign Affairs; and he did not deny my observation, that it 
had been carried on with too much heat by M. de Lavalette at Constantinople. 
Nevertheless, he said, there the question was: the French Government had 
taken a position for which he personally was not responsible, but which he 
could not abandon; and what he desired was, that without embarrassing the 
Porte, this question should be settled honourably for France, and that France 
should not have the appearance of se duped by Russia. In a conversation 
which he had had with Prince Callimachi, he had told him that it could not 
be supposed that the Porte really cared whether the Latins or Greeks were 
most favoured, both being her Christian subjects; but that the Latins being 
under the protection of France, and the Greeks under that of Russia, the real 
nestion at issue was, whether the Ottoman Government preferred the friend- 
ship of France or of Russia. ‘That, for his part, as France had no ambitious views 
in Turkey, and as Russia undoubtedly had, he could not conceive that there 

could be much doubt as to the line of policy which the Porte onght to pursue, 

I asked M. Drouyn de Lhuys whether he would be satisfied with a decla- 
ration on the part of the Ottoman Government that, by the Firman given in 
respect of the Holy Buildings to the Greeks, there was no intention of depart- 
ing from the promises made to France. M. Drouyn de Lhuys replied, that a 
declaration in these terms would be sufficient. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY,

AS a general rule, my object is, if not to suppress the suspicions which

giving expression to them.

despatch No, 184, of the claims of the Russian Government upon those of the 
Principalitics, with the demands of Austria upon the Porte, it is difficult to 
avoid feeling anxiety as to futurity, should these be simultaneously pressed, as 
they readily might be if either one sy other of the claiming Gavariseats

should, with or without reason, become upon less friendly: terms. with the 
Sultan,

apprehend, always involve a certain amouht of danger to Turkey; and I do not

Austrian Envoy, will be regarded as somewhat ominous at Constantinople, —

Once again I would, then, venture to lay before your Lordship the danger

Colonel Rose to the Earl of Malmesbury.—(Received October 28.) 
(No. 89.) 
My Lord, Therapia, September 27, 1852. 

THE French Ambassador has told me that the President had aaid to him 
at Paris, that he could not understand why there should be any differences 
between British and French policy at Athens or Constantinople. His Excel- 
lency has frequently expressed similar sentiments, adding that he approved all 
the leading pAnciples at British policy as to Turkey, and that I should find 
him ready to co-operate with me in support of them, I made suitable 
answers, 

A Violent religious dispute is going on here between two parties of the 
Roman Catholic Armeiian Rayaa. 

= M. de Lavalette has sided with the party favoured by the Court of 
Rome, 

In replying, a day or two ago, to His Excellency's declarations as to 
sympathy with British policy, | observed that there appeared to me to be one 
point as to which divergence existed, and which was, moreover, a cause of un- 
easiness to the Porte. 

“What is that,” said M. de Lavalette, 

: [ replicd ‘‘the Protectorate which France ¢laims of Christianity in the 
cast.” 

« But,” replied M. de Layalette, France only claims the Protectorate of 
the Pope, his rights in the East, and of European Roman Catholic ecclesias- 
tical establishments, which is our right by treaty.” 

“ And not of Turkish Christian Rayas?” I said. 

* Certainly not,” 

“ Not even of a Turkish Christian church or convent ? ” 

“Certainly not,” reiterated M. de Lavalette; “c'est une erreur com- 
pléte, 4{n this Armenian dispute the Porte has dismissed the temporal Arch. 
bishop, I think that she is wrong; but as the Archbishop's is a temporal 
appointment, 1 shall not interfere officially. I only interfere in favour of 


Porte." 

I listened, with as mneh surprise as satisfaction, to these important decla- 
rations. If they represent the sentiments of the French Government, France's 
Protectorate of Christianity in the East, which she has hitherto assumed, loses 
the larger half of its dangerous attributes. 

In order to give all possible formality to these declarations, I replied that 
I had heard them with sincere pleasure, and that I should communicate them 
to Her Majesty's Goyernment, who, | knew, would yeevive the intelligence with 
unmingled satisfaction. | rept 

Your Lordship is aware that M. Guigot in the French Chambers, and 
M. de Bourqueney here, over and over again, have declared that France never 
would surrender the Protectorate of Christianity in the East, The Earl of 
Aberdeen, when he did me the honour to praise in the House of Lords, in 1546, 
my conduct ina Lebanon matter, stated that France claimed this Protectorate, 
In Syria, | repeatedly had to resist the assumption of it. a 

[ will not secupy your Lordship’s valuable time by examining the causes 
of this very-important concession, but merely venture to suggest that 1b would 
be advantageous to obtain, if possible, from the French Government the con- 
firmation of it. And if Russia were to follow, with respect to her co-religion- 
ists in Turkey, 80 good an example, the Porte’s independence and the balance 
of power would be relieved from two dangerous trammels, 

And as regards the Rayas themselves, they will be far safer under the 
weis of civilization, and of the sympatliy of the Powers at large, than under the 
half-and-half protection of two great Powers, one day warmly protected, and 
thus made objects of Ottoman jealousy, and another day abandoned to Ottoman 
vengeance, as it suits circumstances and policy. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) HUGH ROBE,

Colonel Roge to the Earl of Malmesbury.—(Received October 28.) 
(No. 02.) 
My Lord, Therapia, October 1, 1862. 

AFIF BEY, who conveyed to Abbas Pasha the Firman, has gone from 
Egypt to Jerusalem, in order to superintend the execution of the arrangement 
made by the Porte as (o the Holy Places. 

M. de Luvalette now states that his complaint as to the Firman to the 
Greeks is satistied, 

In a previous despateh, I had the honour to state that M. de Lavalette 
complained also of the non-execution of what the Porte had promised him in 
her note to him of the 8th of February last, respecting the Holy Places, 

Your Lordship will see in that note, Inclosure in Sir Stratford Canning's 
Gy Nc No. 31, that the Porte grants to the Latins three keys of the Church 
of Bethlehem, . 

The Grotto of the Nativity is a vault under the Church of Bethlehem, 
and to get to it one must pass through the church. 

The Latins had, up to last February, only a small side-door in this church, 
by which they passed to the grotto, 

M. de Lavalette apprehends that the Greeks will refuse permission to the 
Latins to enter the church by the great door, of which they have now a key.

Colonel Rose to the Earl of Malmesbury.—(Received November 6.)

My Lord, Therapia, October 19, 1852. 


1 HAD a long conversation yesterday with the representative of the 
Greek-'Turkish sect at the Porte respecting the Holy Places. He said that he 
hears that M. de Lavalette has obtained from the Porte some assurances, 
whether verbal or in writing he does not know, which had satisfied his 
complaint as to the Firman to the Greeks. 

He added that the question of the great door of the Church of Bethlehem 
was “grave, tres grave ;” that the Latins insisted on having a key of the great 
door, and entering it in religious procession; that the Greeks, rather than 
consent to that, would have recourse to any extremities. 

M. de Lavalette says, that France would do the same if the Latins 
have not a key of the great door, and the right to pass through in religious 
procession. 

The difference of opinion, therefore, 1s decided ; and the only thing the two 
parties have in common as to the subject of the dispute is their extreme 
violence. 

However, experience shows that hitherto both sides say rather more than 
they do.

Consul Finn to the Earl of Malmesbury.—(Received November 15.) 
(No. 11. Political.) 
My Lori, Jerusalem, October 27, 1852. 


ON the 18th ultimo J had the hononr to report the arrival of Afif Bey 
four days previously on a special mission from the Sultan on matters 
pertaining to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, and other 
sanctuaries. 

On the 2st, arrived M. Basily, the Russian Consul-General, with M. 
Marabutti, the Vice-Consul, and Prince Garari, an Attaché of the Russian 
Embassy. They were received with extraordinary honours: refreshments 
awaited them at three different stations between Jaffa and Jerusalem; the 
Greek Patriarch went out to meet them, and they entered the city with an 
escort of one hundred irregular Cavalry, drums beating, and muskets fired for 
joy. 

M. Boita, the French Consul, and Count Pizzamano, the Austrian Consul, 
had arrived at Jaffa, from Beyrout, in the same steamer with M. Basily: the 
former rode on, and arrived here alone some hours before him; the latter, with 
his lady, came on more slowly afterwards. 

But on Sunday, the 24th instant, M. Basily and the Viece-Consul left 
Jerusalem in great anger and disappointment, the more remarkable after the 
hilarity of spirits in which he had entered Jerusalem. 

‘The interval of the month had been employed in the following manner +— 

After the Corban Beiram festivals were over, and ceremonial visits fully 
exchanged, the Commissioner, Afif Bey, with a suite of the local Effendis, met 
the three Patriarels, Greck, Latin, and Armenian, in the Church of the Resur- 
rection, just in front of the Heyy Sepulchre itself, and under the great dome ;— 
there they were regaled with sherbets, confectionary, and pipes, at the expense 
of the three Convents, who vied with cach other in making luxurious display 
on the occasion, M. Botta was the only Consular person present. 

Afif Bey made an oration upon the desire of His Majesty the Sultan to 
eratify all classes of his subject, and his | rlicular concern for the dilapidated 
state of the great dome above them, which His Majesty ollered to repair at his 
Own expense, 


eet 


65 


The Bey then introduced to notice the architect sent for that task, and 
invited the three communities to appoint a person each to assist him in the 
work. 

Up to that time the only topies of business discussed by the parties com- 
missioned on all sides, had been the repair of the dome, and such matters of 
detail, But M. Basily, with the Greek Patriarch (arrived not long before), and 
the Russian Archimandrite were becoming impatient for the business whic 
had brouglit them here, namely, the public reading of a Firman, which was to 
give to their interest the whole of the Christian Sanctuaries of Jerusalem 
and Bethlehem. 

Afif Bey then invited all the parties concerned to meet him in the Church 
of the Virgin, near Gethsemane, ‘There he read an order of the Sultan for 
permitting the Latins to celebrate mass once a-year, but requiring the altar 
and its ornaments to remain undisturbed. No sooner were these words uttered 
than the Latins, who had come to receive their triumph over the Orientals, 
broke out into loud exclamations of the impossibility of celebrating mass upon 
a schismatic slab of marble, with a covering of silk and gold instead of plain 
linen, among schismatic vases, and before a erncifix which has the feet 
separated, instead of one nailed over the other. 

There, however, were the words of the Firman, and so that proceeding 
ended in nothing. 

M. Basily afterwards called on the Commissioner at his house, and angrily 
insisted upon the great Firman being read. The latter inquired, “ What 
Firman?” ‘That which you yourself drew up, and wrote with your own 
hand, as Second Secretary in Constantinople, declaring that the Latin claims 
to the Sanctuaries are null and void.” 

The Bey explained that he had no directions to read it; that he had no 
copy of it with him, and could not A) beyond his special instructions. 

Thereupon M. Basily sent off Prince Garari to Jafla, to convey these 
tidings to Constantinople in any Arab vessel that could be found. 

At Jaffa the latter stayed six days, detained by contrary winds, 

M., Basily then went to the Pasha of Jerusalom, and demanded to have 
a Special Council assembled, with himself and the Greek Patriarch in attend- 
anee, to receive a final declaration whether the important Firman had been 
sent here or not. 

At that meeting Hafiz Pasha made a smooth speech on the well-known 
benevolence of His Majesty towards all classes of his subjects, and that was 
all that could be said. | 

‘And so ended for the present the business upon which so much excitement 
ee been raised—hoth parties duped by a stratagem characteristic of Turkish 
i0licy. 

The architect is proceeding with protracting his task of surveying the 
Jome. 

There remains the comparative easy question of Bethlehem Sanctuaries. 

The silver star which was stolen in 1847, and which, by the Firman in 
question, was to be replaced at the Latin expense, was supposed to be brought 
on this occasion, having been approved of in Constantinople ; but on inquiry 
i ye found that no one had brought it, or knew where it liad been lett 

rchind. 

The Austrian Consul, who makes no secret of ridiculing French pro- 
ceedings, and French Protection of Christianity in the East, chuckles with 
delight at the failure of both parties, especially since the French would suffer 
no other Roman Catholic Power to assist them in the task of reseuing the 
Sanctuaries from the Schismatics, 

They (the Austrians) claim to be the real efficient supporters of Latin 
interest in Palestine, but in other ways than bya crusade, for which sart of 
measures they consider the time to bu past.

My Lord, : Therapia, November 20, 1862, 
THE question of the Holy Places has become graver, and causes the 
Porte much anxiety. 


All the evils resulting from the contradictory nature of the concessions 
mate in February Inst by the Porte, in the note of the 9th of February and 
the Firman to the Greeks, to the two rival interests engaged in this ill-omened 
difference, are coming into evidence, and striking contrast, as the time ap- 
proaches when Afif Bey, the Porte's Commissioner at Jerusalem, is to perform 
the difficult task of executing the Porte’s conflicting decisions as ta the Sane- 
tnaries. 

A eraver cause of difference than the great door of the Church of Beth- 
lehem has appeared, and taken precedence of it. 

The Porte, under the influence of French and Russian menaces, conceded 
to the French Embassy the note of the 9th February, and the Firman of mi- 
Février to. the Greeks. | 

The Russian Government considers the Firman the charter of rights of 
the Greek Chaorch. The President, and M, de Lavalette, consider it an affront 
to France, because it describes her claims grounded on the Treaty of 1741, 
as “laksig,” unjust, and establishes a status quo, which wholly invalidates 
that Treaty. M. de Lavalette tells me that the Porte promised to M, Sabatier 
that it should not be read at Jerusalem, and he tells the Porte that read it 
never shall be. 

M. d@'Ozeroff tells the Porte, with equal vehemence, that the Firman must 
be read at Jerusalem; he declares that if it be not read, according to usage, in 
the Medgliss at Jerusalem, before the Pasha, Cadi, Members of the Council, 
Patriarchs of the different sects, it will be valucless and a dead fetter, and 
that consequently faith will have been broken with Russia, ; 

The Latin clergy laid claim to a lamp, and means of oti mass, and 
keeping the priestly robes and sacred vessels in the Tomb of the Virgim, where, by 
‘the note of the 9th of August, [February ?] they are now allowed to perform their 
devotions, “ dans les lieux établis.” But M, de Lavalette tels me that he disap. 
proves these pretensions, because they are not sanctioned by the note, and 
that a “maisonnette” is to be erected in Gethsemene, where what is requi- 
site for the churel service in the tomb is to be kept. 

Your Lordship is aware, that the cupola of the Holy cue has for a 
length of time been in decay, and that the violent disputes of the Grecks and 
Latins, as to who shall repair it, are the cause that nothing has been done 
to it. 

It has‘now been decifed that the Sultan is to repair it,and in consequence, 
M. de Lavalette apprehends no dissension on this score. But Fuad Effendi 
foresees that-embarrassments will arise from the pretensions of the rival sects, 
as to whether the inseriptions round the cupola are to be in Greek or ‘Latin ; 
whether the sacred images in it are to be made and habited according to Greek 
or Latin fashions. 

M. de Lavalette tells me that he has had serious discussions with Patriarch 
Valerga and the Latin clergy, and has ‘been obliged to take a high ‘tone in 
order ‘to induce ‘them to withdraw undue pretensions as to the Moly Places, 
which are not sanctioned by the Porte's concessions to France. 

M, d’'Ozeroff says the same to me, ina more modified sense, as to the 
Greek clergy. The Russian Legation is much more under the influence of 
religions feeling and of the clergy than the French Embassy. 

M. de Lavalette speaks, invariably, in the highest terms of the moderation 
and geod fecling evinced ‘by the Pope in the matter of the Holy Places, a good 
example which, he says, is not. followed by the Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem 
and his clergy.

Colonel Rose to the Earl of Mulmeshury—(Receiwed December 11.)

My Lord, Therapia, November 20, 1852. 

THE question of the Holy Places is becoming more serious. France and 
Russia, with the view to coerce the Porte to execute her contradictory conces 
sions of February last to them, have taken the same menacing position towards 
her which they did twelve months ago, only with this difference, that M, de 
Lavalette menaces to defend the advantages he has gained since his return 
from leave, whilst M. d'Ozeroff menaces to regain what he has lost. 

M, de Lavalette has induced the Porte to address him a note, which 
nullifies the status quo established by the Firman to the Greeks, and states that 
nothing can be done by the Porte, affecting the Treaty of 1740, without the 
consent of France. ‘The French Government have expressed their approbation 
of this note. 

M. de Lavalette has also addressed instructions to M. Botta at Jerusalem, 
in which he enjoins him to watch vigilantly over the strict execution of the 
note of the 9th of February, and particularly of the provision in it which he 
says allows the Latins to pass through the great door of the church at 
Bethlehem, without however interfering with the Greeks when they are at 
their devotions, ‘These instructions M. de Lavalette has shown to the Porte, 
who, he says, has expressed her approval of them. With these advantages, 
and the Porte’s promise to M, Sabatier that the Firman to the Greeks ig not 
to be read, M. de Lavalette is satislied, and only protects his position by 
announcing the extreme meastires he would take, should the Porte leave any 
engagements to him unfulfilled. He has, more than once, talked of the 
appearance, in that case, of a French fleet off Jaffa; and once he alluded to a 

rench occupation of Jerusalem, “ when,” he said, “we shall haye all the 
Sanctuaries.” 

M. de Lavalette has obtained these advantages, because he gained a hold 
on the Porte by making her responsible to France, and her ruler, so prompt to 
resent her wrongs, for having issued the Firman to the Greeks, which, his 
Excellency says, “is an insolent denial of the rights conceded to France by 
Treaty, and the note of the 9th of February.” 

The irritation and bitterness caused to M. de Lavalette, and, os he says, 
to the President, by that Firman is excessive. “1 will tell you very con- 
fidentially,” said M, de Lavalette to me, the other night, “the affair of the 
Charlemagne, Tripoli, all our anger with Turkey, tout, tout doit son origine 
au Firman que." 

M.de Lavalette has also said to me lately, ‘‘ If the Porte docs not keep 
her engagements to me, France will make a demonstration; she will then 
accept England's mediation, but the demonstration must first bo tras vive, 
tres. Vive,’ 

Such is the French position. 

The Russian Legation has heard of the note to M. de Lavalette; and 
Russian policy now endeavours, as a set-olf to it, to give validity and dignity 
te the Firman, 

_ A Russian Feldjiger arrived lately here, ostensibly for the purpose of 
bringing mstructions to M. d'Qzeroff, to obtain from the Porte immediate 
satisfaction for an affront, offered some months back, to a Russian merchant 
Hag. Others think that he brought very stringent instructions as to Jerusalem, 
Be that as it may, M, d’Ozeroff, a few days since, in a formal interview with 
the Grand Vizier, accused the Porte of having been guilt of perfidy and 
treachery, and, in language said to be “comminatoire,” demanded that the 
Firman should be formally and publicly read at Jerusalem. 

The Porte, under the influence of thi communication, has instructed 
Afif Bey to cause the Firman te be read, with the least possible publicity, at 
Jerusalem. 

____[ now learn, also confidentially, that besides the Firman, the Porte gave, 
in February last, a vizirial letter, confidentially, to M. de Titoff, promising

Colonel Rose to the Earl of Malmesbury.—(Received December 11.)

My Lord, Therapia, November 23,1852. 

I HAVE the honour to submit a few reflections, founded on local know- 
ledges, Fs 1 ae best mode of hips ths dition question of the Holy Places, 
should it not, by some unexpected turn | erminate ‘ils 
souls ee: y eRe of good fortune, be terminated speedily 

It is quite clear that the present attitude of France and Russia towards 

Turkey menaces her independence, if not her integrity, For the result of 
France's “trés vive démonstration” in favour of an alleged broken treaty 
would be an occupation of Jaffa and Jerusalem, and probably a great deal 
more ; and the consequence of Russia's rapture with the Porte, would, I have 
no doubt, entail her occupation of Wallachia and Moldavia; both eventualities 
being fatal to British policy, and to the balance of power. 
Tt is equally clear that either France or Russia must he in the wrong ; 
and as their difference, if unsettled, must entail a breach of the Convention by 
which the five Powers guarantee Turkey’s independence, Great Britain and 
the other two Powers have a right to require that the Power which is in the 
wrong should not, by the assertion of an unfounded right, nulli the condi- 
tions of a Convention which she has ratified in common with her allies, | 

The first step towards settling a wrong is to examine it. Nobody regrets 
more than I the revival of France’s dormant rights to the Holy Places. But 
they nS of they must he beaten with policy and justice, 

‘lata ‘rench Government, from the be inning, demanded of the ; 
ora of her claims as to the Holy Blagasrwhich she Lea anata, 
ul oe ert Representative still declares, unceasingly, that he wishes nothing 

aa bet ae claims should be thoroughly examined and tried. 

a ut the Emperor of Russia met France's demand for examination, by 
‘a ling in the Porte to refuse all examination; and the Russian Representative 
Pap aac eos tener sense, condemns anything like examination of the dispute as

I think that I have said enough, in this and preceeding despatches, to show 
that the ill-omened difference ought oe to remain any longer in its present 


70 


unsettled state, which discredits Turkey, hurts her independence, and endangers 
the peace of Europe. 3 

It would not be prudent, especially as the world now is, when the 
dangerous power of France is kept within proper limits by the Treaties of 
1815, to disregard her frequent appeals to the rights guaranteed to her by the 
Treaty of 1740, And Great Britain would not cease to regret, were the over- 
throw of Turkey and of the balance of power to ensue from the quarrel about 
a great door or alittle door, a cupboard or no cupboard, when a calm exami- 
nation of France's claim by ‘Treaty, would have settled this momentous differ- 
ance on the safest of all foundations, those of justice and international right. 

Under these cireumstances the time, 1 venture to think, is come when it 
sould be advisable that Great Britain should tell France, Russia, and the Porte, 
that should the settlement of the difference as to the Holy Places be any longer 
delayed, the Convention of 1840, the general peace, and the balance of power 
will be placed in peril; and that therefore it would be desirable that claims 
which one patty grounds on ‘Treaty, and the Sultan, in his letter of last year to 
the Emperor of Russia, called it “un Traité solennel,” should be impartially 
tried by the Porte in enjoyment of her full free agency and of her territorial 
rights as to Jerusalem, aid other legitimate arbitration. Another advantage of 
such a step would be, that Russia would then come to an arrangement with the 
Porte as to the Holy Places; for my belief is, she would never submit her 
claims to a trial with those of France. 

As regards French and Russian influence in Turkey, | agree with the view 
taken of them by the late Grand Vizier and Aali Pasha, that the former is the 
least dangerous. 

France has no geographical influence except in Africa. Her co-religion- 
iste are a few Greek Catholics, Roman Catholics, and Roman Catholic 
Armenians, scattered over the face of Turkey, ‘The only population like a 
mass, are about 120,000 Maronites, who, certainly not warriors, I believe 
respect England more than France, And so little influence has the French 
Ambassador over the Armenians, that he told me only the other day, in much 
irritation, “ que ces ingrats, Ces coquins d’Arméniens” had had the insolence to 
present a petition to the Sultan complaining of his interference in an Armenian 
matter. 2 
But Russia, geographically, encompasses Turkey’s vitality; and nearly, if not 
quite, half of Turkey's subjects are Russia’s co-religionists, blind believers, who 
are taught by their clergy to look on the Emperor of Russia as their protector 
againat ‘Turkish injustice, 

Russia claims the protectorate of the Turkish-Greck Church. The 
ranch Ambassador declares to me that France has no right to that of the 
‘Turkish Roman Catholic Chureh. 

French policy inthe East is noisy and rash. Rmssian policy is silent and 
cautious, 

Abstractedly, therefore, 1 would be better for ‘British policy, that if one 
of the two influences were to be curtailed, it should be Russian. For it were 
idle to suppose that cither France or Russia would go to war for the great 
door ofthe Church of Bethlehem ; the struggle ts for influence in the East, which 
stands behind that door. 

But.in ‘the Jerusalem affair, as 1 had the honour to say before, I think it 
desirable that neither ofthe litigants should gain a triumph. Besides, it would 
hot be-advisable that Russia should isolate herself; for the day may come 
when the Powers, who-for their protection united against Napoleon, may have 
todo the same against his nephew, 

I should observe that both the Emperor of Russia's letter to the Sultan, 
and the Russian advocacy of the Firman to the Greck subjects of the Porte, 
involve an assumption of Russian protectorate of the Turkish Greek Church.

| ascribe this favourable result a good deal to the advice which [ gave to 
Fuad Effendi, on his consulting me what he should do when the Porte was

Both M. de Lavalette and M. @’Ozeroff did not scruple to ring the same 
serious charge, couched in the strongest terms, against the Rorte, in their con- 
versation with myself, and, I hear, with others. 

| saw that their accusations were not only most prejudicial to the credit 
and influence of the Porte, but that the tenacity and asperity with which 
they were repeated, looked ominous, and indicated the possibility of a coming 
demand for satisfaction for continued * perfidy and treachery.” 

I therefore, courteously but frankly, told both M. de Lavalette and M. 
d’'Ozeroff, that I could not admit the justice of these accusations, because the 
coercive nature of French and Russian demands had forced the Porte to give 
conilicting decisions, against her will, her interest, and her conviction ; that 
the Porte had been compelled to act as a judge in a most difficult and, to her, 
distasteful matter, and then deprived of the immunity and independence of a 
judge. All M. d'Ozeroff could reply was, “ Pourquoi done est ce que la
