Colonel Rose to the Earl of Malmesbury.—(Received December 19.) 
(No. 164. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Pera, December 5, 1852. 

M. YOZEROFF has prejudiced much his position, at this important mo- 
ment, by making a formal declaration to the French Ambassador, that Russia, 
by virtue of the Treaty of Kainardgi, protects the orthodox, that is, the Greek 
religion, in ‘Turkey. M. de Lavalette takes this the more to heart, because he 
has lately formally declared that France makes no claim to protect the Turkish 
Roman Catholics. He has made known M, d’Ozerolf’s declaration to his col- 
leagues and the Porte. The Porte has heard this assertion of Russian protec- 
tion of the religious interests of ten or eleven millions of her subjects with 
unmingled dissatisfaction. 

I have the honour to inelose a copy of the two articles of the ‘Treaty of 
Kutchuk Kainardgi, which relate to Russia in connection with the Greek 
Turkish Christians. 

M. d’Ozeroll founds his claim on Article VII; but [venture to think, 
that your Lordship will agree with me that a promise of the Porte to protect 
the Christian religion and churches, docs not bear out the Russian Representa. 
tive in saying that Russia has a right to protect the Greek Turkish Church, 
more especially as the 14th Article expressly limits the right of Russian pro- 
tection of the Greck Church to that of the chapel of the Russian Legation, and 
at new Greek church which the Court of Russia was about to build in 
Galata. 

The Grand Vizier informs me to-day, confidentially, that two deputies from 


73 


Montenegro have arrived here, and are secretly lodged in the Russian Embassy 
House ; this circumstance has of course increased the unfavourable impression 
already existing with respect to Russia at the Porte. 
I have, &e. 
(Signed) HUGH ROSE,

i wrote me a few days bere : fhiee, d : 
Haseeno Government the necessity of its bemg terminated as romney

upon the subject at COMBE I should premise that that Minis Mor 
ee moment of taking office, expressed great regret that the question 8 


rir 


ever have been mooted: he looks upon it as a bad legacy bequeathed him by 
his predecessors; and he has always asserted that his only solicitude was to find 
an honourable means of retreat for France from the false position which she 
had taken: and that though her rights under treaty in regard to the Sacred 
Places were unquestionable, he lamented that they should have been uselessly 
and mischievously put forward. The Emperor also has, on more than one 
occasion, while President, termed it “une question mal engagée, et qu'il était 
bien content de voir terminée,” as he thought it had been by the arrangement 
made hy M. de Lavalette in the spring of the year. 

When, therefore, I spoke to M. Drouyn de Lhuys at Compiégne, he 
repeated his former assurances, and added that the difference must and should 
be settled, He quite understands that it is a question of such vital impor- 
tance to Russia, that she cannot give way upon it, while the interest of the 
Latins he admits to be comparatively small, His only anxiety, therefore, 1s 
to find an honourable retreat for France. He had written, he said, to M, de 
Lavalette, to accept the best arrangement which he could make, and then to 
let the matter drop, I asked him why, if he really wished for an amicable 
adjustment of the difference, he did not desire the French Ambassador at 
Constantinople to put himself in direct communication with the Russian 
Chargé d’ Affaires, instead of leaving to a Musselman potentate the settlement 
of a Christian dispute. I suggested that M, de Lavalette should state to 
M. d'Ozeroff that France had treaties with the Porte which secured to the Latins 
certain privileges in the Holy Places, but that she had no wish to make those 
treaties 1 handle for preventing facilities being afforded to other Christian sects to 
worship in the same places, each according to the form required by their particular 
dogma ; and that he should then enter into friendly arrangement with M, d’Ozeroff 
for preventing any future scandal between the Latin and Greek worshippers, 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys appeared to approve of the suggestion, He said that 
he would turn it in his mind, and speak to me again upon it on my return to 
Paris. 

Yesterday he renewed the subject with me, He said that he had adopted 
my suvestion, and had written in that sense to M. de Lavalette, and he pro- 
josed instructing M. de Castelbajac to make similar overtures at St. Petera- 

rh, He was quite determined that the question should be amicably settled. 

Tam the more anxious that there should be no further delay, because 
M. de Kisseleff informed me confidentially, this morning, that he is in hour! 
expectation of instructions desiring him to enter into some explanations wit 
the French Government upon this matter. I told him that I was convinced the 
French Government was anxious to see it settled, and I informed him of the 
sugcestion which I had thrown out for settling it, He seemed to fear that as 
long as M, de Layalette remained at Constantinople there was no chance of 
terminating the question amicably, He complained that that Ambassador had 
no other argument with the Porte than a menace of the French fleet, giving me 
at the same time distinetly to understand that Russia was prepared with hers. 

With regard to M. de Lavalette’s continued menaces of the French feet, I 
ave the honour to refer your Lordship to my despatch, No. 739, to Lord 
Malmesbury,

with it, can never be sustained in a discussion or ina note, more especially as it 
is founded on the double meanings of a Firman drawn up by the Porte, the 
judge, and then altered, to his views, by the Russian Enyoy, a party im the 
suit. 

lt ig clear that the Envoy felt that the Firman gave, by its real meaning, 
the key in question fo the Latins, because he afterwards obtained a vizirial 
letter to Afif Effendi, instructing him to do all he could to withhold the key 
from them, and if he could not succeed, to refer to Constantinople. 

herefore, as the note of the 9th of February, to the French Envoy, and 
the Firman obtained and altered by the Russian Envoy, concede the key of the 
great door of the Church of Bethlehem to the Latina, the Porte did wisely and 
right in confirming the concession,

of both the opposite intercsts engaged im it, and qualified by Her Majesty’s 
Ambassador and Chargé d’ Affaires a8 an equitable one.

Colonel Rose to the Earl of Malmesbury. —(Received January 5, 1853.) 
(No, 104. Confidential.) 

My Lord, Constantinople, December 18, 1852. 

A SECRETARY of the Russian Legation complained to me, a few days 
since, without my having even alluded to the subject of the Holy Places, of me 
improper and slighting manner in which Fuad Effendi had acted towards the 
Russian Legation in that matter: he seemed to allude particularly to the 
manner in which the Porte’s decision had been communicated to the Legation, 
I replicd that [ fully shared his regret if anything of the sort had taken place ; 
that from the usual extreme courtesy of Fuad Effendi, and the principle which 
he had always advocated, as his invariable rule, to show civility to the foreign 
missions, any neglect of form must have arisen, not from intention, but from 
the awkwardness with which the Porte sometimes transacted affairs. ; 

I lost no time in speaking seriously to Fuad Effendi, telling him amicably 
that I could not conceive anything more impolitie than that the Porte, in 
making what naturally was uk an agrecable communication to Russia, should 

re failed in the least in perfect courtesy. | | 
ee Effendi replied, that the charge was wholly groundless ; that he had 
only been too polite and considerate m all his communications with the Russian 
Legation; that he had even offered to resign at once, if that step would be in 
any way gratifying to them; that the Russian Legation knew all this, but were 
determined to sacrifice him been he had advised the Porte conscientiously 
e decision she had done, : 
. a Eifendi has Ottoman faults, but he is by far the most ractical and 
intelligent Minister the Porte has perhaps had for centuries. In the Loan, and 
all financial affairs, he has heen of the greatest use ; and it would be a circum: 
stance much to be regretted were he to be visited with dismissal, merely be- 
cause he gave what he declares to be a conscientions decision, and one whieh 
he says he would not alter for the sake of his office or any other consideration. 

Fnad Kffendi, so far from haying French tendencies, was always consi- 
dered Russian, If your Lordship were pleased to give him any assistance in 
his dilemma, you would do much service to the Porte. 

M. Balabine also complained of the great disadvantages which must result 
from the claim of France to reopen this dangerous and most delicate question 
when she chooses, ‘This complaint I consider perfectly well founded ; and if 
her Majesty’s Government could induce the French Government to consider 
the present arrangement as a final one, Russia, [ think, would accept it, and 
the peace of the world would be strengthened by a fresh guarantee.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Malmesbury— (Received January 11, 1853.) 
(No. 455.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, December 51, 1852. 

I HAVE had the honour of receiving your Lordship's despatch of the 
14th instant, containing copies of three of Colonel Rose's very interesting 
despatches relating to the dispute of the Greek and Latin Churches at 
Jerusalem. | 

Your Lordship will perhaps recollect the pertinacity with which, during 
the summer and autumn of this year, I continued to allude to the dangers 
which I foresaw would spring from a continuance of these religious, or rather 
these sectarian fends, and it is with infinite regret that I find that my appre- 
hensions were so well founded. 

1 entertain no doubt of the correctness of Colonel Rose’s opinion as to 
political differences being concealed behind such unworthy screens as a church 
door or a yestry cupboard ; but it is not the less true that the whole question, 
from its partly religious character, and from the personal share which he has 
taken in its attempted solution, is one of deep interest to the Emperor. 

His Majesty, with a view to maintaining his religious as well as political 
influence in Turkey, was extremely eager to place his co-religionists in the 
East in the best possible position with regard to their access to the Holy Places, 
and the direct appeal which he made to the Sultan upon the subject rendered 
the question still more personal to himself, 

Further, I cannot doubt that the Emperor—the known champion of 
unlimited monarchy—attaches much greater yalue to the word of a Sovereign 
than to the assurances of a Government; and his application to the Sultan, and 
his Highness's promises in return, cannot fail of having had a powerful eflect 
upon his Imperial Majesty's resolution of abiding by what he considers the 
just, and vested, and confirmed rights of the Greeks at Jerusalem. 

Since the above lines were written I have held a conversation with the 
Chancellor, which only confirms the impression already existing in my mind, 

I commenced the conversation by observing that 1 could not help feeling 
great anxiety about the continued disputes respecting the rights of the Greek 
and Latin Churehes in Turkey, “Et vons avez bien raison,” Count Nessel- 
rode replied, “d'en ttre inquiet, car je ne vous cacheral pas que c'est une 
trés-mauvaise affaire.” |

vernment was simply this:—That after two years of laborious negotiation, an 
arrangement had been effected, fair to all parties, and by which certain con- 
cessions had been made to the Latins; that this arrangement was notified not 
only by a Firman written in February last, but by a formal letter from the 
Sultan tothe Emperor; that the business was suddenly unsettled by the French 
Ambassador, who, under threats of violence, had suspended the reading of the 
Firman ; that certainly this was a state of things which His Imperial Majesty

Sir G..H. Seymour to Lord John Russell. —(Received January 19.) | 
(No. 2.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 6, 1859, 

IN acknowledging the receipt of the Earl of Malmesbury’s despatch 
marked No, 311, of the 2ist ultimo, inclosing various despatches relating to 
the quarrels of the Greek and Latin churches at Jerusalem, your Lordship 
will, I trust, not consider me presumptuous in observing that the moment is 
fully come for putting an end, if possible, to those fonds, threatening as they 
do to become at any moment the motive or the pretext of a trial of strength, 
in the East between the two powerful nations by whom, those religions are 
especially protected, ; 

I would venture to remark, that the chances of a composition are very 
remote, if on one side the French Embassy declares itself resolved not to 
abate a tittle of the claims which it founds upon the concessions made in 1740 
and 1757, while Russia is equally resolute in insisting upon the stafwa qua, the 
strict execution of the Firman of February, 1852, and of the promises ‘Cons 
tained in the Sultan’s letter to the Emperor Nicholas. | 


B4 


Again, if, as Colonel Rose announces in his despatch No. 155, the Porte 
intends to take upon itself the office of settling conflicting claims, with a view 
to making a concession to the Latins at the expense of the Greeks, I can 
hardly doubt that the Sultan, acting as umpire, will lose almost the only 
advantage which he now enjoys in the affair; and that, instead of being consi- 
dered, as at present, a sufferer from disputes in which he has no concern, he 
will be regarded by the Russians as the violator of promises very recently and 
very solemnly given to the Emperor and his co-religionists. 

1 observe, however, from Lord Cowley’s despatch No. 739, that M. D. de 
Lhuys appears sensible that the French Ambassador has run somewhat unne- 
cessarily into this religious dispute, and that probably, under cover of a small 
amount of satisfaction, the French Government would be glad to withdraw 
from the contest. 

It ocenrs to me, therefore, to submit to your Lordship whether the Turks 
might not be adyised to make friends with the French Embassy by delivering 
up to French protection one of those Holy Places which (little to the honour 
of Christendom) are now occupied by unbelievers. 

Of these it appears that there are four, the remains of the Church of 
St. Helena, built on the site of the well where the conversation was held 
between our Saviour and the Samaritan Woman 5 

a. ‘The Church of the Presentation to the Temple; 

3. ‘The Church of the Apostles, on Mount Sion ; and 

4. 'The Church of the Ascension, on the Mount of Olives. 

These last three are represented by the Abbé Michon as being now used 
as MOsqUCs. 

The restoration of one of these to a branch of that religion for whose 
service it was originally )uilt, would perhaps not be too great a price to pay 
for the settlement of a dispute with France; and if the sacrifice be one to 
which the ‘Turks will not submit, it 1s possible that the ruins of the Church of 
St. Helena might be accepted in its place, 

If some such arrangement as the above be considered unworthy and 


i 


impracticable, | hardly know what means could be devised for the settlement 
of the Greek and Latin disputes, unless they were submitted to arbitration, 

It would remain to be seen whether the Russian Government would lend 
iigelf to this proposal ; but, certainly, no conversation which I have held with 
Count Nesselrode warrants my believing that the Emperor will be contented 
with anything short of the exact fulfilment of the promises made to the Greek 
Church and to himself, . 

I have, &c. 


(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

Sir G. H. Seymour to Lord John Russell.—(Received January 19.) 
(No. 5. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 7, 1859. 

SINCE my last despatches were written, the intelligence which has reached 
me is of a nature even more alarming than that which I have already had the 
honour of submitting to your Lordship. | 

A person whose means of obtaining correct information are peculiarly 
good, states that orders have been despatched to the 5th Corps d' Armée to 
advance to the frontiers of the Danubian Provinces, without waiting for their 
reserves; and that the 4th Corps, under the command of General Count 
Tannenberg, and now stationed in Volhynia, will be ordered to hold itself in 
readiness to march if necessary, 

Keach of these Corps consists of twenty-four regiments, and, as your Lord- 
ship is aware, each Russian regiment is composed of three battalions (each of 
about 1000 men), of which one battalion forms the reserve. 

General Liider’s Corps d'Armée, accordingly, being now 48,000 strong, will 
receive a reinforcement of 24,000 men soon after its arrival at its destination, 
and supposing the 4th Corps to follow, the whole force will amount, at least 
according to official returns, to 144,000 men. 


oy 


It is evident that nothing but cither very painful inducements or yery 
excited feelings could induce the Emperor to put such an army in movement at 
a time when the utmost moderation is necessary to preserve ‘Europe from the 
dangers of a war, and when the finances of Russia, already far from flourishing, 
and encumbered with the coming expense of the railroad between St. Peters- 
patel and Warsaw, are so little in a state to encourage unnecessary expen 

iture. 

It is xtremely painful to me to transmil to your Lordship intelligenee of so 
alarming a nature, but the source from which it is derived is such as hardly to 
justify my waiting: for its confirmation. 

I have, &e. 


(Signed) G. H, SEYMOUR,

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 8, 1853. 


THE departure of the Austrian messenger, about to. be despatched to the 
Prussian frontier, having been deferred till to-day, Lam enabled to offer your 
Lordship in a few lines the précis of a long conversation which I have held this 
afternoon with the Chancellor upon the subject of the armed preparations of 
Russia. 

Of the extent of these armaments his Excellency is not prepared to speak 
with certainty ; he believes that marching orders have only been given to the 
sth Corps, and is not aware of the 4th Corps having received directions to 
hold itself in readiness. 

Count Nesselrode treats as exaggerated the apprehensions which I ex- 
Dai as likely to arise in Turkey and elsewhere from the appearance of a 

ussian army on the frontiers of the Suitan’s dominions. The nature of these 
apprehensions was fully explained in a sort of memorandum which | had drawn 
up hastily, and which I read to the Chancellor, Some of the expressions of 
this paper, a copy of which will of course he transmitted to your Lordship, 
Count Nesselrode thought too strong for the occasion, 

His Excellency entered into long explanations and assurances tending to 
prove that the Emperor deprecated the fall of ‘Turkey, and had, under critical 
circumstances, rendered those services to the Porte by which alone such a 
catastrophe could have been averted. 

As regards the present crisis (brought about by the intrigues of the French 
Ambassador at Constantinople), his Excellency expressed the hope and the belief 
that it would be brought toa conclusion by negotiation, but observed that it 
was necessary that the diplomacy of Russia should be supported (appuye) by a 
demonstration of force. It would be required that the Porte should strictly 
fulfil its engagements towards the Greek Church and the Emperor; it would 
further be exacted that a corresponding compensation should be made to the 
Greek, for any new concession mace (I believe his Excellency said, at the open 
of the Emperor's co-religionists) to the Latin Church, Finally, his Excellency 
expressed his firm belief that this alarming question would be brought to a 
satisfactory conclusion, if exertions were made by Her Maley Government 
at Paris and at Constantinople to advocate the rights which the Russian Go- 
vernment are entitled to claim, and to discountenance the pretensions of the 
French Cabinet, 

I beg to apologise to your Lordship for the extreme haste in which this 
despatch is necessarily written. On Thursday next 1 propose despatching the 
messenger in attendance upon the Mission. 


I have, &c.

Memorandum. 


(Confidential. ) St. Petershuryh, January 8, 1863. 

I'l’ is hardly necessary to state that there is no object upon which Her 
Majesty's Government are so intent as upon the preservation of peace in 
Europe, and (as closely connected with this object) upon preventing the down- 
fall of the Turkish Empire. 

It is not to be doubted, that the same importance is attached to these 
objects by the Imperial Cabinet. 

The question then presents itself, will these great ends be promoted by 
the advance of a large Russian ee upon the Turkish frontier ? and it 


7) 
4) 


AB 


should appear that the inquiry admits of only one reply. At a moment when 
‘an unfortunate dispute is carried on at Constantinople,—a dispute in which 
the Porte itself has no interest, one which should never haye been originated, 
and which, without great difficulty, might be arranged,—the appearance near 
the frontier of Turkey of a large Russian army can hardly fail to alarm the 
jealousy of the new French Government—for all new Governments are by 
their nature prone to be jealous—and is likely to produce counter-demon= 
strations on their part. ‘What the consequence would be of the simultaneous 
presence of a Russian and French foree in the East, it would be impossible to 
foresee ; thus much, however, is certain, that it must tend to injure, most 
materially, the inde wndence of Turkey, and to strike, perhaps, 4 fatal blow 
to the authorily of the Sultan. 

But if the presence of a Russian army of the borders of the Principalities 
is likely to arouse the apprehensions of foreign Governments, what. effect is it 
caleulated to produce upon the subjects of the Porte? 

The inquiry may be readily answered. It caunot fail of inspiring the 
Mussulman population with the deepest apprehensions, and is ecually calculated 
to induce the Christian subjects of the Sultan to rise in rebellion against their 
Sovereign ; this, too, ata moment when, besides suffering from severe financial 
embarrassments, the Porte finds its resources severely taxed by the efforts which 
it is compelled to make for putting down the movements which have broken 
out in Syria and in the neighbourhood of Montenegro. 

Tt cannot be that the Russian Cabinet would willing incur the responsi- 
bility of a crisis brought about by a demonstration not called for ai any great 
military or political emergency: But it may be said, that France has uttered 
the threat of making a naval or military demonstration in the Hast, and that 
this menace demands a corresponding demonstration on the part of the Im- 
perial forces. 

To this it may be replied, that the threat, even if sertonsly made, will, 
according. to all appearances, not be acted upon, and that one military act, 
from whieh the Porte would suffer the @reatest inconvenience, could hardly be 

alleged in justification of a similar act, proceeding from another quarter, and 
which would be to the full as detrimental to.the Sultan's interests. 

It has been, by some, assumed that the object of Louis Napoleon in 
reopening the question relating to the Holy Places, has been to produce 
confusion, and. to introduce discord into the councils of the allied Governments. 

Now this suspicion is correct oF itis unfounded; +f wotounded, a resolu- 
tion, the carrying out of which may have the most serions consequences, Will 
have been taken upon false grounds ; if correct, ‘t may be asked, whether it 
would be politic to resort to measures by which the conflict, which it is assur 
to be the desire of France to promote, may be brought about. 

To this may be added the observation that there ts considerable reason 
for believing that the dispute respecting the Latin rights at Jerusalem 
originated not s0 much in the decisions of the Cabinet, ag in the personal 
views of a diplomatic agent; and further, that grounds are not wanting for 
imagining that the French Government may not he reluctant to withdraw, if 
enabled to do so with dignity, from a diplomatic contest entered upon without 
sufficient reflection. ‘To these observations one other might be added,—it 
would be wausual that so strong a measnre &% that of the gathering of an 
imposing military force upon the frontiers of a friendly country, should be 
adopted without notice or warhing } whereas so little notice has been given at 
the Porte of the resolutions which there are appearances of having been earried 
‘nto execution, that it may be remarked that the threat, hitherto made to the 
Porte, has never gone beyond that (of ‘teclf sufficiently alarming) of the 
Imperial Mission being withdrawn from Constantinople, in the event of the 
non-execution of the Sultan's engagements with regard to the Holy Places. 

I cannot be desired by the ‘allies of Russia that the Emperor shonld be 
asked to forego any of those rights 0 which he is justly entitled ; but it may 
“properly be submitted that those rights should not be sought under a demon: 
stration of military force, when, according to all probability, they might be 
attained by the wanal course of negotiation. 

The above rellections are submitted respectfully to the consideration of 
Count Nesselrode, with the expression of a hop that they may be found

The Emperor’s words and manner, although still very kind, showed that 
his Majesty had no intention of speaking to me of the demonstration which he 
‘s about to make in the South. He said, however, at first with a little hesita- 
tion, but as he proceeded, in an open and unhesitating manner, “ The affairs of 
Turkey are in a very disorganized condition; the country itself seems to be 
falling to pieces (menace ruine): the fall will be a great misfortune, and it is 
very important that England and Russia should come to a perfectly good 
understanding upon these affairs, and that neither should take any decisive step 
of which the other is not apprised.” 

T observed in a few words, that I rejoiced to hear that his Imperial Majesty 
held this language ;—that this was certainly the view | took of the manner in 
which Turkish questions are to be treated, 

“Tenez,” the Emperor said, as if proceeding with his remark, “ tenez ; 
nous avons sur les bras un homme malade—un homme gravement 
malade +: ce sera, je vous le dis franchement, un grand malheur si, un de ces 
jours, il devait nous échapper, surtout avant que toutes les dispositions nécessaires 
fussent prises, Mais enfin ce n'est point le moment de vous parler de cela,” 

It was clear that the Emperor did not intend to prolong the conversation, 
but I determined upon having the last word. I therefore said—* Votre 
Majesté est si graciense qu'elle me permettra de lui faire encore une observa- 
tion. Votre Majesté dit que "homme est malades c'est bien yrai, mais votre 
Majesté daigznera m’excuser si je lui fais observer, que c'est i thomme généreux 
et fort de ménager l'homme malade et faible.” 

The Emperor then took leave of me ina manner which conveyed the 
impression of my haying at least not given offence, and again expressed his 
intention of sending for me on some future day. 

Whether the intention will be acted upon, is not to meso certain. Tt 
may be right that | should state to your Lordship that I propose giving Count 
Nesselrode an account of ny conversation with his Imperial master. 

J am conyineed that the Chancellor is invariably favourable to measures 
of moderation, and as far as lies in his power, to English views. His desire, 
then, to actin harmony with Her Majesty’s Government cannot but be strength- 
ened by learning the cordial declarations which the Emperor has made to me 
upon the subject. 

Upon reading over my despatch, [am convinced that the conversation, 
although abridged, has been faithfully reported ; the only point of any interest 
which | am aware of not having touched upon being, that the Emperor observed 
that the last accounts from Constantinople were more satisfactory, the Turks 
appearing to be more reasonable, although by what process they had become 
80) Vind not heen made apparent. 

I will only observe that we have every interest in its being understood that 
no decision should be taken in the allairs of Turkey, without concert with Her 
Majesty's Government, by a Sovercign who can dispose of several hundred 
thonsand bayonets. 

Would the understanding be acted upon?—that indeed may well be 


doubted, and the rather as the Emperor's assurances are a little contradicted ° 


by the measures to which it has been my duty to eall your Lordship’s 
attention, 

Still His Imperial Majesty's words appear to me to possess considerable 
value, and certainly they offer me at this moment an advantage of which T shall 
not be backward in availing myself. 

Your Lordship will pardon me if T remark that, after reflecting attentively 
upon my conversation with the Emperor, it appears to me that this, and any 
overture of the kind which may be made, tends to establish a dilemma by 
which it is very desirable that Her Majesty's Government should not allow 
themselves to be feltered, The dilemma seems to be this:—if Her Majesty's 
Government do not come to an understanding with Russia as to what is to 
happen in the event of the sudden downfall of Turkey, they will have the less 
reason for complaining if results displeasing to England should be prepared, 
If, on the contrary, Her Majesty's Government should enter into the consider- 
ation of such eventualities, they make themselves in some degree consenting 
parties to a catastrophe which thoy have souueh interest in warding off as long 
ns possible, 

The sum is probably this, that England has to desire a close concert with 


91 


Russia, with a view to preventing the downfall of Turkey—while Russia would 
be well pleased that the concert should apply to the events by which this down- 
fall is to be followed,

Sir G, H. Seymour to Lord John Russell.—(Received January 23.) 
(No. 15. Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 11, 1853. 

OWN the Sth instant I had the honour of offering your Lordship a hurried 
abstract of a conversation which I had held that day with Count Nesselrode 
respecting the military demonstrations about to be made upon the Turkish 
frontier. It is perhaps unnecessary that T should now fill wp that outline, but 
[ am desirous of remarking that the Chancellor’s object appeared to be to 
prove that Russia was entitled to negotiate under cireumstances as favourable 
as France, while my object was to demonstrate that the intemperance of one 
party was no exeuse for that of another, directed not against the assumed 
ageressor, but against a third party perfeetly passive in the affair, 

_ ‘Toshow the tendency of my arguments, I venture to report to your Lord- 
ship a very familiar illustration which I made use of when his Excellency 
stated that as the Turks had been seen to give way to French pressure, it was 
only fair that they should be subjected to a little pressure from their the 
Russiin side, | 

_ Getting up from my chair and walking into the middle of the room, I said, 
*M. le Comte, you must allow me to show you to what point your argument goes. 
A man is sitting quietly in his room when a violent neighbour rushes in 
and thrusts him np against the wall; do me the favour to tell me whether this 
act of aggression authorizes a second neighbour to come in and to repeat a 
similar act of violence. You must admit that, if liable to such attacks, the man 
would be driven out of his house, if indeed he were not driven ‘to throw 
himself out of the window.” | 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR,

that in recognising it he would be doing injury to the memory of his brother,

has now in his possession, he continues, some unpublished memoirs of his

Te Deum was celebrated in the presence of the Allies for the return of the 
Bourbons, and when the Emperor Alexander refused to be present, preferring 
to spend the day with Queen Hortense, at: Malmaison. 

Finally, the Emperor states that he has accepted the letters accrediting 
Monsieur de Kisseleff, though he does not deny that the refusal of the Emperor 
Nicholas to give him the title of Brother has greatly pained him; but he adds, 
“My heart has felt it more deeply than my vanity.” His Majesty coneludes 
by saying that he had hoped, where two characters were so much in unison 
as his and the Emperor of Russia’s, in their respect for religion, in their 
desire to preserve social order, to develop the prosperity of their subjects, 
and to promote military discipline, the tithe of Brother would not have been 
refused him; and that if he has accepted the letters, which do not give him 
that title, it has been to show to Europe the conciliatory spirit which animates 
him,

100 


Both these despatches relate to the question of the Holy Places. 

It is with great regret that Her Majesty’s Government have perceived 
that this question is not yet settled, although the instructions given to General 
Castelbajac may lead to a favourable termination of this unfortunate dispute. 
As, however, this happy result may not be attained, it is desirable that you 
should be made aware of the view which is taken of this matter by Her 
Majesty’s Government. 

In the first place, Her Majesty’s Government desire to abstain altoget ier 
from giving any opinion on the merits of the question. Treaties, Conventions, 
and Firmans are quoted with equal confidence on both sides. 

But Her Majesty’s Government cannot avoid perceiving that the Ambas- 
sador of France at Constantinople was the first to disturb the sfatus quo in 
which the matter rested. Not that the disputes of the Latin and Greek 
Churches were not yery active, but that without some political action on the 
part of France those quarrels would never have troubled the relations of 
friendly Powers. ; 

In the next place, if report is to be believed, the French Ambassador was 
the first to speak of having recourse to foree, and to threaten the intervention 
of a French fleet to enforce the demands of his country. . 

I regret to say that this evil example has been partly followed by Russia 5 
and although the report of the march of fifty thousand Russian troops to the 
Turkish frontier appears to have been unfounded or premature, yet it is but 
too certain that if the quarrel is prolonged, the Emperor means to snpport his 
negotiations by arms. ee 

‘ Toa Gavernment taking an impartial view of these affairs, an attitude so 
threatening on both sides appears very lamentable. We should deeply regret 
any dispute that might lead to conflict between two of the great Powers of 
Europe; but when we reflect that the quarrel is for exclusive privileges In a spot 
near which the heavenly host proclaimed peace on earth and goodwill towards 
men,—when we see rival Churches contending for mastery in the very place 
whore Christ died for mankind,—the thought of such a spectacle is melancholy 
indeed. Sy eee 

Your Excellency will understand therefore, Ist, that into the merits of this 
dispute Her Majesty’s Government will not enter; 2ndly, that Her Majesty’s 
Government disapprove of every threat, and still more of the actual employ- 
ment of force ; 3rdly, that as the French have raised this controversy, it is for 
them to set the example of concession and forbearance ; 4thly, that both parties 
should be told, that if they are sincere in their professions of a destre to main- 
tain the independence of the Porte, they ought to abstain from the employment 
of any means calculated to display the weakness of the Ottoman Empire. 
Above all, they ought to refrain from putting armies and fleets in motion for 
the purpose of making the Tomb of Christ a cause of eee Christians, 

Tam, &e, 
(Signed) J. RUSSELL, 


No. 110. 


Lord John Russell to Lord Cowley. 
(No. 87.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, January 29, 1653, 

I HAVE received your despatch No. 61, dated yesterday, and containing 
matters of very serious import. 

The Chargé d'Affaires of France, M, Baudin, spoke to me yesterday in 
the same sense in Which M. Drouyn de Lhuys has spoken to you, _ 

The anxiety felt by the French Government is very natural, and M. Baudin 
observed very justly, that Powers who professed themselves so anxious to 
preserve the status quo in Europe, ought to be the last to meditate so great a 
disturbance of the eaniee of power as the overthrow of the Turkish Empire 
must produce. Yet, notwithstanding this natural antety on the part of 
France, Her Majesty's Government are persuaded that the Emperor of Russia 
will not enter willingly, and certainly not without the consent of England, into 
any schemes for the subversion of the Ottoman Power. 


101 


Her Majesty's Government have reasons quite satisfactory to them for this 
persuasion. 

At the same time, there is no doubt that the Ottoman Empire is in great 
peril. It isso weak, so disorganised, and at the same time so tempting a prize 
to ambition, that each of the great Powers of France and Russia entertain no 
unnatural fear that its conquest may be accomplished to the aggrandisement of 
the other. 

France expects Russia will be the aggressor; the Emperor of Russia 
expects the same of France, 

Thus each Power is induced to action, not from its own ambition, but 
from suspicion of the ambition of another great and formidable Empire. 

These dangers, it must be owned, are increased by the irritating activity of 
Turkey, which, with a restlessness not unfrequently combined with weakness, 
tries to show its vitality by efforts which only exhibit its sense of decrepitude 
and its impatience of decay. 

At the same time, | cannot agree with your Excellency that it would be 
right to go further than we have already done on the subject of Montenegro. 

The title of the Porte to the sovereignty of Montenegro is not contested 
by Austria, and has been allowed by England and France. 

The impradence of asserting that title has been repeatedly pointed out to 
the Porte, both by Her Majesty's late Government and by her present 
advisers. 

Her Majesty’s Government think it desirable, however, that some under. 
standing should be arrived at between the great Powers on this important 
subject, and | will immediately take into consideration the steps that may be 
necessary for this purpose. 

I shall write to your Excellency again on this important subject in a very 
few days. 

Iam, &e. 


(Signed) J. RUSSELL, 


No, 111. 
Lord Cowley to Lord John Russell.—(Received January 29.) 


(No. 61.) 


My Lord, Paris, January 28, 1833, 

M, DROUYN DE LHUYS having requested to see me, | called upon him 
thisatternoon. He told me that he had transmitted yesterday to M. Bandin, for 
communication to your Lordship, the copy of a despatch dated the 23rd instant, 
which he had received from Vienna, and in which M. de Lacour states that he 
has reason to fear that an Austrian expeditionary corps of 6,000 men, under 
the Ban Jellachich, is preparing to enter Bosnia. M. Drouyn de Lhuys, on the 
receipt of M. de Lacour's despatch, directed him by telegraph to ask explana- 
tions of Count Buol, and he received this morning an answer, dated yesterday 
evening, to the following effect, 

The Austrian troops assembled on the Turkish frontier are intended to 
cover the Austrian territory, and to give protection to all those whom pressing 
events may drive over the frontier, Austria has no intention to interfere in 
Montenegro, nor will she enter Bosnia unless to proteet the Catholics, which 
she is entitled to do under treaty. 

Count Leiningen is to proceed to Constantinople on a special mission to 
persuade the Porte to re-establish the status quo as regards Montenegro, to de- 
mand that Hungarian deserters and refugees shall not be permitted to serve in 
the army of Omar Pasha, which is operating on the frontiers of Austria, and to 
endeavour to restore diplomatic relations between Austria and the Porte. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys proceeded to say that, although this latter despatch 
had somewhat reassured him, he could not contemplate without anxiety the 
assembling of Russian and Austrian forces on the Turkish frontier, Advices 
which he had received from Trieste showed that the Austrian forces were also 
collecting in that direction, and he was obliged to ask himself more seriously 
than ever whether there was not some understanding between those two Powers

had questions in reserve on which they appeared to make depend their future 
attitude towards the Ottoman Government, He thought, therefore, that the 
time was fully arrived when Her Majesty’s Government and that of the 
Emperor should prepare for such eventwtalities as the occupation of Bosnia by 
Austria, and of the Danubian Principalities by Russia. What in that case 
should be the attitude of the two Governments? ‘The question was full of 
difficulties, for although they might render effectual assistance against Austria 
hy the Adriatic, they could give but little, if any, against Russia, nor would it 
be a very glorious task to help Mussulmen against Christians. 

{ should not follow M. Drouyn de Lhuys, even if L had time, into the wide 
range of surmises which he proceeded to give me, as to what would be the con- 
duct of Austria and Russia were the Turkish Empire at an end. | said that 
the main point was to prevent such a catastrophe as long as possible, and to 
employ all the influence of the two Governments Co that end. ‘The last time, | 
said, that I had heard from your Lordship upon the subject, you had no reason 
to think that any understanding dangerous to the stability of the Turkish 
Empire existed between Russia and Austria, Whether recent circumstances 
had changed this opinion I did not know. At all events, the first thing to be 
looked to was to prevent: the Porte giving unnecessary nimbrage to those two 
Powers. Now the expedition against Montenegro had been undertaken con- 
trary to the advice of England and France, and this expedition was probably 
the secret though not the jatensible eause of the sudden movement of Austrian 
and Russian troops towards the Turkish frontiers. Should not the first step 
taken by England and France be a renewal of their remonstrances at Con- 
stantinople against an further prosecution of tis expedition, and perhaps a 
menace that if the Turkish troops were not withdrawn within the Turkish 
territory, the two Governments would not interfere, should the continued occu- 
pation of any part of the Montenegrin territory involve the Porte in dispute 
with her powerful neighbours. [could not doubt, I said, that language such 
as this, held firmly but amicably at Constantinople, would induce the Porte to 
abandon Montenegro, and thus remove all further pretext for an armed demon- 
stration on the part of Austria, the proximity of Omar Pasha’s army being the 
exeuse for that demonstration. 

M. Dronyn de Lhuys replied, that if ever & Government was able to 
grapple with the diffieu lies of such a question as the preservation of the 
Turkish Empire, it was Her Majesty's present Cabinet. He therefore entreated 
your Lordship to consider it in all its bearings. Any opinion emanating from 
Her pa haa actual advisers would be most attentively and respectfully con- 
sidered by him. He thought, however, that the time was come when the two 
Governments should endeavour to arrive at a thorough understanding as to 
what their common policy should be under every contingeney which might 
happen to Turkey. No doubt the first object should be to preserve the inte- 
grity of the Ottoman Empire; but would it not be prudent, also, to take into 
consideration that its dissolution may be near athand? 

I have not time to give your Lordship more than this hasty outline of 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys'’s observations. ‘They will be sufficient to show your 
Lordship the anxiety respecting Eastern affairs to which it is too evident he is 
a prey. ‘There being no mail to-morrow, I have thought it better to write at 
once. 

I have, &e.

Lord Cowley to Lord John Russell_—(Received February 1.) 
(No. 66.) 
My Lord, Paris, January 31, 1853. 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS having expressed a wish to see me yester- 
day, and being myself unable to go out, he came to me yesterday evening. 
He said that he had received despatches from Constantinople, dated the 
15th instant, which augmented the disquietude he had previously entertained 
respecting the state of affairs in Turkey. M. de Lavalette had sent him 
the copy of a note, addressed, on the 7th instant, to the Porte, by M, Kletzl, 
the Austrian Chargé d’Affaires, and had given him the details of a conversation 
which he, M. de Lavalette, had subsequently had with Fuad Effendi, Your 
Lordship has, of course, received a copy of this note from Colonel Rose, and | 
need not allude to it further. In the conversation which M. de Lavalette had 
had with Fuad Effendi, the latter had characterised the note as a violation of 
every diplomatic courtesy, and said that it had even been Gieapproved by 
M. Gzeroif, the Russian Chargé d’Affaires. This gentleman had adyised the Porte 
to return no answer to it, as it did not require a reply,—advice in which M, de 
Lavalette had concurred. : 

M. Dronyn de Lhuys has also written to Constantinople, to state that his 
opinion coincides with that of M. de Lavalette. 

M, Drouyn de Lhuys then referred to the question of the Holy Places. 
He said that ie had received despatches from M. Botta, the French Consul at 
Jerusalem, reporting the great irritation which prevailed in the Latin commu- 
nity in consequence of the concessions which had been made to the Greeks, 
The Latin Patriarch had remonstrated at Rome. M. Drouyn de Lhuys added, 
that if the Emperor of Russia was not satisfied with the advantages which 
the Greek Church had gained, he did not know what further concessions the 
Latins could make, short of ceding the Holy Places altogether. He had heard, 
however, that the Greek Patriarch demanded still more; and perhaps no better 
proof could be given that the present arrangement was equitable, than that 
both the Greek and Latin Patriarchs should protest against it. 

The few words I said in reply were strictly based on the instructions con- 
tained in your Lordship’s deanna No. 51. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ language on the question appeared to me less con- 
ciliatory yesterday than it has been for some time past. This may have been 
the effect of momentary irritation, caused by the reports which he had received 
from Jerusalem of the anger of the Latin community at the concessions which 
have been made to the Greek Church ; or it may have been dictated by a more 
general dislike, which is daily gaining ground with him, of the Russian Govern- 
ment. It is, at all events, my duty to report that he stated that the French 
Gos srminet could not, and would not, make greater concessions than it had 
done. 

M. Brennier is to leave Paris, to embark at Marseilles, before the end of 
the week. It is uncertain whether he will still find M. de Lavalette at Con- 
stantinople. 

I have, &e, 
(Signed) COWLEY.

Sir G. H. Seymour to Lord John Russell—(Received February 6.) 
(No. 25. Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 21, 1863. 

I NEED not remark to your Lordship, that the secrecy observed by the 
Russian Government renders it at all times difficult to obtain information re- 
specting their acts and intentions; whilst, as the Emperor's displeasure has 
been excited by the knowledge which lately transpired of the orders which 
had been sent to the 5th Corps d’Armée, it may readily be believed that the 
usual difficulty has been increased, ‘. 

On the night of the 18th instant, a report reached me of a naval aide- 
de-eamp of the Emperor’s having left St. Petersburgh with orders for the 
assemblage of a Russian force destined to proceed to the Albanian coast, «and 
there to form a squadron of observation. — 3 

I was bound to disbelieve the rumours, as.the only naval force disposable 
for such an object would be one which would have to pass the Dardanelles. 
My informant, howeyer, appeared to be convinced that his intelligence was 
not unfounded, and, in the doubt, on the following morning I addressed Count 
Nesselrode the short private letter, of which I beg to inclose a copy. 1 had 
the less hesitation in taking this step, because. I reflected that of the small 
means at my disposal for causing the Imperial Government to pause betore 
taking an imprudent step, none is more likely to produce an effect than that of 
their ia ng rendered sensible that their movements are closely observed, and 
their intentions a little mistrusted. : 

The same day | received from the Chancellor inreply the private note, 
of which I beg likewise to inclose a copy, 

| have some reason for believing that Admiral Kornileff has been ordered 
to proceed to the Dalmatian coast, for the purpose of obtaining correct in- 
formation as to what is passing in the neighbourhood of Montenegro, and if 
this is so, the origin of the report which | mentioned to Count Nesselrode is 
accounted for. 

_ _ Admiral Kornileff is the Chef d'Etat-Major of the Sevastopol fleet, and 
is, in fact, the officer by whom all its operations are directed. 
I have, &c.

Sir G. H, Seymour to Lord John Russell.—(Received February 6.) 


(No, 24. Secret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, St, Petersburgh, January 22, 1858, 

ON the 14th instant, in consequence of a summons which | received from 
the Chancellor, I waited upon the Emperor, and had the honour of holding 
with his Imperial Majesty the very interesting conversation of which it will be 
my duty to offer your Lordship an account, which, if imperfect, will, at all 
events, not he incorrect. . 

I found His Majesty alone; he received me with great kindness, saying, 
that I had appeared desirous to speak to him upon Eastern affairs; that, on 
his side, there was no indisposition to do so, but that he must begin at a remote 
period. ' | 

‘You know,” His Majesty said, “the dreams and plans in which the Empress 
‘atherine was in the habit of indulging; these were vanded down to our time ; 
but while I inherited immense territorial possessions, | did not inherit those 
visions, those intentions, if you like to eall them so. On the contrary, my 
country ig go vast, 80 happily circumstanced in every way, that it would be 
imreasonable in me to desire more lerritory or more power than I possess ; on 
the contrary, Lam the first to tell you that our great, perhaps our only danger, 
ig that which would arise from an extension given to an impire already too 
large. i rose 
srk he Close to us lies Turkey, and in our present condition, nothing better for 
our interests can be desired; the times have gone by when we had anything 
to fear from the fanatical spirit or the military enterprise of the Turks, and 
yet the country is strong cnough, or has hitherto heen strong enough, to 
preserve its independence, and to ensure respectful treatment from other 
comntries, 

“Well, in that Empire there are several millions of Christians whose interests 


109 


I am called upon to watch over (surveiller”), while the right of doing 50 is 
secured tome by treaty. I may truly say that I make a moderate and sparing use 
of my right, and I will freely confess thatit is one which is attended with obliga- 
tions occasionally very inconvenient ; but I cannot recede from the discharge of a 
distinct duty. Our religion, as established in this country, came to us from the 
East, and there are feelings, as well as obligations, which never must be lost 
sight of. 

«Now, Turkey, in the condition which I have described, has by degrees 
fallen into such a state of deecrepitnde that, as I told you the other mght, 
eager as we all are for the prolonged existence of the man (and that Lam as 
desirous as you can be for the continuance of his life, | beg you to believe), he 
may suddenly die upon our hands (“nous rester sur les bras’’) ; we cannot resus- 
citate whatis dead; if the Turkish Empire falls, it falls to rise no more; and I 
put it to you, therefore, whether it is not better to be provided beforehand for 
a contingency, than to ineur the chaos, confusion, and the certainty of an 
European war, all of which must attend the eatastrophe if it should occur 
unexpectedly, and before some ulterior system has heen sketched; this is the 
pein to which I am desirous that you should call the attention of your 

iovernment. 

“Sir” | veplied, “your Majesty isso frank with me, that lam sure you will 
have the goodness to permit me to speak with the same openness. [ would then 
observe, that deplorable as is the condition of Turkey, it is a country which 
has long been plunged in diffienlties supposed by many to be insurmountable. 

* With regard to contingent arrangements, Her Majesty's Government, as 
your Majesty is well aware, objects, as a general rule, to taking engagements 
upon possible eventualities, and would, perhaps, be particularly disinelined to 
doing so in this instance. If I may be allowed to say so, a great disinelination 
(répngnance) wight be expected in England, to disposing by anticipation 
(d'escompter) of the succession of an old friend and ally.” 

“'The rule is a good one,” the Emperor replied, “ good at all times, especially 
in times of uncertainty and change, like the present; still it is of the greatest 
importance that we should understand one another, and not allow events to 
take us by surprise; ‘maintenant je désire vous parler en ami et en gentleman, 
si nous arrivons 4 nous entendre sur cette affaire, fAngleterre et moi; pour le 
reste, peu m'importe, il m’est indifferent co que font ou pensent les autres. 
Usant done de franchise, je vous dis nettement, que si l'Angleterre songe A 
s'établir un de ces jours 4 Constantinople, je ne le permettral pas; je ne vous 
préte point ces intentions, mais il vaut micux dans ees occasions parler claire: 
ment; de mon coté, je suis également disposé de prendre engagement de ne pas 
m'y établir, en propriétaire, il s'entend, car en dépositaire je ne dis pas; il 
pourrait se faire que les cireonstances me missent dans le cas doceuper Con- 
stantinople, si rien ne se trouve prévu, si Von doit tout laisser aller au eee 

{ thanked His Majesty for the frankness of his declarations, and for the 
desire which he had expressed of acting cordially and openly with Her 
Majesty’s Government, observing at the same time, that such an understanding 
appeared the best security against the sudden danger to which His Majesty 
had alluded, | added that, although unprepared to give a decided opinion 
upon questions of such magnitude and delicacy, it appeared to me possible 
that some such arrangement might be made between Her Majesty's Giovern- 
ment and His Majesty, as might guard, if not for, at least against, certain 
contingencies, 

To render my meaning more clear I said further: “T can only repeat, sir, 
that in my opinion, Her Majesty’s Government will be indisposed to make 
certain arrangements connected with the downfall of Turkey, but it is possible 
that they be ready to pledge themselves against certain arrangements which 
might, in that event, be attempted.” . 

His Imperial Majesty ten alluded to a conversation which he had held, 
the last time he was in England, with the Duke of Wellington, and to the 
motives which had compelled him to open himself to his Grace ; then, a8 now, 
His Majesty was, he aie eager to provide against events which, in the absence 
of any concert, might compel him to act in a manner opposed to the views of 
Her Majesty’s Government.

Sir G. H. Seymour to Lord John Russell.—(Received February 6.) 
(No, 28. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petershurgh, January 25, 1852, 


| HAVE. held some interesting conversation with General de Berg, an 
officer who is very much in the confidence of the Emperor, and one of the very 
few who are ever disposed to express any opinion as to the events of the day. 

© You have had a sharp alerte,”” General de Berg said, “and during a few 
days I dare say that you thought some serious events were at hand ;—it is 
natural enough, but when you have been here longer you will see that this 
sort of thing oceurs frequently. Decisions are taken in a hurry, orders are 
given—then they are cancelled, and in a few days everything 1s forgotten, 

“You must always bear in mind that the ey is as peaceably inclined 
as you can be, and that if you dread the downfall of the Turks, he dreads. it 
even more, All the old policy upon'these subjects is altered. We could go 
to Constantinople if we pleased, thatis clear, but no one is so little disposed as 
the Emperor. 

“'The fact is this, our interests are perfectly well understood: Moscow, St. 
Petersburgh, these are the seats of a national foree, which constitutes our 
strength; if we extend ourselves to the south, our national feeling is destroyed, 
and the Empire loses its vitality. ee 

“ We pass for being profound politicians, and yet our policy is of the 
simplest order ; our great affair is to have weak pliant neighbours. 

* This advantage, among others, we possess—our two maritime issues are 
in the hands of weak States, and we are very much interested in their prolonged 
continuance. From weak neighbours we obtain all the facilities we can require, 
and this without those inconveniences and dangers which we must incur were 
we to take possession of their territories. In a word, then, the Emperor may 
be obliged by some extraordinary circumstances to march upon Constantinople ; 
but he will never possess Constantinople, neither will his son, nor, in all pro-

T informed Count Nesselrode that Her Majesty's Government had shown 
themselves as desirous as himself that the utmost moderation should be 
observed by Omar Pasha, but begged that he would not lose sight of the fact 
of a series of very wanton aggressions haying been perpetrated by the Monte- 
negrins; that if, then, under such provocations, the Turks retaliated severely, 
they would only act as the Austrian Government had done towards the same 
offenders in the year 1836 or 1838, 

Count Nesselrode, as of late he has been in the habit of doing, expressed 
opinions the most unfavourable of Fuad Effendi, eaying that he is a man whose 
word 1s not to be trusted, and that he appears destined to involve his Sovereign 
in the greatest embarrassments, 

[ will here remark to your Lordship (as [ ought to have done sometime 
since) that, according to the Russian version, Fuad Effendi is at present 
devoted to the interests of France, his services having been retained by the 
French Ambassador, ' 

We spoke again of the critical posture of affairs in Turkey, and | must 
observe that the opinions which I had expressed in the written paper, a copy 
of which was inclosed in my No. 10, opinions, at the time considered by Count 
Nesselrode to be exaggerated, appear now to be precisely those which he him- 
self entertains, 

He did not hesitate to speak of the inflammatory spirit of the Christian 
opulation of Turkey, remarking that any excesses committed against the 
hristian population might cause that spirit to break out in extensive flames. 

Once again Count Nesselrode desired to impress upon my mind the dread, 
the sincere dread, with which the Emperor regarded the great probability of a 
dissolution of the Ottoman Empire. 

“1 believe,” his Excellency said, “that, involved as they unquestionably 
are, the Emperor takes too dark a view of ‘Turkish affairs; of the sincerity of 
his feelings, however, no one who has had good opportunities of judging ean 
doubt; in short, no state of things can serve our interests better than that 
which now prevails in Turkey,”

The question raised by his Imperial Majesty is a very serious 908 WN 15,

In these circumstances it would hardly be consistent with the friendly 
feelings towards the Sultan which animate the Emperor of Russia, no less than 
the Queen of Great Britain, to dispose beforehand of the provinces under his 
dominion. Besides this consideration, however, it must be observed, that an 
agreement made in such a case tends very surely to hasten the contingency for 
which it is intended to provide. Austria and France could not, in fairness, be 
kept in ignorance of the transaction, nor would such concealment be consistent 
with the end of preventing an European war, Indeed, such concealment 
cannot be intended by his Imperial Majesty. It is to be inferred that as soon 
as Great Britain and Russia should have agreed on the course to be pursued, 
and have determined to enforce it, they should communicate their intentions to 
the great Powers of Europe, An agreement thus made, and thus communi- 
cated, would not be very long a secret; and while it would alarm and alienate 
the Sultan, the knowledge of its existence would stimulate all his enemies to 
increased violence, and more obstinate conflict. They would fight with the 
conviction that they must ultimately triumph; while the Sultan's generals and 
troops would feel that no immediate sucecss could save their cause from final 
overthrow. Thus would be produced and strengthened that very anarchy 
which is now feared, and the foresight of the friends of the paticnt would prove 
the canse of his death. 

Her Majesty's Government need scarcely enlarge on the dangers attendant 
on the execution of any similar Convention, The example of the Succession 
War is enough to show how little such agreements are expected when a 
presse temptation urges their violation. he position of the Emperor of 
Russia as depositary, but not ar of Constantinople would be exposed 
to numberless hazards both from the long-cherished ambition of his own nation 
and the jealousies of Europe. The ultimate proprictor, whoever he might be, 
would hardly be satished with the inert, supine attitude of the heirs of Mahomet 
the Second, A great influence on the alfairs of Europe seems naturally to 
belong ta the Sovereign of Constantinople, holding the gates of the Mediter- 
ranean and the Black Sea. 

That influence might be used in favour of Russia; it might be used to 
control and curb her power,

desire more territory or more power than I possess. On the contrary,” he 
observed, ‘our great, perhaps our only danger, is that which would arise from

Sir G, H. Seymour to Lord Jon Russell—(Received February 14.) 


(No. ‘44. Confidential.) visi 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, February 3, 1855. 

I LEARN from an officer who is about the Emperor's person, and in the 
enjoyment of his full confidence, the correctness of the report of Prince 
Menchikof! having received.orders to repair to Constantinople... | 

“ Our diplomacy,” this person observed, “has for some time been too. 
inactive in Turkey ; it is time that Russian interests should be better protected, 
when attempts are made to dispossess us of our rights.” nels ; 

From other parts of the conversation, it appeared that T had been correct 
in stating, as I did some weeks ago, that much greater importance was attached 
to the word of the Sultan than to any acts of the Turkish Ministry. 

 Qur position,” my acquaintance observed, “is this:—we have the 
Firman of last. year, indorsed by an autograph letter of the Sultan’s, securing 
us richts of which we (the Greek Church) have been in the enjoyment for 140 
years: the reading of the Firman was delayed by Fuad Effendi, and the 
status quo has, since the reading took place, been altered under the dictation 
of France: this we cannot submit to.” I observed, that I had not been back- 
ward in blaming the activity and violence of M, de Lavalette, but that common 
fairness required that we should all recognize the conciliatory spirit of late 
manifested by France to settle the disputes respecting the Holy Places with 
the Russian Government. This plea, my Russian acquaintance observed, was 
not admissible; Russia had nothing to do with France in this question; the 
point was one to be settled between the Emperor and a Sovereign whose word 
the Emperor held. ‘What Prince Menchikoff may do,” he added, 1 do not 
know: but I can say this, that were I to be sent in his place to Constantinople, 
my first demand would be the expulsion of so false a man as Fouad Effendi 
from the Ministry.” 

It occurred to me that a Russian, high in place and favour, is not apt to 
talk of the line of political conduct which he should pursne, unless he had 
previously made himself well acquainted with the feelings of his master; and 
[ inferred that the conversation of which I have given the outline, ought to 
be notieed to your Lordship. 


I suppress any report of what passed further with respect to the Mon- 


tenegrins, the object of my acquaintance being to prove that those people 
were unjustly attacked, whilst mine was to show that Montenegrin inde- 
endence was one question, and the right which seems claimed by them to 
plunder and murder with impunity is another and a widely different one. 

On this, as on all occasions, I endeavour to demonstrate that the very 
interest taken by the Emperor in the Montenegrins should be shown by efforts 
to restrain their appetite for acts of lawlessness. and violence ; that, as I have 
expressed it, a person may keep a dog without allowing him to go about-biting 
the neighbours. 

T have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H, SEYMOUR,

Sir G. H. Seymour to Lord John Russell —(Received February 14.) 
(No. 56.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, February 5, 1859. 
I WAITED yesterday, by appointment, upon the Chancellor, and held a 
conversation with him upon Turkish affairs. 
It commenced by my expressing my satisfaction at the conciliatory attitude 
of the French Cabinet, remarking that, with such amicable dispositions on 


their part, it was impossible but that the question of the Holy Places should 


be speedily disposed of. 

His a eaticicy replied, that the conduct of the French Government was 
becoming more conciliatory, “qu'il semblait_ mettre de eau dans son vin;” 
that a communication had been received from the Marquis de Castelbajac 
upon the subject of the religious question, and that he proposed soon to reply 
to this overture; the reply, when made, would be communicated to me. 

Count Nesselrode then said, that he desired to acquaint me that Prince 
Menchikoff had received orders to prepare for departure for Constantinople, 
where the affairs of the Russian Mission had been for some time conducted by 
a Chargé d’Affaires, whose rank did not give him the weight which was 
required in affairs of such gravity as those now pending. . 

His Excellency wished to assure me that the instructions with which 
Prince Menchikolf would be provided were of a conciliatory nature, and that 
although bred to arms, the Prince himself was animated by intentions the most 
pacific. 

I inquired whether Prince Menchikolf would be instructed to occupy him- 
self with the affairs of Montenegro, as well as with that of the “* Lieux 
Saints; and was acquainted that would he the case. 

The conversation then turned to the war in Montenegro, and Count 
Nesselrode spoke with animation of the bad faith exhibited by Omar Pasha, 
who was waging a war of extermination, when, according to the promises of 
the Porte, a defensive war was alone about to be undertaken. 

I endeavoured to show that the Montenegrins had been the notorious 
aggressors, and that however deplorable the fact, so it is, that with Turks as 
with Christians, violent attacks were apt to provoke violent retaliation, “‘Are 
you,” | inquired, “prepared to advance that this unfortunate feud was com- 
menced by the Turks?” 

Count Nesselrode replied, that certainly he made this assertion ; that the 
Sultan’s troops had endeavoured to possess themselves of a tract of country 
belonging to Montenegro, and that this attempt had brought down the Monte- 
negrins in defence of their countrymen; that subsequently operations had 
been carried on with great violence by Omar Pasha, and that, in proof of the 
fact, he would state that a convent which had been defended by the moun- 
taincers had, upon their expnision, been burned by the ‘Turkish troops. 

I remarked that such acts of violence were common to all wars; that it 
appeared to me that the great point to be sought by all parties was to put a 
stop to hostilities, but that 1 must be permitted to retain my opinion, and to 
suggest that when tranquillity shall be restored to Albania, an inquiry (enqueéte) 
should be instituted as to the causes and the authorsof the war. I would then 
only request that it should be observed whether my statements were or were 
not borne out by evidence. Some slight controversy upon the point continuing, 
I concluded the conversation by requesting permission to use a familiar ex- 
pression which, as I stated, 1 had just employed in speaking with M. de 
Soniavine, “The intercst,” I said, *M. le Comte, which you feel in the 
mountaineers is very intelligible; so is the affection often felt towards a dog ; 
remember, however, that the proprietor or the protector of a dog is bound to 
prevent his becoming a nuisance to the neighbours ; and permit me to observe 
that in the present case the dog passes as belonging to you.” 

The observation was taken, aa it was intended to be, in good part, and 
piers the slight merit, not always belonging to diplomatic conversations, of 
eaving no doubt as to the speaker's meaning. 

I have only to add, that as I left the room I said, “Tt will be satisfactory

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, February 6, 1865. 

THE Chancellor was good enough to place inm hands yesterday five 
despatches, dated the 25th ultimo, which he had receive from Baron Brunnow: 

They relate severally :—to the establishment of diplomatic relations 
between Russia and Belgium ; to the question of the communications of the 
8th May to the German Diet: to the marriage of the French Emperor; to 
a conversation held with the Karl of Aberdeen by Baron Brunnow, on the 
question of the Holy Places; and to the non-communication of the memorandum 
of the 8rd December to the French Cabinet. b 

Tn this last paper 1 found a confirmation of my notion of its being sul 
peeted by the Russians that some private understanding had been entered imto 
between Her Majesty’s Government and that of France with regard to the 
Secret Act. Taken as a whole, the correspondence offered a’ fresh indication 
of Baron Brunnow’s desire to promote the best intelligence between the Court 
at which he resides, and that which he representa with so much credit to him- 
self and advantage to his Imperial master.

Mr. Jerningham to Lord John Russell.—(Received February 18.) 


(No, 18. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Paris, February 17, 1853. 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS expressed himself to me to-day as he has 
more than once done to Lord Cowley regarding the Hast, namely, in the sense 
that Austria and Russia might be speculating on the fall of the Turkish 
Empire, and that such a possibility rendered of the utmost importance a good 
and intimate understanding between England and France, not only in fact but 
in appearance ; whilst he feared that foreign Governments might be shaken in 
their belief of such an understanding by circumstances like the recent speeches 
of Sir James Graham and Sir Charles Wood relative to. the Emperor, a& well 
as by the armaments of England, 

M. Dronyn de Lhuys expressed satisfaction with the late explanations of 
your Lordship and the Earl of Aberdeen, excepting your Lordship’s statement 
that the French Government were increasing their navy, which M. Ducos had 
since assured him was completely erroneous; adding, that M. Ducos had pro- 
mised to make him a written statement on the subject, which he would commu- 
nicate to me as soon.as it should reach him. 

I observed to M. Drouyn de Lhuys respeeting the English armaments, 
that our object appeared to mo to be simply to place England in the state of 
defence rendered advisable by the existence of steam navigation, and by the 
uncertainty of the future, while it must not be forgotten that this defensive 
armament began before the Revolution of 1848. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys expressed himself as being also much preoccupied 
with the question of Ciba: and he represented it as another reason why Eng- 
land and Hance ought to appear hong united,

No. 196, 
Lerd John Russell to Colonel Rose. 


(No. 27. Confidential.) 


Bir, Foreign Office, February 19, 1855. 

THE Russian Minister at this Court has read to me a despatch from 
Count Nesselrode to M. Kisseleff, giving an account of the result of General 
Castelbajac’s explanations of the views of the French Government in reference 
to the Holy Places. 

The open and conciliatory language of the French Government appears 
to have produced a favourable impression on the Emperor of Russia. Yet 
there is no disposition to recede ris the terms of the Firman of February, 
1852; and it appears that Prince Menchikoll is about to proceed to Constan- 
tinople, to express the firm resolution of the Russian Government not to rest 
satistied with the departures from the terms then proclaimed by the Sultan, 
and assented to both by France and Russia, 

The British Government has never concealed from, the Government of 
France its conviction that, apart from the merits of the case, the fresh demands 
made by the French Embassy at Constantinople, on this matter, were ill-tinmnedd 
and likely to prove a source of embarrassment, 

You are, therefore, instructed to hold to the Sultan’s Minister, to Prince 
Menchikoff, and to the French Minister, language calculated to bring back 
the state of this question to its position of February in the last year, ‘This 
should be effected in the manner most consistent with the dignity ot the French 
Government, which has been somewhat compromised by the language of 
M. Layalette. 

It is said that the Emperor of Russia will demand the dismissal of Fuad 
Effendi. On this question, you will take no part, one way or the other. 


If the Russian, troops should advance to the frontier, you must give 
immediate information to Her Majesty's Government. 

I trust I need not suppose the case of their advancing beyond the frontier 
to the attack of the capital. In such a case, Viscount Stratford de Redeliffe 
will be upon the spot, furnished with the requisite instructions. 


Tam, &c. 
(Signed) J. RUSSELL.

Colonel Rose to Lord John Russell.—(Received February 21.) 


(No. 30) 
My Lord, Constantinople, January 28, 1858. 

| HAVE very great satisfaction in informing your Lordship that I have 
every reason for believing that the dangerous and yery difficult question of the 
Holy Places of Jerusalem is terminated. ‘The French Ambassador declares to 
me that, as far as he is concerned, it is settled, and that France will not again 
revive it 

The Russian Chargé d’ Affaires, also, told me on the 26th instant, that the 
settlement of the question, as already announced by me to your Lordship, was 
a “chose faite?” only, he added, that he feared that further discussions must 
be opened respecting it, becanse there were one or two details as to the settle. 
ment, which were interpreted very disadvantageously to the Greeks; that the 
Latins claimed to have the ‘Tomb of the Vir in, one day, exclusively for them- 
selves: that such an arrangement would very disagreeable, and produce 
much discontent amongst the Greek pilgrims. Finding that M. d’Ozeroff's 
observations were well-founded, and that I should do a bad service to the 

caceful and disinterested policy of Her Majesty's Government, and to the 
interests of peace and good policy, were I to allow one little cause of difference 
to prevent the settlement of this most grave difference, | quite unostentationsly 
and unofficially told M. de Lavalette of the observations of my Russian 
colleague. His Excellency instantly, and in the most conciliatory manner, 
declared that with the view of preventing any collision between the sects, he 
merely wished that the Latins, and other sects, should have possession of the 
tomb for the time that was necessary for the performance of their devotions ; 
but that for the rest of the day, the Sanctuary should of course be open to the 
Greeks and other sects. M. de Lavalette assured me further that, a though if 
he had strained the meaning of the note of the 9th February, he might have 
demanded that the Latins should have lamps and images in the tomb, he, from 
a feeling of moderation, had forborne to do so, and had thus consented that the 
Lating should not have the privileges in the tomb which all the other Christian 
sects, even the Copts and Blacks, ad, 

| communicated to M, d’Ozevoff, who dined with me Since M. de La- 
valette’s explanations, and he seemed quite satisfied with them. I cordially 
concurred with my Russian colleague's wish that this ill-omened question 
should never again be mooted, and assured him that I had written strongly in 
that sense to my superiors, 

Roth the French and Russian Representatives exhibit now most laudable 
moderation in the matter of the Holy Places. And | cannot praise too highly 
the excellent feeling exhibited by the Greek Patriarchs of Constantinople and 
Jerusalem. They have borne the disappointment as to the key in a manner 
which docs the highest honour to them as Christian prelates, and to the feel- 
ing of duty which animates them towards their Sovereign, 1 bear willing 
record, that, by so acting, ches have gained more influence, and acquired more 
respect for the Christian creea, which has produced such Chiristain results, than 
if they had acquired, by discussion or by arms, all the Sanctuaries. 

Y wish that I could say as much for the Latin Patriarch Valerga, who, un- 


127 


mindful of the great moderation evinced by the Pope in this question, has 
entered at Jerusalem a violent protest against the settlement of the question of 
the Holy Places by Afif Bey. M. de Lavalette blames highly, and does not 
intend to pay the slightest attention to the objections of the Patriarch, who 
will therefore have gained by his ill-advised step nothing but the notoriety of 
having alone, of all the great and numerous interests concerned in this im-= 
potent discussion, in vain sought to continue a religious difference which might 
ve involved the world in war.
