Sir G. H. Seymour to Lord John Russell,—(Received February 21.) 
(No. 62, Confidential.) 


“My Lord, St. Petersburgh, February 10, 1853, 


THE Minister of Greece has spoken to me of the affairs of Turkey, and 
of his extreme apprehension that the effects of internal decay, hastened, 
possibly, by external pressure, may bring about the dissolution of the Ottoman 
Empire before Greece will be sufficiently consolidated to assert successfully 
her pretensions to a portion of the inheritance. 

I did not fail to point out to M. de Zographo, that no Power can be more 
interested than Greeee in the maintenance of the status quo in ‘Turkey; and 
that cone ne it should be the object of the Greeks to avoid in every way 
increasing the embarrassments with which their neighbours were contending, 

M. de Zographo concurred entirely in these views ; and informed me that 
a few days since he had sought a conversation of the Chancellor, for the purpose 
of expressing his pee | respecting the military demonstrations of the Russian 
Government, which he teared might lead to very serious consequences. 

M. de Zographo had, he said, felt at liberty to arestin ths Chancellor as 
to the probability of war taking the place of negotiation; and had done so 
upon the ground that if there were any question of military operations being 
resorted to, he thought it would be advisable that his Government should be 
placed upon their euard, and that precautions should be taken for preventing 
the inflammable spirits among the Greeks from being so acted upon as to be 
induced to take up arms. 

_ The answer returned to the Greek Minister by Count Nesselrode leads 
him to infer that he is sanguine as to existing difficulties being surmounted 
without an appeal to arms; and the more so, a5 his Excellency observed, that 
no one deprecated more sincerely than himself the disruption of the Turkish 
Empire,—a catastrophe, he observed, which might lead to an European war 
of fifty years’ duration. 

I have, &c.

Sir G. H. Seymour to Lord John Russell —( Received February 21.) 


(No. 70.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, February 10, 1853. 

IN speaking ta me yesterday of Prince Menchikoff’s instructions, which 
were again represented to be moderate in their character, the Chancellor 
observed that there was necessarily some vagueness in his orders, a8 on one 
aide it was hardly ascertained to what extent the rights, secured last year 
to the Greeks, had been infringed ; and, on the other, there could be no 

vestion of attempting to regain from the Latins any of the privileges which 
they might subsequently have acquired at Jerusalem. The object to be sought 
for was therefore an equivalent for any privilege lost by the Greeks. “Thus,” 
Count Nesselrode observed, “ we have no wish to demand the restoration of the 
koy of the Bethlehem Church.” 

‘As it is always desirable to guard against misapprehensions, I ventured 
to inquire whether, in this case, a key meant an instrument for opening a door, 
only not to be employed in closing that door against Christians or other sects ; 
or whether it was simply a key—an emblem. 

Count Nesselrode replied, unhesitatingly, that his meaning was that the 
key was to be used in giving the Latins acecss to the church, but not to be 
used for securing the door against Grecks and other Christians, 

I then took the liberty of inquiring how the Austrian Cabinet regarded 
the views of the Russian Government upon these, 80 termed, religious questions. 
Count Nesselrode’s answer was, that no difference with regard to them existed 
between the two Governments; that Austria had been jas to by France, 
gome months ago, to join her upon the question of the Holy Places, but that 
the overture had been rejected; the Emperor of Austria, although an ardent 
Catholic, not considering the pretensions of Russia exorbitant, and being 
withal opposed to that supremac in religious questions in the East, which the 
French were inclined to claim for themselves. 

With regard (to the affairs of Montenegro, the Chancellor seemed to fcel 
considerable anxiety, and but i ae snelination to speak of them, He observed 
only, that it was an unfortunate usiness, ( méchante question”); that it might 

very well be settled forcibly befere the two Imperial Missions reached Con- 
stantinople ; but that ft must not be forgotten that history shows that the 
Turks have been able to overrun Montenegro, without being strong enough to 
retain possession of the territory.

No. 146, 

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 
(No, 1.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, February 26, 1863, 


THE Qucen has been pleased to direct that at this critical period of the 
fate of the Ottoman Empire your Excellency should return to your Embassy 
for a special pups: and charged with special instructions. 

Your Excellency is aware that the preservation of the independence and 
integrity of Turkey enters into the general and established system of European 
policy; that the principle is solemnly declared and sanctioned by the Con- 
vention of 1840, and is a civerdeaged’ by all the great Powers of europe. 

But while the general principle is acknowledged, the inclination of different 
Powers is very different, and must be carefully borne in mind, 

Great Britain adopts it in all sincerity, without mental reservation: is 
antialed by sincere friendship for Turkey ; and has no after-thought on the 
subject. 

France is likewise desirous to maintain it, partly from the traditions of 
her policy, partly from jealousy of the Powers which, being the nearest neigh- 
bours to Turkey, would claim to possess (he fairest portion of the inheritance 
in case of her dissolution. 

Austria is likewise disposed, from policy and interest, to maintain the 
independence of the Porte; but several causes of dissension have arisen of 
late years, and her passions may lead her to depart widely from the road of 
her true interest and her conservative policy. 

The case of Russia is altogether different. ‘The possession of Constanti- 
nople was a favourite dream of the Empress Catherine. The wars which 
Russia has waged with Turkey, both during her reign and down to the period 
of the peace of Adrianople, have all ended in the aggrandizement of Russia, 


132 


and the depression of the Mahometan Power. The conquest of Constantinople 
‘s a favourite object of national ambition. Millions of Christian subjects of 
the Porte long to reverse the triumphs of the lifteenth century, and to make 
the Crescent inferior to the Cross. 

But the possession of Constantinople by Russia, giving her a commanding 
position al once on the Baltic and the Mediterranean, would not be seen with 
complacency by other Powers. The difficulty of arranging this point prevented 
; cordial alliance between Napoleon the First and the Emperor Alexander, An 
attempt to cut the knot by Ruasia would, at this moment, unite against her all 
the Powers of Europe. The Emperor Nicholas ts conscious of this difficulty, 
and, with a moderation at once magnanimous and wise, iscontent to forego the 
prospect of this brilliant prize. 

But the weakness of the Turkish Empire, and the presumption of its 
rulers, may bring on a danger which no one seems willing to invite, and hasten 
a crisis which no one is anxious to precipitate. 

The object, therefore, of your Excellency’s mission at this time is to 
counsel prudence to the Porte, and forbearance to those Powers who are urging 
her compliance with their demands. You are instructed to use every effort to 
wardolfa ‘Turkish war, and to versuade the Powers interested to look to an amii- 
cable termination of existing disputes, 

The disputes which more immediately demand attention, are those which 
relate to Montenegro and the Holy Places. 

The defence of Montenegro may be prolonged, or the Mountaineers may 
submit to the Turkish force ; and, in either case, the Sultan may be nnwilling 
fo return to the status quo that has been peremptorily insisted upon by 
Austria. 

But the question of the Holy Places in Syria offers more danger to the 
peace of ‘Turkey. However indifferent to their respective merits, the Porte is 
now nnavoidably exposed to the rival pretensions of Russia and France, each 
animated by a political interest as well as by religious zeal, and both appealing 
to engagements alleged to have been contracted towards each of them by the 
Porte. ‘Threatened from both sides, and unable to satisfy one party without 
displeasing the other, the Sultan is placed in a position of embarrassment and 
danger, rendered more eritical by the internal weakness of the Empire, and the 
special character of the points at issue. 

It is, therefore, to be feared that if the three Governments do not noni 
their demands, and should continue to maintain towards the Porte the dictatorial, 
if not menacing, attitude they have lately assumed, they may, without any de- 
liberate intention of departing from those principles of Huropean policy to 
which I have above alluded, accelerate the dissolution of the Turkish Empire, 
and produce the catastrophe that all are concerned in averting. 

England, however, is ina position to neutralize, by her moral influence, 
these alarming contingencies ; for England has the important advantage 
having no special interest in the pending questions, and of being viewed by the 
Porte with less mistrast, and stronger hopes of eventual assistance, than any 
other Power in Christendom ; and the Porte will learn with satisfaction that, 
even before your arrival at Constantinople, the best efforts of Her Majesty's 
Government have been directed to restrain encroachment, and to obtain every 

fair concession calculated to settle the existing dilferences. | 

With this object your Excellency ig instructed to proceed to Constanti- 
nople, by way of Paris and Vienna. . 

You will inform the French Minister for Foreign Affairs that Her 
Majesty’s Government have great satisfaction in believing that the interests of 
France and England in the East are identical, and that nothing, therefore, need

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, February 17, 1855. 

AS 1 am particularly anxious at this moment not only to be upon intimate 
terms with the rench Minister but to jet it be known that Lam so, | called upon 
him this day, as 1 do now about twice a week, for the purpose of bearite what 
he might have to communicate, and of imparting any information which | 
might have to offer him. 

1 found M. de Castelbajac more reassured than I had lately seen him as to 
coming events, and possessed with the idea that present difficulties would be 
surmounted. : 

He did not conceal from me his objections to the wathering of Russian and 
Austrian troops in the vicinity of ‘Turkey, but professed his belief in the fair 
intentions of the Emperors of both countries. 

With regard to the bith Corps d'Armée no doubt could, M. de Castelbajac 
said, exist as to its having received orders to complete its ranks, but no orders 
had been sent, he was confident, for their advance, neither did he think that any 
would be issued, 

As regards the proposition made by the French Cabinet, General Castel- 
bajac was, he said, ready to admit that he had not been empowered to enter into 
detailg—he had not been even enabled to do so by the information afforded him ; 
he could, therefore, understand the expediency of the affair being discussed 
rather at Constantinople than here, and had written to Paris to say thab the 
auestion to be decided was suply whether the Firman of last February, con- 
firmed by the Sultan’s letter, cot d be admitted by his Government as the basis 
of negotration. 

General Castelbajac then desired to read moa long despatch which he had 
addressed on the 14t and J5th instant to M, Dronyn de Lhuys, in which he 
had endeavoured to lay before his Government his opinions as to the questions 
pending with Russia.

Sir G. H. Seymour to Lord John Russell.—(Received March 6.) 


(No. 83.) 
My Lord, St, Petersburgh, February 18, 1853. 

THE impression may be erroneous, but 1 cannot divest myself of the 
idea of ‘Turkish affairs never having been in so critical a state as at present, 

I am willing to believe that Htussia may be indueed to abstain both from 
open interference with the Sultan’s authority, and from those alarming de- 
monstrations which are ealenlated to produce the same results; but I should be 
sorry to conceal from your Lordship my persuasion that if a Russian force 
were to enter Turkey, the war which would ensue would in all probability 
he the last which would ever take place upon European soil in the defence of 


no attempt at arresting 4 trial the result of which is go plainly before me. 

With these ideas I held some conversation with Count f esselrode yester- 
day, and omitted no consideration which [ could call to mind to impress upon 
him the immense danger which would be ‘neurred at the present moment by 
any rash step taken in the affairs of Turkey. 

In addition to other considerations, the volcanic state of Italy, as proved 
by the late insane attempt at Milan, offered me a fresh argument in favour of 

rudence and caution ott the part of those Governments who were more 
particularly interested in guarding against & renewal of the scenes of 1848. 

I found Count Nesselrode less anxious about Eastern affairs than he and 
others had been three or four days ago; he even expressed his belief that all 
would yet be settled amicably, now that the Turkish armies were not seen to 
he advancing to the heart of Montenegro. ‘This pause, he said, looked as 
if the mission confided to the Count de Leiningen were taking a favour- 
able turn. 

What particularly struck me was that upon this occasion Count Nessel- 
rode never advocated fontenegrin independence ; he spoke only of a return to 
the status que hitherto existing in Montenegro. “ ‘And now,” Count Nesselrade 
gaid, “* put yourself into our position, and judge what you would have felt if a 

ulation looking to you during « century for assistance, your brothers iti 
religious belief, a community whom you had fed when they liad not bread to 
eat, had suddenly been threatened with extermination!” 1 begged Count 
Nesselrode to remember that the advice given to the Porte upon this matter 
by Her Majesty's Government had been of quite as merciful a character as 
any which he could have tendered ; but observed that, although J deprecated 
contests of words, I should be always ready to prove by evidence that the 


138 


struggle which gave us all so such mneasiness had been provoked by the law- 
less and cruel behaviour of the Montenegrins. — 

After adyerting to the attempts made by a Russian, Budberg by name, to 
stir up revolt in Bulgaria, I turned to the accounts which had reached me of 
the naval preparations at Sevastopol, observing that they were of a nature to 
increase materially the anxiety already felt by Her Majeaty’s Government. 

Count Nesselrode surmised that I had been misinformed, and believed that 
the only preparation then making was that of a steamer fitting out for the 
conveyance of Prince Menchikoff. | 

Upon my assuring the Chancellor that it was hardly possible that any 
mistake should exist with regard to a point upon which I ad received direct 
intelligence, he replied that he hadno knowledge of any such preparations as 
1 had alluded to, but that he should lose no time in speaking upon the subject 
to the Emperor. 

1 will not conclude my despatch withont repeating that Count Nesselrode 
inveighed bitterly against the encroachments still carried on, as he asserts, by 
M. de Lavalette upon the rights of the Greek Church. They, he said, must 
be puta stop to, and the firm representations, in this sense, of Her Majesty's 
Government both at Paris and at Constantinople would conduce powerfully 
towards averting those serione consequences which England and Russia were 
so desirous of guarding against. 

T have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H, SEYMOUR,

My Lord, St, Petersburgh, February 21, 1868. 

‘THE Emperor came up ‘tome last night, ata party at the Grand Duchess 
Hereditary’s, and in the most gracious manner took me apart, saying that he 
desired'to speak tome. After expressing, in flattering terms, the confidence 
which he has in me, and his readiness to speak to me without reserve upon 
matters of the greatest moment, as, His Majesty observed, he had proved ina 
late conversation, he said: “And it is well it ig 40; for what 1 most desire 18, 
that there should ‘be the greatest ‘intimacy between the two Governments: it 
never was so Necessary as at present. Well,” the Emperor continued, “ so 
you have got your answer, and you are to bring it to me to-morrow ?” 

“Tam to have that honour, sir’ I answered; “but your Majesty is 

aware that the nature of the reply is very exactly what ‘I ‘had led you to 
expect,” 
sat So ‘I was sorry to hear; but I think your Government does not well 
understand my object. [ amnot so eager about what shall be done when the 
Bear dica, al am to determine with England what shall not be done upon 
that event'taking place,” 

* But, sir,’ LT replied, “ allow me to observe, that we have no reason (to 
think that the Bear (to use your Majesty’s expression) ts dying. ‘We are as 
much interested as we ‘believe your Majesty'to be in his continuing to live ; 
while ‘for myself, | will venture to remark that experience shows me that 
countries do not die in such a hurry. I have seen by our archives, ‘both in 
'Purkey and Portugal, that these two countries have for years past! been con- 
sidered in a perishing state, and yet there they remain; and there Turkey will 
remain for many a year, unless some unforeseen erisis should oceur. It is 
precisely, sir, for the avoidance of all circumstances likely to produce such a 
crisis, that Her Majesty’s Government reckons upon your generous assistance.” 


“Then,” rejoined the Emperor, ‘| will tell you, that if your Govern- 
ment has been ‘led to believe that Turkey retains any elements of existence, 
your Government must have received incorrect information. | repeat'toyou, 
that'the: Bear is dying: you may give him musk, but even musk will not long 
keep him alive; and we can never allow such an event to take us by surprise. 


We must come to some understanding ; and this we should do, lam convinced 


139 


if I could hold but ten minutes’ conversation with your Ministers—with Lord 
Aberdeen, for instance, who knows me so well, who has full confidence in me, 
as Lhave in him, And remember, I do not ask for a treaty ora protocol; a 
general understanding is all I require—that between gentlemen is sufficient ; 
and in this case I am certain that the confidence would be as great on the side 
of the Queen's Ministers as on mine. So no more for the present; you will 
come to me to-morrow, and you will remember that as often as you think your 
conversing with me will promote a good understanding upon any point, you 
will send word that yon wish to see me.” 

I thanked His Majesty very cordially, adding that I conld assure him that 
Her Majesty’s Government, I was convinced, considered his word, once given, 
as good as a bond, 

It is hardly necessary that I should observe to your Lordship, that this 
short conversation, briefly but correctly reported, offers matter for most anxious 
reflection, 

It can hardly be otherwise but that the Sovereign who insists with euch 

rtinacity upon the impending fall of a neighbouring State, must have settled 
‘1 his own mind that the hour, if not of its dissolution, at all events for its 
dissolution, must be at hand. 

I will only remark to your Lordship, as a point of evidence which goes 
far towards establishing a settled purpose, that the expression of “musk being 
insufficient to keep alive the sinking Turk,” was used tome ten days ago by one 
of the Emperor’s most confidential servants. 

Then, as now, I reflected that this assumption would hardly be ventured 
upon unless some, perhaps reneral, but at all events intimate understanding, 
existed between Russia and Austria. 

Supposing my suspicion to be well-founded, the Emperor's object is to 
engage Her Majesty’s Government, in conjunction with his own Cabinet and 
that of Vienna, in some scheme for the ultimate partition of Turkey, and for 
the exclusion of France from the arrangement. 

T have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H, SEYMOUR.

Sir G. H. Seymour to Lord John Russell —(Received March 6.) 


(No. 88. Secret and Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, February 22, 1855, 

1 HAD the honour of waiting yesterday upon the Emperor, and of’ hold- 
ing with His Majesty one of the most interesting conversations in which 1 ever 
found myself engaged. My only regret is my inability to report in full detail 
a dialogue which lasted'an hour and twelve minutes, 

The Emperor began by desiring me to read to him aloud your Lordship’s 
“Secret and Confidential” despatch, marked No. 38, saying that he should 
stop me occasionally, either to make an observation, or to call upon me for the 
translation of a passage. 

‘Upon arriving at the fourth paragraph, the Emperor desired me to pause, 
and observed, that ‘he was certainly most desirous that gome understanding 
should be entered into with her Majesty's Government, for providing against a 
contingency so probable as that of the downfall of ‘Turkey; that he was, 
perhaps, even more interested than England could ‘be in preventing a Turkish 
catastrophe, but that it was constantly impending ; that it might be brought 
about at any moment, either by an external war, or by a feud between the 
old Turkish’ party and that of the “new superficial French reforms,” or 


again, by a rising of the Christians, already known to be very impatient of 


shaking ‘off the Mussulman yoke | “)ong As regards the first cause, the 
Emperor said that he had a good right to advert to it, inasmuch as, if he had 
not stopped the-victorious progress of General Diebitch in 1829, the Sultan’s 
authority would have been at an end. 

The Emperor likewise desired me to remember that he, anil he only, had 


140 


hastened to the assistance of the Sultan, when his dominions were threatened 
by the Pasha of Egypt. 

| proceeded to read, and was again stopped at the sentence beginning, 
‘In these cireumstances it would hardly be consistent with the friendly 
feclings,” when the Emperor abserved, “that Her Majesty's Government did 
not appear to be aware that his chief object was to obtain from Her Majesty’s 
Government some declaration, or even opinion, of what ought not to be 
permitted in the event of the sudden downfall of Turkey.” I said, * Perhaps 
your Majesty would be good enough to explain your own: ideas upon this 
negative policy” ‘This His Majesty for some time declined doing; he ended, 
however, by saying: “ Well, there are several things which I never will 
tolerate: 1 will begin by ourselves, I will not tolerate the permanent occupa- 
tion of Constantinople by the Russians; having said this, I will say that it 
never shall be held by the English, or French, or any other great nation. 
Again, I never will permit an attempt at the reconstruction of a Byzantine 
Empire, or such an extension of Greece as would render her a powerful State ; 
still less will 1 permit the breaking up of Turkey into little republics, asylums 
for the Kossuths and Mazzinis, and other revolutionists of Europe; rather than 
submit to any of these arrangements 1 would go to war, and as long as I have 
a man and a musket left would carry it on. 

These,” the Emperor said, “are at once some ideas, now give me some inl 
return.’ 1 remarked upon the assurance which would be found respecting the 
English resolution of never attempting to possess Constantinople, and upon the 
disinclination of Her Majesty’s Government to enter into eventual arrange- 


ments; but upon being still pressed by His Imperial Majesty, 1 said: “ Well,. 


sir, the idea may not suit your Majesty, may not suit Her Majesty’s Govern- 
ment: but what is good between man and man is often a good system between 
one State and another ;—how would it be if in the event of any catastrophe 
occurring in Turkey, Russia and England were todeclare that uo Power should 
be allowed to take possession of its provinees,—that the property should remain, 
as it were, under seals until amicable arrangements could be made as to ita 
adjudication ?” 

«| will not say,” the Emperor observed, “that such a course would be 
impossible, but, at least, it would be very difficult; there are no elements of 

ravineial or communal government in Nirkey : you would have Turks attack- 
ing Christians, Christians falling upon Turks, Christians of different sects quar- 
rolling with each other, ; in short, chaos and anarchy.” 

Sir,” [then observed, “if your Majesty will allow me to speak plainly, 
I would say that the great Jifference between us is this, that you continue to 
dwell upon the fall of Turkey, and the arrangements requisite before and after 
the fall; and that we, on the contrary, look to ‘Turkey remaining where she is, 
and to the precautions which are necessary for preventing her condition from 
becoming worse.” “ Ant” replied the Emperor, ‘that is what the Chancellor 
is perpetually telling me, but the catastrophe will oceur some day and will take 
us all unawares.” 

1 request your Lordship’s attention to the accidental evidence thus 
obtained, of the wisdom and prudence of Count Neaselrode’s views. 

His Imperial Majesty spoke of France; God forbid,” he said, “that I 
should accuse any one wrongfully, but there are circumstances both at Con- 
stantinople and Montenegro which are extremely suspicious ; it looks very much 
as if the French Government were endeavouring to embroil us all in the Hast, 
hoping in this way the better to arrive at their own objects, one of which, no 
doubt, is the possession of Tunis.” 

The Emperor proceeded to say, that for his own part he cared very little 
what line the French might think proper to take in tern affairs, and that 
little more than a month ago he had apprised the Sultan that if his assistance 
were required for resisting the menaces. of the French, it was entirely at the 
service of the Sultan !

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received March 11.) 


(No, 131. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, March 10, 1853. 

M. DROUYN DE LITUYS having sent this morning’ to express a desire 
to see me, | waited upon him this afternoon. He read to me extracts of @ 
despatch and private letter, dated the lst instant, which he had received this 
morning from St. Petersburgh. 

The contents of them are very satisfactory. It appears that M. Dronyn de 
Lhuys had not been pleased with the answer of the Russian Cabinet to the 
conciliatory overtures which he had made some time back for the settlement 
of the question of the Holy Places: and that he had, on the Lith of last 
month (while I was in England), addressed a despatch to M. Castelbajac, in 
which he had stated, that if the Russian Government replied to the conciliatory 
overtures of France by reeriminations, there would be no hope of establishing 
an understanding between the two Governments. M. Castelbajac reports, 
that Count Nesselrode had been much distressed at finding that which he had 
intended to be a simple statement of facts, looked upon by the French 
Government in the light of a recrimination. The Count had assured him that 
the Emperor had received with s lively satisfaction the conciliatory declara- 
tions of France, and desired to respond to them in the same terms, and that he 
had every hope that the question of the Sacred Places would now be settled 
without any disturbance of the peace of the East. The recall of M. de Lavalette 
and the appointments of M.M. de la Cour and Bourqueney were looked upon 
as an earnest of the good intentions of the Emperor of the French. 

Count Nesselrode had further expressed to M, de Castelbajac the opinion, 
that the danger which menaced the East was greatly reduced by the success 
of Count Leiningen’s mission. ‘The intelligence of it had given the Emperor 
go much pleasure, that he had rushed out of breath to communicate it to the 
Empress, The Emperor, Count Nesselrode assured M. Castelbajac, would be 
too happy to act with France to prevent a dissolution of the Turkish Empire. 
It was the last thing which His Imperial Majesty desired, ‘The movements 
of troops towards the Turkish frontier were not made with any intention of 
attacking the Turkish Empire, but were, on the contrary, intended to prevent 
its dissolution, by acting on the fears of the Turkish Ministers, to force them 0 
give way on points, a persistance in which would bring about the catastrophe 
all wanted to avoid. 

M. Dronyn de Lhuys stated further, that his reports from Vienna, in regard 
to Turkey, gave him equal satisfaction.

Colonel Rose to Lord John Russell, (Received March 14.) 
(No. 59.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, February 22, 1855. 

IN compliance with the ‘nstructions in your Lordship’s despatch No. 16, 
I brought, at the earliest moment, the important considerations which it con- 
tains before Fuad Effendi, taking care not to furnish his Exeelleney with a 
copy of the despatch, or of an of its inclosures. 

Fuad Effendi listened with marked attention to the powerful reasoning in 
your Lordship’s despatch, which I translated to him into French, dwelling 
on, and drawing his Excelleney’s particular attention to, all those passages 
which bore on the policy which the Porte ought to follow under existing 
circumstances. . 

I endeavoured to induce his Iixcellency to come into the views of Her 
Majesty's Government re eeting the advantage of the Porte’s sanctioning aly 
arrangement about the oly Places, which might be recommended for its 
adoption conjointly by the French and Russian Governments. 

Fuad Effendi did not seem to approve the plan, alleging that it would be 
an acknowledgment of the right of Russia to interfere in and protect the Greek 
interest in ‘Turkey ; and he put off further conversation on the subject by say- 
ing, that it would be better to await the arrival of M. Brennier. 

L have reason to believe that M. de Kleal failed also in inducing the Porte 
to act in the sense recommended by Her Majesty's, and, as it would appear, by 
the Emperor of Austria’s Government also. 

However, on receiving your Lordship's despatch® No, 19, with its im- 
portant inclosures, I was enabled to renew, with more efficacy, my arguments 
in favour of the adoption of your Lordship's suggestions. 

Your Lordship will be glad to hear that Fuad Efendi yielded; he said 
that he now viewed the matter much as I did, and that he would recommend 
the Council to adopt the suggestions of Her Majesty’s Government, 

1 venture to congratulate your Lordship on the favourable manner in 
which the Governments of France and Russia have received the well-timed 
advice of Her Majesty's Government, conveyed to them by your Lordship in 
language as persuasive as ‘¢ was unanswerable, respecting the settlement of 
the question of the Hol Places, I anticipate the best result from this mode 
of proceeding, which I had the honour to recommend in my des vatches of last 
year to the Earl of Malmesbury, The wisdom and influence of Great Britain 
must ultimately prevail, when she appeals in the name of Christianity, policy 
and humanity, to France and Russia not to plunge Europe in perhaps inter- 
minable war on account of a dispute as to the scenes of the sufferings of Him 
who died telling mankind to pay evil with good. Such a war would be a 
great hypocrisy, and an irreparable injury to Christianity. It would be a 

roclamation to the infidel world that great Christian and civilized Powers 
sacrificed the heavenly to the worldly part of their religion, its perfect 
essentials to the puerililies and passions ‘vith whieh man has disfigured it; that 
Christians, for the sake of an inanimate symbol, or a sectarian triumph of their 
religion, violate its most important recat 

But having watehed this dep arable contention, and the actors in it, 80 
vigilantly and so long, it is my duty to tell your Lordship that I anticipate 
far more good from the counsels of Her Majesty's Government to France 
and Russia than from the direet negotiations between those Powers themselves. 

If they give due weight to the rights of public opinion, peace, and Ohris- 
tian obligations, the difference will be speedily settled. But if they both strive 
for political influence in the East, France bringing forward her ill-omened 
Treaty, and Russia her right to protect Greek ay Rey never agree. 

ve, &e. 


(Signed) HUGH ROSE.

Inclosure in No. 162. 
Memorandum by M. E, Pisani. 


Constantinople, February 26, 1859. 

IT is essential to be remembered that the Russian Envoy, M. de Titoff, 
was duly informed, through his first interpreter, of the intention, and subse- 
quently of the decision, of the Porte to yield and accede to the arrangement 
contained in the note which was sent in fo the French Embassy on the 9th of 
February, 1852, touching the Sanctuaries of Jerusalem. hen the Porte 
communicated the contents of the said note to M. de Titoff, and also offered to 
give him some explanation on the subject, he refused to receive any oral or 
written declaration, explaining the motives and grounds upon which the Porte 
was compelled to concede to the Latins the right of officiating at the Holy 
Virgin’s Shrine, and to grant them the key of the principal coor of the Church 
of Bethlehem, and also one of the keys of each of the two doors of the Crib, 
M. de Titoif fears that the concessions made to the Latins would increase 
the pretensions of the French, and embolden them to seck for more advantages, 
induced him to protest against any arrangement which would have for ellect to 
change the status quo of actual possession. 

in order to dissipate the apprehensions entertained by the Russian Envoy, 
the Porte proposed to grant a Firman to the Greek community, explaining 
the arrangement entered into, and giving guarantees for the future. In that , 
Firman it is clearly stated, that the three keys (the grant of which was so long 
resisted by the Russians) were to be given to the Latins. 

Before concluding, | think myself called upon to observe that M. de Titoff 
was duly apprised of the Porte’s intention to give the note, which was pre- 
sented to M. de Lavalette on the 9th of February last; and that the Firman, 
which was subsequently given to the Greek Patriarchs of Jerusalem and Con- 
wrap and in which the three keys are distinctly mentioned, was for 
several days under the consideration of the Russian Envoy, who amended it 


according to his wish, 
When Afif Bey was sent to Jerusalem to carry into execution the arrange- 


148 


contained in the note given to M. de Lavalette, M. d'Ozeroll, who suc- 
moved M. de Titofl applied Ms and obtained from, the Porte a vizirial ree 
instructing Afif Bey to endeavour to avoid giving the keys in se ee 
Latins. But this could not in fairness be executed, and Alif Bey thought it mM 
duty to carry into effect his former instructions.

Sir G. .H. Seymour to Lord John Russell.—(Received March 14.) 


(No. 101. Secret and Confidential.) 


My Lord, St, Petersburgh, March 1, 1869. 

I LEARN from one of me diplomatic acquaintances that he overheard 
by accident a conversation which passed last week at the palace fete between 
the Emperor and Count Zichy, a visitor, and | believe a casual one, at St. 
Petersburgh. 

His Imperial Majesty, as T had an opportunity of observing, went up to 
Count Zichy as he sat at supper and spoke with him during some minutes, 

It now appears that his Majesty stated “that he had just been writing to 
the Emperor of Austria,” anil that he added, “in this letter, which will be 
conveyed by Baron de Lieven, I have told his Majesty that I approve highly of 
the threatening attitude which he has taken avainst the ‘Turks, and that I hope 
he will not recede from it, as 1 know well that nothing is to be obtained from 
that people but under menace. | feel the more strongly upon the subject, as 
Lam convinced that the refugees and renegades in the ‘Turkish service are in 
communication with the revolutionary committees, und are endeavouring to 
carry out their objects.” 

I took the liberty to remark to my informant that what he had heard 
stated as a fact was, I was disposed to beheve, a mere conjecture or 
assumption, and that I must be allowed to say that it appeared to me extra- 
ordinary that advice so well calculated to Eee the Sultan's authority and 
to light up a war in Europe should proceed from a monarch who professed his 
undeviating attachment to Conservative principles. 

| will only add that the impression loft upon the mind of my acquaintance 
(who has followed the late transactions in Turkey attentively) is that the hostile 
disposition manifested by the Emperor of Austria towards the Sultan is the 
result of the feelings of resentment occasioned by the hospitable reception given 
by his Highness to the Hungarian exiles. 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR,

received the despatches which have been so long expected from Constantinople.

weather. M, de Lavalette has also reached Paris, and has completed by word

Colonel Rose, it is not necessary that 1 should say more than that the French 
Government, although rejoicing that the matter is terminated, are not the less 
sensible of the humiliation to which the Porte has-been subjected by the haughty 
conduct of Austria, : 

I understand that M. de Lavalette’s language respecting the internal state 
of Turkey is so far satistactory, that he does not see any extraordinary signs of

The Russian Representative so far forgot himself as to try and give a

he induces that same Sovercign’s alter eqo, the Grand Vizier, to write seeretly a

out that the secret letter, which enjoined the breaking of the Sultan's faith,

Envoy and the Greek nation in a Firman, gave the Russian Government a 
right to complain, because the provisions of that dishonourable letter had not

From the ill-fated time that France revived her Treaty of 1740, and 
demanded dormant or neglected rights as to the Holy Places, the Porte, in 
her weakness, has been coerced by France and Russia to give contradictory 
decisions. 

Nor can I give your Lordship a better idea of the humiliating position in

cive manners of these powerful suitors, than by quoting a recent speech of

' Some recent confidential conversations with M, d’Ozeroff and M. de Bala- 
bine, convinee me that it is the object of Russian policy to engage Her 
Majesty’s Government and their representative here to ignore the validity of 
the French Treaty of 1740. I told these gentlemen that I thought that it 
would be wise and politic for Her Majesty's Government, appealing to the 
civilization, the religion, humanity, and good sense of France, to use all her 
influence to induce her to be satished with what she had already gained by her 
Treaty, and not to appeal to it again. But that, should all these Spats of 
ersuasion prove fruitless, I would never advise that the sacred rights of 

aty, the safeguard of justice and peace throughout the world, should be 
sacrificed or set aside; and that, as regards policy, we should never forget 
that if we became parties to a breach of French treaty in Palestine, we eould 
no longer protest against a breach of the treaties which now confine warlike 
and ambitious France within limits which she once overstepped to make 
Europe one vast battle-lield. And it is here apposite that 1 should express my 
regret that Count Nesselrode, as appears by Sir Hamilton Seymour's Aaeiieh 
No. 7 to your Lordship, should have endeavoured to make him believe that 
the Wench Convention (should be Capitulations) of 1740 has not all the value 
of a treaty, By the inclosed report trom MM. Frederick and Etienne Pisani, 
the former and present first interpreters to Her Majesty’s Embassy, your Lord: 
ship will see that the French Capitulations of 1740, on which France grounds 
her claims as to the Jerusalem Sanetuaries, and the validity of which the Rus- 
sian Government attack, are exactly the same as. our Capitulations with the 
Porte, by virtue of which, and by which alone, Great Britain possesses her 
rights in Turkey. 

The attempt of Russia to deprive France’s Treaty, or Capitulations of 
1740 with the Porte, of its just value, shows that she, knowing that those 
Capitulations give France felts as to the Holy Places, has nothing left for it 
but to discredit that Treaty, But this is not just or politie. It is unwise to 
irritate France by ignoring her Treaty; but appeal should be made to her best 


= 


153 


and wisest feelings; she should be asked, for the sake of the world’s happiness, 
to allow that Treaty to moulder, as it has done for so long, in its archives. 

Count Nesselrode speaks much of injustice and wrongs done to the Greek 
Church by the Porte’s late decision as to the Sanctuaries. 

I admit most fully the deplorable impolicy of reviving the Treaty of 
1740; and nobody feels more than I do the necessity of the Porte’s conciliating 
her numerous Greek Rayas, who feel as much hurt in a religious point of view 
as Russia can do, at any concessions as to the Holy Places made to the Latins. 
But these very Greek Rayas, and the most powerful and influential of them, 
have assured me again and again, that they would infinitely prefer that Latin 
monks should have the key of the Church of Bethlehem, and walk through 
that church to pray in the Grotto of the Nativity, than that French cruisers 
should destroy their commerce, and French serew line-of-battle ships bombard 
their villazes and homes on the Bosphorus, &c. 

The Russian Government would be astonished if they heard the names of 
the Greek Rayas who have held this and similar language to me,—who have 
declared that they abhor the idea of a war, destructive to all their interests, on 
account of the Holy Places; that even in the important matter of the Cupola, 
which they acknowledge France has the right by treaty to repair “oxclu- 
givement,” they, the Greek Rayas would, if left to themselves, come to an 
equitable arrangement with Franee and the Porte; that they deplore that 
Greek Rayas and a religious question are used by Russia as instruments for 
the sake of upholding her political influence. 

As regards the mere matter of abstract right, if French and Russian 
claims as to the Holy Places were referred to any eminent barrister, he would 
certainly award eight, and probably many more, sanctuaries to France, instead 
of the key, and the very limited right to pray iu the Tomb of the Virgin, 
ceded to her by the late arrangement.

rotest against that arrangement, which certainly looks as if the Latins viewed 
it rather as a defeat than us a victory. 

Lalso have the honour to iheloe copies of the several Articles of the 
Capitulations of 1740, or as the French official list terms it, “* Traité entre la 
France et la Porte Ottomane,” relating to the Holy Places at Jerusalem.

Inclosure 2 in No, 170. 
Protest of the Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem and Guardian of Shrines. 


(Translation.) Jerusalem, December 23, 1852. 


WE, the undersigned, have become acquainted with the resolutions which 
the Porte has thou At fit to adopt in the quetigy of the Holy Places at 
Jerusalem, and for the execution of which she has sent thither as her Commis- 
sioner Afif Bey, 

From the vast interest and sanctity which the cause of these august 
memorials of the Redemption bear in our eyes, and in those of all Catholics, 


154 


we are under the painful necessity of declaring, that the said resolutions are 
far from meeting our just wishes, or according in the least with the solemnly 
recognized rights proved by the evidence of the Porte’s own declaration ; slie 
having at all times proclaimed, and more especially last March, in an official 
note to the Ambassador of France at Constantinople, that they were to be 
respected, All things considered, and for the moment resigning oursclyes, 
under the eyes of the protecting Consul, to the painful position in which we 
are placed by the execution, imperfect and strewed with obstacles, of wealk 
and insufficient arrangements settled at Constantinople, which we would fain 
view as the beginning of redress, we deem it our duty to adopt all necessary 

recautions, as a safeguard to the incontestable and authenticatedly established 
rights of Catholicism in the Holy Land. We therefore protest, by this present 
document, as in effect we have protested through the medium of Afif Bey 
to the Porte, and to the Ambassador of France through his Consul at 
Jerusalem :— 

Firstly Against any attempt whatever made by the last resolutions of 
the Porte upon the rights euarantecd solemnly by treaty stipulations between 
France and Turkey, as also against the usurpations to which the Frank clergy 
have been subjected from 1740. till the present day, in defiance of pledge 
faith: and we protest in the same terms and form that the Ambassador of 
France protested last March at Constantinuple. 

Secondly,—Against, the Porte’s pretension to rebuild herself, and at her 
own expense, the larger dome of our Lord's Sepulchre, 

'Thirdly,—Against the atone as took place the 28th November last, 
at Jerusalem, of the Hatti'S eri! granted to the Greeks in the spring of that 
year; protesting, firstly, beeause such a public and official document ts 
derogatory to, and infringes on, the rights as guaranteed to the Frank clerg 
by the Treaty of 1710; and secondly, because in this note the Porte, which 
neither is nor ean be other than one of the interested parties in this question of 
the Holy Places, constitutes herself as sole and exclusive judge, without the 
intervention of the other contracting party ; finally, as no one is unaware of 
the promise made by the Ottoman Cabinet to the French Embassy, that the 
Hatti Sheriff! wonld neither be read nor published at Jerusalem, 

Fourthly —Against the strange provision adopted by the Ottoman 
Government, in remitting to the Frank clergy the keys of the gate of the 
great chureh at Bethichem, without at the same time recognizing the fact of 
their possession, and consequent legitimate use of that possession. ‘This 
protest becomes more rigorously incumbent on us, in the case of the Porte’s 
having meant to deline by that provision that. the ancient firmans, in which it 
is stated repeatedly that the Frank clergy have been at all times possessed of 
all the keys of the church, should be understood as denoting the possession of 
the keys only, and not of the use of the church, Does not common sense 
declare, that whoever has the posseasion of a spot, naturally enjoys the use of 
that possession. 

‘ifthly —Against the method adopted in replacing the star on the spot 
of the Nativity in Bethlehem, as executed by the agents of the Porte solely, 

Sixthly.—Resigning ourselves with much pain to the condition in which 
the Latins are placed as regards the exercise of their worship in the Church of 
the ‘Tomb of the Virgin in Gethsemane, we, the undersigned, reserve to our- 
selves, in all integrity, the incontestable rights of Catholicism over this 
sanctuary; and until it please Giod to reinvest us with the full aceomplish- 
ment of these rights, we shall not cease to demand that the Latins be placed, 
provisionally, and till full justice be rendered to them, on perfect equality 
with the Greeks and other sects, as regards the exereise of Worship in this 
sanctuary, in conformity with the terms contained in the note transmitted to 
the French Ambassador in Constantinople, wherein it is stated “that the 
Latins shall be able to exercise their worship in this sanctuary in the same 
way and manner as the Cirecks and Armenians. 


(Signed) THE PATRIARCH OF JERUSALEM. 
TH GUARDIAN OF THE HOLY PLACES.

Colonel Rose to Lord John Russell.— (Received Mareh 19.) 
(No, 76.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, March 7, 1853. 

CIRCUMSTANCES connected with the mission of Prince Menchikoff 
have gradually come to light, and cause grave apprehensions for the indepen- 
dence, if not the destiny, of Turkey. 

No expense or efforts have heen spared for the purpose of imparting to 
the Russian Embassy all the advantages which accrue {rom personal influence, 
display, and entertamment, 

rince Menchikolf is an Admiral and Minister of the Marine, and he is 


156 


accompanied by tke Chancellor's son, Prince Galitzin, the Emperor's Aide-de- 
Camp, and a large suite. It is stated that 10002 a month, some say double 
that sum, is allowed to Prince Menchikoff merely for entertainment, and that 
the secret service money is unlimited. 

Whilst then the Russian Government have neglected no means for render- 
ing this Embassy influential, and agreeable to Orientals, they have been equally 
careful to impart to it the most powerful of influences amongst ‘Turks, in- 
timidation. Ste 

The Embassy is perfectly arranged, and is deficient in only one essential, 
and that is smeerity. ; 

A day or two after the arrival of Prince Menchikofl, another man-of-war 
steamer arrived here, conveying Vice-Admiral Korniloff, of the Black Sea 
fleet, Aide-de-Camp and Adjutant-General of the Emperor; and General 
Nikapotchinski, Chief of the Staff of General Radiger’s two corps darmeée, with 
other military officers. ‘The presence of these superior officers of the naval 
and military forces, which are to act against the Porte should she not comply 
with Russian demands, had its due effect, particularly as it is known that the 
Sth and 7th corps have been concentrated, and placed on the war footing 
under the command of General Rudiger, whose head-quarters are at Kiskereff, 
in Bessarabia. I also had further information that General Danneberg, com- 
manding the cavalry of the 5th corps, had pushed his advance euard as far as 
Skubery and Areny, up to the very Moldavian frontier, within two hours of 
Jassy; that large funds had been transmitted to Russian merchants in 
Wallachia and Moldavia, for the purchase of provisions for the Russian troops ; 
finally that the fleet at Sebastopool was getting ready to sail at the shortest 
notice. 

Unfortunately Prince Menchikoll’s first public act evineed entire dis- 
regard on his part ofthe Sultan's dignity and rights, which, combined with the 
hostile attitude of Russia, created the impression that coercion, rather than 
conciliatory negotiation, would distinguish his Exeellency’s mission, — 

His Excellency transmitted his credentials to Fuad Effendi, and the next 
day, with his whole Embassy, waited on the Grand Viaier at the Porte; it is 
an invariable rule that a new ambassador mukes the second visit of ceremony 
to the Minister for Foreign Affairs. But Prince Menchikoff, after leaving the 
Grand Vizier, although invited by Kiamil Bey, the ® Introductenr des Ambassa- 
deurs,” to visit Fuad Effendi, whose apartinvent adjoins those of the Grand 
Vizier, declined to do so; and Prince Menchikoll, passing by the line of troops 
and Kayasses, and the very door of Fuad Effendi, which had been opened to 
receive him, left the Porte. 

The allront was the more galling, because great preparations had been 
made for the purpose of receiving the Russian Ambassador with marked 
honours, and a great concourse of people, particularly Greeks, had assembled 
for the purpose of witnessing the ceremony. : : 

The incident made a great and most painful sensation. The Grand Vizier 
expressed to me his indignation at the premeditated affront which had been 
offered to his Sovereign; and the Sultan’s irritation was excessive, 

M. Benedetti and myself at once saw all the bearing and intention of the 
affront. Prince Menchikoff wished, at his first start, to create an intimidating and 
commanding influence, to show that any man, even a Cabinet Mimster, who 


had offended Russia, would be humilitated and punished even in the midst of 


the Sultan's Court, and without previous communication to His Majesty. 
Prince Menchikol! wished to take the cleverest man out of the Ministry, 
humitiate it, upset it, and establish in its place a Ministry favourable to his 
viows. [f this manoeuvre had succeeded, a second treaty like that of Un-

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, March 9, 1853. 
A PERSON who is upon friendly and confidential terms with Baron 
Meyendorif, has inquired of him, how he explained the remarkable accordance 
of views exhibited by the two Governments of Austria and Russia, in the 
questions which just at present excite such absorbing interest, 
Baron Meyendorfl, under injunction of secresy, replied that the expla- 


nation was more simple than appeared possible; that the Emperor of Russia 
had been deeply wounded at the conduct of his brother monarch with regard to 
the style of address employed towards Louis Napoleon (Mon Frere”), and that 
with a view to dispelling unpleasant feeling, His Imperial Majesty had resolved 
to place himself as much as possible under Russian cuidance with regard to the 
questions afloat in Turkey. 

[ean affirm with certainty, that this explanation has been given by Baron 
Meyendorff; and 1 am not prepared to express doubt in its correctness up to 
a certain point, } 

It may be the truth, but I question whether it be the whole truth, as I 
suspect that it will some day be proved that a certain understanding with regard 
to the affairs of Turkey existed between the two Imperial Courts soripaaly to 
the recognition of the French Empire, 

1 will entreat your Lordship to consider this communication as strictly 
confidential. 

To be able to report with any correctness the proceedings of this Court, it 
is most essential that the attention of the Russian Government should not be 
drawn towards the reporter.

My Lord, St, Petersburgh, March 9, 1853. 

WHEN calling upon Count Nesselrode on the 7th instant, L stated that it 
was highly desirable that I should be informed what credit was to be attached 
to the rumours which reached me from so many quarters as to military pre- 
parations in the course of being made. 

Count Nesselrode said, that he believed he might state that 1 had not 
heen correctly informed, 

& Toes your Excellency," I inquired, “authorize me to assert that you are 
not arming, or am I only to report that you believe you are not arming,” 

After gome hesitation, the Chancellor said that he would not assert, but 


that he believed (croire), that he had reason for believing (lieu de eroire), that 
the tendency was to slacken (ralentir), rather than to urge on, military prepara- 
tion, ae the successful termination of Count Leiningen’s mission had beg 
learned. . 

I apprehend this relaxation of preparation to allude to the order for the 
purchase of horses, which has been rescinded, | 

A somewhat desultory conversation ensued. We spoke of General 
Leiningen’s mission, and I took an op vortunity of observing that the pressure 
lately applied to the Porte was such as, in the opinion of Her Majesty's 
Government; could not be safely earried on. 

The Chancellor replied, that, to use my own expression, great part of the 
pressure would now cease ; that, as regarded Montenegro, there had been 
periculum in mor” (sic); that hours were of importance when Christians were 
being massacred,—when there was question of the extermination of whole 
Christian populations! But this was not the case with the question of the 
Holy Places, about this there was no immediate hurry; that Prince Menchikoif 
had been provided with very extensive powers, and that (he would add in 
confidence) the Prince had been made the bearer of a letter from the Emperor 
to the Sultan, drawn up in more friendly terms than had been employed in his 
letter by the Emperor of Austria. 

{ may here observe that intelligence has been received of Prince 
Menchikofi’s having embarked at Odessa on the 44 ultimo, He will, therefore, 
probably have reached Constantinople two days later. 

Before dismissing the subject of Montenegro, | remarked to Count Nessel- 
rode, that 1 thought very unnecessary importance had been attached to the 
circumstance of some of the Hungarian and Polish refugees having been 
employed in Omar Pasha’s army. 

The Chancellor appealed to me whether it were not very natural that 
danger should be apprehended by a Government, who found that men of this 
description were serving in a military capacity near its own frontiers. I 
replied that I had no wish to cast reflections upon the Austrian Government, 
but that 1 begged attention to one point :—* If,” Lsaid, ‘there is danger to a 
powerlul and well-established monarchy like that of Austria, from the neigh- 
bourhood of a handful of refugees, may there not be danger, and very extreme 
danger, toa weak Government like that of Turkey, in the approach to its 
frontiers of large foreign armies ?” 

I proceeded to speak of Constantinople, and of the promising aspect of 
athirs there, as described in Colonel Rose’s despatch No. 30, of the 28th 

anUary. 

L observed that I was about to be guilty of the irregularity of reading to 
his Excellency a report not intended for communication, 

Lread out accordingly the whole of the despatch, with the exeeption of 
the sentence beginnings “J cordially concurred.” 1 did so for the reasons, Lst, 
that I might exhibit the extremely conciliatory and impartial part taken by 
Colonel Rose, in affairs in which he has most unjustly been accused of siding 
unduly with the French Embassy, and 2nd, because I thought it of great 
importance to establish that Prince Menchikoif must have found affairs, upon 
his arrival in Turkey, in a train of amicable arrangement, and, therefore, that if 
not carried on in the same spirit, the blame would attach to the new-comer. 

Count Nesselrode expressed his warm satisfaction at the honourable and 
important testimony borne by Colonel Rose to the Bo! conduet of the Greek 
clergy, and took notes of some of the facts which are reported in Colonel 
Rose’s despatch, 

We proceeded to speak of the Holy Places question, and Count Nesselrode 
remarked, that he had heard with real pleasure from Baron Brunnow of the 
exeellent instruction addressed by Lord John Russell to Lord Cowley upon this 
matter. 

With respect to the Emperor's views, Count Nesselrode again observed, 
that it was impossible that his Imperial Majesty should recede from the position 

secured to the Greeks by the Firman of last February, confirmed as it had 
been hy the Sultan’s letter. 

That this very Firman was, in fact, a concession to the Latins, who in 
stn eel obtained two favours in lieu of the one granted to the Greek

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—-(Received March 19.) 


(A. Secret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, March 9, 1863. 


WHEN I waited upon Count Nesselrode, on the 7th instant, his Excellency 
said, that in pursuance of orders which he had received from the Emperor, he 
had to place in my hands a very confidential memorandum, which his Imperial 
Majesty had caused to be drawn up, and which was intended as an answer to, OF 
4 comment upon, the communication which 1 had made to his Imperial Majesty 


At first Count Nesselrode invited me to read the paper; he subsequently 
observed that if, instead of reading it at the time, | chose to take 1b awa, I was 
at liberty to do so—that, in fact, the paper was intended for my use (sic 

Very little conversation upon the subject passed between the Chancellor 


1 have the honour of avatees to your fordebip a copy of what, under the 
circumstances which have attended its drawing up and delivery, cannot fail of 
being considered as one of the most remarkable papers which have heen issued, 
IL do not say from the Russian “ Chancellerie,” but from the Eimperor’s secret 
cabinet, : 

It would not be difficult either to controvert some of the facts which the 
memorandum advances, or to show that the impression under which it has been 
framed is an incorrect one, that impression eins evidently that, m the disputes 
carried on between Russia and France, Her Majesty's Government has leant 
partially to the latter Power, f . 

Three points appear to me to be fully established by the Imperial memo- 
randum—the existence of some distinct understanding between the two Imperial 
Courts upon the subject of Turkey, and the engagement taken by the Emperor 
Nicholas neither to possess or establish himself at Constantinople, or to enter 
into arrangements Speers the measures to be taken in the event of the 
fall of the Ottoman Empire without previous concert with Her Majesty's 
Government, : ay Re 

The wording of this engagement, coupled with the conversation which f hae! 
the honour of holding with the Emperor, leaves upon my mind the impression 
that, whilst willing to undertake not to make himself the permanent master 
of Constantinople, his Majesty is ‘ntentionally inexplicit as to its temporary 
occupation, 

othe as a certain and now acknowledged fact, the existence of an 
understan er compact between the two Emperors as to Turkish affairs, 1t 
becomes of the deepest importance to know the extent of the engagements 


164 


entered into between them, As to the manner in which it has been concluded, 
I conjecture that little doubt is to be entertained. 

Its basis was, no doubt, laid at some of the meetings between the 
Sovereigns which took place in the autumn , and the scheme has probably been 
worked out since under the management of Baron Meyendorif, the Russian 
Envoy at the Austrian Court, who has been passing the winter at St. Peters- 
burgh, and is still here. 

For such subterraneons negotiation Baron Meyendorff is admirably 
qualified by his acuteness, by his Jesuitical qualities, ani by the circumstance 
of his being the brother-in-law and imtimate friend of Count Buol. 

By degrees it becomes more intelligible why the assistance of Russia has 
been afforded to Austria in proceedings, for the justification of which it has 
been necessary to resort to the current fables respecting the persecution and 
massacre of Christians by the infidels; and why, in her turn, Russia is recely= 
ing the full support of a Government as Roman Catholic and as much under 
the influence of priests and Jesuits as that of Austria, towards obtaining 
objects to be carried by the Greek against the Latin Ohureh, 

With whatever view the overtures made by the Fimperor to Her Majesty's 
Envoy may have been resolved upon, I ean hardly doubt that the advantage 
obtained has been for Her Majesty's Government, who are now in possession of 
gome knowledge of obscure transactions, and some recorded security against 
eventual dangers. 

The evils of a close alliance between the Emperors of Russia and Austria, 
upon the basis of advantages to be wrung from a weak neighbour, are certainly 
very great; but it may be that time mayassiat us in this matter, and that, as 
experience and wisdom are rained, the Emperor Francis may perceive that too 
high a price may be paid for the acquisition of a Turkish province. 

Supposing the schemes, which may now with some fairness be attributed 
to Russia and Austria, really to exist, ib may be conjectured that the next 
stage in the transaction will be to prepare Prussia for coming events, and, it 
may be, to give her an interest in their arrival. 

In conclusion, I will venture to observe, that [ am convineed that very 
serious offence would be taken by the Emperor of Russia, if he should ever 
ascertain that the inclosed most secret paper, or the report of the communica- 
tions by which it was preceded, had been brought to the knowledge of any 
foreign Cabinet. 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR,

My dear Count Neasselrode, Bt. boablawi dt ; ae ee 
THERE is an observation regpecting the very Hmporls) theme 

placed yesterday by your Excellency in m y hands, which I feel obliged Mf make. 

~~ Tam most anxious to observe that this paper must have been drawn up

under the impression of English policy at Constantinople having been very 
different from what in reality it has been. 

I can affirm, conscientiously and distinctly, that the object proposed to 
themselves, as well by the late as by Her Majesty's present Government, has

ae) that ample satisfaction should be given to the demands which His

This assertion I should have no diffienlty in substantiating by written 
evidence ; and I will add, that in any: just demand which England may have to 
make upon a Foreign Cabinet, 1 only desire that the conduct of a friendly 
Power towards us may be that which quietly and unostentatiously the Engli 
Government has pursued in the complicated question of the Holy Places with 
regard to the claims of Russia. 

I request your Excellency’s good offices for causing this, the real state of 
the case, to be rightly understood; at all events, for preventing a contrary 
belief from being adopted until it shall be clearly ascertained whether or no 
my statement is correct.

M. E. Pisani to Colonel Kose. 


March 8, 1853. 

A FRIEND of mine, closely connected with the Russian Embassy, informed 
me this morning, in the most conlidential manner, of a conversation he had 
with one of the aides-de-camp of Prince Menchikoff, at which M. de Balabine 
was present, He said that the Prince was not sent here to negotiate, but to 
make some peremptory demands ; that the Emperor of Russia was ready for all 
emergencies; that this time the scene will be at Constantinople ; that the 
Latins had no right to interfere with the Sanctuaries of Jerusalem 5 that the 
Cupola shall belong exclusively to the Greeks ; that the Prince Menchikoff gave 
the most. positive assurances to the Greek Patriarch that the Emperor had taken 
up the affair, and they may stay quiet, and not make any re resentations to the 
Porte, He also said that the treaty between the Porte and France was of no 
value in the Emperor's eyes, in comparison with the political exigencies of the 
Emperor, which were of far greater weight ; that he suspected that the English 
fleet would probably come to assist the Turks, but that before it could arrive, 
“Je coup serait porté ;” that Enplent and France were not yet acquainted with 
the policy of Russia ; and that I ussia could excite all the Christian populations 


to revolt. 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) FE. PISANI.

LE 9 Mai, 1833, au moment of la cession du territoire d’Adana venait 
de mottre un terme aux derniéres difficultés qui, malgre les efforts réunis de 
la France et de |'Angleterre, s'opposaient encore & la conclusion de la paix 
entre "Empire Ottoman et Egypte, le Général Comte Orloff, aide-de-camp de 
'Empereur Nicolas, qui, a une époque peu éoignée, avait déji rempli une mission 
en Turquie et y avait Jaissé de bons souvenirs, arrive a Constantinople avec le 
double titre d’Ambassadeur Extraordinaire et de Commandant-en-chef des forces 
Russes qui oceupent le Bosphore. 

Dans les premiers temps de son séjour, les efforts du Comte Orloff, malgré ses 
Hiiaedietarig réitérées aux Ambassadeurs de France et de l’Angleterre, tendaient 

provoquer la reprise des hostilités, en conseillant au Sultan la résistance, et en 
Ini promettant l'appui de la Russie ; mais les mouvemens des troupes Russes, qui 
vont camper vis-a-vis les iles des Princes, un plan @oceupation des Dardanelles, 
déja répoussé par la Porte, et reproduit avec plus d'insistence, ne laissent que 
trop prévoir de quel prix la Turquie paierait les secours qu’on veut lui imposer. 
C'est, dit-on, en s'elforcant de thir renoncer le Grand Seigneur & la cession 
d'Adana que le Comte Orloff espére arriver au but quil se propose, ou que du 
moins l’arrivée incessante de nouvelles troupes Russes dans le Bosphore autorise 
A lui supposer. 

Cependant, vers la fin du mois de Mai, la retraite d'Tbrahim Pasha com- 
menee a s'elfectuer, et en méme tems certaines ouvertures, faites ila Porte par 
'Ambassade de Russie, donnent A penser que le Comte Orloff, contraint par les 
efforts réunis de la France et de l’'Angleterre, de respecter la paix qu'il a trouve 
faite 4 son arrivée, cherche, en désespoir de cause, 4 conelure avee le Sultan un 
traité offensif et defensif, qui permetira aux Russes d’exercer sur la Turquie une 
influence exclusive, leur donnera le droit d’intervenir sans etre obligés.d’en pré- 
venir qui que ce soit, eben un mot, les autorisera A commander dans le Bosphore 
au moindre symptome de refroidissement dans les rélations de la Turquie avec 
quelquautre Puissance. 

Ces bruits deviennent au bout de quelques jours une certitude; le Comte 
Orloff, qui rencontre chez la plupart des membres du Ministere une vive rési- 
stance, veut agirsur le Sultan lui-meme, et c'est au palais qu'il cherche des allies; 
Ahmed Pasha, Mushir du Mabein du Sultan Mahmoud, et dévoué a la Russie, 
\ni préte le coneours le plus actif; des revues, des fétes auxquelles le Sultan est 
invité A assister, ’entretiennent dans les dispositions qu’on a su lui suggeérer, et 
le 8 Juillet le traité, qui doit porter le nom d’Unkiar Skelessi, est signé par le 
Seraskier Ahmed Pasha et le Reis Effendi, sans avoir été délibéré en Conseil. 

Peu de jours apres, les troupes Russes se rembarquent ; le Comte Orloff part 
pour Odessa sur le vaisseau le «'chesme,” et pendant dix ans la Turquie s'est 
trouvée unie 4 la Russie par des liens qui ont entravé sa liberté d’action dans 
toutes les questions, qui lui ont aliéné les sympathies des Puissances Occidentales, 
qui ont failli enfin amener les plus graves complications.

{ HAVE the honour to inform you that Prince Menchikof, accompanied 
by all the persons attached ta his Embassy, was received m audience to-day by 
the Sultan, After he had presented his credentials, he said that he had been 
particularly desired by his august master, the Emperor, to present, his friendly 
compliments to His Majesty the Sultan, and to assure him how anxioms he (the 
[mperor) was to see the coolness which had latterly existed between the two 
Governments give place to more friendly relations. | 

Subsequently, all the attachés, and M. d’Ozerott himself, withdrew, and the 
Prince remained alone with M. Argyropulo, in private converse with the Sultan, 
in the presence of the Minister for Foreign Affairs and the first Interpreter of 
the Divan. 

It would appear that the presence of the latter was not very agreeable to 
the Prince, who cast furious glances at M. Argyropulo. He did not enter imto 
any details touching the object of his mission; but only spoke ™ general terms 
of several matters that required settlement, without specitying their nature, and 
added, that it was his intention to communicate thereon with His Majesty's

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon——(Reeeived March 21 )

My Lord, Paris, March 19, 1R53, 


TES despatches addressed to the French Government from Constanti- 
nople, on the Sth and Gth instant, conveyed by the regular packet to Marseilles, 
and those transmitted on the &th, brought by an English steamer to the same 
port, reached Paris—the former yesterday, the latter this mornmg. he tele- 
graphic notice already received, respecting the nature of the intelligence con- 
tained in them, had created considerable anxiety m the Government, an anxiety 
which had been shared by the public at large. , 

M. Benedetti’s despatches give an account of the arrival of Prince Men- 
chikoff at Constantino le of his visit to the Porte, and of the change the 
Ministry of Foreign 4 ffairs, Your Lordship will have received ample intelli- 
gence on these matters, and 1 do not pursue them further, Beyond this, the 
statement of the French Chargé d’ Affaires is confined to, surmises 28 to the 
nature and scope of Prince Menchikoft’s mission ; for it appears that, up to the 
Sth instant, nothing was distinctly known 2s to the demands whieh he was to 
make upon the Porte. M. Benedetti, however, seems to have no doubt that 
they included a summons to restore the status quo at Jerusalem,—0 recogmition 
by the Sultan of the Protectorate of Russia over the Greek Religion in Turkey, 
—the election of the Greek Patriarch for the future by the Greek subjects of 
the Porte, such eleetion to be confirmed at St. Petersburgh,—the liquidation of 
various claims pending between the Russian Legation anc the Divan,—and the 
settlement of the frontier separating the two empires Asia Minor, It was 
also rumoured that the Russian Envoy was to ask. of the Porte a treaty which 
should give her some such rights as those she obtained under that known by the 
title of “Unkiar Skelesst.” To conclude the summary thus furnished me of 
M. Benedetti’s despatches, Colonel Rose had thought that matters had taken 
go serious & turn, that he had requested Admiral Duudas to approach the Darda- 
nelles with the fleet under his comma, 

''o the anxiety felt by the French Government, 98 mentioned in the be- 
ginning of this despatch, has now been superadded irritation and impatience. 
The conquest of Turkey 15 looked upon as decided on, and even undertaken by 


171 


the Emperor of Russia; and the hasty imagination of some of the Ministers 
already sees a Russian army in possession of the Principalities, and & Russian 
fleet before Constantinople, although the French Government does not in fact 
-et know what are the real demands of Prince Menchikoff, and whether they can 
be reasonably granted by ‘Turkey or not. 

Thad long conversations with M, Drouyn de Lhuys, both yesterday and 
today, He expressed surprise this morning at not having received any answer 
to a despatch which hie had addressed, the day before yesterday, to Count 
Walewski, and in which, it appears, he expressed the hope that some joint 


course of action might be decided upon by the Governments of Great Britain 
and France, I observed upon the impossibility of coming to a decision upon 
facts that were not yel known, 

M, Drouyn de Lhuys continued the conversation with great imitation of 
manner. He said that what he had always predicted had come true,—that 
while Russia was eajoling us at St. Petersburgh with assurances of a friendly 
disposition towards ‘Turkey, she was preparing the vast resources at her disposal 
for crushing the Ottoman Empire,—that the question of the Sacred Places was 
a pretext, the humiliation and finally the subjugation of ‘Turkey, the intention, 
—that Turkey could not be attacked without violating the Treaty of 1841,— 
that it behoved the Powers, parties to that ‘Treaty, to oppose that violation, and 
that France would do so, even if she stood alone,—that the French fleet had 
heen ordered to the coast of Greece, not with any immediate hostile intention, 
but to be prepared for any eventuality, 

My reply to M, Drouyn de Liuys was to the following purport -—That Her 
Majesty’s Government was as anxious as could be that of the Emperor for the 
preservation of the integrity and independence of the Ottoman Empire. If, how- 
ever, that integrity and independence were menaced, whose fault wasit? Con- 
scientiously I must say that if was the fault of France and of Austria,—of France 
in raising without consideration the question of the Holy Places, which had 
Kren Russia the pretext for her present proceedings,—of Austria in setting 

ye example of menace and intimidation, Even now, I said, unless events had 
marched with a rapidity hitherto unknown in ‘Turkish negotiations, the projects 
of Russia, such as were imputed to her by France, might be baffled, If Russia 
hod demanded the status quo in Jerusalem, it was more than probable that she 
had done so under the conviction that France would refuse lier consent, and 
that she (Russia) would consequent! be justified in asking an exitivalent for 
what had been granted to France; that e uivalent might be the Protectorate 
of the Greek religion, or, in other words, the supremacy of Russia in the Euro- 
pean provinces of Turkey, Let ‘France, however, accept the status quo at 
Jerusalem, the Russian scheme would probably be ilefeated. 

Nothing could be more fair an honourable than the way in which M. 
Drouyn de Lhuys admitted, as far as his personal “opinion was concerned, the 
error committed by the French Government, not ‘only in the matter of the 
Sacred Buildings, but in the naval demonsttation undertaken last year against 
Tripoli, * But,” he said, * France has already expiated her faults ; for what has she 
obtained in comparison to what she demanded, and'to what she is entitled by 
treaty? She cannot make greater. concessions; this is not my opinion only ; 
the Emperor would rather be pounded ina mortar (* broyé dans un mortier ’) 
than yicld to the dictation of Russia, The honour of’ France would not 
permit it,” 

1 rejoined that there was no questionof yielding to the dictation of Russia ; 
that Russia, in proposing the re-establishment of the status quo, gave up the Fir- 
man which she had obtained, and which sceured to her advantages equivalent, at 
the least, to those which Franee enjoyed; and that, for my part, I could see 
nothing dishonourable in two great countries making mutual concessions for 
THROU the peace of the world. 

Teould obtain nothing more from M. Drouyn de Lhuys than this—that 
there was nothing in the concessions made to the French which, in his: opinion, 
rendered impossible the exceution of the irman given to the Greeks; in other 
words, that France could not openly give up what had been conceded to her, 
but would not look too closely into any arrangement made with Iussia, whether 
it militated against her interests at Jerusalem, oF not, 

I have been more particular in giving your Lordship these short details of 
two very long conversations, because it ts impossible not to see that the French 


172 


Government may make this matter very dangerous. Irritated at their own 
want of foresight, in raising ® question which has given Russia her present 
anrEntaee in the East, they are endeavouring to make it appear that it is not 
the settlement of a religious dispute which Russia meditates, but that it is her 
supremacy in Turkey which she asserts. I shall, as occasion offers, continue 
the language which | have never ceased to hold on this question,—that we have 
no right to doubt the peaceable intentions of the Emperor of Russia, or of his 
desire to maintain the integrity of the Ottoman Empire, assurances to that 
effect having been so re weatedly given both to Great Britain and France at Bt. 
Petersburgh, until we have proofs to the contrary; and 1 shall endeavour to 
ealm, as far as depends on me, that “rritable humour which leads the French 
so constantly to act upon the spur of the moment, and, consequently, with a 
rashness of which they have often to repent in the sequel of events, 

I have, &e. 

(Signed) COW LEY.
