My Lord, Foreign Office, March 22, 1859. 

YOUR Excellency's despatches, to No, 164 inclusive, have been received 
and laid before the Queen, and | have the satisfaction to inform you that Her 
Majesty entirely approves of the language held by you to M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
upon the events that have recently taken place at Constantinople. 

I had yesterday a long interview with Count Walewski upon the same sub- 
ject. The information received by the French Government appears to corres- 
pond precisely with that which has reached Her Majesty's Government, and 
Count Walewski gave me the same report as is contained in your Excellency’s 
despatch No, 161, of the views and feelings of his Government. 

T told his Excellency that when the intelligence from Constantinople was 
analysed, and divested of the colouring imparted to it by local excitement, it 
would be found to consist chiefly of street rumours, Russian gossip, Turkish 
alarm, and diplomatic zeal; and that there was but one fact to deal with, viz., 
that General Menchikoff, in pursuance of the orders of the Emperor of Russia, 
announced nearly two months ago, had declined to hold offieial intercourse with 
Fuad Effendi, because that Minister, in the opinion of His Imperial Majesty, 
had acted with bad faith to Russia. Fuad Effendi had accordingly resigned ; 
but Prince Menchikotf had not required this, and he had deelared that no dis- 
respect was intended to the Sultan by the omission of the customary visit to his 
Minister. 

Under these. circumstances, I’ said Her Majesty’s Government liad not 
thought Colonel Rose justified in requesting that the British fleet should come 
to Vourla, and they had learnt, with mueli satisfaction, that Admiral Dundas 
had considered’ it his duty to remain at Malta until he received’ instructions 
from Mngland, 

For similar reasons, | told'Gount Walewski that Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment regretted the order given to the French fleet to sail for the Greek waters, 
as the delay of a few hours would have put the French Government in possession 
of information that might have led ‘to the same conclusions that Her Majesty's 
Government have arrived at on the subject ; and I ventured to remark to His 
Excellency, that a policy of suspicion was neither wise nor safe, and often led 
to hasty determinations. 

Her Majesty's Government, I added, were disposed to place reliance on the 
Emperor of Russia, from whom they had often received the most solemn assur- 
ances thatit was both his interest and his intention to uphold the Turkish Empire, 
and that if any change in this policy were contemplated by His Imperial Majesty, 
the intention should he communicated without hesitation or reserve, 

No such communication baying been made, Her Majesty's Government 
were hound to believe, until they lind proofs to the contrary, that the mission of 
Prince Menchikoff was not of a character menacing to the independence and 
integrity of Turkey. 

1 further informed Count Walewski that Thad just had a conversation with 
Baron Brunnow, to whom [ had unreservedly communicated the reports that had 
reached ws from Constantinople respeeting the objects of ioneral Menchikoif's 
mission, and that Baron Brunnow had assured me, of his own knowledge, that 
no frontier question would be mooted ; that no change in the mode of appointing 
the Greek Patriarch would be proposed; and that there was no intention Beteacte! 
ing the Latins of advantages they possessed in the Holy Places, though the 
Emperor would insist upon the promises made to him in favour of the Greek: 
Church being fulfilled. |

Her Majesty’s O arsisente who are fully aware that, in the event of any 
understanding with reference to future contingencies being expedient, or, 


2A 2 


176 


indeed, possible, the word of His Imperial Majesty would be preferable to any 
Convention that could be framed. 

Her Majesty's Government persevere in the belief that Turkey still 

possesses the elements of existence, and they consider that recent events have 
roved the correctness of the opinion expressed in the despatch of my pre- 
ecessor, that there was no sufficient cause for intimating to the Sultan that he 

cannot keep peace at home, or preserve friendly relations with his neighbours, 

Her Majesty's Government have accordingly learnt with sincere satisfac- 
tion that the Emperor considers himself even more interested than England in 
preventing a ‘Turkish catastrophe; because they are convinced that upon the 
policy pursued hy His Imperial Majesty towards Turkey, will mainly depend 
the hastening or the indefinite postponement of an event which every Power 
in Europe is concerned in averting, Her Majesty's Government are convinced 
that nothing is more calculated to precipitate that event than the constant 
prediction of its being near at hand; that nothing can be more fatal to the 
vitality of Turkey than the assumption of its rapid and inevitable decay; and 
that if the opinion of the Emperor, that the days of the Turkish Empire were 
numbered, became notorious, its downfall must occur even sooner than His 
Imperial Majesty now appears to expect. 

But on the supposition that, from unavoidable causes, the catastrophe did 
take place, Her Majesty's Government entirely share the opinion of the 
Euaperor, that the occupation of Constantinople hy cither of the great Powers 
would be incompatible with the present balance of power and the maintenance 
of peace in Hurope, and must at once be regarded as impossible; that there are 
no elements for the reconstruction of a Ryzantine Empire; that the systematic 
misrovernment of Greece offers no encouragement to extend its territorial 
dominion; and that as there are no materials for provincial or commercial 
government, anarchy would be the result of leaving the provinces of Turkey to 
themselves, or permitting them to form separate republies. 

The Emperor has announced that sooner than permit a settlement of the 
question by any one of these methods, he will be prepared for war at every 
hazard; and however much Her Majesty’s Government may be disposed to 
agree in the soundness of the views taken by His Imperial Majesty, yet they 
consider that the simple predetermination of what shall not be tolerated, does 
little towards solving the real difficulties, or settling in what manner it would be 
practicable, or even desirable, to deal with the heterogencous materials of which 
the Turkish Empire is composed. 

England desires no territorial aggrandizement, and could be no party toa 
previous arrangement from which she was to derive any such benefit, England 
could he no party to any understanding, however general, that was to be kept 
seeret from other Powers; but Her Majesty's Government believe that no 
arrangements could control events, and that no understanding could be kept 
secret, ‘They would, in the opinion of her Majesty's Government, be the signal 
for preparation for intrigues of every description, and for revolts among the 
Christian subjects of the Porte, Each Power and each party would endeavour 
to secure its future interests, and the dissolution of the Turkish Empire would be 
preceded bya state of anarchy which must aggravate every difficulty, if it did not 
render a peaceful solution of the question impossible, 

The only mode by which such a solution could be attempted would be that of 
an European Congress but that only atfords an additional reason for desiring 
that the present order of things in ‘Turkey should be maintained, as Her 
Majesty's Govaninient cannot without alarm reflect on the jealousies that would 
then he evoked, the impossibility of reconciling the different ambitions and the 
divergent, interests that would be called into play, and the certainty that the 
treatics of 1815 must then be open to revision, when France would be prepared 
to risk the chances of an European war to get rid of the obligations which she 
considers injurious to her national honour, and which, having been imposed by 
victorious enemies, are a constant souree of irritation to her, 

The main object of Her Majesty's Government, that to which their efforts 
have been and always will be directed, is the preservation of peace; and they 
desire to uphold the Turkish Empire, from their conviction that no great ques- 
tion can be agitated in the East without becoming a source of discord in the 
West, and that every great question in the West will assume a revolutionary 


biti 


character, and embrace a revision of the entire social system, for which the 
continental Governments are certainly in no state of preparation. 

The Emperor is fully cognizant of the materials that are in constant fer- 
mentation beneath the surface of society, and their readinesa to burst forth even 
in times of peace; and His Imperial Majesty will probably, therefore, not dis- 
sent from the opinion that the first cannon-shot may be the signal for a state of 
things more disastrous even than those calamities that war inevitably brings in 
its train. 

But such a war would be the result of the dissolution and dismemberment 
of the Turkish Empire; and hence the anxiety of Her Majesty's Government 
to avert the catastrophe. Nor can they admit that the signs of Turkish decay 
are now either more evident or more rapid than of late years; there is still 
great energy and great wealth in Turkey; a disposition to improve the system of 
government is not wanting; corruption, though qnforesantaty great, is still not 
ofa character, nor carried to an extent, that threatens the existence of the State; 
the treatment of Christiansis not harsh, and the toleration exhibited by the Porte 
towards this portion of its subjects might serve as an example to some Govern- 
ments who look with contempt upon Turkey as a barbarous Power, 

Her eae 8 Government believe that Turkey only requires forbearance on 
the part of its allies, and a determination not to press their claims in a manner 
humiliating to the dignity and independence of the Sultan,—that friendly sup- 

ort, inshort, that, with States as with individuals, the weak are entitled to expect 
rom the strong,—in order not only to prolong its existence, but to remove all 
cause of alarm respecting its dissolution, 

It is in this work of benevolence and of sound European policy that Her 
Majesty's Government are desirous of co-operating with the Emperor; they 
feel entire confidence in the rectitude of His Imperial Majesty’s intentions, and 
as they have the satisfaction of thinking that the interests of Russia and England 
in the ast are completely identical, they entertain an earnest hope that a 
similar policy there will prevail, and tend to strengthen the alliance between the 
two countries, which it is alike the object of Her Majesty and Her Majesty's 
Government to promote, 

You will give a copy of this despatch to the Chancellor, or to the Emperor, 
in the event of your again having the honour to be received by His Imperial 
Majesty. 

Tam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

No. 190. 


Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.— (Received March 25.) 


(No. 172. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Paris, March 24, 1868. 

I REPORTED to your Lordship on Saturday afternoon last the 19th 
instant the resolution to which a Council, over which the Emperor had presided 
im the morning, had come, of ordering the flect at Toulon to procee to the 
eoast of Greece, I was somewhat surprised by this decision, because | had no 
reason to believe’ that it was in contemplation. The despatches received the 
day before from the French Chargé Affaires at Constantinople had dis- 
couraged any such demonstration, and an indirect inquiry, which | had made of 
M. Drouyn de Lituys, liad led me to suppose that he was likewise opposed to it, 
On asking why it had been judged necessary to take this serious step, I was 
told that it had not been done with any hostile intention; that it was evident 
from Colonel Rose having sent for the English fleet, that he considered the 
crisis at Constantinople as one of great gravity, and that the french Goyern- 
nient had resolved tobe prepared for any eventuality. But we were, at this, 
time, without any information as to the reasons which had induced Colonel 
Rose to take the step in question. It appeared to me, tlerefore, that however 
necessary and advisable the presence of the French fleet in the Archipelago 
might eveitually become, the decision to send it had been taken prematurely, 
The French Government had no precise knowledge of the nature anid extent, of 
the demands to be made by Prince Menchikoff on the Porte; Her Majesty's 
Government had not yet received their despatches from Colonel Rose; and it 
was most desirable that no false move should be made, which might prove a 
source of future embatrassment. I took, therefore, such steps as I thought 
might induce the Emperor to pause, until His Majesty had a thorough know- 
ledge of all that had occurred at Constantinople, It seemed to me that. no 
disadvantage could ensue from a short delay, for one of two things would pro- 
bably have happened at Constantinople: either Prince Menchikotf would have 
insisted upon the ateeptance of his demands, with an energy which would have 
SSC his ends before an English or French fleet could have been near 
Constantinople, or he would haye entered into a course of negociation with the 
Porte, which would allow time for England and Franee to interfere, if the two 
Governments judged it necessary. 

My overtures were il) received on all sides, An attempt which I made to 
see the Emperor himself, failed from unwillingness, I believe, on his part to 
enter into any discussion of the matter, and the “Monitenr” of Sunday 
morning had announced officially that orders had been sent to the fleet to sail 
for the coast of Greece. Nevertheless, on Sunday evening it was intimated to 
me, | cannot help thinking with the Emperor's concurrence, that the orders for 
the French fleet to sail had not then been sent, becanse the instructions for the 
Admiral had not been completed. I was at the same time given to erie 
that if Her Majesty's Government would assure that of the Emperor that Great 
Britain would co-operate with Franee to prevent the dissolution of the Turkish 
Empire, and would promise at the same time that “les bons offices” of Her 
Majesty's Embassy at Constantinople should be employed for the settlement of 
the question of the Haly Places in a way which should not be dishonouring to 
France, the French fleet might be sent to some port in the Mediterranean for 
the present rather than into the Archipelago. 


‘The communications which I have at various times received from Her 
Majesty's Government, enabled me to assure my informant that no Government 
could be more desirous for the preservation of the Ottoman Bens than was 


that of Her Majesty, and that Lord Stratford’s instructions already enabled 
that Ambassador to employ in the manner suggested his great talents and his 
efforts for the settlement of the question of the Sacred Buildings. 


180 


Tealled the next day on M, Drouyn de Lhuys in the expectation of finding 
him willing to abide by the declaration made to me the previous evening. 
Unfortunately a Council had been held in the morning, at which less conciliatory 
advice had prevailed, and I was informed that it was too late to make any 
alteration in the destination of the fleet. It was impossible, M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys said, to recall orders which had been published in the “Moniteur.” His 
manner was greatly irritated when speaking of Russia. He was surprised, he 
said, that England was so little alive to the character of Prince Menchikoifs 
mission, ‘This officer had arrived at Constantinople with an immense staff, after 
reviewing the Russian army and fleet at Sevastopol, had treated the Sultan’s 
Ministers with extreme disrespect, and was currently reported to be about to 
make demands of the Porte, the acceptance of which would annihilate the 
independence of Turkey. This state of things had seriously alarmed the 
English Chargé d'Affaires at the Porte, and he had informed his French 
colleatue that he had summoned the British fleet to Constantinople, Was it 
extraordinary that France should not wish to remain inactive where the inde- 
pendence of Turkey was in danger, and the Treaty of 1841 threatened, perhaps, 
with violation ? | 

M, Drouyn de Lhuys continued in this strain for some time, contrasting 
the apathy of the British Government now with its alacrity when the Porte was 
threatened by Austria and Russia in the question of the refugees, and hinting 
that it sugested the idea of a change of policy on our part in regard to 
Eastern affairs. 

[ assured M. Drouyn de Lhuys, that he was quite mistaken in his latter 
supposition; that [ would answer that Her Majesty’s Government were as 
anxious as any of their predecessors for the maintenance of the integrity and 
independence of the Ottoman Empire ; but that if [ remonstrated against the 
departure of the French fleet, it was because neither Government had any facts 
batore them on which to found a concerted action, and that until facts proved 
the contrary, we were bound to trust to the solemn assurances made by the 
Emperor of Russia of lis pacific intentions, . 

1 will not, however, weary your Lordship with a more detailed report of the 
arguments which I employed on this and other occasions, first, to prevent the 
departure of the fleet, and finding that impossible, to prevail on the French 
Government to give a less hostile and menacing appearance to its. arrival at 
Salamis, whither it is bound, by sending orders that it should anchor for a few 
days at Naples and other ports between ‘Toulon and the coast of Greece. 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys would do no more than promise to submit my obser- 
vations to the Emperor, He informed me subsequently, that they had not 
induced His Majesty to alter the orders already given, and that the fleet would 
sail on the morning of the 22nd. He repeated at the same time, that there 
was no hostile meaning in the movement of the fleet; it was a simple measure 
of precaution, 

I have received a confidential confirmation of this latter assertion from a 
person who has read Admiral de la Susse's orders. [fe is instructed not on 
any account to leave the waters of Greece, unless under a written demand from 
the Freneh Ambassador at Constantinople. 

[ have thought it necessary to trouble your Lordship with a summary of 
my proceedings during the last three or four days, in order that Her Majesty's 
Government may be assured that I have left no means untried to prevent the 
consummation of an act conceived in ignorance and haste, and carried out with 
petulanee and obstinacy. . 

It only remains for me to state, ina few words, the motives which have 
actuated the Emperor and his Ministers on this occasion. In the first place, 
‘i is a common saying with them, that Louis Philippe fell in 1840, and not in 
1848; meaning, that the conduct of Louis Philippe, in permitting the settle- 
mont of astern affairs in 1840 without the participation of France, cnused the 
eventual fall of the Orleans family. ‘The Emperor 1s determined not to commit 
any such mistake 

Secondly.—The vanity of the nation is flattered by the announcement that 
the French fleet is sent towards troubled waters—though the nation neither 
knows nor enres what the fleet is to do. 

Thirdly. —There is jealousy, and perhaps a little mistrust, of England. 


181 


The idea that our fleet should alone be summoned to Constantinople excited 
irritation and # sentiment of rivalry. 

Fourthly —The question of the Sacred Buildings at Jerusalem is not yet 
settled, and the French Government, without having any definite object in 
view, thinks, no doubt, that the approach of the Trench fleet towards Turkey 
may be useful in the ensuing negotiation.

My Lord, Paris, March 24, 1855. 

I HAVE the satisfaction to acquaint your Lordship that the tone of the 
French Government in regard to its relations with Russia is much calmer, and 
more conciliatory. 

M. de Kisslett received despatches yesterday from St, Petersburgh, dated 
the 15th instant, which he communicated to M. Drouyn ile Lhuys in the course 
of the day. 

In them Count Nesselrode reiterates the sincere desire of the Emperor to 
terminate the question of the Holy Buildings amicably, In reply to an 
observation made by M. Drouyn de Lhuys, through M. de Catelbajac, that he 
sees no reason why the Porte's note of the Sth of February, 1852 to M. de 
Lavalette, together with the instructions given to Afif Bey, the Porte’s Com- 
missioner at Jerusalem, in which documents are contained the concessions 

ranted to the Latins, are not reconcileable with the Firman obtained by 
L. de Tito for the Greeks. Count Nesselrode says that he has no knowledge 
of the two former documents; that they have never been communicated either 
by the Porte or by the French Government, to him, and that he can conse- 
quently give no opinion about them ; that if they are communicated to him 
now, he will take them into consideration, and instruct Prinee Menchikoif 
accordingly. ‘The Count remarks, “That if the communication had been made 
frankly at the time, all that has since taken place mizht have been avoided.” 
‘To a proposition which appears to have been made by M. Drouyn de Lhuys, that 
a conference of French, Russian, and Turkish Commissioners should be 
established at Constantinople, for the purpose of regulating the claims of the 
contending partics, Count Nesselrode answers, “ That it would be better that 
the French and Russian Representatives should understand each other before 
addressing themselves to the Porte." Assurances are miven that there is no 
intention on the part of Russia to disturb any arrangements made between 
France and the Porte in regard to the Sacred Buildings; but it is laid down, 
that if concessions have been made to the Latins, an equivalent will be required 
for the Greeks, ‘The whole tenour of the correspondence shows further, that 
the Emperor of Russia has no hostile feeling towards Turkey, and is anxious 
for the maintenance of the integrity of the Ottoman Empire, 

Prince Menchikoff, Count Nesselrode says, will meet whoever may he 
the French Representative at Constantinople with the utmost frankness and 
cordiality. ‘

amicably ; hut the Russian Envoy docs not appear to have refrained from

himself, on the plea of the Russian armaments near Glew: to which M. de

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley.

My Lord, Foreign Office, March 29, i853. 

ON the 25th instant Count Walewski informed me, by the direction of his 
Government, that the French fleet had orders to proceed to Salamis, and that 
communications of a satisfactory mature (is reported in your Fixcelleney’s 
despatch No. 175) had been received from Russia with respect to the instruc- 
tions given to Prince Menchikoff concerning the Holy Places. 

Count Walewski said that the French Admiral was directed not to proceed 
further than Salamis, and that the fleet was sent there not as a menace to 
Russia, but as a measure of precaution ; that serious events might arise in the 
East, for which ib was ‘neumbent on France to be prepared, and that it was 
thought necessary to send the French fleet to Salamis im order that it might be 
on the same line as the English fleet at Malta, which, otherwise, would have 
heen nearer to the theatre of events; but that, should the necessity for it 
arise, the French Government hoped the two fleets would act together im sup- 
port of the common ‘nterests of both countries in the Hast. 

I told Count Walewski that I saw no reason tor altering the opinion I had 
more than once expressed to him, and that I still thought the orders for the 
sailing of the fleet were given hastily and without sufficient reason ; and that, 
although I hoped the two Governments would always act together when their 
policy and their interests were identical, yet | must frankly say that the recent 

roceedings of the French Government were not the best calculated to secure 
that desirable result; for the fleet had been ordered to sail without consultation 
or communication with us, at & moment, too, when the French Government 
were either in possession of their despatches from Constantinople, or were hourly 
expecting their arrival, and when, moreover, they knew from him (Count 
Walewskt) that Her Majesty's Government hoped and believed that the Admiral 


185 


at Malta would not comply with the request addressed to him by Colonel Rose ; 
and that, notwithstanding the earnest request of your Excellency, no delay in 
the departure of the fleet nor change of its destination could be procured. 

I added further, that coldness and suspicion all at once appeared to exist 
towards us, in the place of previous cordiality ; that we were thought to be 
taking part with Russia against France, and placing undue confidence in the 
former, while we looked with unaccountable indifference at the approaching 
destruction of the Turkish Empire; whereas, T said, the French Government 
must know that we had acted with perfect sincerity towards them ; that in their 
differences with Russia we had endeavoured, without expressing any opinion 
upon the claims of either party, to bring about an amicable arrangement ; that 
se had stated our reasons for thinking the Emperor of Russia entitled to con- 
fidence, and that [ had informed him (Count Walewski) of the assurances which 
had been given to me by Baron Brunnow, and which had been fully confirmed 
by the communications made by M. Kisseleff to M. Drouyn de Lhuys; and 
lastly, that the French Government were woll aware that it always had been 
and would be the poly of this country to maintain the integrity and 
independence of the ‘Turkish Empire. 

ane assured Count Walewski, however, that I had not adverted to these 
ints of difference by way of remonstrance or complaint; but that, with 
overnments ag with individuals, 1 thought it best, when any disagreement 
arose, frankly to seek and to give explanations, and that | was sure such a 
course would tend to promote those friendly relations between the two countries 
to which Her Majesty's Government attached so much value. 

Count Walewski received these remarks in the same spirit of cordiality 
and good humour with which they were offered; he said, that any Suspicion of 
the good faith of Her Majesty's Government would be most unfounded, and 
he admitted (though, of course, in confidence) that M, Drouyn de Lhnys had 
been unnecessarily disturbed and precipitate ; but he assured me that the views 
of the Emperor were not those of his Minister,

M. Nicolaievitch declared that M. Garasechanin was entirely innocent of the 
charge, 

After reflecting on this information, I requested M, Nicolaievitch to come 
to me the next day, when I advised him to write to the Prince of Servia, and 
suggest to him that it would be well if he replied to the demand in terms of 
respeet and perfect civility, that. by the constitution of Servia, which was 
guaranteed by Russia and the Porte, no public servant could be dismissed with- 
outa trial; and that the Porte, as Suzerain of Servia, would of course take 
umbrage if the Prince of Servia dismissed a Minister on the official demand of 
Russia, without even her knowledge; that, under these circumstances, the 
Prince hoped that Prince Menchikotf would communicate with the Porte on the 
subject, and that he engaged himself to do prompt and ample justice to any 
complaint which might be addressed to him against M. Garaschanin, in conformity 
with the rights of Russia, the Porte, and the institutions of Servia, 

t observed, that Her Majesty's Ambassador was expected here immediately 
and that his Excellency would, I was sure, aid with his powerful influence the 
Prince of Servia in obtaining justice for a Minister who ba always manifested 
a sincere and effectual sympathy for the rights of the Porte and British 
interests, 

‘The demand in question of Prince Menchikoff, and the threat which aceom- 
panee it, show how yaried are the real objects of Prinee Menchikoff's mission ; 

iow different they are from those which were announced: and how unscrupulous 
are the means employed for carrying them out,

My Lord, Paris, March 80, 1853. 

AT the ball given by the Corps Légistatif to the Emperor on Monday last, 
His Majesty came up to meas soon as he saw me, and said that he hoped that 
the misunderstanding which I had had with M. Drouyn de Lhuys concerning 
the departure of the French fleet had passed over, 1 replied that I had had no 
misunderstanding with the French Minister for Foreign Affairs, though I had 
certainly differed in opinion with him, both as to the necessity for and the pru- 
dence of the French fleet leaving Toulon; and I had felt that the act was at 
variance with the assurances so constantly given me of the desire of the French 
Government to consult with that of Her Majesty in all questions concerning the 
affairs of the Hast. The Emperor observed that he did not know whether 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys had explained to me correetly the reasons which had 
induced His Majesty to consent to the immediate departure of the fleet, or the 
munner in which His Majesty viewed the duties and obligations of France in the 
East. Although he had every wish of acting generally in concert with England 
in Eastern affairs, there was at this moment a shade (« nuance’) of difference 
between the interests of the two Governments in Turkey. There was the 
general question of the integrity and independence of Turkey, on which he 
should be always most ready and desirous to act in unison with the British 
Government, and there was the question of the Sacred Places, whieh concerned 
France more particularly, and in which she must consult her own interests. 
Now those interests appeared to him to require that France should shew that 
she was not indifferent to what was passing at Constantinople. 

The place in which this conversation occurred was not favourable to dis- 
cussion, The Emperor spoke with some warmth and animation of manner. and 
he had already, | observed, attracted the notice of bystanders, Without, there- 
fore, remarking, as 1 might have done, upon the inconsistency of vindicating the 
departure of the French fleet by the present state of ithe question of the holy 
places, instead of attributing it to the true motive, namely, the proceedings of 
Colonel Rose in regard to the English fleet, | said, (as your Lordship’s despatch 
No, 25 to Sir Hamilton Seymour had enabled me to do,) that Her Majesty's 
Government, although they had not disguised from the I'rench Government the 
concern with which they had viewed the departure of the fleet, were yet disposed 
to make every allowance for the peculiar position of France in recard to the 
holy places, and had used all the influence which they possessed at St. Peters- 
burgh, in order to induce the Russian Government to respect the natural suscep- 
tibility of the French nation on this point, I remarked, however, that it was 
mistake to suppose that any question of importance regarding Turkey could 
long be kept a separate question. The Turks themselves, by asking advice 
first on one side, and then on the other, would soon render it European and 
when armies and fleets were put in motion, all Europe took the alarm, . 

The Emperor replied, that he had some reason to complain that the 
Russian Government had never given him the same pacifie assurances which 
they had given to the Queen’s Government, Had they done so the French 
fleet would never have left Toulon. | 

_ I said that His Majesty, at all events, ought to see in the regret which Her 
Majesty's Government had evinced at the single action of France at this moment 
the sincerity of the oft-repeated assertions of their desire that a common under 
standing should prevail between the two Governments in all questions where 
their policy was identical; that it was os mere matter of fact very immaterial 
to us where the French fleet was stationed, but that it was of great importance 
that other Powers should not imagine that a difference of opinion had soning up 
where unity of principle was asserted; that I trusted that for the time all 
danger of complications in the East was at an end, and that we should for the 
faite ice as if these incidents had not oceurred, assuring His Majesty that it

No. 203. 
The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 


(No. 81. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, April 1, 1850. 

ON Tuesday last, Count Walewski informed me that he had that morning 
received letters from Paris which left no doubt on his mind that the Emperor 
had to a certain extent been deceived with respect to the recent intelligence 
from Constantinople, as precedents had been quoted to him which were not 
applicable; and that in fact he had given a decision without having completely 
examined the whole question, and in error as to the course that Her Majesty's 
Government would pursue. 

The Emperor, however, having discovered his mistake (in consequence, as | 
inferred, of Count Walewski’s representations), had declared that, if the sailing 
orders had not been improperly published in the * Moniteur,” the French fleet 
should not have left Toulon; and he would not listen to the persons who had 
advised him ill, and who, finding their views unsupported by facts, had sought 
to cast blame upon Her Majesty's Government for abandoning France and pre- 
ferring Russia, which was the cause, Count Walewski said, of that absence of 
cordiality respecting which J had spoken to him on a previous occasion. 

Count Walewski renewed his assurances that the fleet would not proceed 
further than Salamis, and said he was charged to express the carnest hope of the 
Emperor that this incident would not alter the relations between the two 
countries, nor, should it become necessary, prevent their cordial cooperation in 
the Kast where the interests of both were so entirely identified; and, added 
Count Walewski, “I can give no better proof of how much the Emperor has the 
English alliance at heart than the fact that in order to preserve it he would be 
ready to sacrifice even the holy places.” 

~The conversation, of which [ have now given you the substance, was of con- 
siderable length, and as much of it was of a confidential character, and inter- 
spersed with messages from the Emperor, and expressions not altogether friendly 
to M. Drouyn de Lhuys, no doubt was left on my mind that Count Walewski 
spoke from the direct instructions of the Emperor; and your Excellency will 
therefore consider this despatch as strictly for your own information, 

Alluding to M. Drouyn de Lhuys, Count Walewski said, “I have been 
reproached for not having sulticiently defended the order for the sailing of the 
fleet, and my answer was that I could not defend a course which | considered to 
be unjustifiable,” 

Count Walewski more than once pressed upon me that whenever a question 
of diffieulty arose, it was most desirable that your Excellency should communicate 
with the Emperor, to whom he knew it would always be agreeable. 

The communication of the French Ambassador was of course received by 
me in the most friendly spirit, and I said I never entertained a doubt that 
frank espana one would remove the momentary difference that had arisen, | 
admitted that the sailing order having been published in the “ Moniteur,” it could

ACCORDING to the reports received from Constantinople, Prince 
Menchikoff, after his more formal audience, Was admitted to a private interview 
of the Sultan, at which he had the honour of presenting the letter of which he 
was the bearer from the Emperor.

Prince Menchikoff said all that was necessary to quiet his Highness’s appre- 


hensions. At a previous conference with the Grand Vizier, Prince Menchikoff 


had requested that some commissioner might be named to negotiate with him, 
and that the person selected might not be Fuad Effendi.

resignation,

BARON BRUNNOW yesterday communicated to me a ceahesh a 
Count Nesselrode expresses his satisfaction at the entire Be Naren: “ath

I assured Baron Brunnow, and you will repeat the assurance to Count 
Nesselrode, that that confidence remains unabated. 

I at the same time informed Baron Brunnow that, from various quarters, 
reports reached Her Majesty's Government of vast military armaments and 
preparations in the Southern Provinces of Russia, which, if true, hardly appeared 
consistent with the pacific determinations of the Emperor; and I asked him if 
he could give me an explanation of those statements, which, being published in 
the newspapers, had, as he was aware, created considerable uneasiness. 

Baron Grunnow was unable to give me any information on that subject, or 
upon the mission of Admiral Korniloff to Athens, where, as you will see by the 
inclosed copy of a despatch from Mr. Wyse, he had arrived, and where his pre- 
sence had caused some excitement, 

You will therefore ask for information on these points from the Chancellor, 
and you will at the same time make known to him that Prince Menchikoff 
appears to have told M. Benedetti that. Montenegro was the real object of his 
mission, and that the holy places were a secondary question wpon which he was 
about to inform himself. 

With respect to the latter part of Count Nesselrode’s despatch, which 
complains of the conduct of Colonel Rose, I have to inform you that, as there 
was no opportunity for forwarding the instructions of Lord John Russell before 
the 24th of February, they could not have reached Her Majesty’s Chargé 
d'Affaires on the 9th ultimo; but you will long since have been aware that the 
conduct of Colonel Rose, in requesting that the British fleet should come to 
Vourla, was not approved by Her Majesty’s Government. He appears to have 
participated in the alarm of the Turkish Government, and the great excitement 
of the Greck population, caused by the arrival and first proceedings of Prince 
Menchikoff, together with the rumours that obtained general credit at Constan- 
tinople of the advancing army and fleet of Russia; but Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment are unwilling to believe that, on the part of Colonel Rose, there existed 
any design to thwart the objects of Prince Menchikoff's mission, or to encourage 
the Turkish Government in opposition to the just demands of the Emperor. 

Tam, &e. 


(Signed) CLARENDON,

No, 212. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received April 9.) 
(No. 219.) 
My Lord, 


Paris, April 8, 1853, 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS is much pleased with the assurances which 
M. de Bourquenay has received since he has been at Vienna, of the desire of 
the Austrian Government to maintain the integrity of the Turkish Empire. 
These assurances appear to have been even more categorical than those given 
to Lord Stratford; Count Buol having declared to M. de Bourqueney that 
Turkey must live, and that Austria would neither act alone, nor with one or 
two, but always with the five Powers, on all questions relating to the existence 
of the Turkish Empire. 

L have; &c,

Russia may learn that unlimited authority, although current within her 
own broad borders, is not to be practised with impunity beyond her frontiers. 

Austria, that the alliance of an overgrown military State, although afford- 
ing great powers of repression against her own subjects, would not be a full 
security against the hostility of foreign countries. 

France, that too great a price may be paid for the petty advantages extorted 
by diplomacy from a weak ally; and ‘Turkey, that there is less danger in the 
refusal of a foreign demand, than in the attempt to reconcile contrary interests, 
and in playing off one powerful foreign ally against another. 

There is another Power in Europe by which a very useful lesson may be 
learned from recent events; | allude to the public press of England, 

What has lately occurred may, it is to hy hoped, have the effect of satis- 
fying a very influential portion of that press, that there is no great wisdom in 
encouraging the ambitious views of Russia, and at the same time in alienating 
from us that Government, whose goodwill, at all times of the utmost importance, 
becomes indispensable when circumstances render it necessary that a check 
should be given to Russian encroachment. 

I have, Xe. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

My Lord, St, Petersburgh, March 29, 1853, 

I WAITED yesterday at his desire upon the Chancellor, who was desirous 
of learning, if possible, the truth of the intelligence reported from Paris as to 
Colonel Rose having sent for the English squadron. 

It was of course out of my power to give any information upon the subject, 
and it was my object to point out that, even should the intelligence prove 
correct, there was no reason why that incident or accident should give rise to 
any difficulties. 

[ represented that Colonel Rose might have been influenced by incorrect 
reports as to naval or military movements on the part-of the Russian forces ; 
that there would probably be ample time for sending counter-orders, supposing 
them to be called for, and that even in the extreme case of the English squadron 
approaching the Dardanelles, they would only be in waters which they are more 
usually in the habit of visiting in the course of the winter or spring. — 

Count Nesselrode inquired what degree of responsibility an English 
Chargé d'Affuires was at liberty to incur? To which I replied, that when only 
private risk was to be weighed against public advantage, | thought it difficult 
to enED. any limits to the responsibility of an English diplomatic agent of what-

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, March 31, 1853- 
SEVERAL indications lead me to ‘afer that the Russian Government have 


not been insensible of the dangers which they were incurring by their hostile

I did not like to inform your Lordship of a report that reached me that a

The truth is, that Russia did not make her present formidable demonstra-

accession to power of Reshid Pasha’s Administration, and the question of the 
refugees, has lost gradually her commanding influence here, and now wishes to 
regain it, All Russia’s acts prove this. Members of her own and of the 
Austrian Embassy do not scruple to declare it. 
The means she has recourse to are a warlike demonstration, and, for the 
present, the fairest words.

My Lord, Constantinople, March 19, 1853. 

| HAVE the honour to acknowledge the receipt of Lord John Russell's 
despatch, No. 27, confidential, and to say that | have executed the instructions 
which it contains. 

Rifaat Pasha, Prince Menchikoff, and M. Benedetti, received the communt- 
cations which I made to them, in obedience to those instructions, in the 
following manner. ’ 

Rilaat Pasha said, that Prince Menchikoff had told him that 1 had received 
instructions from my Government respecting the holy places, and asked him 
whether I had communicated them to him. Fis Excellency then asked my 
opinion as to the cupola, saying, that according to his information, which he 
considered correct, it would ‘nat without repair for four or five years more, and 
that his intention was, if the question was mooted by the Russians, to let it 
remain for the present in the status quo. 1 replied that I could not express an 
opinion on the subject, as I had no instructions respecting the cupola. Rifaat 
Pasha requested me to let him have a memorandum of what I had said to him. 
| replied, | would think about it; but as the instruction is & confidential one, 
and Rifaat Pasha has said nothing more about it, 1 thought it more prudent not 
to give him the memorandum. te 

Baron Menchikoff approved the communication of my instructions, but 
dwelt upon the firman to the Greeks as the basis of the solution of the question 
of the holy places, saying, however, that the ees in a concessional spirit, 
would not come back on the past, that is, would not demand back the key of 
the Church of Bethlehem. 

M. Benedetti said, on my holding language to him in the sense of Lord 
John Russell’s instructions, “that he desired nothing better than to adhere to 
the position of the holy places of February in the last year.” 

As this declaration was ostensibly very satisfactory, I thought it advisable 
to say no more, as any further conversation might have carried M. Benedetti 
‘nto an assertion of M, de Lavalette’s protest in favour of the Treaty of 1740, 
which also forms part of the position of the question in February 1852, and 
from the protest to the ominous matter of the cupola; the right to repair the 
cupola being, in the opinion of the French Embassy, secured to France by that 
Treaty and the protest, 

bn the other hand, Prince Menchikoff told me ona previous occasion, 
that the cupola, and the right to repair it, belonged to Russia. ' 

The position of the question of the sanctuaries in February 1852, 1s one 
of contradictions, because the note of the 9th of February, and more particu- 
larly the French protest of that same month, are contradicted in some essential 
respects by the firman to the Greeks of that month, which has beside a double 
Meaning. | 

France has always hitherto declared that she considers that firman a5 an 
affront to her dignity, and an attack on her Treaty rights. 

When, therefore, Prince Menchikoff and M. Benedetti say that they agree 
to the position of the question of the sanctuaries in 1852, they probably make 
mental reservations that they only agree to so much of that position as suits their 


VIEWS. 
9E 2 


But it is very satisfactory if de facto France and Russia, from motives of 


prudence and conciliation, aceept the position of February 1852, even allowing 
that their mutual reservations will come into operation when the cupola must be 
repaired, a few years hence. At any rate, the dangerous question will be as the 
French Government says, ‘enterré,” and rendered harmless for a few years, by 
the end of which time the parties interested in it may have become cooler and 
wiser, or political events may have altered their positions. 


Prince Menchikoff was indisposed ; I therefore communicated M, Bene- 


detti’s adhesion to the position of the Sanctuaries Question in 1852 to Count 
Nesselrode, whom Prince Menchikoft sent to me, he expressed much satisfac- 
tion at the communication. 


Of course the Porte will be only too happy to escape out af the dangerous 


labyrinth in which the peremptory and contradictory demands of the two 
powerful rivals in this great suit have placed her ; she will hasten to ratify the 
position of February, 1852. 


Prince Menchikoti’s language about the holy places is much more satis- 


factory and moderate than that o 'M. d’Ozeroff; he says that it isa question for 
monks more than statesmen; that it should from the first have been treated as a 


matter of secondary importance. 

M. Pisani reports to me that M. Argyropulo has changed his tone, and uses 
the same language to the Porte, having said only yesterday that the Sanctuary 
Question was “ Papasishee *“—matter of monks. 

M. Benedetti now talks less and more moderately about the question than 
he did. [think that the wise counsels of Her Majesty’s Government have 
‘nduced both France and Russia to wish to back out of the question. 

Under these ¢ircumstances I really hope that 1 may congratulate your 
Lordship on the settlement of this dangerous question. 

I have, &e.

IN execution of the instructions in Lord John Russell’s despatch No, 22, I 
abstained from giving my advice or opinion. In the matter of the Holy Places till 
[received his Lordship's despatch No, 27, and 1 confined myself to recom- 
mending moderation and caution in any step taken as to that matter by any of 
the Forcign Ministers here. | 

The detail as to the holy places, as to which the French and Russian 
Representatives evineed the least moderation, is that of the cupola; and 
although i cannot say that I have modified their determination to yield nothing 
of their supposed rights as to possession of it, yet I think that I have dimi- 
nished their wish to enter into a discussion of the subject. 1 think that both are 
inclined to shut their eyes, for the present, and allow the cupolato be a dormant 
question till the repair of it become necessary, Nor do | think it impossible 
that the French Government would not object, were the Grecks, very unostenta- 
tiously, to make such repairs in the cupola as may become necessary for the pur- 
pose of preventing its fall, For I said one day to M. de Lavalette, ‘* Afterall, you 


save been so moderate as to say that you consider the question of the Holy 
Places definitively settled ; but if, as you now state, the repair of the cupola is to 
revive the question, it is not settled, Surely you would not object to the Greeks 
quietly putting in a beam now and then to keep the cupola together, Do not 


let a beam give the world as much trouble as the key did.” 
M. de Lavalette laughed, said nothing, but seemed pleased with the idea.

Colonel Rose to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 15.) 


(No. 109.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, March 21, 1853. 

L HAVE again had a curious proof of the unwillingness of Turkish Greeks 
that there should be a war between Russia and Franee, even on account of the 
cupola, ‘The chief man of the nation, although a most active Russian agent, 
and now all devotion to Prince Menchikoff, said to me, the other day, in a long 
and confidential conversation, that he was willing to make concessions as to the 
cupola ; that even if it were necessary he would consent that the Sultan should 
repair it, without any inseription, except the following ; The Sultan gives this 
cupola to the Christian world ;” he added that I might tell the Porte that if she 
thought proper to ask for this opinion in writing he would give it. He said 
emphatically that neither he nor his nation wished that a war with France should 
ensue about the sanctuaries. I asked him if he thought that the Russian 
Government were of the same opinion. He reflected a little; and said, Russia 
does not wish to go to war with France. 

The fact is that if Russia, even aided by Turkey, went to war with France 
she would be a loser, unless indeed Russia occupied and fortified the Dardanelles. 
That is in all probability the secret aim of Russia. She wishes to establish a 
Turkish Ministry favourable to Russian views, prevail on that Ministry to make 
a favourable treaty, perhaps an offensive and defensive one, with Russia, and then 
give some decision in favour of some great Russian political object, such as 
Montenegro or the holy places. 

I the Western Powers resisted such a decision, Russia would throw off the 
mask, and then Europe would understand that it was neither the ill-judged 
language of M. de Lavalette, nor the key of the Chureh of Bethlehem, nor 
Omar Pasha's supposed propagandism, which had caused the warlike attitude of 
a Russian fleet and of three corps d’armée, and the transmission, a couple of 
months ago, of 700,0001, in gold imperials from England to Russia. 

If Russia once possesses and tortifies the Dardanelles and the Bosphorus 
(she will tell Turkey that she does so im her defence), then she will have a key 
whinh she values more than that of Bethlehem; she will have the key of the 

st, 

Russia has assumed a warlike position menacing to Turkey, and the com- 
inercial interests of the world—a position which enables her to place, in afew days, 
with ease 15,000 or 20,000 men in the Dardanelles ; she has assigned no 
legitimate reason for this most grave act, which is inno way justified by France's 
attitude, which I believe is pacitic. 

Under these circumstances 1 venture to think that either Russia should be 
moved to resume a pacific position ; or that Great Britain, singly or in concert 
with other Powers, should take such steps as would protect the balance of power 
and vast commercial interests from any sudden aggression. 

1 have, &e. 
(Signed) HUGH ROSE.

Vizier and Rifaat Pasha, in vain endeavoured, as he told me himself, to elicit

The important revelations made to me by Rifaat Pasha and the Grand 
Vizier, form the subject of a further despatch. Many usually well-informed 
persons supposed that Prince Menchikoff had merely made general declarations 
as to the nature of his demands respecting the holy places, the 'Turco-Russian 
frontier, and Montenegro; and that he was endeavouring to carry out his views in 
those respects by reorganizing a Russian party, and by influencing, through 
their means, the Sultan and the Valideh in his favour, The extreme activity 
and intrigues of Hussein Bey, the Secretary of the Valideh, Iahseen Bey, and 
other known Russian agents, rendered this report probable. 

The great object of Prince Menchikoff is to overthrow the present ministry, 
which he considers opposed to him. In order to second his views, the Russian 
party, Ahmet Fethi Namick and Heir-ed-deen Pashas, Hussein and Jahseen Beys, 
have endeavoured openly in the Council and secretly in the palace, to effect the 
failure of the proposed new Constantinople Bank. The present ministry have 
very much identified themselves with that measure, which they consider to be 
one of great national benefit. The Grand Council, with the exception of the 
Russian party, has approved the contract for the new bank; it was sent to the 
Sultan yesterday for his Tradeh, but so powerful are the influences brought to 
bear on His Majesty and so susceptible is he to them, that I should not be 
surprised were he at the last to put aside the very plan which he, more than any 
one else, has favoured and developed. 

If Russtin presents, which are most freely given, shall have converted the 
Valideh into an opponent of the bank, nothing is more likely than that the 
Sultan, who is devoted to his mother, should refuse his sanction to it. 

Hosrew and Ahmet Fethi Pashas would probably be at the head, Namik 
and Sarim Pashas, Chekib Effendi, and Hussein Bey, being members of the new, 
that is,a Russian ministry. All of them are of the retrograde party.

Colonel Rose to the Earl of Clarendon. —(Received April 15.) 


UNo. 125). 
My Lord, Constantinople, March 28, 1858. 

MUCH has been said in late French despatches as to Russian endeavours 
to create amongst the Turkish Greeks disaffection towards their Mahommedan 
Governors, and of their organization against the Porte; the only mistake is the 
supposition that such efforts and organization are of a recent date. 

Since the time of Empress Catherine + has been the unvarying object of 
Russian policy to make ‘Turkish Greeks believe that the Emperor of Russia is 
their mereiful protector against the fanaticism and injustice of their T urkish 
rulers. But an anomaly has always distinguished this policy, this sympathy for 
Christians, which is, that Russia, neither collectively nor individually, has ever 
ureed on the Porte the adoption of any benevolent measure of sound policy 
which would have reconciled the Christians to Turkish rule; on the contrary, 
the tendency of Russian policy has ever been to keep alive the causes of 
grievance Which estrange Christians from the Porte, and thereby to draw them to 
Russia, Russian poliey 15 amputation, not cure ; amputation, which enables 
province of the Porte, injured by her misrute, to revive under semi-Russian rule 
or influence ; witness Moldavia, Wallachia, Montenegro, und Servia. 

Greece was severed, but not reconciled, 

Russia, it is true, has often resisted the dismemberment of Turkey, but that 
was when she feared lest Egypt or Syria might fall under non-Russian power and 
influence. 

The benevolent and guecessful efforts of Hor Majesty's Ambassador in 
favour of ‘Turkish Christians were, | believe, generally single-handed. Russian 
cooperation was not given, 1 believe, at Constantinople, certainly not in Syria, 
in support of onc of the greatest benefits granted to Christians in the East—the 
recognition of the valitity of a Christian oath against a Mussulman oppressor. 

lf this great principle of justice be only very partially carried out, stil it has 
received birth, and is in slow but certain progress, 

M. Basily, who is under the direct patronage of the Synod of St. Petersburgh, 
always decried reform, of which the main feature was the amelioration of the 


position of Turkish Christians. His language to me, invariably, was, ‘Ces bons 
vieux Tures qui donnaient des coups de baton et pau des tétes, valaient 
ussians of higher position 


mille fois mieux que les Tures civilizés de Resehid.” 
than M. Basily have said the same. 


it is not that these gentlemen really approved these barbarous acts; but

that they saw with alarm the birth of civilization in Bakes) which introduced 
liberal principles, and threatened to win back the stray allegiance of Turkish 
Christians from Russia to the Porte. } 

The liberal administration of Reschid Pasha indisposed Austria and Russia. 
The question of the refugees completed their estrangement from the Porte. 

Russia affected to pardon; Austria declared, more frankly, that she never 
would forgive the wrong. Butthe Emperor of Russia eaid, “ Elle mela payera ; " 
and those few words were of more omen than Austria's denunciations. 

Since the time of the refugees, Austria and Russia have secretly made the 
Christians of European Turkey instruments of their policy and of their ill-will 
towards the Porte: only with this difference, that Russia has merely had to 
revive, to recall into action her historical mode of doing so, whereas Austria has 
had to learn her lesson how to do so. 

Daniel Petrovich in Montenegro only acts over again the part which “ Little 
Father Stefuno’”’ played there in former days. 

Russia appealing to the Sclavism, common language, origin, and religion of 
the Bulgarians, Bosnians, Servians, and Montenegrins, prepares them and the 
Greeks for the moment when she shall proclaim to them the anti-Turkish 
denunciation contained in the Sclave prayer-book, published in 1851 by the 
Bishop of Kief, “avec la bénédiction du Saint Synode,” and industriously circu- 
lated by Russian agents. 1 have this prayer-book in my possession, and 
inclosed is a copy of this remarkable passuge. 

T have also 4 curious proof of the endeavours to make the Bulgarians is 
Russian as possible. The Russian Embassy here, in opposition to the wishes of 
the Greek Patriarch of Constantinople, insists that the Bulgarian liturgy in the 
Sclave, that isa Russian dialect, should take the place of the Greek liturgy 
hitherto used ; and further, that Selave, and not Greek, should be taught in the 
Bulgarian schools, ‘The intention 1s that Bulgaria, so important by its position, 
fertility, and manly race, should become as Russian as possible. 

Both Austria and Russia for the last three or four years have, by means of 
seeret agents and the local elorgy, striven to revive and increase an anti- 
Mahotedan feeling in the bigoted populations of European Turkey ; in short, to 
organize a sort of Christian militia, ready to be called out at the appointed 
time. 

The Porte has unfortunately by her misrule always played the game of 
Russia. Her Administration, it is true, is now more humane than formerly, but 
‘tis also weaker. She is consequently less disliked but) less feared than she 
was by the Christians. 

The Porte is certainly in a critical state; but ina further despatch I shall 
have the honour to show how she can extricate herself from it. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) HUGH ROSE.

Colonel Rose to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 15.) 
(No. 129.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, March 31, 1853. 

SINCE the date of my late despatches to your Lordship, I have had inter- 
views on the state of affairs here with the Grand Vizier, the Seraskicr, Rifaat 
and Numick Pashas. 

It results from the confidential statements made to me on these occasions 
by the ‘Turkish Ministers, that Prince Menchikoff has not as yet made any 
distinct demand with respect to Russian complaints, except as to the question 
of the holy places. The same remarkable vagueness or indecision marks his 
Excellency's negotiations as has been the case from the first. 

It is not that Prince Menchikoff does not know what to demand from the 
Porte: but that before doing so, his Excellency wished to have the conviction 
that what he asks will be granted, 

But he could not have this conviction so long as the present Ministry, 
which he considers anti-Russian, and favourable to the British and French 
connection, is in office. His Excellency felt certain that the retirement of Fuad 
Efendi, and the intimidation caused by the menacing movements of Russi, 
would have long since effected the dismissal of the present, and the appointment 
of a Russian Ministry. 

But the suecess of the Government in the matter of the new bank made 
Prince Menchikoff understand that all his endeavours, although aided by a 
perfect system of intrigue and an expenditure of 48,0001, secret-service money, 
could not upset the Ministry, which relies chiefly on British support. His Excel- 
lency therefore now endeavours to make the best of the present Ministry; and 
he begins, as I learnt yesterday from the Grand Vizier, by trying to exact a promise 
from Rifaat Pasha, before he makes known to him the nature of his mission and 
of his demands, that the Porte shall make a formal promise that she will not 
reveal them to the British or French Representatives. Rifaat Pasha declined, 
and at once Prince Menchikoff became angry, declaring also that if the object of 
his mission were not promptly settled, he must leave Constantinople, as he was 
fur too old a man to engage in a long and arduous negotiation; but he modified 
this declaration by declaring that he did not mean thereby to imply that his 
retirement would be the signal for war, 

Rifaut Pasha asked Prince Menchikof’ for explanations respecting the 
monaeing movements and attitude of the military and naval forces of Russia, 

_ _ The inclosed copy of a report of M. Chabert will give your Lordship full 
information as to the explanations which took place between Rifaat Pasha and 
Prince Menchikoff on the subject. 
_ Talso incloge the copy of a previous report of the Grand Vizier's conversa- 
tion with me on the 28th imstant. 

These documents will give your Lordship full information as to the latest 
proceedings of Prince Menchikoff, Your Lordship will see, with much regret, 
that Count Nesselrode's and Baron Brannow’s assurances that Russian negotia- 
tions at Constantinople were to be carried on in conformity with the views of 
Her Majesty’s Government, and in cooperation with their servants, have not

My Lord, Constantinople, April |, 1853. 


AFTER midnight this morning the French Chargé d’ Affaires called on me 
for the purpose of communicating to me very important written information 
which he had just received, that ata conference, which took place yesterday between 
Prince Mene tikoft and Rifsat Pasha, and which lasted five hours, the Ottoman 
Minister had consented that three Plenipotentiaries should be named on the 
part of the Ottoman Government for the purpose of holding conferences with 
the Russian Ambassador. | 

M. Benedetti expressed great alarm, and his conviction that a secret 
‘Treaty would be the certain result of these conferences; and he earnestly 
begged me to use all my endeavours at the Porte to avert so great a disaster. 


Although 1 doubted, after the disclosures which the Porte had made to me 


of Russian designs, that she would venture to enter into a secret Treaty, I 
thought it safe, in such critical times as the present, to neglect no precaution. 


Notwithstanding the character given to me by gentlemen of the Embassy of 
Rifaat Pasha, I was in possession of information of his corruption, of his having 
heen in very long conferences with the first Russian dragoman and Russian agents 
for three days previous to his appointment as Foreign Minister, and further that his 
son and interpreter had paid last night two long visits to the Russian Embassy. 

One of the most experienced of Russian statesmen, who has at his disposal 
a menacing army and fleet, a perfect Embassy, the sympathy of co-religionist

48,0001, secret service money, uses all the ckill of Russian diplomacy to obtain 
a secret Treaty from a Turkish Ministry, of which the Foreign Minister 
probably, and the Minister of Commerce certainly, is a Russian partizan. 

Under these circumstances, I deemed it necessary to take prompt measures 
for averting the fatality which the French Chargé d’ Affaires considered imminent, 
This morning early I despatched M. Chabert with an energetic instruction to 
the Foreign Minister; Mr. Hughes with a similar one to the Seraskier; I myself, 
accompanied by Mr. Doria, proceeded to the Grand Vizier at his country-house 
on the Bosphorus. Besides making an immediate impression on the Turkish 
authorities, I wished to see whether the three leading ‘Turkish Ministers would 
make similar statements as to the nature of Prince Menchikoff's conference yes- 
terday with Rifaat Pasha. ‘The result of this combined movement has been 
satisfactory. ‘The replies of the three Turkish Ministers to the several demands 
{ addressed to them, agree in denying the correctness of M. Benedetti’s infor- 
mation, Inclosed are copies of Mr. Doria’s and Mr. Chabert’s reports. 

But your Lordship will learn from Mr. Doria’s report, the fresh proofs which 
the Grand Vizier this day gave me of the bad faith of the Russian Govern- 


ment. They offer to defend the Porte with 400,000 men against the Western 
Powers, of which England 15 one, if the Porte will make a concession to her 
which will make the Emperor of Russia a sort of co-Sultan of Turkey, by making 
him sole protector of the Church of the Greek Christians, who form nearly half 
of the population of the Ottoman Empire. And I venture to direct your Lord- 
ship's particular direction to the anti-English feeling which, by the Grand 
Vizier's revelations to me, appears to characterize the policy of Prince Menchi- 
kaff, His Excellency, talking to me, ‘troduced quite unnecessarily, the subject 
of the refugees, and said: “ The English protected Kossuth, but hanged the 
Cephalonians.” I replied that the cases were quite different; that the Copha- 
lonians had burnt British-protected subjects in their houses, murdered men, anid 
violated women—crimes to which all well-regulated States applied capital 
punishment. | 

Tt would be dangerous not to contemplate present Russian, and I may say, 
Austrian policy also, a5 to Turkey in all its very serious reality. 

These two countries are determined to induce the Porte, by force or per- 
suasion, to conform to their policy, and to give up the Western influences which 
acted on her in the refugee question. 

If Austria and Russia gain over the Porte by diplomacy, then, with Russian 
garrisons on the Bosphorus and in the Dardanelles, it may be doubtful whether 
England and France would think it worth while to engage in the great war 
which would be necessary for the recovery of the lost balance of power, 

If Austria and Russia cannot 80 gail over the Porte, then arises the ques- 
tion—Will they try force ? 

There are those who think that Russia never would have goné so far as she 
haa done, if she had intended to recede without & struggle. 

But it is certain that if Russia and Austria go to war with England, France, 
and the Porte, they go to certain defeat, unless, indeed, we allow the Russians 
to surprise the Dardanclies. ‘Then with the ‘Turkish fleet captured, a Russian 
fleet off the Dardanelles, the rear of those forts protected an fortified, like the 
front and flank faeces, with Paixhaus guns, English and French forces would meet 

with an obstinate resistance—perhaps @ defeat. 

Under all these circumstances, { earnestly venture to suggest that Her 
Majesty's Government should, without any loss of time, play the game which 
she now has in her hands. Notwithstanding all obstacles and dithculties, the 
Porte is still true to us; she wishes us to protect her: she invites us to approach 
and protect the keys of her possessions and of the Kast, She tells us State 
secrets as to Mussin, which if known to Russia, will cause that Power at once to 
go ta war with her. But if the Porte sees that Great Britain hesitates to avail 
herself of her confidence and friendship, ana of her geographical strength, she 
rust unwillingly throw herself into the arms of her historical and geographical 
enemy, 

; L have, &e.

No. 237. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 16.) 
(No. 161.) 
My Lord, 


St. Petersburgh, April 6, 1853. 

I HAVE heard from several persons belonging to the Court, and as well 
from three or four of my colleagues, of the warm approbation which has been 
expressed repeatedly by the Emperor of the attitude of Her Majesty’s Govern- 
ment during a crisis which gave rise to so much anxiety at Paris: an anxiety, | 
may remark, which I must confess myself to have fully shared. 


This indirect testimony is, perhaps, more valuable than any expression 
addressed to a servant of Her Majesty's Government. c 

The last report of the kind which reached me was from the Bavarian 
Minister who, having been accredited to the Court of Sweden as well as to this, 
is upon the point of setting off for Stockholm. 

Count de Bray had the honour of an audience of the Emperor on the 3rd 
instant, when His Majesty, after immediately observing that the conduct of the 
English Government on a late occasion had been all that he could have desired, 
added, In fact our relations with England are now of the most friendly nature, 
the only point of difference between us is that relating to the Refugees, and 
upon that we must suppose that there is little to be expected. 

His Majesty's expressions upon this occasion were the more satisfactory, as 
he had heated only a few hours previously a telegraphic message bringing 
intelligence of the arrests which have taken place at Berlin, Were the 
Emperor's feelings towards Her Majesty's Government and our country other- 
wise than very fricndly, it is certain that no time would have been lost in 
conforming to the common continental practice, of attributing to the agency of 
the foreign revolutionists in London every fresh attempt at seditious movements 
which takes place in any part of Europe. 

lt remains to be seen whether any proofs can be adduced in support of the 
assertion, at first very confidently made here and elsewhere, as to the Vienna 
assassin having been the instrument of the London Committee, 


I may here mention, which I omitted to do at the time, that I took the 
precaution of stating to Count Nesselrode, and to many other persons, that there 
was primd facie evidence of the falsehood of this assertion, inasmuch as it was 
not very probable that an association, as was stated, disposing of considerable

I would here observe that I am very far from asserting that the feeling 1s 
justified. I believe it not to be. I am assured that it is not by a Russian officer 
of acknowledged merit who served in the Hungarian campaign; but I take note 
of a fact which Austria may have cause to regret. 

Another point is worthy of attention. Until lately the Austrian Govern- 
ment had a certain security against the encroachments of a powerful neighbour 
in the sacred obligations of Treaties, but the value of these has been put an end 
to by the new Conservative principles laid down by Count Buol and his colleagues. 
When it is once established that legality means self-murder, and that Con- 
ventions are to be regarded as poison, an appeal to international law can be 
nothing more than a comparison of the number of bayonets which the respective 
States hold at their command, 

According to this new code, the legal rights which Austria possesses over 
Sardinia, Sardinia over Parma, and Parma over the Republic of San Marino, 
may some day be invoked by Russia against Austria herself; Russia having at 
her command above a million of bayonets, and the common Conservative policy 
pursued by the two Imperial Cabinets having singularly increased the inclination 
felt for making use of them. 

| observed in a preceding part of my despatch upon the military turn which 
the events passing in Turkey had given to the ideas of boys and striplings here ; 
but the observation is not applicable to them alone. I heard from a Russian 
acquaintance the details of a conversation which nassed some days since among 
some of the generals, and in which that very cautious soldier and courtier 
Marshal Paskewitch took part. 

The conversation turned upon the readiness with which Turkey might be 
oceupied, After some discussion, it was decided that no serious obstacle existed 
on the part of the Turkish army, and that as for England and France, if one 
Power sent 10,000 and the other 40,000 mento the assistance of the Sultan, it 
was the utmost that could be expected ; while as for Russia, she might pour in 
100,000 men, or 200,000, or as many more us might be required, 

{ mentioned Marshal Paskewitch as having been present at the con- 
versation, and his conclusions, as understand, were quite in favour of the 
ready means of execution of the plan under discussion. [I have, however, 
reason for believing that such influence as he has exerted here has been 
favourable to temperate measures and a policy of peace. 

Unfortunately his fear of incurring an Imperial frown 1s so great as rarely 
to permit his putting forward any opinion which is not entirely conformable to 
those of his master. 

As your Lordship is aware, the ostensible object of the Marshal's prolonged 
visit to St. Petersburgh, has been the duty imposed upon him of presiding over 
the court of enquiry into the robbery committed upon the Invalid Fund, I have, 
however, reason to believe that a better reason existed in the wish entertained by 
the Emperor of having at his side a man whose military experience would make 
his opinions of great value in the event (according to the Russian phrase) of 
war with Turkey becoming inevitable, or (as it might more properly be 
Sepia) in the event of its being considered expedient to declare war against 

urkey, 

Reverting to Count Buol and his colleagues, | would only venture to 
remark that it appears to me that Prince Metternich’s friends can desire no 
better justification of his policy than that afforded by the contrast which it 
offers to that of his successors. 

Whatever may have been his errors, I believe Prince Metternich to have 
been as incapable of handing over his country to the tutelage of Russia, and of 
sneering down the value of an international engagement, as he would have been 
of placing a Russian body-guard about the person of his Sovereign, or of 
inviting France to tear up the ‘Treaties of the year 1815.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received April 16.) 


(No. 164. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, April 7, 1853. 


THE Chancellor, when I called upon him yesterday, observed that he could 
not do better than to place in my hands a despatch, not yet dated, which he had 
just addressed to Baron Brunnow, and which is to be forwarded by a Russian 
courier who will set off this day for London. 

The whole language and purport of this paper (which I perceived with 
regret Baron Brunnow has no order to communicate to your Lordship) gave 
me very great pleasure, 

Count Nesselrode expresses the warmest satisfaction at the despatch 
No. 25, which L had been ordered to commiumieate to him, and in general at 
the confiding, noble, and at the same tine politic attitude taken by Her Majesty's 
Government at a moment of unnecessary alarm. 

The departure of the English and French fleets for the Levant would, it ts 
observed, have been a demonstration so closely resembling a menace that it 
would have rendered it impossible for the Emperor to. act as he desired to do in 
Turkish affairs: the presence of a French fleet in the Levant had its incon- 
veniences, but such as the attitude of Her Majesty's Government was sufficient 
to neutralize: it would be the same with regard to any rinforeseen difficulties 
which might arise at Constantinople. 

With regard to the objects sought by Russia, they were precisely those 
which had from the outset been professed; all the ambitious schemes imputed 
to her were not exaggerated rumours, but rumours devoid of all foundation. 

The Emperor was desirous of attending to your Lordship’s recommen- 
dations, and was prepared to “ ménager’ even the susceptibility of the French, 
although he had learned that concessions in that quarter led only to further 
demands: but thut to these attempts at settling uflairs amicably the Cabinet 
of Paris must lend its assistance. 

There was no question of taking back from the Latins any one advantage 
which had been granted to them. I s'agissait simplement de faire concorder 
ces concessions (to the Latins) avee les dispositions du hatti-cherif, en les 
dépouillant de ce qu'elles peuvent avoir dexclusif, dobtenir aux Grees quelques 
compensations pour le tort qui leur a été fait, et surtout de les mettre i Vabri 
contre le retour de nouveaux préjudices,” 

A preceding passage of the despatch, and one which makes it very desirable 
that Her Majesty’s Government should be placed in possession of the document 
from which | was permitted to copy the above lines, is that in which the 
Emperor is made to declare his constant desire for the maintenance of the 
independence of ‘Turkey, and to renew his promise of duly apprizing Her 
Majesty's Government, should his intention in this respect undergo any change. 

AL the close of the despateh, Baron Brunnow is informed that his conduct 
has been highly approved ot by the Emperor. 

The three points which appear to me to be established by the paper of 
which | have offered your Canis a summary, are: first, the satisfaction felt 
by the Emperor at the proof of confidence in his word manifested by Her 
Majesty's Government—this is expressed in plain words; second, which is plainly 
to # seen, tho apprehensions entertained by the Russian Cabinet of an alliance, 
having for its object a joint action upon the affairs of Turkey, between England 
and France; and third, the almost equally evident desire of proving that such 
an alliance must, from the opposing interests of the two parties, exist more in 
appearance than in reality,
