My Lord, St. Petersburgh, April 7, 1853. 

I FOUND the Chancellor yesterday very much pleased with the accounts 
which had reached him under date of the 24th ultimo, from Constantinople, and 
with those of different dates which he had received from Vienna and Paris. 
‘Vous me trouvez,” he said, “in the highest spirits.” 

We spoke of the differences which required settlement between the nomi- 
nally conflicting pretensions of the Greek and Latin Churches, and Count Nessel- 
rode was eager to admit that they were very align He had, he said, now had an 
opportunity of comparing the Porte’s note to the French Ambassador dated the 
8th February of last year, with the firman communicated to Russia on the 10th 
of the same month, and the difference was so inconsiderable as to render tt 
extraordinary how the French Cabinet should have raised a question upon a 
point so little deserving of serious notice. 

| observed that with the peaceful prospects which were now opening on Us, 
| flattered myself his Excellency could now give me the assurance that military 
preparations were laid aside; at all events, that there was some commencement of 
discontinuance of military preparation. 

Count Nesselrode replied that he did not feel at liberty to give me that 
assurance, but that he did not hesitate to express to me his conviction that the 
negotiation at Constantinople would be brought, and speedily, to a happy 
conclusion.

Sir G. H, Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received April 16.) 
(No. 166. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, April 7, 185d, 

IN addressing Her Majesty’s Government I observe one constant rule, 
which is, to express plainly my opinions both of men and of affairs; I hold it to 
be my duty to have no concealments with those under whose orders I have the 
honour of serving, and feel sure that when concealment is required, your Lord- 
ship will provide that no publicity shall be given to my reports. | 

It is frequently my business to express disapprobation of what I witness, 
but it is infinitely more agreeable to me to bestow praise, and this a recent. cir- 
cumstance connected with the alarm lately experienced at Constantinople enables 
me to do at present. 

Some private letters which have passed lately between Baron Brunnow and 
the Chancellor, and which the latter has allowed me to read, show that the 
Russian Government are in fact well aware that in writing to Admiral Dundas, 
Colonel Rose was acting in conformity with the expressed wishes of the Porte. 

Baron Brunnow, however, being aware that an. official knowledge of this 
fact might tend to complicate the Turkish difficulties, appears to have been 
careful to avoid such Se NiaTaioas as would have confirmed what he had learned 
privately upon the subject, and, as 1 had an opportunity of hearing, this reserve 
has met with Count Nesselrode’s complete approbation. 

I have, &c.

The French Minister has, however, questioned Count Nesselrode very 
closely as to the policy which the Russian Cabinet is pursuing at Constantinople, 
his inquiries being directed principally to these two points, 

Do the Russian Government, after the negotiation opened with the French 
Mission here, contemplate conducting the arrangements respecting the Holy 
Shrines at Constantinople without the concurrence and approbation of the French 
Ambassador ? 

Can the Russian Government, after all the pacific assurances which have 
been so repeatedly given, offer any reasonable explanation of these continued 
military armaments and preparations, for which there exists such slight ostensible 
reason ¢ 

Upon neither of these points docs General Castelbajac appear to have 
received such explanations as he would be warranted in considering as perfectly 
sutisfactory, He looks, as he is justified in domg, with great disapprobation 
upon the intimidation employed for diplomatic purposes in Turkey, and with 
some mistrust both upon the arrangements to be made with regurd to the holy 
places, and to the large gathering of troops on the Turkish frontiers. 

General Castelbajac spoke with some warmth of the manner in which, by 
some perversion of language, Count Nesselrode still represents the assemblage of 
these large Russian armies as made in the interest of the Sultan, and witha 
view to a demonstration which is to render war unnecessary. As regards Count 
Nesselrode’s views, General Castelbajac is disposed to consider them as agreeing 
with his own, and as differing from those of the Emperor, whose personal agency 
he traces in the direction given to these critical affairs, 

Having learned upon certain authority, that the French Mission have been 
taught to believe that Her Majesty's Government have acted a double part by 
France on a late occasion, | have endeavoured, and I believe with some success, 
to combat such a notion, As regards Constantinople, I have shown that nothing 
ean be less like an abandonment of France than our policy has been; that from 
the first moment, as now, Her Majesty’s Government deplored the forward zeal 
of the Marquis de Layalette upon a question of no interest to England, and 
which was certain to arouse the susceptibility of Russia; that as regards the 
despatch of the two fleets, no concert upon the subject existed, the plan having 
appeared at once to Her Majesty’s Government very injudicious; but that Her 
Majesty's Government, far trom seeking to place itself by contrast with France 
in an advantageous point of view to Russia, had carefully pointed out why it 
was that an English Minister had heen enabled to have greater confidence in the 
intentions of the Emperor than could be expected from a Minister of France; in 
fine, that Her Majesty's Government never ceased feeling and expressing the 
greatest anxiety that the honour and rights of France should be carefully kept 
in view in the arrangements to be made about the holy shrines, a point which | 
had been directed to press constantly upon the Chancellor's attention. 

In a word, my abet has been, and continues to be, to prove to my French 
colleague, that the conduct of Her Majesty's Government towards France has 
been of a perfectly friendly nature, and at the same time to avoid all such appear- 
ance of concert with the French Mission as might injure the position of Her 
Majesty's Mission, without offering corresponding advantage to that of France, 

Under the supposition of some great event having taken place at Constanti- 
nople, a8 was suggested by the first news of the summons sent to the English 
and French fleets, the case was different; | was then desirous of showing every 
readiness to act heartily with my French colleague. 

According to Count Nesselvode’s expression already quoted to your Lord- 
ship, in these uncertain times it is difficult to say in what quarter, at the end ofa 
few days, a Government is to look for its allies.

(No. 114.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, April 18, 1853. 

COUNT WALEWSKEL has read to me a despatch from M. de Benedetti, 
which appears to have given some uneasiness to the French Government, and 
particularly as regards a secret Treaty, similar to that of the 8th July, 1833, 
which is suid to have been pressed upon the acceptance of the Porte by Prince 
Menchikoff. 

I told Count Walewski that the same information had been communicated 
to Her Majesty's Government by Colonel Rose, but I had reason to believe that 
the Treaty in question would be nothing more than a written agreement with 
respect to the holy places, and the mode of conducting divine worship und reli- 
gious ceremonies there by the Greek and Latin communities. 

[ then read to Count Walewski some extracts from the last despatches of 
sir H. Seymour, which fully confirmed the assurances given by Baron Brunnow 
of the pacific intentions of the Emperor of Russia towards Turkey, 

These extracts seemed to be quite satisfactory to Count Walewski, but his 
Excelleney said that as things were not yet settled, and as Russia might still 
invade Turkey, he wished to know whether, in the opinion of Her Majesty's 
Government, it would not be prudent now to announce tothe Emperor of Russia 
that all questions involving the fate of the Turkish Empire must in future be 
settled, not by one Power singly, but by the five Powers acting together. 

[ replied that such a course would be doing either too much or too little; 
too much, if France and England still meant to confide in the honour of the 
Emperor of Russia, which events had hitherto justified; too little, if the Emperor 
violated all, his engagements, and, for the gratification of his ambition, ran the 
risk of an European war, 

I therefore considered that such a declaration at this moment might do 
some harm, but could be productive of no good result, 

Count Walewski appeared to agree in this opinion, and did not press the 
matter further, His Excellency did not say whether the proposal originated 
with himself, or whether he had been instructed to make it by M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys.

Colonel Rose to the Barl of Clarendon.—(Recetved April 19.) 


(No. 136.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, April 3, 1853. 

| THOUGHT it my duty again to ask explanations of Prince Menchikoff 
respecting the late warlike movements of Russia, 1 commenced the con- 
versation by reading to his Excellency Mr. Vice-Consul Cunningham’s report to 
yous Lordship of the 28th of March, as well as the substance of Mr. Consul 

eames’ Jast report. [read also, as [had done before to M. d’Ozérott, Lord 
John Russell’s despatch No. 18 to Sir Hamilton Seymour, and the memo- 
-andum in his confidential despatch No. 10 to his Lordship. On a previous 
occasion, I had read to his Highness Mr. Consul Yeames’s report to me of the 
4th of March. 

On all these occasions I have dwelt on the difference of the assurances 
made at St. Petersburgh and London respecting the pacific intentions of Russia 
in the East, and the unceasing warlike movements and pre) rations made by 
her in all parts of her territory from which an attack could be directed against 
Turkey. 1 thought also that I could not do better than use on these occasions 
the excellent arguments employed by Sir Hamilton Seymour in his memorandum 
of the 8th of January last. 

L have urged also, that if Russta had cause to complain of the language 
of M. de Lavalette, the sympathy shown for her in that matter by her allies, by 
the recall of M. de Lavalette, and the retirement of Fuad Effendi, must be con- 
sidered a satisfactory reparation ; that Montenegro had been evacuated ; that in 
short, none of the causes alleged by Russin as causes for a hostile attitude 
existed any longer; but, that notwithstanding this, Russian inereased her warlike 
preparations, and that with a mystery which only increased their very serious 
gravity ; that yesterday the Nestor of the British merchants came to me and 
expressed a just alarm at the menacing aspect of affairs ; that the hostile and 
unexplained attitude of Russia had placed a responsibility on the British Repre- 
sentative here which he had no right to bear; that if he told his countrymen 
of his suspicions, and his ignormice as to the objects of Russia’s armament, he 
might, perhaps, needlessly create alarm, and check or stop enterprizes in which 
they were engaging; that if he did not tell them, they considered his silence ns 
a guarantee that they had no cause of apprehension, and might safely embark 
their capital in peaceful commerce ; that for these and other reasons, agents had 
n right to ask for explanations from the Representatives of a Power who 
assumed, without assigning a valid cause, a hostile position; that his Excellency 
had stated that the reports of the Consuls were exaggerated ; that they had 
made a fuss because a few troops had been embarked, and a little biseuit baked ; 
that waggons could not have been pressed for the troops, because they had their 
own wagzons; that he had told me before that the troops were only in their 
eantonments; that only a few troops could be embarked on board ten suil-of- 
the-line, which constituted the whole effective Russian navy in the Black Sea; 

that General Riidiger had not been placed in command of two corps, that only 
one corps had been put in a state of preparation, and that he really knew very 
litte about the number or position of the Russian troops. 

| replied, that I had good information that large and very unusual quantities 
of biscuit had been ordered to be got ready for large bodies of troops, and what 
was remarkable, to be consumed by Russian troops in Turkish provinees; that 
besides the ten sail-of-the-line, there were other numerous transports at 
Nicolaieff und Sevastopol, all of which had been ordered to be ready for sea; 
that two divisions, that is, « whole corps d’armée, had embarked or was about to 
do so: that the fact that only one corps had been put on a war footing, was 
different from the accounts [had scen from Petersburgh and elsewhere ; that | 
concluded that his Excellency would be able to give me information as to the 
troops, because 1 had heard that he was commander-in-chief of the naval and 
military forces which supported his Excellency’s negotiations. 

Prince Menchikoff made a reply to this last observation, which was $0 
confused that I could not understand it, 

I have also urged that the Porte’s independence, guaranteed by all the 


230 


Powers, required that she should negotiate, uninfluenced by a formidable mili- 
ber demionabration, more especially as Russia had never even given her notice 
of it. 

__ Prince Menchikoff is a very clever diplomatist, and always endeavours to 
shift the discussion from the Russian armaments, which is very disagreeable to 
him, to the refugee question, respecting which he is very discursive, That is 
the grievance which he and M. de Klezl cannot forget, and which they always 
bring forward as a sort of justification for every illegitimate position which 
Austria and Russia take up in Turkey: and it is remarkable how completely 
what these two gentlemen say to me on this subject, tallies with the menace 
which they urge on the Porte to induce her to abandon England and France, 
and give her hand to Austria and Russia. 

In reply to an observation of his Excellency, that England always encou- 
raged Socialists and Revolutionists, I answered that Russin ought not to 
complain of our institutions, which had so often preserved the peace of Europe ; 
that England was a medium between democracy and despotism, which had 
frequently prevented a conflict between their antagonistic principles ; that by 
not opposing too violently democracy in 1848, we had acquired an influence 
over France which we had used for the benefit of other States; that England 
had, by such means, prevented the march of a French Republican army into 
{taly for the purpose of constituting Italy an united Republic. I asked his 
Excellency whether he did not approve that result of British policy. Prince 
Menchikoift replied that he had not heard of it before, and that it was an 
excellent result, 

1 coneluded by telling Prince Menchikoff that I trusted that he would be 
able to give me pacilic assurances. He replied, “I cannot promise you that we 
will disarm.”’ 1 said. “But if the Russian troops could retire ;” he reflected 
and said, “All I can tell you is, that I have the most pacific intentions.” 

My impression from all Prince Menchikoff said was, that he made light of 
Russia’s hostile position for the purpose of retiring from it with as good a grace 
as possible, |

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received April 23.) 


(No, 259, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, April 22, 1853. 

M. DE KISSELEFF has been kind enough to read to me the despatches, 
dated the 6th instant, which he communicated lately to M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
with respect to the question of the Holy Places, and to which reference is made 
in my despatch No, 264. 

As your Lordship will no doubt have been made acquainted with these 
papers through the agency of M. de Brunnow, I will not refer to them further 
than to say that although Count Nesselrode, after examination of the notes (they 
are three in number) addressed by the Porte to the French Ambassador on the 
8th of February, 1852, finds that the concessions made to the Latins are greater 
than he was aware of (he mentions particularly certain houses purchased by the 
Sultan for the use of the Latin monks at Jerusalem), he 1s still sutisfied to abide 
by them, and he thinks that the Porte may find means to reconcile the promises 
made by the Sultan’s hatti-sheriff of the 10th February, with the concessions 
civen to the Latins on the 8th. 

M. de Kisseleff gave me further some details of the conversation which he 
had had with M. Drouyn de Lhuys, He had requested that Minister, if he 
believed in Count Nesselrode’s words, to have a little patience and not to trust 
to ey report which might reach him from Constantinople, and act upon it 
directly. 

Prince Menchikoff was fulfilling his mission regularly. He could not put 
himesclf in communication with the French Embassy at Constantinople until he 
had come to some arrangement with the Porte. He was but following the 
course marked for him by M. de Lavalette, who had obtained concessions for the 
Latins, not only without communicating with the Russian Mission on the subject, 
but without even informing the Russian Government of the nitture of the con- 
cessions after they had been obtained. Prince Menchikoff was charged with a 
migsion to the Porte: as soon as its object should be accomplished, as it con- 
eerned also the French Government, he would communicate with the French 
Embassy, and it would then be the business of the two Ambassadors to assist 
each other to smooth any difficulties which might remain. Until this was done, 
M. de Kisseleff entreated the French Government to be patient. They had 
already dune harm by sending the French fleet to Salamis. Its departure 
from Toulon had, he knew from the language held both at Constantinople and 
by the Turkish Ambassador at Paris, raised the hopes of the Ottoman Govern- 
ment to be enabled, as was their policy, to play off one Power against another. 
Demonstrations of this kind, or promises of support, would only delay the 
settlement which the Russian Government was sincerely desirous of 
obtaining. 

M, dé Kisseleff expresses himself satisfied with the tone employed by M. 
Drouyn de Lhuys in his reply.

(No. 174.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, April 13, 1853. 

GENERAL CASTELBAJAC has read to mea long despatch, dated the 
lat instant, which he has received from his Government, and in which was 
inclosed the last report which had reached Paris from M. Benedetti. 

The chief points of interest which 1 noticed in M. D, de Lhuys’ despatch 
were first, an indication of the hope entertained of a satisfactory settlement of 
the question of the Holy Places ; second, the observation of the difference of 
the position assumed by Her Majesty's Government and that of France being 
more ostensible than real, the presence of an English squadron at Malta 
answering very closely to that of the French fleet now at sca in the Mediter- 
ranean; third, an intimation that events may take a turn in Turkey, which 
would bring the Governments of France nud England into closer connection, 
and an assurance that the contingency of such events is looked to by France, 
not fom mistrust in the Emperor of Russia’s intentions, but from a considera- 
tion of the consequences which the military demonstrations of his armies may 
possibly involve; fourth, @ mention of the orders given to the Queen's 
minister at St. Petersburgh, to endeavour to impress upon the Russian Govern- 
ment a due consideration of the dignity of France in the arrangements about to 
be made at Constantinople. 

These orders, as General Castelbajac is well aware, met with the immediate 
attention of Her Majesty's Mission, 

M. Benedetti reports in his despatch a conversation which he had held with 
Prince Menchikofi, 

He represents the Prince as accounting for the military preparations of 
Russia by the necessity which existed for being in a position to act energetically 
‘a the affair of Montenegro, and as having stated that he had up to that time 
(M. Benedetti’s despatch is dated the 14th ultimo) received no orders for entering 
into negotiation with the French Embassy. 

With respect to the Prince's explanation, it may be observed that what 
might have been a valid reason before the result of Count Leiningen’s mission, 
cannot be admitted as such from the moment that the Porte gave way to the 
wishes or injunctions of Austria, 

With regard to the fact stated by Prince Menchikoff, it appears from a 
veference to dates, that the instructions respecting which M, Benedetti had made 
inquiries ought (after the assurances which had been given to General Castel- 
bajac), to have reached the Russian Plenipotentiary before the middle of March. 

As bearing upon this latter point, my French colleague read to me a note, 
and one it appeared to me very judiciously drawn up, which he had addressed 
on the 6th instant to the Chancellor, and in which, referring to various commu- 
nications, the precise dates of which are given, he insists strongly upon the

obligation contracted by the Russian Government, not to conclude any arrange- 
ment regarding the holy places without the concurrence of the French ambassador 
at Constantinople.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recewed April 26.) 


(No. 8.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, April G, 1853. 
1 HAD an interview at the Porte to-day with the Grand Vizier and Rifaat 
Pasha, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs. 
After some complimentary expressions, they entered at once on the subject 
of the pending discussions with Russia. They informed me that since the arrival 


His sa Nigh Se eee 6, <> OES “SREP Bie a Mea mg NITE ete 


of Prince Menchikoff, the language held by the Russian Embassy to them had 
been a mixture of angry complaints and friendly assurances, accompanied with 
positive requisitions as to the holy places in Palestine, indications of some ulterior 
views, and a general tone of insistance bordering at times on intimidation, = 

‘The points of complaint were, that the Sultan had not responded like his 
father to the Emperor's offers and acts of friendship, that he was too much 
influenced by Governments and individuals ill-disposed towards Russia, and that 
he had more particularly of late displayed a marked disregard of the consideration 
due to that Power. ei . 

The assurances were those of a willingness to promote the continued 
existence of the ‘Turkish Empire, and to renew those cordial relations which had 
been attended on former occasions with so much benefit to the Porte. — ; 

‘The requisitions as to the holy places were that the Porte, after giving satis- 
faction for a vacillation of conduct offensive to Russia, should adhere with 
steadiness to the arrangement proclaimed by the Sultan's tirman, and pledge 
itself toa complete and undisturbed maintenance of the status yuo in future by 
some form of written engagement, A disposition was at the same time expressed 
to acquiesce in the privileges already obtuined for the Latins, und also a deter- 


241 


mination to have the cupola of the Church of the Nativity at Jerusalem repaired 
according to the actual, that is, the Greek forms. 

With respect to indications of ulterior views, there was still some uncer- 
tainty in the language of Prince Menchikoff. In the beginning he had sounded 
the sentiments of the Porte as to a defensive alliance with Russia, but, receiving 
no encouragement, had desisted from the overture. His intimations were now 
rather directed to a remodelling of the Greck Patriarchate of Constantinople, so 
as to make the election of the Patriarch henceforward an appointment for life, 
independent of the Porte; to a more clear and comprehensive definition of 
Russian right under Treaty to protect the Greek and Armenian subjects of the 
Porte in salsa matters; and to the conclusion of a formal agreement, com- 
prising those points between the two Governments. 

The tone of intimidation adopted by the Russian Embassy was explained to 
consist in a peremptory demand of reparation for an alleged offence, in an unre- 
laxing insistance on the Porte’s coming to an early and almost immediate 
decision, in repeated intimations of the Emperor's displeasure in the menace of’ 
interrupting diplomatic relations should any part of the pending negotiations 
transpire, and of retiring to Odessa should the Porte continue much longer to 
protract its hesitation. All this might justly be said to take a deeper colouring 
from the advanced positions taken up by considerable portions of the Russian 
army, and from Prince Menchikoff's official connection as well with them ns 
with the Russian fleet at Sevastopol. 

The Ottoman Ministers informed me that nothing had yet been settled 
between the Porte and the Russian Embassy ; that the nofe verbale containing 
Prince Menchikoff’s propositions respecting the holy places, and modified at 
their suggestion, would probably be laid before the Council in three days, or, it 
might be, on the following day; that they had insisted on being at liberty to 
communicate its contents to the French Embassy, whose opinions must neees- 
sarily depend on the Ambassador newly arrived from the seat of Government. 
Their impressions seemed to be favourable to the probability of a friendly solu- 
tion, and their anxiety was principally directed to the remaining-proposals 
expected from Prince Menchikoff, and to the difficulty of dealing with them so 
us not to compromise either the independence or the tranquillity of the Empire, 

Their anxiety took the form of numerous conjectural inquiries as to what 
was to be done in certain cases, whether supposed altogether or founded on 
communications more positive than they chose to avow, did not exactly appear. 

The sum of what 7 said in reply is this: Endeavour to keep the afuir of 
the holy plices separate from the ulterior proposals, whatever they may be, of 
Russia. The course which you appear to have taken under the former head 
was probably the best; and Tam glad to find that there is a fair prospect of 
its success to the satisfaction of France, as well as of Russia. Whenever Prince 
Menchikoff comes forward with further propositions, you are at perfect liberty 
to decline entering into negotiation without a full statement of their nature, 
extent, and reasons. Should he ground them on any existing Treaty, it would 
be equally incumbent on him to afford a full explanatory statement in the first 
instance. Should they be found, on examination, to carry with them that 
degree of influence over the Christian subjects of the Porte in favour of a foreign 
Power, which might eventually prove dangerous or seriously inconvenient to the 
exercise of the Sultan’s legitimate authority, Hie Majesty's Ministers cunnot be 
denied the right of declining them, which would not prevent the removal, by 
direct. sovereign authority, of any existing abuse, or the more strict execution, 
by the Porte itself, of any treaty engagement, affording to Russia a fair ground 
of remonstrance, 

The personal character of the Emperor Nicholas, his obligations, in common 
with the other greut Powers of Christendom, and his frequent declarations of 
respect. for the independence of the Turkish Empire, exclude the suspicion of 
any attempt to carry his point by mere arbitrary foree. He lies under the 
restraint of moral as well as political considerations. He could not throw off 
the mask and compel the Porte to uccept, on no distinct grounds of Treaty, 
propositions materially affecting the Sultan's relations with a large portion of 
his subjects; and, consequently, to a certain degree, his position in the general 
scale of power, without exposing himself to severe censure, and risking interests 
of the most important description. Were it, however, ta turn out, contrary ta

In the conversation which ensued, | took occasion to touch upon the prin- 
cipal points of your Lordship’s instructions; and I had the satisfaction to find 
the Sultan disposed to enter upon these with apparent frankness and confidence 
in Her Majesty's Representative. 

Referring to Count Leiningen’s mission, 1 explained the circumstances 
which had made it impossible for me to arrive here at that time, and expressed 
a hope that, however to be regretted in some respects, the manner in which the 
negotiations had terminated, would have the advantage of placing Austria in a 
more natural position towards the Porte, and reviving those friendly sentiments 
which had heretofore prevailed between the two Governments. I said, that the 
language of the Austrian Government, when | passed through Vienna, went far 
to warrant this hope. The Sultan spoke to me of Montenegro, and assured me 
that the sole objects of his expedition against that country had been the pro- 
tection of his peaceable subjects, and the vindication of his just authority. | 
replied, that unfortunately right and sound policy did not always go together. 
The Sultan, while assenting to this remark, and agreeing with me that good 
might in future result from the settlement of his differences with Austria, 
appcared to retain a remnant of the painful impressions which must necessarily 
have accompanied a transaction so vexatious and disparaging to him. 

The question of the holy places came next into view. I expressed the 
gratification which I had derived from learning that it bid fair to be settled in a 
manner satisfactory to all parties. I assured His Majesty that we took no 
interest in the affair except inso far as it was a cause of embarrassment and 
eventual danger to him; that language calculated to moderate the pretensions of 
France and Russia had been employed by the Queen's Representatives at Paris 
and St. Petersburgh ; and that without presuming to volunteer any interference, 
I was prepared to afford my good offices whenever they were deemed available 
for purposes of conciliation and friendly arrangement. His Majesty said that 
he placed the fullest confidence in me. 

Alluding to the secret demands as brought forward by Prince Menchikoff, 
l expressed my conviction that the Sultan, in making every reasonable conces- 
sion for the sake of peace and good neighbourhood, would be careful to admit 
no innovation dangerous to his independence, 

These questions, | added, if properly managed, would soon in all likelihood 
pass away, or be amicably settled; but there were other matters of deeper and 
more lasting importance, which depended entirely upon the Turkish Government, 
and affected interests bearing on its very existence. I explained my meaning to 
the Sultan, by reminding him of incidents which, having occurred in this country 
during the last few months, had produced throughout Europe impressions 
singularly unfavourable to the eredit and prospects of the Ottoman Empire. I 
urged the necessity of striving to remove these impressions by the early adop- 
tion of comprehensive and effectual improvements in the administration of the 
Empire, and the management of its vast resources. His Majesty declared, im 
general terms, his willingtiess to act in this sense, and gave credit to the English 
Government and nation for the friendly sentiments which induced them to desire 
the adoption of such measures, He maintained, nevertheless, with some warmth 
of manner, the justice and expediency of his conduct in refusing to ratify the 
loan contracted at Paris without his sanction, T admitted the right, and was 
proceeding to intimate a doubt of the policy, when His Majesty mentioned the 
new bank which he was about to authorize, and which he described as fraught 
with much eventual benefit to the State, affording the advantage without the 

inconveniences of a loan, and relieving his Government from several burthens 
which had long pressed heavily on its interests. He said, that if the plan suc- 
ceeded, its operations might be extended, so as to lead to the introduction of 
railways aud other useful enterprizes, 

His Majesty's language was so far promising, and I have no reason to 
question its sincerity. But more communications must take place upon the 
same subject before | can venture to entertain o sanguine expectation of such 
changes in the spirit and mode of proceeding, as may constitute a real system of 
improvement entitled to the confidence of Murope. 

That His Majesty had every appearance of being inclined to listen to me is, 
meanwhile, un encouraging circumstance; and | hope to find an early oppor- 
tunity of submitting to your Lordship a report of such further steps as | may

serious opposition from France. The Article relating to this matter, and two 
athers, are still reserved for consideration by the Porte. 

But the anxiety of the Turkish Government is not confined to the one 
ostensible object for which Prince Menchikoff was understood to have been sent 
to Constantinople. His Excellency has addressed secretly to Rifaat Pasha a new 
set of propositions, fur more important and comprehensive than those which are 
already known to your Lordship. Although the Turkish Ministers were the first 
to speak to me on this subject, and to solicit my opinion respecting it, 1 have 
found much difficulty in obtaining an unreserved statement of the particulars. 
This combination, of alarm seeking for advice, and of reluctance to entrust me 
frankly with the whole case, is attributable to the threatening language of Prince 
Menchikoff, and to the character of his proposals. Rilaat Pasha has been 
emphatically warned of the danger which he would be sure to incur if any of 
those proposals were to transpire; and the earnestness with which the Russian 
Ambassador insists on an early reply, increases the embarrassment and appre- 
hension of the Porte. 

All the proposals or demands in question, with two or three exceptions, 
refer to the Greek clergy and churches in Turkey. They amount, in substance, 
to the conclusion of a Treaty, stipulating that Russia shall enjoy the exclusive 
right of intervening for the effectual protection of all members of the Greck 
Church and of the interests of the churches themselves; that the privileges of 
the four Greek patriarchs shall be effectually confirmed, and the patriarchs 
shall hold their preferment for life, independently of the Porte’s approval. 

The exceptions are, the protection of Greek pilgrims in Palestine, the con- 
struction of a Russian church at Jerusalem, and the confirmation, with due 
enforcement, of all Imperial rescripts granted to Russia from time to time. The 
whole is put forward as an explanation of the Treaty of Kainardji, necessary for 
its seals execution, 

As the Treaty thus evoked to serve as the basis of another more stringent 
and comprehensive one is doubtless within your Lordship’s reach, I will only 
observe with reference to it that, of the four Articles, which alone, as 1 am 
assured, have any bearing upon this subject, the VIIth allows of a limited 
Russian interference only for one particular church and its ministers, and of no 
direct protection at all; the ViIIth relates exclusively to pilgrims; the X1Vth 
accords to Russia the right of protecting one specified church in this neighbour- 
hood; and the XVIth applies exclusively to Wallachia and other provinces 
restored to Turkey by the Treaty. . 

The advice which I have given to the Turkish Ministers, at their repeated 
solicitation, is to endeavour to keep the terins of arrangement touching the holy 
places separate from the propositions which relate to the Greek clergy and 
churches in general, and to avoid, if possible, entering upon the merits of the 
latter until the former are disposed of by a suitable understanding. 

The Russian Government would, in all probability, be more or less discon- 
tented, if not offended, by the Porte's rejection of the proposed Treaty ; but 
they would not find it easy to justify any overt act of resentment on that account ; 
and the repeated declarations of the i'mperor Nicholas are so many guarantees 
of his adherence to the principles of justice and moderation in his present trans- 
uctions with the Porte. 

It may be presumed that the immediate objects of the Court of St. Peters- 
burgh are to acquire a broader and more effective influence over the Greek 
popuntion in this Empire, and to throw a heavier yoke of responsibility on the 

ultan’s Government when seeking to evade the natural consequences of such a 
Protectorate, ‘There are also, no doubt, the less questionable motives of wishing 
to simplify relations of delicacy subsisting between two Empires which border 
upon each other, and to afford a more efficient protection to those who naturally 
elaim the sympathy of Russia on grounds of humanity and religion. 

Regarding the question from an European point of view, | venture to think 
that your Lordship will not be surprised at the Porte's repugnance to proposals 
of such a nature, when coming from such a quarter. ‘Though here and there an 
individual Minister may be found ready, for private reasons, to take the proposals 
of Russia on trust, I have reason to believe Fant all parties agree in viewing them 
with suspicion and alarm, The opinion expreased by one ‘Turkish Minister, to 
the effect that an acceptance of the proffered Treaty would be a virtual partition 
of the Empire, may be exaggerated, but it must, nevertheless, be taken as repre. 

2K 


senting a very prevalent impression, and showing a degree of foresight which it 
might be dangerous to disregard. ; | sea 

In communicating with the Turkish Government or with any of my col- 
leagues on so delicate a subject, I shall not lose sight of the important interests 
which may be affected by it; nor, while sensibly alive to the objections involved 
in its principle, be unprepared for the eventual introduction of amendments 
calculated to disarm it of evil in the application. ees ¥. 

The prospect in this direction would be more promising if Russia were to 
show signs of being disposed to act on Christian rather than on sectarian pring 
ples. But it appears that the protection which her Government wish to ex oree 
with so little control or limitation, is of a strictly exclusive character; and it has 
reached me, from more quarters than one, that, among the motives for increasing 
their influence in this country, is the desire of repressing Protestantism wherever 
it appears.

T request that your Lordship will consider it for the present as a secret

I have to add in few words that the several conversations which I have 
held since my arrival here with Prince Menchikoff, M. de la Cour, and 
M. de Klezl, have left on my mind the following impressions with regard to the 
instructions under which they are now respectively acting. 

First as to the Russian ambassador. His tone is considerably softened ; 
his object is to reinstate Russian influence in ‘Turkey on an exclusive basis, and 
in a commanding and stringent form; there is no question of a defensive 
Treaty, and, unless as a consequence of the late naval movement from Toulon, 
no thought of military intimidation for the present, but at the same time a 
fixed intention as to carrying certain points of his plan for settling the question 
of the holy places. 

The French Ambassador is prepared, 1 conceive, to make the best bargain 
he can on that subject; but after some increase of pretension, he appears to 
have prepared himself for concession, provided appearances be saved, us indeed 
they are in the principal matters, for the satisfaction of French feelings of honour. 
1 am given to understand that he reckons upon my good offices, and that 
the squadron at Salamis will make but a short stay there, and give to its visit 
the appearance of an evolutionary movement, proceeding in turn to other stations 
in the Levant. 

‘The Austrian Chargé d’Affaires is evidently instructed to communicate 
confidentially with me on the subject of the pending discussions. He tells me 
that his Government was pleased with the language which I held at Vienna, and 
although there is still a leaning towards Russia, | am under an impression that 
he will not support Prince Menchikoff in any proposals tending to increase 
the influence of that Power at the expense of Turkish independence. 

Upon the whole there is reason to hope that the clouds which have 
lung over Turkey of late, will finally disperse without a storm, though not, 
perhaps, without some further causes for anxiety, and the interference of friendly 
counsels,

tenor of it was, that the French Chargé d'Affaires at Athens hod reported to 
his Government that Admiral Korniloff had arrived at Athens in a Russian 
man-ol-war steamer ; that whilst at Athens he had made assurances to the Greeks

respecting the ample protection which Russia would give her co-religionists in 
all matters relating to their religion ; that Admiral Korniloff had besides secretly 
endeavoured to induce the Greek Government to send armed bands, or banditti, 
from Greece into the neighbouring Turkish provinces, for the purpose of exciting 
troubles and revolt amongst their Greek inhabitants, 

Rifaat Pasha also informed me that the Turkish Charge d’Affaires had gone 
to Mr, Wyse, and the French Minister at Athens, to ask them to make repre- 
gentations to the Greek Government respecting Admiral Korniloff’s proeeedings ; 
that he could not see Mr. Wyse because he was il in bed ; that the French Minister

By Viseount Stratford de Redclifie’s directions, I requested Mr. Wyse to 
transmit his Excellency information on this subject. 

The Russian steamer with Admiral Korniloff on board, was the same which 
took soundings off the Dardanelles. ‘ 

Admiral Korniloff is a Greek by birth, who took a Russian name ; he is a 
very good officer, second in command of the Black Sea feet, and accompanied 
Prince Menchikoff to Constantinople. 

The proceedings of Admiral Korniloff are another link of the long ehain of 
proof which shows that the policy of Russia with respect to Turkey is 
dangerous. 

A short review of the principal features of that mass of proof is instructive. 

An Ambassador Extraordinary, in a time of profound peace, Commander- 
in-Chief of and supported by a vast army and fleet, prepared for immediate war, 
for a four days’ expedition as well as a naval and military campaign, having at his 
disposal #00,000/, secret-service money, negotiates with the Porte for the 
purpose of inducing her to throw off her connection with England and France, 
and to become for the future an instrument of Russian policy. The Russian 
Embassy offers to protect the Porte, should she aecept her proposal, with 400,000 
men anda fleet, telling the Sultan's Ministers that England and France are 
“ ill-disposed powers.” 

The day before 1 ceased to act as Chargé d’Affaires, the Porte’s Foreign 
Minister informed me confidentially, as Mr. Chabert reported “with some indig- 
nation,” that Prince Menchikoff had just made a demand, of which the purport 
was, that the Emperor of Russia should take charge of the affairs of the Greek, 
and the Sultan those of the Mussulman subjects of the Porte; the result of 
which arrangement would be that His Imperial Majesty would be a Co-Sultan 
of Turkey, in violation of the spirit and of the conditions of the Convention of 
1841, to which the Five Powers were parties. 

Prince Menchikoff premises negotiations so prejudicial to British interests 
and the balance of power, by threatening the Porte formally, that if she reveal 
them to Eng and, he will instantly break off relations with her, the Porte. 

But besides armies, and some sixty or seventy pennants hovering over 
Turkey, Russia has prepared other aggressors, who duly wait for the signal of 
attack—the Christian garrison of Montenegro, and the able-bodied men of some 
12,000,000 of Turkish Greeks, who have been taught by Russian traditions 
and their Russian prayer-books, that they are “to destroy impious Turkish vale,” 
and substitute for it that of * the Orthodox Emperor.” And as if all this were 
not enough, Russian agents bring to hear against the Porte the decrees of an 
avenging Providence and unerring prophecy; they circulate a pamphlet amongst 
fanatical populations which, after stating that ingland and Protestantism are 
Satanic, declares that a saint has prophesied that this very Turkey is to be destroyed, 
and her Greek subjects set free, after having undergone 400 years of Turkish 
oppression and tyranny, ‘And it jg remarkable that it is in this very year that 
Russia appears to have let loose Pandora's box on Turkey. She has even 
succeeded in inducing the “Times,” which sets itself up as the protector of 
British commercial interests, to advocate a partition of Turkey, which would not 
only be the ruin of those interests, but the destruction also of our Indian power 


and of our influence as a nation, The possession of European Turkey, and of 


the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles, would enable Russia to increase the sixteen 
gnileof-the-line which she now has in the Black Sea, to twice that number ; 
Malta and Egypt could not stand before such maritime strength. 

| have the honour to conclude, by reporting that Prince Menchikoff, not- 
withstanding the great resources at his disposal, has not succeeded in obtaining 


253) 


from the Porte any concession which compromises British interests, the Porte's 
independence, or the Convention of 1841. 

_ ‘fhe manner in which Prince Menchikoff effected the dismissal of the 
Minister of the Prince of Servia, was certainly an infraction of Servia’s and of 
the Porte's rights; but still that incident is not of a went nature, and is as 
nothing in comparison with the concessions which his Excellency has in vain 
endeavoured to obtain from the Porte—concessions involving the peace and 
interests of the civilized world. | Ee 

It would be a source of general satisfaction were the pacific intelligence 
from Odessa, communicated in my last despatch, confirmed. The circumstances 
which made it doubtful, were the fresh demand made by Prince Menchikoff, 
and the non-confirmation of the pacific reports of Mr. Black's Odessa corre- 
spondents, who were all Greeks, by Her Majesty’s Consul in that city.

(No. 17.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, April 16, 1853. 


1 HAVE had some further conversation with Prince Menchikoff this 
morning on the subject of his discussions with the Porte. I have not time, nor 
is it necessary for me, to go into the particulars of what passed between us ; 
but two or three of the leading points may be found not altogether unworthy of 
your Lordship's attention, 

The Russian Ambassador, though he spoke favourably of our French 
colleague's personal qualities and character, complained a little of the manner in 
which he had met the concessions spontaneously made by the Prince himself. 
He saw in M, de la Cour's insistance a proof of the encroaching spirit of that 
Church which proclaims itself universal, and looked for its real cause in the 
unceasing desire of the same Chureh to extend the sphere of its action and 
influence at every favourable opportunity. On that account alone it had 
become necessary for Russia to fix some limit to so objectionable a tendency 
and also to obtain a positive security in some conventional form, no matter 
wena provided it had the foree of treaty, against the vacillations and bad faith 
of the Porte. 

In addition to this essential point, he described the same difficulties as 
those presented to M. de la Cour, observing that he did not despair of coming 
to. an understanding with the French Ambassador on a portion of them, j 

_ He quoted several instances of bad faith on the part of the Turkish 
Ministers, whether correctly or not I can hardly presume to say, and enforced: 
thereby the justice of his claim to a precise and durable guarantee. 

According to his statement, the much-talked-of cupola is of wood, un- 
marked with religious symbols of any kind; and it would seem that the 
masonry beneath, which bears the figures of the four Evangelists, is not in want 
of repair, The difficulty made by the French Ambassador, relates to the intro- 
duction of the Greek Patriarch as charged with superintending the repairs; and 
there is reason to think that M. de la Cour, at all events, will not abstain from 
reserving the rights of his Government on that point. 

I sounded Prince Menchikoff as to his being disposed to wait for a reference 
to Paris, but without refusing categorically, he showed no willingness to extend 
his Dearne far. | 

Ve did not close our conversation without touching upon tt ior 
demands of Russia relative to the whole Greck Church an Mee anel tn 
Turkey. He again sought to attenuate their extent and effect; but | drew a 
clear line of distinction between the confirmation of epecial points already 
stipulated by Treaty, and an extension of influence having the virtual force of a 
protectorate to be exercised exclusively by a single foreign Power over the most 
Important and numerous class of the Sultan’s tributary: subjects. We both 
avoided enterin into a discussion, which might have proved irritating, on this 
question ; and | was glad to learn from Prince Menchikoff, that notwithstand-

THE messenger Ridgway arrived here on the night of the 14th instant, 
although the state of the roads and rivers has been such that for two previous

Lam now in possession of your Lordship’s despatches down to No. 38 
inclusive, 

With reference to the orders contained in your Lordship’s despatch 
No. 85 of the 5th instant, I have made inquiries of the Chancellor respecting 
the object of Admiral Korniloff’s visit to Greece, and with regard to the con- 
tinued armaments of Tussia. 

As to the first point the Chancellor replied, without hesitation, that Admiral 
Korniloff iad not been charged with any mission; that he had proceeded to 
Greece upon an ordinary excursion (une simple promenade); and that he must 
have returned to Constantinople before the intelligence of his departure had 
reached Her Majesty’s Government. 

With respect to the armaments, the subject was one upon which it was 
manifest that the Chancellor was unwilling to be questioned, and that, as 1 
really believe, because he was unable to return a satisfactory answer. 

He replied, that he believed that the armaments were not in progress, but 
that certainly he could not take upon himself to say that orders had been given 
for their abandonment. Such orders as he had before stated, would not be 
issued until a certainty should be obtained of a pacific solution of the question 
of the holy places: pending at Constantinople, at 

With reference to the conversation of Prince Menchikoff with M. Benedetti, 
Count Nesselrode observed, that the Prince had stated correctly that Monte- 
negro was the chief object of his mission; that the question was, as it hap- 
pened, decided before his arrival, but that it must be in my recollection (which 
is perfectly true), that he, the Chancellor, had on more than one occasion 
remarked to me, that Montenegro alone had caused him serious anxteties ; that 
he had ever been of opinion that the question of the holy places was one which 
would be settled without much danger of war. 

Count Nesselrode maintains that Prince Menchikofl’s arrival at Constanti- 
nople has given rise to much excitement among the Greck population of 
Turkey,

(No. 185. Secret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, St, Petersburgh, April 20, 1853, 

1 HAVE taken an opportunity of stating to the Chancellor that one of my 
private correspondents, usually very well informed as to passing events, had 
written me word that he could afhrm that a Treaty of Alliance, offensive and 
defensive, was in course of being negotiated, if it had not been already, between 
Russia and Turkey. 

Count Nesselrode denied the correctness of the statement, and after some 


O55 


little hesitation said, that he did not know what objects could be derived from 
an offensive alliance with Turkey. Having then changed the form of my inquiry, 
the Chancellor replied, that he would again state that the report was mcorrect, 
but that it was true that the Emperor had caused it to be intimated to the 
Sultan, that he might count upon the protection and aid of Russia in case an 
attack should be made against Turkey by France, in consequence of any conces- 
sion made in favour of the Greek Church by his Highness in the affair of the 
Holy Places, 

This overture probably explains much of what has appeared so little intel- 
ligible in the warlike attitude assumed by the Imperial Government. 

It is however to be observed, that upon this point a clue had in fact been 
furnished by the Emperor himself. His Majesty, in the conversation which was 
reported in my secret and confidential despatch, No, 88, of the 22nd February, 
having stated “that he had apprized the Sultan, that if his assistance were 
required for resisting the menaces of the French, it was entirely at the service of 
the Sultan.” I have, &e.

(No. 189. Secret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, April 20, 1853. 

THE Emperor on rising from table when | had the honour of dining at the 
Palace on the 18th instant, desired me to follow him into the next room. 

His Majesty then said that he had wished to state to me the real and 
sincere satisfaction which he had received from your Lordship’s despatch marked 
Secret and Confidential, No. 23, of the 23rd ultimo. 

It had been, His Majesty said, most agreeable to him’ to find that the over- 
tures which he had addressed to Her Majesty's Government had been responded 
to in the same friendly spirit in which they were mae; that, to use a former 
expression, there was nothing in which he placed so much reliance as * la parole 
dun gentilhomme;” that he felt that the relations of the two Courts stood upon 
a better basis now that a clear understanding had been obtained as to pomts 
which, if left in doubt, might have been productive of misintelligence, and, as 
His Majesty was pleased to add, he felt obliged to me for having contributed 
towards bringing about this friendly entente. 

And His Majesty said, “1 bez you to understand that what I have pledged 
myself to will be equally binding upon my successor; there now exist inemo- 
randums of my intentions, and whatever | have promised, my son, if the changes 
alluded to should occur in his time, will be os ready to perform as his father 
would have been.” 

The Emperor proceeded to state that he would very frankly offer an 
observation or two—it might be a criticism, on your Lordship’s despatch. 

The despatch spoke of the fall of the Turkish Empire as an uncertain and 
distant event: he would remark that the one term excluded the other; uncertain 
it was certainly, but for that reason not necessarily remote: he desired it might 
be, but he was not sure that it might so prove, 

His Majesty desired further to observe that he could not doubt that Her 
Majesty's Government had taken too favourable a view of the stute of the 
Christian population in Turkey ; the Sultan might have intended to better their 
condition, might have given orders in that sense, but he was quite certain that 
his commands had not been attended to, 

Upon my remarking that Her Majesty's Government were understood to 
receive very aecurate reports of what passes in Turkey, the Emperor replied with 
considerable animation that he called this fact in question; that he believed on 
the contrary that some of the English Consular Agents were incorrect (His 
Majesty made use of a stronger expression) in their reports: he would only 
refer to Bulgaria; the greatest discontent prevailed there, and His Majesty 
would affirm thet were it not for his continued efforts to repress the manifesta- 
tion of feelings of the sort, the Bulgarians would some time since have been in 
insurrection, 

His Majesty proceeded to contrast the threatening attitude which had been 
assumed by Count Leiningen with the peaceable character of Count Menchikoff's 
mission, not, however, that he desired to blame the Emperor of Austria, a 
noble Prince whom he loved sincerely, and all of whose acts he approved; the 
difference existed in circumstances, und when Montenegro was threatened with 
utter devastation, the Emperor of Austria was obliged to act with energy; His 
Majesty's would, he said, have acted in the same manner,” 

lam desirous of remarking here, that part of the Emperor's observations 
were, it was Obvious, addressed to me personally, and were intended as a reply 
us well to an allusion whieh I had meas as to religious intolerance in Tuscany, 
us to my comments to the Chancellor upon the conduct of the Austrian Cabinet 
with regard to the lute contiseatory measures in Lombardy, 

By this time His Majesty had become still more animated, and after 
observing that according to the accounts just received (those of the 29th ultimo) 
little or no progress had been made towards an adjustment of difficulties at 
Constantinople, said that as yet ho had not moved a ship or a battalion; that 
he had not done so from motives of consideration for the Sultan and from

old capitulations which were quoted by the French in support of various preten- 
sions were represented as having the value of Treaties; that it was therefore 
desired that an arrangement, which it was intended should be permanent, should 
possess an unquestionable character of this description. 

Count Nesselrode proceeded to remark upon the proofs of moderation 
which the Russian demands upon the Porte, as explained by Prince Menchikoff's 
note, exhibited, and contrasted them with the threatening messages and 
fornatable ultimatum of which the Prince had been represented to be the 

earer. 

As regards the two parties with whom the Porte has to deal,—one, his 
Exeeclleney observed, represented a very extensive, the other a very tolerant 
religion. On one side was a solitary convent, and some eighty travellers, 
attracted chiefly by motives of curiosity; on the othen ten millions of subjects of 
tee Sultan, and great crowds of foreign pilgrims, animated by fervid religious 
eelings. 

Count Nesselrode proceeded to pet of the last accounts which he had 
received from Constantinople, and which, although inconclusive, were, as far as 
they went, satisfactory. 

Prince Menchikoff’s interview with Rifaat Effendi led to the belief that the 
dispositions of the Porte were conciliatory: the same report had been made of 
the language held by the English and French Ambassadors. 

The greatest difficulties apprehended by the Chancellor are those connected 
with the repairs of the Church of Bethlehem ; and these, his Excellency con- 
ceived, might be the more readily avoided as, if necessary, the repairs might be 
deferred for a few years, 

I was careful to remark, that this: suggestion had been made originally by 
Colonel Rose, whose conduct had nevertheless licen on some occasions consis 
dered as uneonciliatory. Count Nesselrode’s language gave me to understand 
that if the rights of the Greek Church were once solemnly recognized and 
secured, every disposition would exist on the part of that church to enter into 
such arrangements as would be found acceptable to the Sultan. 

On the whole, I collect that Count Nesselrode anticipates a satisfacto 
solution of church difficulties; and supposing such an adjustment to be made, 
cannot doubt that few weeks will elapse before reasonable men of all ereeds will 
look back with astonishment upon the stir which has been made about objects 
of such trifling importance. 

My conversation with his Excellency took place on the 19th instant.

faith, would have found means to conciliate their conflicting claims, 

Notwithstanding that M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ language was throughout this 
interview positive as to not admitting certain of the pretensions of Russia, I am 
under the impression that the French Government will accept any arrangement 
that M. de la Cour may make, even if he admits all that Russia asks for in the 
Convention of which I have given the analysis, 

If | have not mistaken the real feeling of the French Government, it 1s 
that M. de la Cour should take upon himself the responsibility of settling the 
question, no matter how, that they may be able to say at Rome, the affair is 
settled, and although we aye the arrangement, we cannot consent to open the 
question again. M. de la Cour would be sacrificed, but there would be an end 
to the matter, 

Unfortunately M. de la Cour either does not or will not understand what is 
required of him, and appears just as anxious that the responsibilit of any 
arrangement should rest with M, Drouyn de Lhuys, as M. Drouyn de Lhuys is 
desirous that it should remain with M. de la Cour, .

My Lord, Paris, May 2, 1853. 

SINCE writing my despateh No. 980, reporting the substance of the last

have received through your Lordship’s kindness copies of the latest reports 
addressed to you by Lord Stratford. 

In comparing them with those written by M, de la Cour, L observe that 
the Porte has been much more frank and unreserved in its communications with 
Lord Stratford than it has been in its relations with the French Ambassador. 

I have further to remark, that the draft of Convention proposed by Russia 
for the settlement of the question of the holy places has not been communicated 
in its original form to M. de la Cour, but with the modifications introduced into 
it by the Turkish Ministers, and M. de la Cour appears to have no knowledge of 
the original text. On the other hand, Articles III, V, and VIL, which in the 
copy given to Lord Stratford had been reserved for further deliberation, are filled 
up in the copy furnished to M. dela Cour, ‘The substance of them is much the 
same as that proposed by Russia, but the words employed are, as in the other 
amended Articles, less positive, and consequently less likely to meet with oppo- 
sition from Trance. 

I endeavoured to obtain, for your eee information, a copy of the 
Convention as submitted for the consideration of M. de la Cour, but M, Drouyn

improvement has been remarked of late in the tone and demeanour of Prince 
Menchikoff, It is remarkable at the same time that Count Nesselrode appears 
to have made no mention whatever of the ulterior and very important propo- 
sitions brought forward here by the Russian Ambassador. This reserve cor- 
responds with the endeavours made by Prince Menchikoff to insulate the Porte 
in its eventual negotiation respecting them, and his endeavours for that purpose 
are the more significant, as the principal interpreter of the Russian Embassy 
is alleged to have said in conversation within the last few days, that if the 
Prince failed in carrying his points, he would simply embark the Embassy, and

Consul Yeames to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


(Extract.) Odessa, April 11, 1853. 

THE concentration of each of the three divisions of the 5th corps d’armée 
is at the present day completed, namely, the 13th division of infantry at 
Sevastopol; the 14th at Odessa; and the 15th at Leovo, on the Pruth, The 
artillery of the corps, usually kept in the rear on the left, bank of the Dnieper, 
has already joined the divisions; and the 5th division of cavalry, composed of 
four regiments, 18 in march from Wornozensk to the Pruth. Such is the front 
of the demonstration; of the actual movements in the rear, necessary for its 
support, I have great doubt. It is certain that the 4th corps d’armée was from 
the first ordered to take a part in these operations, and that the reserves were 
called together from both the 4th and Sth corps. The cantonments of the 4th 
lay facing the frontier of Galicia, extending from the kingdom of Poland to the 
Dneister, with its centre and head-quarters at Kremenetz, It was by a flank 
movement to concentrate in Upper Researabia, with its advanced division at 
Lipkani, on the Pruth: but [ believe that no such movement has commenced ; 
and that it is utterly impossible in the present state of the roads of Volhynia 
and Podolia. These troops, therefore, cannot be in the positions designed 
within, at the least, six weeks; and so long will the 5th corps be entirely 
unsu pported ; 

‘The division at Sevastopol is of course prepared for an ex vedition by sea ; 
ane we are told of the troops being exercised in the operation of embarking and 
anding. 

The division here is destined for the same kind of service. Every man, 
including officers, is to carry rations for four days. No baggage will be taken, 
otherwise conveyed, and no horses are to be shipped. 

With regard to the object of these embarkations, 1 have no information 
whatever, The ficet at Sevastopol may, it is said, take on board a complete 
division of infantry for a short voyage, No transports have been assembled, 
nor have any merchant ships been engaged. A division is composed of sixteen 
battalions, and its field artillery of eight batteries. The present effective 
strength of the battalion cannot exceed 800 men; so that at each of the three 

ints, Sevastopol, Odessa, and Leovo, the force assembled is under 13,000 men, 

he reserves called to their standards in January, were to muster at ‘Toula, 
Ove}, and Woronije. They compose four battalions for each division, and they 
are still very far in the rear, 

Preparations in front continue in great activity; of those in the rear T have 
doubts; and it is still whispered that the reserves are not advancing. The fleet 
has not moved, and the ships have not yet left their winter berths. 1 need 
searcely say that the newspaper reports of reviews by Prince Menchikoif of 
armies and fleets, before proceeding on his mission, are entirely unfounded, It 
‘s the fashion likewise to talk of a popular feeling in this country for war with 
Turkey ; now, there are no popular feelings in Russia, and most assuredly none 
would find utterance, ‘There is no ardour for such a war even in the army, 
usually desirous of acti: Comfortable quarters in the two Danubian princi- 
alities may be thought of; but it is not Forgotten that 300,000 men perished 
ignobly in the two miserable campaigns of 1828 and 1829. No one will 

Feaume to affirm that there is now more ability or less corruption than 

ormerly ; and all are aware that the want of the one, and the prevalence of 

the other, have been the causes of Russian disasters, In the science required 

for the preservation of armies, no prowers has been made. Already disease is 

spreading among the troops now here assembled, in the form of scurvy and 

ophthalmia, which cause at times eu ravages. Of the three battalions

(No. 16.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, April 16, 1853. 

| SAW the French Ambassador this morning, before he went to have his 
appointed conference with Rifaat Pasha. The principal object of my visit was 
to let M, de la Cour know on what points it might be expected that Russia 
would make no concession, and to dissuade him from committing himself on 
those points towards Rifaat Pasha, if, as J hoped, he did not mean to render am 
amicable solution of the whole difficulty impossible. 1 explained that the points 
in question were those of the cupola, of a Greek porter in the church at Beth- 
lehem, and of Greek precedency as to the time to be fixed for the performance 
of certain religious functions, not only there, but also in the Chapel of the 
Virgin at Gethsemane, 1 gave him to understand that I thought the Greek 
pretension stood on strong ground im these respects; and I urged him to bear 
in mind the great European interests at stake; the declared moderation of his 
Government : the ‘satisfaction already given by Russia to France as to the 
key" and the ‘‘star;” and the importance of regulating all that concerns the 
holy places, without further delay, in order that the ulterior propositions of 
Russia might rest upon their own merits, and be dealt with accordingly ; not 
for the extension ofa single influence, nor for the benefit of a single class of 
Christians, but on true principles of European policy, and, if possible, for the 
advantage of all the Sultan's tributary subjects. 

| must do M. de la Cour the justice to state that he appeared to enter Into 
the spirit of my suggestions, at the same time that he did not give up his objec- 
tions to the Russian plan of settlement. He read to me some concinatory, but 
still rather antagonistic passages from a despatch addressed to him by M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys, but also intimated that he was not prepared to give way Gn every 
point to the Russian Ambassador, with whom he had held a long conversation 
the day before. : 

As I am to have an account from both parties of whatever may occur at 
the approaching interview between them, and shall then, in all likelihood, be at 
liberty to take a more decided course for helping to remove the obstacles to a 
mutual understanding, it is unnecessary for me to trespass further on your 
Lordship’s time at this moment, 

I have, &e, | 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

My Lord, Constantinople, April 20, 1853. 

| AM now able to report that the discussions between Rifaat Pasha and 
the Ambassadors of France and Russia, respecting the BF places, have every 
appearance of drawing to an amicable and satisfactory conclusion. The points 
of difference which remain have very little importance in the sight of an impar- 


' 
2% a 


aie eds a 


ent 


n 7 
i Se 
i = 


275 


tial observer. They are matters rather of form than of substance, and in 
number they do not exceed two or three, 

I had some conversation upon the subject this morning with Prince 
Menchikoff, and subsequently with M. dela Cour. 1 endeavoured, as I had 
done before, to bring them to a more complete understanding, without putting 
myself forward beyond what they appeared themselves to desire. I had hoped, 
indeed, that the result of their direct communications with each other would 
have rendered my interference superfluous, ‘The remaining antagonism between 
them consists chiefly in this: the Russian Ambassador, suspicious of future 
encroachments, strives for every particular belonging to the status quo; while 
the French Ambassador reserves what he conceives to be his right under the 
Treaty of 1740, and seeks, by maintaining the Latins on an equal footing with 
the Greeks, to open a door for further advances hereafter, at some period more 
or less distant. 

In communicating with Rifaat Pasha, 1 have suggested whatever appeared 
to me best calculated to conciliate the existing differences. I have urged him 
most earnestly to settle all that relates to the holy places before he enters upon 
the ulterior demands of Russia, conceiving it to be highly desirable that the two 
questions should be kept separate ; and I have expressed my opinion that it was 
daily becoming more urgent for the Porte to terminate the discussion by the 
promulgation of a firman incorporating the terms agreed upon, and deciding 
equitably the still-disputed points, respecting which it seems to me that the 
Porte might in fairness almost entirely side with Russia. 

The real difficulties and just causes of anxiety to the Porte remain to be 
considered. ‘They are already known to your Lordship, and they are formidable, 
though [am happy to say that Prinee Menchikoff, aver a second conversation 
between us on the subject of his demands concerning the Greek Chureh, has 
informed me that he no longer means to press that part of them which regards 
the Greek Patriarchs and their patents of privilege. He explained this 
important change of pine by stating that he recognized the impossibility of 
separating the political from the spiritual character of the Patriarch, and that 
his Government disclaimed all intention of interfering with the Sultan's subjects 
in any political sense, He has since read over to me his amended draft of a 
Convention framed with the view of repeating and confirming the privileges 
secured to the Greek religion and its places of worship in Turkey by former 
Treaties, and particularly by that of Kainardji. | 

This agreement, whatever may be its name or its form, is to have the force 
of a Treaty, and the preamble is in the customary solemn style of that kind 
of instrument. As fur as my memory serves, the terms are such as to give to 
the Russian Representative here a virtual right of protection over the Greek 
Church and clergy throughout the Sultan’s dominions, and by a necessary, 
though underhand consequence, a vast exercise of influence on the Greek popu- 
lation at large, This advantage would result from taking Article VIT of the Treaty 
of Kainardji with some modification of its terms, from extending the provisions 
of Article XVI, which concerns the Danubian provinces alone, to the whole 
empire, and from adding in substance, with a slight management of the terms, 
that Article of the Treaty of Carlowitz which gives to Austria the nght, not 
indeed of protecting the religion of Roman Catholic subjects in Turkey, but of 
calling the Porte’s atteution to any just matter of complaint in that respect. 

As Prince Menchikoff assured me, at the same time, that the proposed 

fonvention was limited to an explanatory confirmation of existing Treaties, 
necessary as a guarantee to Russia, and only granting to its coreligionists what 
Austria already possessed with regard to hers, 1 am willing to hope that the 
Impressions retained by me would disappear on a closer and moro leisurely 
examination of its terms. [ did not, however, leave him without remarking 
that the Sultan’s promise to protect his Christian subjects in the free exercise 
of their religion differed extremely from a right conferred on any foreign Power 
to enforce that protection, and also that the same degree of interference might 
be dangerous to the Porte when exercised by so powerful an empire as Russia 
on behalf of 10,000,000 of Greeks, and innocent in the case of Austria, whose 
influence, derivable from religious sympathy, wis confined to a small number 
of Catholics, including her own subjects, 

_ The other ‘Articles of Prince Menchikoff’s draft were not of a nature to 
involve any objectionable or ulterior consequences; but an enumeration by

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received May 9.) 
(No. 25.) 


My Lord, Constantinople, April 25, 1853. 

I HAD an interview yesterday with the Grand Vizier and Rifaat Pasha, at 
their request, at the country-house of the former. 

They confirmed to me the final settlement of the question concerning the 
holy places, and expressed warmly their thanks for the part which I had taken 
in bringing it about, 

They next informed me that the Government was determined neither to 
enter into # Convention with Russia on that subject, nor to accept Prince Men- 
chikoff’s proposals respecting the protection of the Greek Church in Turkey. 

The line of conduct to be otherwise pursued by the Porte in dealing with 
Prince Menchikoff was an object of anxious inquiry to both of them. After 
presenting the matter in various lights, they agreed with me in thinking that if 
the Russian Ambassador were to offer an amended draft of his Conventiou, the 
best course would be to receive it for examination, and on finding it inadmissible 
as to any essential points, to decline negotiating without a previous distinct 
withdrawal of the objectionable parts, and to intimate at the same time a doubt 
whether the remainler would be worth the trouble of a negotiation. Were his 
Excellency to express a different opinion, preferring a simple confirmation of the 
Articles of existing Treaties concerning the Greek religion to no Convention at 
all, it might, we thought, be more advisable, on the whole, to meet his wishes 
in that respect than to hazard the consequences, whatever they might be, of his 

retiring in disgust. 

1 urged them strongly to complete the firmans relating to the holy places 
with all practicable specd, and to invest the official note, which is to accompany 
the communication of them to the two Ambassadors, as much as possible with 
that character of guaranty to which the Emperor of Russia appears to attach the 
highest importance. 

In the course of discussion I learnt from Rifaat Pasha that the French 
Ambassador had warned him not to admit any contradiction between the firmans 
and the note delivered by Aali Pasha to the French Embassy in February of last 
year, and | presume that his Excellency would, in the contrary ease, make a 
special reservation of his rights, The two Ministers assured me that no such 
contradiction existed, and that I should have the firmans to look over before 
they were finally delivered. The Council is to meet the day after to-morrow, 
and whatever remaing to be done as to these matters will be taken into formal 
consideration. 


Before we separated, I returned to the great ane of reform, I endea- 


voured to make the two Ministers sensible, first, of the advantages which they 
would derive from solemn ty confirming and rendering more practically effective 
and comprehensive the privileges and immunities conferred by successive Sultans 
on the tributary subjects of the Porte; and, secondly, of the necessity which 
urged their Government to lose no time in striving to recover their position in 


ui 

: urope by a system of improvement acting 
on all the branches of administration, developing the resources of the empire, 
and bringing it into harmony with the spirit of the times, the claims of humanity, 
and the just expectations cf commerce. In support of my counsels I pointed 
out the causes of those humiliations which they had lately undergone, and gave 
them, though guardedly, some insight into the dangers from which they had not 
yet entirely escaped, and which, if removed for the time and not destroyed in 
their causes by the application of adequate means, would infallibly return with 


augmented force at no distant period. 
They appeared to adiit the truth, they could hardly doubt the sincerity, of 
my suggestions; and fam authorized by their assurances to expect the adoption 
of such measures as | may recommend or approve, as s00n As their present 
difficulties with Russia shall be overcome, Experience will not allow me to be 
sanguine in this respect ; and, ag to any immediate extension of Christian privi- 
leges, I feel more hope than confidence,
