Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received May 9.) 


(No. 299.) 
My Lord, Paris, May 8, 1653. 

THE Constantinople mail of the 25th ultimo reached Paris this morning, 
and I have seen M. Drouyn de Lhuys this afternoon. I am happy to be able 
to state to your Lordship that it brings intelligence of a mature similar to that 
which had alrendy reached Her Majesty’s Government by telegraph, and that the 
question of the Sacred Places may be considered as settled. 

It would appear from M, de la Cour's reports, that Prince Menchikoff had 
at leneth lent himself to enter into amicable conferences, and that the result had 
been an amicable arrangement. 

The question of the repairs of the cupola of the Church of the Holy 
Sepulchre had been solved in the manner indicated in one of Lord Stratford's 
first despatches to your Lordship; that is, the wood-work surmounting the 
whole, on which no images or inscriptions could be placed, was alone to be 
repaired. ‘The under part was to remain in statu quo. Instead of giving the 
Greek Patriarch the superintendence of the repairs, as required by Russia, it is 
enid that he may make observations respecting them if he pleases. 

The question of precedence is arranged thus: The Greeks will possess it

of so doing, and had written to M. de la Cour to say that he considered the 
arrangement might be accepted, or rather that the French Government had no 
objection to raise ugainst it, 

Yor throughout this conversation M. Drouyn de Lhuys, although constant! 
making use of the words ‘accepted by France,’ or “ objected to by France,” 
when speaking of the different points in dispute, was careful to impress upon me 
that he considered France to be rather a tacit spectator of the arrangement made 
with Russia, than a participator in it. He never could have put his name, he 
said, to any document sanctioning it; for France would, in so acting, have been 
surrendering the rights of Rome. As it was, he feared that Rome would be 
much displeased, and would remonstrate with the French Government: there- 
fore, he added, “we have rather shut our eyes to what Russia is doing (nous

My aa hee St. Petersburgh, April 27, 1853. 
dk French Minister has had the kindness to read to ut af the 
ssa rei mh he has received from Paris. ee ee 
espatch from M. Drouyn de Lhuys, dated the 15th instant, is of consi 
i | , tant, is of consi- 
derable interest. Its chief purport is to show that France, although disposed 
act ® conciliatory part with regard to the holy pluces, cunnot entirely give u 
nghts which have been secured by ancient Capitulutions ; and above all, to make 
it clear that an attempt on the part of Russia to settle this affair without the 
participation of the French Embassy, would inyolve a direct breach of faith. 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys almost sees that the despatch [which Marquis 
O02

Piel 


Castelbajac took upon himself to suppress, had not been communicated to the 
Chancellor; and adduces, as a proof of the dictatorial tone assumed by Russia 
in Turkish affairs, the fact of the Imperial Cabinet having called upon. the 
Prince of Servia to dismiss his Minister Garaschanin, contrary to the wishes of 
the Prince and of the country, the result being, as M, Drouyn de Lhuys states, 
that Servia is actually demanding the support of the Sultan against Russian 
encroachments, 

Of the two inclosures to the French Minister's despatch, the one is a despatch 
dated the 31st of March from M. Benedetti, who speaks of the mystery in which 
Prince Menchikotf’s negotiation is involved, and of the objects which he is 
supposed to be pursuing. He conjectures that he has in view the conclusion of 
an offensive and defensive alliance between Russia and Turkey, and has some 
reason for believing that he has offered to extricate the Turks from their present 
financial difficulties by means of a loan; Russia—who, as | may observe, would 
have to borrow at 4 per cent.—being, M. Benedetti states, ready to advance 
money to the Porte at 24 per cent. 

The second inclosure, a despatch from M. de Bourqueney, of the 28th 
ultimo, isa very remarkable paper. 

M. de Bourqueney gives an account of a conversation with Count. Buol, 
which goes to prove that little difference exists between the Cabinets of Vienna 
and Paris in their view of Turkish affairs, 

Count Buol is represented as approving warmly the conciliatory conduct of 
France in the question of the holy places, as ready to support the very reason- 
able objects which are pursued by France, and as so little disposed to concur in 
the policy adopted by the Emperor of Russia towarks Turkey, that, in speaking 
of Turkish affiirs, he observed, ‘Tout par les cing Puissances, rien par quatre, 
ni par trois, ni par deux;" an expression which appears to me well worthy of 
being recorded. 

In a second despatch, like the other under date of the 15th ultima, 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys informs my French colleague that the good offices of France 
have been and will continue to be employed for the adjustment of difficulties 
between Austria and Sardinia. He further states that negotiations are on fool 
between Austria and the Swiss Confederation, which warrant a belief that the 
just demands of the former will be complied with without that reeourse to 
violence which would be open to so many objections. 

Before leaving me, General Castelbajac informed me that it appears from a 
report received at Paris from M. de Varennes, that Baron Manteutfel views 
with as little approbation as Count Buol, the conduct which the Russian Cabinet

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, April 30, 1853, 

THE Chancellor, upon whom 1 called yesterday by appointment, had the 

kindness to read to me several passages from a despatch and a private letter from 
Prince Menchikoff, of the date of the 16th instant, which produced a favourable 
Impression upon my mind, 
Not only was the manner in which the Prince speaks of his English and 
French colleagues such as to indieate his being upon terms of friendly inter- 
course with them, but in the account which he gives of his official interviews 
with M. de la Cour, it appears that in so far as any latitude has been left to him 
it has been his wish to conciliate the rights of the Greek with the demands of 
the Latin Church. 

One great point is, at all events, established by these reports. 

It has been proved that there is no intention on the part of the Russian 
Embassy of concluding the arrangements respecting the holy places without 
atvemating to secure the cooperation of a French Negotiator. 

ith regard to the objects of Prince Menchikoff’s mission, again Count 
Nesselrode assured me that they were no other than have been made known to 
Her Majesty's Government and Her Majesty's Legation, and he once more 
repeated that the wish, the intention I should rather say, of causing the forth- 
coming arrangement to be embodied in an Act, was dictated solely by the 
urgency of making the arrangement final, of giving it a more binding character 
than could be derived from a firman, and for placing it at the least upon a 
footing of equality with those cipitulations to which the French are apt to 
ascribe the force of Treaties, 

After leaving the Foreign Office, I held some conversation with Count 
Orloff, I found him sanguine as to the negotiations carried on (and, as he 
observed, carried on slowly) at Constantinople, being brought to a satisfactory 
cose, 

He begged me, however, to bear in mind that the Emperor would not, and 
could not, give way as to points, apparently of insignificant value, but to which 
Breat Importince was attached by a Sovereign who was bound to respect the 
religious leclings of his people; those feelings, he said, being in the highest 
degree sensitive upon all matters connected with the holy places of Jerusalem, 

[will not conclude my despatch without stating to your Lordship, as in

justice to Baron Brunnow I am bound to do, that in a private letter to the

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received May 9.) 
(No, 209.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, April 30, 1853, 

WHEN I saw M. de Séniavine three or four days since, 1 took occasion to 
speak to him of the extensive armaments in progress in this country, of which I 
have heard reports from so many quarters. 

M. de Séniavine said he should be glad to know who had reported to me 
upon the subject. 

The list, | replied, would be a long one; I hear the accounts from London, 
and Berlin, and Gilseie: and Constantinople, and Taganrog: to give you the 
names of the persons who have written to me upon the subject, would be in 
other words to give a list of my correspondents. 

An English gentleman who arrived here three days since, after leaving 
Odessa on the 12th instant, states that great mystery was observed there as to 
the movements of the army, and that General Liiders was supposed to know as 
little as the troops under his command what was their destination, 

On his journey to St. Petersburgh the traveller in question observed that 
the military colonies on the Bug, especially Elizabethgrad, were deserted, 
Between Toula and Orel near Msensk, he met large trains of ammunition- 
waggons proceeding south; these, as soldiers informed him, were conveying 
3000 pounds of gunpowder. ‘This occurred on the 20th instant, 

The accounts brought here by messenger Wright show that the movements 
of ammunition are not confined to the south of Russia, 

On the 10th instant, while proceeding to Berlin, Lieutenant Wright over- 
took (he believes near Wilkomar), twenty-eight carts loaded with powder; on 
the 25th instant, whilst on his return to St. Petersburgh, he found a second 
convoy halting near Dunaburgh—twenty-four waggons were driven up in sight 
on the face of a hill, and as Lieutenant Wright imagines, he saw only half the 
number of which the convoy was composed. 

T have, &c. 
(Signed) G, H. SEYMOUR.

Count Buol had, it appeared, expressed to the Russian Chargé d’ Affaires

made to him by Lord Westmorland in consequence of orders received from your 
Lordship and had stated that for a considerable time the same good feeling had 
not existed between the two Governments, 

Reverting to the affair of the holy places, Count Nesselrode said; 

“My only remaining fear is that of our not coming to a good understand- 
ing with France. As regards the Turks we have no longer any apprehensions, 
but we believe the French Ambassador not to be provided with sufficiently 
extensive powers, and fear that the business will hardly be settled without his 
referring to his Government, or sheltering himself behind a reserve or a protest.”

No. 294, 
Sir G. WH. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon. — Received May 13.) 


(No. 217. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, May 5, 1853. 
ONE of my colleagues remarked to me, the other day, upon the difficulty 
of comprehending the actual policy of Russia, and of reconciling the objects 
professedly sought by her at Constantinople, with the amount of military pre- 
parations and expenditure which has for some months been observable, 
It ocenrred to me, that if this difficulty was experienced by a sensible man 


trained to diplomatic pursuits, long resident in this country, and well acquainted ” 


285 


with the Emperor's feelings, it may well be conceived that the doubts thus 
suggested should be extremely embarrassing to the European public in general. 

The explanation, as more generally noes is not to be sought in one 
cause, It is, I apprehend, the result of various causes. 

First, It must never be forgotten that any question relating to the holy 
places is of great interest to the Emperor and the whole of his people. It has a 

at hold upon the personal feelings of the one, and of the religious and fanatical 
tlings of the other. 

Second. The possibility is to be assomed of the decision of the Porte upon 
the questions set on foot by M. Lavalette being so displeasing to France, that 
those threats which were uttered with an intemperate disregard of consequences 
may be acted upon. 

In this event the Emperor would be bound in honour to protect the Sultan 
from injury, and would be still more impelled to do so by attention to that 

parently-recognized principle (recognized, that is, in this country), that hence- 
forward the existence of Turkey must be dependent upon the will of her tradi- 
tional rival; that what happens to her of weal or of woe, must be bestowed or 
inflicted by Russia. 

Third. It is next to be considered, that the influence of the Russian 
Mission at Constantinople had been allowed to run down, to use an expression 
which I heard employed by one of the Emperor's most constant associates, 
During the absence of M. Titoff, and under the direction of M, Ozeroff, the 
Russian Mission had ceased to speak with the same authority which it had 
previously possessed in Turkey, 

This state of things had been already felt at St. Petersburgh, and it was 
felt still more keenly after the diplomatic coup de main achieved by Count 
Leiningen had rendered the Emperor Francis more formidable in the eyes of the 
Turks than the Emperor Nicholas himself. 

It was at once held to be desirable that the fears excited by 40,000 
Austrian troops should be obliterated by those which the neighbourhood of a 
Russian force of triple that amount would arouse, 

When, to the above considerations is added, that of its being, as it should 
appear, expedient to subject Turkey to a series of agitations and crisises which 
shall prevent the country ever recovering any degree of stability; and when it 
is remembered that the long exercise of unlimited authority over many millions 
of subjects, and a million of soldiers, has rendered His Majesty a little reckless 
as to the manner in which he indulges, I will not say his warlike, but his mili. 
tary tastes, it may be the better understood how, without having any actual 
design of overrunning Turkey, he should haye assembled upon her frontiers an 
umount of force which is generally considered threatening to the existence of 
a weakened Government and a degenerate race, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received May 18.) 
(No. 331.) 
My Lord, Paris, May 17, 1853. 


M. DROUYN DE LHUYS received last night the despatches brought by 
the ‘Chaptal,” which boat left Constantinople, us Thad the honour to inform 
your Lordship yesterday, on the 7th instant; but he ts not yet in possession of 
M, de la Cour’s previous despatches of the 5th. He ts consequently still without 
accurate information of all the circumstances which have occurred at Constanti- 
nople since the 25th ultimo, and which have led to Prince Menchikofi's note of 
the Sth instant, alluded to in my despateh No, 425. 

A copy of this note was brought by the “ Chaptal,” and M, Drouyn de 
Lhuys read it to me this morning. It must already be in your Lordship’s hands, 
and [| need not allude to its contents except for the purpose of stating the 
impression produced on the French Government by its contents. | 

If it shall be found, on the arrival of M. de la Cour's despatches of the Sth, 
that the question of the holy places has been settled by the two firmans to which 
reference is made in Prinee Menchikoti’s note, the French Government has no 
objection to offer. There is nothing m those firmans, in M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ 
opinion, at variance with the concessions made to the Latins in the note 
addressed by the Porte to M. de Lavalette on the Bth of February, 1852, and 

France consequently is perfectly satisfied. But, observed M. Drouyn de Lhuys, 
these concessions are far less than France has a right to ask under her Capitula- 
tions with the Porte: and the aspect of the question hecomes changed when the 
Porte is required, as appears by Prince Menchikoff’s note and annex, to engage 
by a Convention that this state of things shall never be altered. We have no 
wish or intention to insist on a more literal fulfilment of the rights conferred on 
France by the Capitulations of 1740, but at the same time we cannot admit that 
a Convention, signed at the present day between the Porte and Russia, can overe 
ride prior Treaties signed between the Porte and us, 

L observed to M, Drouyn de Lhuys that it would be better not to raise that 
question now ; that there was no use in putting such an axiom upon paper; that 
as a general proposition it was one in which every one must concur, and that 
whatever the Porte might sign with Russia could not invalidate the previous 
engagements of the Porte towards other Powers. . 

My object in using this language was to prevent any further discussion of 
the rights of France; at the same time that I admitted that those rights, what- 
ever they might be, remained unimpaired by any transaction of the present day 
to which France herself was not a party. 1 doubt however whether, should the 
Porte consent to give Prince Menchikoff the solemn assurance he demands, 
France will not reserve her rights, but if so, it will be done, | trust, more as a 
matter of form, and without comminatory language. 

‘The question of the holy places settled, continued M, Drouyn de Lhuys, 
there remains the general one of the po one demanded by Russia over the 
Greek Church and religion. Upon this France has no pretension to act alone, 
Whatever may be the conduct of the Porte, whether she yields the point or not, 
we have no more interest at stake than have the other great Powers, and we 
shall be quite ready to consult and act with them. 

1 have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received May 19.) 
(No. 34. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, May 3, 1853, 

THOUGH more than a week has elapsed since I was entitled to consider 
the question of the holy places as virtually settled, I am still unable to report 
‘ts formal and definitive conclusion. ‘Two firmans, embodying the terms of the 
arrangement, have been prepared and communicated to the Embassies of France 
and Russia, ‘These firmans, being accepted by both parties, are to be invested 
with the usual forms and again communicated to the two Embassies, with an 
official note addressed respectively to each. Of the firmans and note, as 
intended for communication, I have now. the honour to inclose copies, in the 
hope that those shadows of mystery and indecision which. still float over them, 
will soon be dispersed for ever. 

Lam, nevertheless, informed that the note has met with some opposition in 
the Council, and that it is now before the Sultan with the disadvantage of having 
been rejected by a majority of that assembly. 

The firrans and the note were both referred to me for consideration before 
they were finally adopted by the Ministers, and I suggested two or three altera- 
tions in the latter, which were approved by the Grand Vizier and Rifaat Pasha. 
L have since addressed myself in private to the Sultan, urging him to confirm the 
decision of his Ministers, and to empower them to make their final communica- 
tion without further delay. As Russia continues to insist upon a guarantee, the 
note may fairly be preferred by them as being the simplest form of compliance 
with that requisition. 

Your Lordship may rest assured that I have spared no pains to hasten the 
conclusion of this delicate and protracted question. — 

Unfortunately the dangerous illness of the Sultan's mother, and the lateness 
of the Greek Raster, have furnished excuses for hesitation and delay. Petty 
additions or changes, proposed by interested parties after the main points were 
settled, have not been set aside without a strong remonstrance on my part. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

My Lord, Constantinople, May 5, 1853. 
EVEN if I had the necessary time at my disposal, I should hardly think it 

worth while to trouble your Lordship with the particulars of my long conver- 
sation with M. d’Ozeroff. As soon as Prince Menchikoff is well enough to 
receive ie, I shall probably have to go over the same ground again, and his 
previous knowledge of my sentiments in the present stage of his discussions 
with the Porte, will help to bring on, if he be so inclined, a more complete 
disclosure of his real views. The present appearances are that the Emperor of 
Russia, though moderate in his requisitions as to form, and in some measure as 
to terms also, is determined to obtain a treaty guaranty for the strict execution 
of the Porte's engagements, as well with respect to the holy places as for the 

rotection of the Greco-Russian Church throughout Turkey; and that Prince 

fenchikoff, on failing in the attainment of this object by means of negotiation, 
will break off his relations with the Porte, and open the door for his Government 
to take any measures more or less coercive on the Porte, which the Emperor's 
policy or sense of offended dignity may Reon

The Porte will not accept the Ambassador's proposals, as embodied in the 
projet, of which I transmitted a copy to your Lordship soon after my arrival 
here, I do not see how it is possible for the Porte to accept them without 
disparaging her authority, and endangering her independence. It remains 
to be seen whether by standing to a refusal of those demands, and at the same 
time affording Prince Menchikoff an opening for other more moderate prope: 
sitions, she may gain the advantage of either carrying with her the favourable 
opinion of Europe, should Russia resort to strong measures, or of embarking 
in a negotiation capable of terminating in a safe and durable adjustment of 
differences, 

My counsels are requested in face of this dilemma, and such are the diffi- 
culties and dangers of the case under its present appearances, that in giving

No, 303. 
Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon,.—(Recewed May 19.) 


(No. 38.) 

My Lord, Constantinople, May 5, 1853. 
SINCE I addressed your Lordship on the 3rd instant, | have had some 

further conversation with M. de la Cour, M. de Klezl, and M. dOzeroff, 

Principal Secretary of the Russian Embassy. I called on Prince Menchikoff, 

but did not find him at home. He has had a return of his previous indisposition, 

and is now confined to his bed. 


It results from these several communications that the two firmans and ~ 


official note prepared at the Porte with reference to the holy places, would 
suffice to terminate that portion of the pending questions in a manner 
satisfactory to the respective Parties; but that a certain degree of doubt and 
uneasiness is still kept up by the variable language and procrastination of the 
Turkish Ministers. It is more than time for this ill-omened vacillation to cease, 
and my opinion has been strongly and repeatedly expressed, not only to the 
Grand Vizier and Rifhat Pasha, but even to the Sultan himself. The Grand 
Vizier was to see His Majesty this morning, for the express purpose of 
engaging him to declare his final decision without further delay. 

I liad scarcely finished the preceding sentence, when I was interrupted by 
a-report from M. Pisani, whom I had sent to obtain intelligence from Rifaar 
Pasha before the departure of the messenger. He writes me word that the 
Sultan has cnctioned the firmans and the note, and that they have been imme- 
diately forwarded to the Russian Embassy with the date of this day, and, as 
| understand from M. Pisani’s letter, in the terms already made known to your 
Lordship. If any alteration has been introduced, either into the firman or into 
the note, it will appear from the copies, which have been also sent in a more 
official manner to this Embassy, together with a memorandum suggested b 
me, and intended, I believe, for communication to other friendly Powers, as well 
as to Her Majesty's Government. 

It will scarcely be possible for me to receive the translations of these papers 
in time for transmission to your Lordship by the present opportunity ; but I may 
be allowed to congratulate your Lordship upon the peaceful termination of those 
discussions, respecting the holy places, which have so long occupied the attention 
and threatened the tranquillity of Europe. 

The difficulties which unfortunately remain to be overeome before the 
relations of the Porte with Russia can be settled on a stable and friendly basis, 
appear, from my last communications with the Russian eae to be still of a 
very scrious character, I hope, nevertheless, that it will not be impossible for 
me to contribute towards go desirable a result, by persevering in that line of 
conciliation and firmness of which | have hitherto found no reason to repent. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFIE,

Lord Cowley to the Earl af Clarendon.—(Received May 20.) 


(No, dd) 
My Lord, Paris, May 19, 1853. 

I HAVE the honour to inclose herewith an article published in the 
‘‘Moniteur” of yesterday, relative to the present state of affairs at Constanti- 
nople. Your Lordship will remark that it is written in terms which accord 
perfectly with the language held to me by M. Drowyn de Lhuys. 

Nevertheless it is to be regretted that it should have been published, nor 
is it possible to overrate the mischief which is done by these almost official 
declarations of the French Government, I believe that the object of the Govern- 
ment in the present instance was to calm the agitation which had begun to 
manifest itself in the money market in consequence of the vagueness of the 
reports circulated as coming from Constantinople; but your Lordship will pro- 
bably agree with me that that object could have been attained without employing 
language which can hardly fail to irritate the Russian Goresune nls 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

“rance,

No. 307. 


Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received May 22.) 


(No. 42.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, May 9, 1853. 

SINCE I transmitted to you on the 6th instant what may be called Prince 
Menchikoff's ultimatum, though he has prudently, and I hope with intention, 
avoided the use of that word, my time has been entirely occupied with commu- 
nications relating to it. Your Lordship may easily conceive that so abrupt and 
peremptory a step could not be taken in secret, and that the public would not 
be slow in catching the excitement, and sharing the apprehensions of the Porte, 

The Russian note and accompanying Projet were conveyed to me with a 
request from the Ottoman Secretary of State for Foreign Atlairs, that T would 
acquaint him with my impressions respecting them at an carly hour next 
morning, preparatory to a meeting of the Couneil, 

In reply to this message, I suggested what follows : 

1. To make the communication of the Russian papers common to the 
British and French Embassies in a strictly confidential form. 

2. To prepare a written answer to the Russian declaration as exhibited in 
the official note, the Projet de Sened, and the note verbale of April the 19th, 

8, To frame the answer in a spirit of conciliation and firmness, giving 
every assurance of a cordial intention on the side of the Porte to act towards 
Russia on principles of strict good faith and friendly consideration; to place in 
their proper light, clearly but sa Mea the proceedings and requisitions of 

Russia in connection with Prince Menchikoff’s embassy ; and to declare, not- 
withstanding, an unalterable readiness to entertain his Excellency's propositions, 
in so far as they were free from objections bearing on the Sea hes oe dignity and 
independence of the Sultan, however ce they might as to the 
question of the Holy Places in Palestine already settled to the satisfaction of all 
parties; to redress any grievances fairly made out on behalf of the Greek Church, 
and to confirm and carry into effect all the established rights and privileges 
secured already by Imperial favour to the Christian religion, and its ecclesiastical 
property throughout the Empire. 

4. ‘To communicate the note containing an answer of this kind, together 
with the three abovementioned documents, to the Representatives of the four 
great Powers who, in common with Russia, were parties to the Treaty of 1841, 

The Secretary of State conferred with the Grand Vizier, and expressed his 
satisfaction with the advice which I had tendered; authorizing me at the same 
time to place the Russian papers, as confidentially as they had been sent to me, 
in the hands of the French Ambassador. 

My next step was to see M. de la Cour, I found his Excellency at home, 
and after reading the documents in our possession, we talked over their contents 
and the general features of the crisis, with a total absence of reserve, equally, in so 
far as | could perceive, on his partason my own. I left him with the impression 
that we were both on the same ground; that he, no more than myself, contem- 
plated an spe to the squadrons without express orders from home; that he 
disapproved of the proposed Sened, even in point of form ; that he fully appre- 
ciated the dangers involved in the terms of its first and second Articles, and 
deprecated the peremptory attitude assumed by the Russian Ambassador; at 
the same time that he entered into all those considerations which naturally 
result from the weakness of the Ottoman Empire, and the occasional imprudence 
of its Government, 

We separated with an understanding that each of us would see the Turkish 
Ministers and Prince Menchikoff, holding to both parties the same kind of 
language, and meeting again afterwards for our mutual information. 

The Russian Ambassador called upon me and also upon M. de la Cour in 
the course of the day. His visit to me had the air of a private attention, irre- 
spective of politics. 1 took occasion, however, to bring up the topic nearest to 
my thoughts, and also, in all probability, to his also. Avoiding with care any 
warinth of expression which might lead to an unpleasant discussion, | intimated 
i strong impression that the Porte was not more likely to accept his new than

No. 315. 
The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, 


(No. 49.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, May 26, 1853. 

THE repeated and explicit assurances received by Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment from Sir Hamilton Seymour and from Baron Brunnow, rendered it im- 
possible to doubt that the sole object of Prince Menchikoff’s mission was to 
obtain a final and satisfactory settlement of the question of the holy places, and 
that no other matter remained behind, and that no demands were contemplated 
that could lead to difference between Russia and the Porte. 

Her Majesty's Government have accordingly thought themselves not alone 
justified, but called upon entirely to discredit the many rumours inconsistent 
with the above assurances that circulated since the arrival of Prince Menchikoif 
at Constantinople; and for the same reason when it recently became clear that 
he was about to make demands with which the Porte could not comply, Her 
Majesty's Government were induced to believe that Prince Menchikoff was 
acting on his own responsibility, and not upon instructions from Mis Court, of 
which Her Majesty's Government had no knowledge. 

It was therefore with extreme surprise and regret that they received the 
note in the form of an ultimatum (inclosed in your Excellency’s despatch, 
No, 41, of the Gth instant), and Project of Convention, which had been pre- 
sented on the 5th by Prince Menchikoff to. the Porte, and to which a definitive 
answer was demanded in the space of five days. ; 

Your Excellency was not furnished with instructions to meet a course of 
proceeding that Her Majesty's Government had such abundant reason for not 
contemplating: to have sent instructions upon a question that must have been 
determined before it came to the knowledge of Her Majesty's Government 
would have been useless; but upon that point they felt no uneasiness, because 
their general views and policy were well known to your Excellency; and in 
earrying them out, they relied upon the ability and experience, os well as the 
local knowledge and well-earned influence of your Excellency with the Porte. 

That confidence has been fully justified; and I have the pleasure to convey 
to you the entire approval of Her Majesty's Government of all your proceedings, 
as stated in your No. 42 of the 9th instant. 

Her Majesty’s Government view the proposed Convention and the practical 
operation that it would have in Turkey, in the same light as your Excellency 
appears to do: they consider that its acceptance by the Porte in its present form 
would have been incompatible with the honour and independence of the Sultan ; 
and that the advice given by your Excellency to the Turkish Ministers as to the 
mode of meeting this demand, was alike prudent and dignified; and Her 
Majesty's Government most especially approve of your answer to the Grand 
Vizier, advising him that demonstrations calculated to increase alarm and pro- 
voke resentment, should be avoided so long as the question retained what your 
Excellency considered to be its moral character. 

Her Majesty's Government observe with satisfaction, that M. de la Cour 
appears to haye adopted the views of your Excellency, and to have held the 
same language as yourself to the Porte. The co-operation of the Ambassadors 
of England and France at this important crisis of Eastern affairs cannot fail to 


give confidence to the Porte, and is in conformity with the desire of their 
respective Governments, 


Lam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

Lord Cowley to the Karl of Clarendon.— (Received May 30.) 
(No. S68, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, May 29, 1853. 
M.DROUYN DE LHUYS has received despatches from Vienna respecting 
the views of the Austrian Cabinet in regard to the present aspect of Eastern 
affairs, with which he is satisfied. M, de Bourqueney describes Count Buol as 
disapproving both the matter and form of Prince Menchikoff's ultimatum. 

M. de Hitbner has also read to M. Drouyn de Lhuys a despatch upon the 
subject from Count Buol ; but its terms, if Lam correctly informed, are hardly 
us strong us those given in M, de Bourquency's reports, M.de Hiibner is desired 
ta express the hope of the Austrian Cabinet that modifications, especially in 
form, may yet be introduced into Prince Menchikoff’s demands, so as to render 
them acceptable to the Turks. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys asked, what was meant by form? [f it meant that 
words might be changed while the sense remained unaltered, or that the Russian 
hegotimtor was to put on an uniform instead of a great coat, he did not see that 
the sting of the ultimatum was reduced. If on the other hand it meant that the 
rights, privileges, and immunities of the Greek Church, of which Russia wished 
to make herself the guarantee, were to be secured by some fi 
act of the Sultan, such a modification might be acceptable. 

M. de Hibner replied that he could do no more than give M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys the text of Count Buol's despatch, but he asked whether he might report 


the French Minister’s words to his Government, to which he ree

No. 323. 


The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 
(No. 54.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, May 31, 1853. 
THE latest despatch received at this office trom your Excellency, is No. 51, 
dated the 15th instant, and Her Majesty's Government are therefore wnin- 
formed respecting the negotiations which took place between the 15th and 
the 22nd, on which day Prince Menchikoff quitted Constantinople, nor do they 
yet know whether the rupture between the Russian Ambassador and the Porte 
was of a character to preclude all hope that negotiations might be resumed. 

* See Inclosures in No, d35, 


2 


ols 


Nevertheless the departure of Prince Menchikoff, followed by the entire 
Russian Mission, is a fact in itself of such grave importance, the military 
preparations of Russia on the ‘Turkish frontier are upon a scale of such vast 
manitude, and the danger which threatens the Porte may be so imminent, that 
it ap ears indispensable to take measures for the protection of the Sultan, and 
to Ht his Highness in repelling any attack that may be made upon his territory. 

L have accordingly to inform your Excellency that by Her Majesty's com- 
mands the fleet now stationed at Malta is placed at the disposal of your 
Excellency, and that orders will be sent to Admiral Dundas to conform to the 
‘astructions he may receive from you, and to repair to such place a8 you 
may direct in the event of your considering the presence of a British force 
absolutely essential to the safety of the Turkish Empire. Her Majesty's 
Government, however, are desirous that your Excellency should distinctly 
understand that in coming to this determination they by no means intend to 
depart from the moderate and conciliatory course which they have always 
adopted between the Porte and its Allies; but in the use of the power now 
confided you, involving as it may do the momentous question of peace or war, 
Her Majesty’s Government place the fullest reliance on the discretion of your 
Excellency. | 

A declaration of war by Russia against Turkey, the embarkation of troops 
at Sevastopol, or any other well-established fact noting intentions of unmis- 
takable hostility, would in the opinion of Her Majesty's Government entirely 
justify your Excellency in sending for the fleet, which however would not pass 
the Dardanelles except on the express demand of the Sultan; but the use of force 
should only be resorted to as a last and unavoidable resource for the protection 
of Turkey against an unprovoked attack, and in defence of her independence 
which England is bound to maintain.

(Signed) CLARENDON.

No. 324. 
The Earl of Clarendon to Sir G, H. Seymour. 
(No. 81.) . 
Sir, Foreiyn Office, May 31, 1853. 


YOU will have learned by my despatch No. 69 of the 17th instant, that 
great anxiety prevailed here with respect tothe negotiations then pending between 
the Russian Ambassador and the Porte. Subsequent intelligence tended to increase 
that anxiety, and a state of painful excitement was created on Saturday last, when 
the news arrived that diplomatic relations between Russia and the Porte were 
broken off; that Prince Menchikoff had quitted Constantinople on the 22n 
instant, and that the remainder of his Embassy was to follow him in three days. 

Her Majesty’s Government are at present uninformed of the immediate cause 
that led to this rupture; but the undoubted fact of Prince Menchikott's departure 
‘s to them @ source of deep regret; nor can they view without the utmost 
alarm, an event that may lead to war between two Powers 1m close alliance with 
England, and which must consequently endanger the peace of Europe. But in 
state of affairs so critical and so full of peril to the best interests o society, it Is 
indispensable that between England and Russia no misunderstanding neal 
exist, and Her Majesty’s Government feel that they should be wanting im ar 
perfect confidence which has hitherto prevailed, and whieh they trust wil 
always continue to exist between the two Cabinets, if they did not at once seek 
from the Russian Government the most frank and unreserved explanations, 

For this purpose it becomes necessary to revert to your correspondence 
during the present year, which conveyed the assurances given to you ig ayes 
the policy and intentions of Russia towards Turkey, that, on the part o ist 
Majesty's Government, were received, as they were entitled to be, with unreserve 
confidence. , 

It appears then by your despatch No. 7 of the Sth of January, that on the 
8th of January, in a conversation which you held with Count Nesselrode ee 
pecting the reported armaments in the South of Russia, the Chancellor eae 
you that the Emperor deprecated the fall of Turkey, and that as regarded the

present crisis, Count Nesselrode hoped it would be brought to a conclusion by 

negotiation, but that the diplomacy of Russia must be supported by a demon- 

stration of force, and that the Porte would be required strictly to fulfil its 

engagements towards the Greek Church and the Emperor, and that a corresponding 

Soipeneeion most be made to the Greek, for any new concession to the Latin 
ureh, 

In a conversation (No. 13, of the 11th January) which you had the honour 
to hold with the Emperor on the following day, the 9th of January, His Imperial 
Majesty said that it was very important that England and Russia should come 
to a perfectly good understanding on the aifairs of Turkey, and that neither 
should take any decisive step of which the other was not apprized. 

By a despatch from Count Nesselrode dated January 14, it clearly appears 
that the sole object of Russia at that time was “un arrangement qui puisse 
rendre au firman la validité qu’on lui a étée; rétablir 4 Jérusalem les deux rits 
are pied d’égalité; et concilier leurs prétentions sans léser les droits de Yun ou 

e Tautre.” 

On the 5th February (No. 56), you stated that Count Nesselrode told you 
that Prince Menchikoff was going to Constantinople, where a person of greater 
weight than a Chargé d’Affaires was required; that his instructions would be of a 
conciliatory character; and that the Prince was himself animated by the most 
pacific intentions, Count Nesselrode also added that Prince Menchikoff would 
be instructed to occupy himself with the affairs of Montenegro, as well as with 
the question of the Holy Places, 

On a subsequent occasion (No. 70, 10th February), Count Nesselrode still 
represented Prince Menchikoff’s instructions as moderate, observed there was 
necessarily some vagueness in his orders, as it was hardly ascertained to what 
extent the riglits secured to the Greeks last year had been infringed; but there 
would be no question of attempting to regain from the Latins any of the 
privileges which they might aubeequently have acquired at Jerusalem—the 
object to be sought for was an equivalent for any privileges lost by the Greeks. 

Count Nesselrode said (No. 116, March 9), there was no such hurry in 
settling the question of the Holy Places as that of Montenegro; that Prince Men- 
chikoff had been provided with very ample powers: that it was impossible for 
the Emperor to recede from the position secured to the Grecks by the firman of 
February 1852, and the Sultan’s letter; that Prince Menchikois mission had 
long been determined upon, and only delayed on account of his health. 

In reply to your inquiry (No. 134, March 24), whether an adjustment of 
the difficulties respecting the holy places would settle all matters in dispute 
between Russia and the Porte, or whether Prince Menchikoff had other grievances 
to bring forward, Count Nesselrode said he was not aware that any such existed ; 
there might be some outstanding private claims, but he knew of no other demands ; 
in short, of none except such as might exist between any two friendly Govern- 
ments, and form part of the current business of every Chancery. 

Count Nesselrode remarked (No. 151, March 29), that the only moment 
during the late transactions when he had felt apprehension was that at which the 
urgency of affairs at Montenegro had called for the mission of Count Leiningen ; 
that he had never contemplated the chance of the question of the Holy Places 
leading to war; and that his anticipation of a speedy conclusion of all matters in 
dispute, had been confirmed by Prince Menchikoff’s despatches of the 17th, 
which represented affairs as gomg on satisfactorily. 

Count Nesselrode said (No. 160, April 5), that there had been no sort of 
demand for the dismissal of Fuad Effendi; no ultimatum; no demand for exten- 
sion of territory; no attempt at procuring for Russia the nomination of the 
Greek Patriarch; no wish was entertained of calling upon France for the 
restitution of any rights in regard to the holy places which she had obtained ; 
and that the Emperor was only waiting for a confirmation of the peaceful 
intelligence which he had received from the South, when orders would be issued 
for discontinuing all warlike preparations. 

Count Nesselrode's language on a subsequent occasion (No. 165, April 7), 
still alluded to the question of the Holy Places as the only one under discussion, 
und the speedy arrangement of which he looked forward to with confidence. 

_ . Ina despatch to Baron Brannow (April 7), Count Nesselrode repeats that 
it is the desire and resolution of the Emperor to respect the independence and 
integrity of Turkey, and if his views in that respect should change, he would be the

Tt now becomes necessary to advert to the proceedings of Prince Menchikoff

Prince Menchikoff, in his note of the Sth of May, recapitulated the pro- 
posals he had previously made to the Porte on the 22nd March and 19th April; 
but in addition to those of the 22nd March relating to the holy places, Prince 
Menchikoff simultaneously made other proposals far more important and com- 
prehensive in their character, accompanied with warnings of the danger which 
Ritnat Pasha would incur if any of those proposals were permitted to transpire, 

These last proposals amounted in substance to the conclusion of a Treaty 
stipulating that Russia should enjoy the exclusive right of intervening for the 
effectual protection of all the members of the Greek Church, and of the interests 
of the churches themselves; that the privileges of the Patriarchs should be 
effectually confirmed, and that. the Patriarchs should hold their preferment for 
life independently of the Porte’s approval, the protection of Greck pilgrims in 
Palestine ; the construction of a Russian church at Jerusalem; and the confir- 
mation and enforcement of all Imperial reseripts granted from time to time to 
Russia. These demands were put forward as an explanation of the Treaty of 
Kainardji, and necessary for its complete execution,

No. 325. 


Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received June 1.) 
(No. 53.) 


My Lord, Constantinople, May 19, 1853. 

PRINCE MENCHIKOFF and the Russian Legation are still here; and 
itis not easy to divine why they are so, after what has occurred. The fact, 
however, still affords a chance of their being induced to postpone their depar- 
ture indefinitely without any improper sacrifice on the part of the Turkish 
Government. With the view of improving that chance, if possible, 1 proposed 
a meeting of the four Representatives, which accordingly took place this morning 
at the French Ambassadors, 

Before I mention the substance of what passed at this meeting, I must 
apprize your Lordship of the state of things as now existing between the Porte 
and Prince Menchikoff. It may be described in a single sentence. The Russian 
Ambassador has declared his mission to be terminated, the whole of his legation 
to be on the point of leaving Constantinople, and the interests of Russian trade 
and shipping to be consigned to the Director of the Chancery, who is to remain 
here with the persons employed in his department. 

A copy of the note by which his Excellency has made this declaration to 
the Porte, 1s inclosed herewith. I received it last night from Reshid Pasha, and 
at his request communicated it to the French Ambassador, the Prussian Envoy, 
and the Austrian Chargé d' Affaires, 

Prince Menchikoff sent in this decisive note after he had received a visit 
the same day from Reshid Pasha, who, passing over considerations of etiquette 
suggested by the previous interruption of the Ambassador’s personal relations 
with the Porte, as signified officially by himself, called upon his Excellency in 
the hope of disposing him favourably to the reception ot the Porte's definitive 
communication, prepared, but not yet delivered. 

_ The Porte was thus prevented from making any official communication 
of its last intentions, and the Russian Ambassador's all but hostile declaration 
arrived when the Ottoman Council, composed of unusual numbers, had decided 
on maintaining its previous resolution by a majority of forty-two members out 
of forty-five, . 

To make the course of this unhappy business still more clear to your 
Lordship and Her Majesty's Government, I have the honour to inclose herewith 
in copy a short eoereypangenser which had taken place between Reshid 
Pasha and Prince Menchikoff two or three days before. 

(Of the Porte’s intended note, it is but justice to gay, that it declared a 
readiness to concede every point demanded by Russia with the single exception 
of that form of guarantee, [ mean an engagement with the force of Treaty, 
which the Porte conceives to be inconsistent with its independence and sovereign 


* Bee Inclosures in Nos, 397, 342. 
2U 


o24 


dignity, and which opinion is more or less entertained by every one who may be 
supposed to have acquired 8 competent knowledge of the subject. 

I now return to the meeting which I held this morning with my colleagues 
of Austria, France, and Prussia. It afforded me sincere satisfaction to find that 
there was no essential difference of opinion in our judgment of the emergency 
and of its bearings. We could not question the soundness of the Porte’s views 
in resisting the extreme demands of Russia; we could not but acknowledge the 
spirit of conciliation displayed by the Sultan's Ministers; we agreed in our 
anxiety to find some means of averting the rupture which was all but carried 
snto effect ; and unfortunately we could not but agree in the difficulty, not to 
say impossibility of reconciling, after all that had passed, the requirements of the 
adverse parties. We finally determined on making an overture to Prince 
Menchikoff in the form least calculated to give umbrage. On the one hand we 
had some cause to hope that his Excellency would not be sorry to find a reason- 
able excuse for improving his position towards the Porte. On the other, we saw 
no reason to doubt that he would hesitate to avail himself of any proposal 
coming in an ostensible shape from an union of four Representatives, Ve 
thought to secure the advantage, and to avoid the danger, by requesting 
M. de Klezl, who had thoughts of paying a farewell visit to Prince Menchikoff 
the following day, to apprize him of the sorrow with which, individually, we all 
contemplated the rupture of his relations with the Porte, to express the lively 

tification which a friendly solution of the present difference, if that were still 
possible, would afford us, and to ascertain whether he was disposed to receive 
through a private channel the Porte’s intended note, and to give it a calm con- 
sideration, notwithstanding the measures which he had officially declared. 

The prospect of success to be expected from this step is far from encourag- 
ing; but your Lordship will probably agree with me that the motives for making so 
doubtful an experiment overbalance the objections to incurring the risk of failure. 

M. de Klezl is not at liberty to make this communication to Prince Menchi- 
koff without having previously obtained the assent of Reshid Pasha. Whatever 
may be its result, there ‘s room for consolation in the limited extent of Prince 
Menchikoff's admonitions. 

Their tone is harsh, and their aspect is threatening; but there 1s at 
least no threat of immediate war, no hint of an approaching occupation of the 
principalities, Whatever perils may be involved in the rupture of diplomatic 
relations between Russia and Turkey, they do not appear to be immediate ; and 
I cherish a sanguine hope that the exertions of European influence will check the 
ebullitions of resentment, and ultimately ward off those contingent evils which 
it is now the business of Prince Menchikoff to paint in imposing colours.

(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

current business of every Chancellerie.” 

The Chancellor threw no doubts upon the correctness of my report, but 
maintained that an adjustment of Church difficulties was precisely the object all 
along given out, and the attainment of which was now sought by the Sened. 

LT admitted haying, some considerable time since, learned from his Excellency 
that it was considered essential that the two firmans should be remforced by, or, 
if he pleased, embodied ina Convention, but that there was entirely new matter 
in the “ Projet de Traité” brought forward by Prince Menchikoft; that there 
was now question of granting to the Emperor a right of protection over 
10,000,000 of Greeks, which would render him more powerful in Turkey than 
the Sultan himself, which would make them all look up to a foreign Sovereign, 
and not to their own master. 

Have they looked, Count Nesselrode replied, for the last hundred years in any 
other direction? No: believe this Convention upon which we so. strongly 
insist is perfectly inoffensive and anodyne (sic); it changes nothing in the state 
of affairs; it does not tend to weaken the Sultan’s authority, and it is in some 
measure calculated to strengthen it since it removes the possibility of such con- 
testations as those which we have lately witnessed, 

I rejoined that I could not admit that the proposed Act contained no inno- 
vation ; that, beyond being a confirmation, it was a very great extension of the 
rights secured to the Russian Crown by the Treaty of Kainardji; that the old 

rights applied to the Danubian provinces, whilst those proposed were to range 
over the whole of Turkey. 

The Chancellor could not give up his position, and testified his great regret 
at the view of the subject which has been taken by Her Majesty's Ambassador 
at Constantinople, an expression which I met by assuring his Exeellency that no 
difference upon the point existed between Lord Stratford de Redcliffe and Her 
Majesty’s Government, 

Count Nesselrode hoped that this would yet prove not to be the case; the 
opinion of Her Majesty's Government had been formed upon the original 
“Projet de ‘Traité” presented by Prince Menchikoff, and would by this time 
be considerably modified by the amended draft which Baron Brunnow had been 
directed to communicate to your Lordship. 

The last expressions employed by Count Nesselrode appeared to me to 
sound ominously. 

The Emperor had, he said, shown the greatest consideration for ‘Turkey 
in the docuands which he had made upon her; great latitude had been left in 
Prince Menchikofl’s hands, of which a full use had been made by the Prince in 
attempting to meet the objections of the Turkish Government and of Her 
Majesty’s Embassy; and further alterations of form might be possibly admitted ; 
but from the substance (le fond) of his demands, His Imperial Majesty could not 
recede, and “a dreadful responsibility would be assumed by any Government 
which by counselling the rejection of these demands might bring about the 
downfall of the Ottoman Empire.” 

T have omitted to state that when the Chancellor remarked, as he did in the 
eourse of the conversation, that it was only asked that the Emperor of Russia 
should be put in possession of a right similar to that enjored by the Emperor of 
Austria ; I replied that besides that the demand now made was a new feature in 
the transaction: there was this difference between the two Sovereigns, that one 
possessed a hold over some thousands of Catholics, and that the other would 
obtain the same influence over some millions of Greeks. 

It may indeed be argued that this influence is already possessed by Russia, 
and that although the right to interfere generally on behalf of the Greek subjects 
of the Porte is not yet secured to her, the practice of so interfering lias long 
prevailed; allthis may he true, but it is not less certain that a long-cherishe 
object is seen to have been sought by a tortuous path, and that if words be not 
intended to disguise rather than to manifest intentions, Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment have good right to look with surprise upon the demands made upon the 
Sultan, in the name of his master, by Prince Menchikot. 

I have, &e.

No. 334. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon —(Received June 3.) 


(No. 43.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, May 10, 1853. 
IN one of my preceding numbers I mentioned that I had seen the Sultan 
in private. The interview took place yesterday morning, Rifaat Pasha accom- 
panied me to the Sultan's apartment, and then withdrew. I found His Majesty 
to all appearance much cast down, and having an air of weakness as well as 
melancholy. The loss of the Validé Sultana was no doubt weighing on his 
spirits, but the demands of Russia and the attitude assumed by Prince Men- 
chikoff, were also, 1 conceive, among the prominent causes of their depression. 
Reminding the Sultan of the disposition he had shown to receive my 
counsels, I said that I had hitherto confided them to his Ministers, not wishing 
to trespass personally on His Majesty's indulgence without necessity. I added 
that in the present critical juncture of affairs the case might be different, and 
His Majesty might like to know what [thought from my own lips. I then 
endeavoured to give him a just idea of the degree of danger to which his Empire 
was exposed, first from an increasing opinion of its decline entertained in one 
and proclaimed in another part of Europe, with a corresponding disposition in 
the north to provide as for an approa hing crisis, and a growing indifference in 
the west to an event more or less considered as unavoidable. The immediate 
danger had been arrested for the time, if not removed, and Her Majesty's 
Government had nothing more at heart than to assist in rescuing the Porte 
from everything which might threaten a return of it, while the Porte itself 
was careful to meet the demands of Russia in a spirit of conciliation, equity, 
and prudence, united when necessary with firmness and resolution. ‘The success 
which had fortunately attended the negotiations relating exclusively to the holy 
places at Jerusalem, promised well for an eventual arrangement of the subse- 
quent discussions, and I was happy to find that His Majesty’s servants, both 
Ministers and Council, were not less inclined to gratify the Russian Ambassador 
with all that could be safely conceded to him, than determined to withhold their 
consent from every requisition calculated to inflict a serious injury on the inde- 
pendence and dignity of their Sovereign. I had waited to know their own 
unbiassed impressions respecting the kind of guarantee demanded by Prince 
Menchikoff, and I could not do otherwise than approve the decision which they 
appeared to have adopted with unanimity. My own impression was, that if 
His Majesty sanctioned that decision, the Ambassador would probably break off 


his relations with the Porte, and go away, together perhaps with his whole 
Embassy ; nor was it quite impossible that even a temporary occupation, how- 
ever unjust, of the Danubian Principalities by Russia might take place ; but I felt 
certain that neither a declaration of war nor any other act of open hostility was to 
be apprehended for the present, as the Emperor Nicholas could not resort to 
such extremities on account of the pending differences, without contradicting 
his most solemn assurances, and exposing himself to the indignant censure of 
all Europe. 1 conceived that under such circumstances the true position to be 
maintained by the Porte was one of moral resistance to such demands as were 
really inadmissible on just and essential grounds, and that the principle should 
even be applied under protest to the occupation of the pi apn not in 
weakness or despair, but in reliance on a good cause and on the sympathy of 
friendly and independent Governments. A firm adherence to this line of con- 
duct, as long as it was possible to maintain it with honour, would in my judg- 
ment offer the best chances of ultimate success with the least practicable degree 
of provocation and present disturbance of commercial interests. 

L concluded by apprizing His Majesty of what I had reserved for his private 
ear, in order that his Ministers might take their decision without any bias from 
without, namely, that in the event of imminent danger I was instructed to 
request the Commander of Her Majesty’s Forces in the Mediterranean to hold 
his squadron in readiness. 

‘he whole of this language appeared to interest the Sultan deeply, and also 
to coincide with His Majesty's existing opinions. He said that he was well 


dal 


aware of the dangers to which I had alluded; that he was perfectly prepared in 
the exercise of his own free will to confirm and to render ctive the protection 
promised to all classes of his tributary subjects in matters of religious worship, 
including the immunities and privileges granted to their respective clergy, 
observing that his ancestors had been more liberal in promise than exact im 
performance; and he gave me the fall measure alike of his apprehensions and 
of his resolution by saying, with reference to the loss of his mother, that having 
now «o little to attach him to life, the sacrifice even of that would scarcely cost 
him a feeling of regret. He showed me the last communications in writing 
which had passed between his Ministers and the Russian Embassy; he thanked 
me for having helped to bring the question of the holy places to an arrange- 
ment; he professed his reliance on the friendly support of Great Britain, and 
finally dismissed me with gracious expressions of confidence and satisfaction. 

T have since learned from the Grand Vizier, to whom the Sultan had men- 
tioned his private reception of me, that His Majesty had been much gratified by 
the tenor of my communications. 

] have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received June 3.) 


(No. 44.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, May 14, 1853. 

1 ADDRESSED you last on the 10th instant. I have now to continue 
my statement of the principal incidents relating to Prince Menchikoff’s ill-omened 
difference with the Porte. 

The first object to which | have the honour of soliciting your Lordship’s 
attention is an official note addressed to the Prince by Rifaat Pasha, on the 10th 
of this month. A copy of it is inclosed herewith ; and, agreeably to my advice, 
it has been communicated to the French, Prussian, and Austrian Representatives, 
The communication is confidential. 

Your Lordship will observe that the note has been framed in general with 
reference ore suggestions, as stated in my despatch No. 41, of this year; but 
any responsibility which may in consequence devolve upon me, does not extend 
beyond the principal heads, excluding composition, and the reserve of unnoticed 
points. The object of the note was to declare the Porte’s readiness to accept 
all the Russian demands not utterly inadmissible; to comply with those wishes 
of Russia which could not be demanded on any ground of right; and to offer 
such guarantees as the Sultan could give without a sacrifice of his independence 
and sovereign dignity, 

_ On the following day Prince Menchikoff sent in a rejoinder, expressing 
dissatisfaction with the terms proposed by the Porte, and insisting, though with 
somewhat more of courtesy than before, on a more complete and immediate 
acceptance of his own. This note bears a date equivalent in our style to 
Wednesday, May 11; and Rifaat Pasha was given to understand that Saturday, 
the 14th, would he really the extreme goal of Russian forbearance, The interval 
was occupied with private or indirect endeavours to obtain a more liberal allow- 
ance of time, and to discover some mode of bringing the adverse parties within 
reach of an accommodation. { képt myself in communication with the French 
Ambassador and the Austrian Charge d’Affaires; I put Rifaat Pasha in posses- 
sion of whatever struck me as at all calculated to smooth down the existing 
obstacles without a surrender of the main point at issue, and, acting through a 
seeret channel, | endeavoured even to dispose the [Russian parly to more 
accommodating terms, notwithstanding the positive manner in which Prince 
Menchikoff had closed every avenue to negotiation hut that which required a 
ticket of surrender at its entrance, 

The Prince himself, though shunning, in the country, all contact with his 
diplomatic colleagues, and stickin yertinaciously to his basis, was busy in 
knocking at every door where the slightest chance existed of gaining a vote in

(Transilation.) Shahan 2, 1269. (Mey 10, 1853.) 


| HAVE had the honour to receive your Excellency’s note dated the Sth of 
May, x. s. The contents of the other papers having reference to it, have been 
into due consideration. | : 
es has been His Imperial Majesty the Sultan's earnest and constant desire 
to maintain and inerease by every means the strong relations of sincere friend- 
ship and concord between the Sublime Porte and the illustrious Government of 
Russia, and more especially to confirm and consolidate those same relations 
which for a long time have been happily established on a firm basis between His 
Imperial Majesty the Sultan and His Imperial Majesty the Emperor of Russia. 
Tt is therefore the sincere desire of the Porte in pursuance of the relations of 
good neighbourhood and a sincere and generous friendship, to settle any Hussian 
claims which do not in any way injure or affect the independence, the special 
interests, or the rights of the Porte. ‘The Sublime Porte m reserving to itself 
the power of giving a decisive reply, if it should be expedient, to the matters 
contained in the waper inclosed in your Excellency’s note, desires earnestly that 
your Excellency Heat take into your friendly consideration the following points. 
"fhe Sublime Porte will not decline to negotiate on the demands made by 
Russia concerning a church and a hospital at Jerusalem, and relative to Russian 
subjects, monks, and pilgrims, in so fur as they do not militate against the rights 
of the Porte, and to give a written assurance in harmony with the decision 
ich may be come to. 
i at ublime Porte, and more especially His Imperial Majesty the Sultan, 
in his royal solicitude on behalf of his subjects, has been ever desirous that the 
religious privileges enjoyed by his Christian and other subjects should be fully 
preserved, While the Imperial Government of Russia, having conceived certain 
doubts concerning the religious privileges of the Greek subjects of the Porte, 
: ances in that respect. 
ae oat rrapesal M reaty the Sultan being extremely desirous that the 
ancient privileges of his Greek as well as his other subjects should be perpetually 
preserved, it is not only His Majesty's intention that these religious privileges 
should be by no means destroyed, but constant care and attention is given for 
confirming and preserving them in perpetuity, However friendly may be the 
reciprocal sentiments of the Sublime Porte und the Government of Russia, it is 
contrary to international rights that our Government should conclude a Treat 
with another on a dangerous matter, affecting not only those things in which 
her independence is grounded, but as it 1s well known her independence itself 
in its very foundations. 
‘. The gent and valid objections entertained by the Porte on this subject, 
will be generally acknowledged, and more especially so by His Majesty the 
Emperor, whose sense of justice is so widely known, | 
“In like manner as the Porte has hitherto fully preserved the many 


aa 


religious privileges which she has, of her own free will and from a very remote 
period, conceded and granted to her Christian subjects, and more especially to 
the Greek subjects and monks; she will likewise henceforward, in harmony 
again with her own rights, be careful to continue and duly preserve them. 

Tt is the decided intention of the Porte hy again specially proclaiming His 
Imperial Majesty’s resolution and unalterable views in this respects to the world, 
at large, to afford a decisive proof of His Royal solicitude on behalf of his 
people; and there can be no doubt whatever that this measure will serve as 
a real and full security to all, 

In making this communication te your Excellency by order of His 
Imperial Majesty, 1 avail myself, &c. :

(Translation.) Shaban 7, 1269. (May 15, 1853.) 
PRINCE MENCHIKOFF’S last note has been laid before the Sultan. 

_ His Execllency the Prince has already been informed, both directly and 
indirectly, that owing to the change in the epartment, it is impossible to give 
4 precise answer on a matter of such delicacy as this of the religious privileges, 
without acquiring sufficient information thereon; but as His Imperial Majesty 
is most desirous that all manner of friendly relations should be maintained with 
the illustrious Government of Russia, the Prince is informed that the Sublime 
Porte is sincerely desirous that an arrangement, conveying assurances satisfactory 
to both parties, should be come to; that a delay of five or six days will be 
sufficient for this purpose, and that it will be sateen to settle the matter 
earlier if possible,

No. 347, 


Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received June 3.) 
(No.207. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Berlin, May 30, 1853. 

| CALLED on Baron Manteuffel yesterday, his Excellency having pre- 
viously informed me that he wished to see me on the subject of the late news 
from the East. 

He began by observing that he had been desired by the King to make 
known to me the concern which His Majesty's felt at the departure of Prince 
Menchikoff from Constantinople, as reported by the telegraph, and the probable 
suspension of the diplomatic relations of Russia and Turkey, and then said that 
he wished to now whether L could communicate to him any intelligence that 
would guide him as to the policy of Her Majesty's Government at this juncture, 
[ replied that I had no instructions relative to the turn which these affairs had 
taken, but that I was so far aware of the opinions of Her Majesty's Government 
that I could assure him they were unprepared for the “ Sened " or Convention 
which had been proposed by Prince Menchikoff—a document having nominally 
for its object the better protection of the Greck subjects of the Porte in the 
exercise of their religion, but which would in reality give to Russia a right of 
interference in the internal affairs of Turkey incompatible with her independence. 
I then communicated to his Excellency, and I trust your Lordship will approve 
of my having done so, your despatch to Sir Hamilton Seymour No. 69 of the 16th 
instant, for which he thanked me, saying the opinions which it contained quite 
coincided with those of the Prussian Government, and the knowledge of them 
would be of the greatest value to him. Baron Manteuffel went on to say that 
the impression which had been made on him by the intelligence received from St. 
Petersburgh, and from other quarters, was the same as that stated by your Lord- 
ship, and that it appeared that the Cabinets of Berlin, London, and Paris, had 
been all led to believe that when once the question of the holy places was settled 
nothing else of importance remained to be done by Prince Menchikoff; conse- 
quent: as no intimation to the contrary had reached him from the Russian 

overnment, the King was inclined to believe, and he fain y*shed to be of the 
same opinion as His Majesty, that Prince Menchikoff had overstepped his instrue- 
tions and must be disavowed. 

I replied that this would he the most satisfactory way of getting out of the 
difficulty, but that disavowals were not usual in Russian diplomacy; and that, 
further, Baron Budberg, to whom I had just been speaking, gave me to under- 
stand that he believed Prince Menchikoff had not acted without instructions, 
and that the draft of Convention which he had proposed, had actually been sent 
from St, Petersburgh. I added that I had had a good deal of experience of the 
system pursued by Russia in matters relating to the Kast, and that I had always 
found the Government, though disposed to communicate at times with frankness 
upon the affairs of Western Europe, unwilling to act in the same wayas regards those 
of Turkey, and moreover that it invariably considered its position towards that 
country exceptional, and was therefore reserved in her communications ; that 
her confidences as to her plans never went further than she considered likely to 
answer her own immediate purposes, and to advance her own selfish interests, 
and that I thought this was clearly demonstrated by her present conduct. 

Buron Manteuffel then said that he thought of writing to St. Petersburgh, 
and expressing the astonishment with which the last news from Constantinople 
had been received here; that the Prussian Government had expected to learn a 


he ee 
- re? De . Se 
SS ———— 


346 


totally different termination to Prince Menchikoff’s embagsy; and that he con- 
jared the Russian Goyernment so to act towards Turkey, that while attending to 
the wants of the Christians, there should be no attempt at interference with the 
independence of the Porte, which Prussia, in common with the other Powers, 
was interested and bound in maintaining; and, that further, in consequence of 
the difficulties which had arisen, the Prussian Government offered the services 
of their Mission at Constantinople, if they could be made available in bringing 
about a settlement of the difference with the Porte. 

I replied that I was sure Her Majesty's Government would learn with 
satisfaction the feelings which the proceedings of Prince Menchikoff had pro- 
duced, but I thought that before taking this step, he should await the arrival of 
his despatches from M, Wildenbruch; that he ad as yet only received a tele- 
graphic account of the occurrences ab Constantinople; that in a yg of days 
we should probably have some news from St. Petersburgh, and that I therefore 
thought he could safely delay a short time before sending off this instruction, 
when he would be in possession of further details. 

He agreed with me that there was no immediate hurry, and he said that 
he had been the more anxious to unburthen his mind to me, as he had spoken 
on the subject to the Russian Minister, who had told him that any commmmica- 
tion of this nature from Berlin would be very displeasing to the Emperor, and 
that it should be avoided. 

I then said that I was glad to see the independent course he was about ta 
adopt at this important crisis, and I trusted that although he might be disposed 
to modify his instructions according to the news which he must shortly receive 
from different quarters, nothing would deter him from carrying out his present 
intentions. 

Baron Manteuffel rejoined that I might depend upon this being done, 
adding, “Je tiens & constater que nous ne voulons pas étre a le remorque de la 
Russie.” 

The impression which has been made by the last reports from Turkey is 
most unfavourable to the Russian Government, Baron Manteuffel considers 
Prince Menchikoff to have gone far beyond everything that we were given to 
expect, and that the endeavours of the Great Powers must now be directed to 
discover some loophole by which # reconciliation of the differences can be effected 
anda rupture avoided. I think that I may safely assure your Lordship that 
the conduct of the Russian Government is generally condemned, and that the 

inion of the public and of the diplomatic body here is united in deprecating 
the proceedings of Prince Menchikoff; all agree that it is impossible for the 
Porte to sign this Treaty, without incurring the loss of her independence. 

The language of my Austrian eons is that he believes his Government 
does not object to the substance of the ussian demands, but to the form in 
which they have been put, and that the Great Powers should endeavour to come 
to an understanding as to the establishment of a conference on the affairs of 
Turkey, the basis of which to be, that none of them should act singly against 
the Porte, and that the determination of the Five to uphold her dignity and 
independence should be thus proclaimed. 

The Russian Minister's language has lately been in contradiction of his 
former assurances, but still lam not aware that he ts fully informed as to the 
nature of the instractions which have been sent to Prince Menchikoff; but he 
has certainly given me to understand that the terms of the “Sened” were not 
invented by Prince Menchikoff, but sent from St. Petersburgh; and, further, on 

my observing that the departure of M. Ozeroff was impossible, as it would 
imply a rupture of diplomatic relations between the two Courts, he said that he 
believed it was probable. In reply to a further question I put to him as to what 
was to happen next—whether the Russian armies would advance, he said that 
he did not believe they would; that time would ny allowed for negotia- 
tions; but that, if the French squadron passe the anelles, the Russian 
troops would enter the Principalities, 


T have, Xe, 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.
