No. 355. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—{ Received June 6.) 


(No. 397.) 


My Lord, Paris, June 6, 1853. 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS has just informed me that he saw the Emperor 

esterday, and that, after acquainting His Majesty with the resolution taken by 

Ter Majesty’s Government, in consequence of the intelligence lately received 
both from Constantinople and St. Petersburgh, to order Admiral Dundas to 
approach the Dardanelles, and to place himself under the orders of Lord Strat- 
ford de Redcliffe, he stated to His Majesty the strong desire which your Lord- 
ship had expressed, that the two Governments should act entirely in concert for 
the maintenance of the independence of the Porte, and of the integrity of the 
Ottoman Fmpire. 

His Majesty inquired whether it was certain that Admiral Dundas had been 
actually ordered to leave Malta, and on being assured of the fact, acquiesced in 
telegraphic orders being sent to Marseilles, to order the “ Chaptal” to get under 
weigh with despatches for Admiral de la Susse and M. de la Cour. 

These despatches, being sent by telegraph, were naturally short, but as 
both the Admiral and M. de la Cour were provided with ample instructions at 
an earlier period, it is only necessary that they should now be informed of the 
movements of Her Majesty's fleet, and that the one should be enjoined to act in 
concert with Admiral Dundas to execute any orders which may be transmitted 
from Constantinople, and that the other should be instructed to consult and 
come to an understanding with Lord Stratford de Redcliffe as to the orders which 
the Admirals are to receive. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys was good enough to read me the instructions now 
sent by the “ Chaptal,” as also those with which M, de la Cour was furnished in 
March last, on taking his departure for the East. As these latter will be com- 
municated to your Lordship confidentially by Count Walewski, I need only add 
that the most complete authority is given by them to M. de la Cour to bring the 
French fleet, under certain eventualities and at the demand of the Turkish 
Government, within the Dardanelles, and, should more be required in conse- 
quence of actual hosilities on the part of Russia, to dispose of the material force 
of the fleet for the Sultan's assistance. 

Neither must I omit to record the satisfaction with which I read that M. de 
la Cour was enjoined, the case arising, to inform Her Majesty's Representative at 
Constantinople of any determination to which he might come; that if (what is 
admitted to be most unlikely) no demand for assistance should be made of 
England when it is made of France, he should urge the Turkish Government to 
place the two countries in a similar position; and that, finally, the Mrench 
Admiral is to be desired, if the British fleet should arrive after the French fleet 
had taken a decided step, to enter into immediate relations with his British 
colleague, and offer to share with him whatever plan of action had been or might 
be agreed upon, 

In the despatches transmitted by the ‘ Chaptal,”” M. de la Cour is referred 
to these instructions; he is told that Her Majesty’s fleet is placed under Lord 
Stratford's directions, and that the two fleets will rendezvous at Besika Bay, 
there to await orders from Constantinople. 

Admiral de la Susse is desired to make for Besika Bay, where he is told he 
will find the English fleet. 

Some misunderstanding has arisen with respect to this latter point. I was 
asked, as having some acquaintance with Turkey, where it was probable the 
English fleet would go, and I replied that in summer Besika Bay, which is at 
the mouth of the Dardanelles, would very likely be the rendezvous, M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys took what I mentioned as a probability for a certainty, aud gave orders 
in consequence. I have called his attention to the error which he has made, 
but as it is more than probable that a part, if not the whole, of the British fleet 
will make for that anchorage, I trust that the error will be of no material 
consequence, I have, Xe, 


(Signed) COWLEY,

establishing a sort of conference of the four Powers at Vienna.

cannot pronounce herself until she has heard from St. Petersburgh ; that she 
could not consent to a conference from which Russia should be excluded; and

never approved of the selection of Prince Menchikoff for the embassy on which

but still he could not be disavowed. He then repeated the old worn-out argu- 
ments that Russia must have security for the future good conduct of the 
Turkish authorities reapecting the Greek Church, and added that nothing short 
ofa Convention drawn up perhaps little “differently would satisfy the Emperor ; 
and that he was full of hope that the last communication made to your Lord- 
ship by Baron brunnow, would smooth the way for an arrangement. He talked 
of the admirable condition of the fleet in the Black Sea, and seemed to think that 
it required but the will of the Emperor to drive the Turks from Europe ; for 
that the Christians would one and all, if the least effort was made to rouse them, 
join the Russian standard, but that nothing was further from the Emperor's 
wishes than having recourse to such a proceeding, 

It did not appear to me that Baron Budberg was aware of the conversation 
which Sit Hamilton Seymour had held with Count Neaselrode, as reported in 
that Minister's despately No. 261. He came to me, however, prepared to allow 
that Prince Menchikoff’s negotiation had been badly managed, but determined 
to convince me that, although faults had been committed, his Highness would 
be supported, Further he would not allow that there had been any serious 
discrepancy between the assurances given at St. Petersburgh to Her Majesty's 

Minister and by Baron Brannow to your Lordship, and the proceedings of 
Prince Menchikoff; neither would he admit that any ill effect had been produced 
here or at Vienna, by what had eked out relating to the proceedings of his 
Government.

M. le Comte, Paris, le 5 Juin, 1853, 

J'AL recu les déptches que vous m’avez fait 'honneur de m’¢erire jusqu'au 
No. 272, et j'ai placé sous les yeux de VEmpereur celle of vous mannoncez 
que l'escadre commandée par M. PAmiral Dundas est mise A Ventiere dis- 
position de Lord Stratford. Sa Majesté Impériale se félicite de Videntité de 
vues et d'action qui existent entre son propre Gouvernement et celui de Sa 
Majesté Britannique, et elle espére que son effet sera d'empécher les com- 
plications qui pourraient surgir en Orient et menacer sérieusement la paix 
générale. 

Das le début de la mission de M. le Prince Menchikoff, nous avions congu 
des inquictudes sur son résultat; mais nous n'avions jaamis douté que du moment 
ob le Gouvernement de Sa Majesté Britannique partagerait nos apprehensions, 
des intéréts communs et un désir égal de maintenir Vintégrité et l'indépendance 
de Empire Ottoman dans leurs conditions actuelles ne dussent réumir vers le 
méme but les efforts de la France et de Angleterre. C'est dans cette confiance 
si pleinement justifice, que javais, Wapres les ordres de l'Empereur, rédigé les 
‘nstructions de M. de la Cour, et qu’en lui donnant, A la date du 22 Mars, 
Yautorisation d’appeler V’escadre Frangaise aux Dardanelles, je lui recommandais, 
si cette grave mesure lui paraissatt nécessaire, de stentendre avec Lord Stratford 
pour combiner autant que possible les mouvements de nos forces navales avec 
ceux de la flotte Anglaise. 

L’Ambassadeur de Sa Majesté Impériale, M. le Comte, se trouve done 
déja muni de toutes les directions dont il a besoin pour prendre une attitude 
absolument semblable & celle de ‘Ambassadeur de Sa Majesté Patan Ge et

de se rapprocher des Dardanelles et de mouiller dans la Baie de Besica, Le 
by Chaptal,” qui lui porte cet ordre, @ quitté Toulon hier, et de cette fagon les

constater l'accord des deux Gouvernements, ef nous espérons fermement qu'une 
telle démonstration, autorisée par les armements de la Russie elle-méme, sutfira 
pour donner a la diplomatic le temps de prévenir une rupture plus compléte 
entre le Cabinet de St. Pétersbourg et la Porte Ottomane. C'est dans le Traite de 
1841 que nous puisons notre droit; il ne saurait dés-lors étre dans nos inten- 
tions de ne pas observer fidélement, tant qu’aucun acte agressif n'aura pas mis 
la Turquie dans le cas d'une légitime défense, Nous attendrons done pour 
franchir les Dardanelles, que ja Russie ait commencé les hostilités par terre ou 

mer contre |'Empire Ottoman, et que la Porte, en nous adressant une 
demande d’appui, nous ait déclaré qu'elle se considére comme en état de guerre. 
Ce jour-1i, M. le Comte, le Traité de 1841 sera méconnu par Vune de ces Parties 
Contractantes, et, en vertu de l'esprit qui l'a dicté, & raison des immenses intéréts 

ui font du maintien de la Turqme une necessité d'équilibre Européen, nous 
réterons a cette Puissance tout le concours qu'elle récla de nous. Il est 
bien entendu, d'ailleurs, M. le Comte, que non-obstant les circonstances qui 
peuvent survenir, nous he cesserons de faire, & tout moment, de loyaux efforts

No. 367. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received June 7.) 
(No. 263.) 
My Lord, 


St. Petersburgh, May 31, 1853. 
HALF-AN-HOUR after the departure of the messenger who left St. 
Petersburgh on the 28th instant, I received a note from Count Nesselrode who 
desired to see me on the following day. 1 requested that our meeting might 
take place immediately, as [ was aware that a Feld-Jiger from Prince Menchi- 
koff had arrived in the morning. I learned, however, from his Excellency that 
the papers which he wished to communicate to me would be returned to him 
only on the 29th. 

On the 29th accordingly | waited upon the Chancellor, who gave mean 
account of the circumstances which had led to the departure of Prince Men- 
chikoff from Constantinople, and read to me various documents in explanation 
of his withdrawal. 

These papers were the letters addressed by Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to 
Prince Menchikoff, and the Prince’s reply; the “Projet de Note” which had 
been prepared by the Russian Embassy for the signature of the Sultan's Minister ; 
and the short despatch in which the Russian Ambassador relates the events 
which led to his embarkation for Odessa. Count Nesselrode, as before, laid 
great stress upon the moderation of the Russian demands: they were only for 
a confirmation of the Emperor's rights, and such as | had always been led to 
expect; they bore upon no exclusive privilege, they should be received as a 
roof of the wish of removing all grounds of dissension between Russia and 


urkey. 

If the demands too were moderate, the manner in which they were urged 

was not less so. ‘To meet the views of Her Majesty’s Ambassador a Sened had 
been prepared in lieu of a Treaty, and subsequently an ordinary official note 
had been substituted for the Sened; conciliation could hardly be pushed further, 
whilst, as I had heard, it was the Queen's Ambassador who had prevented the 
acceptance of those moderate terms which the most prudent of the Sultan's 
advisers had considered essential for the safety of Turkey. 
‘To this I replied that I must repeat that 1 had been informed several times 
by his Excellency that it was intended that the status que which had been 
troubled at Jerusalem should be re-established by firmans, the foree of which 
should be sanctioned by an international Act, but that L had never understood 
that there was question of any new rights being conferred by that Act upon the 
Crown of Russia. 

At the close of our conversation, Count Nesselrode, who is evidently much 
pained by the events which he had been communicating to me, observed that it 
could not be denied that the state of affairs was very alarming; that the position 
of the Emperor was one from which it was impossible for His Majesty to recede, 
and that he would not conceal from me that a continued rejection of the terms 
offered to the Porte, would be followed by the issue of orders for the entrance of 
the Russian armies into the Principalities, His Excellency was desirous of 
remarking to me that war could hardly be undertaken by the Sultan under more 
disadvantageous circumstances than when it was brought about by a refusal of 
those conditions the acceptance of which was so warmly desired by the whole 
Greek population of Turkey, and which carried with them the sympathy of the 
co-religionists of this country. 

It only remained for him to say that he Jad been ordered to apprize me 
that, if 1 desired to sce the Emperor, His Majesty would receive me on the 
following day; to which I answered that there was but one reply to such an 
intimation, and that of course [ should have the honour of obeying the Emperor's 
commands, 

It is right that I should report to your Lordship that the Chancellor then 
suggested that I should unhesitatingly entreat of His Majesty to refrain from 
issuing orders for the advance of the Russian forces until the opinion of Her 
Majesty’s Government should be learned upon the late events, intelligence of 
which, as I found, has been conveyed to London by Count Dimitri Nesselrode. 

3 A2 


ons 


1 will likewise observe that Prince Menchikoff, whilst relating particulars of the 
activity displayed by Viscount Stratford de Redeliffe in urging the Turks to 
reject his demands, and of course taking the line of blaming his Excellency’s 
conduct, makes no allusion to the attitude assumed by the French Ambassador 
during the late critical transactions. 

Before concluding my despatch, 1 am desirous of stating to your Lordship 
that a very manifest change has taken place of late in the public feeling of the 
Russian society, which is now seen to be very favourable to matters being 
pushed to extremity with the Turks. 

The language commonly used, and which has been repeated to me by some 
of my diplomatic colleagues, is that further negotiation is idle trifling; that the 
course which ought to be followed is to fall upon Turkey and to settle differences 
at the point of the bayonet. 

1 have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H, SEYMOUR. 


No. 368, 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recewed June 7.) 


(No. 263. Seeret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, Si. Petersburgh, May 31, 1853. 


I HAD the honour of holding yesterday a long and extremely interesting 
conversation with the Emperor, the most important parts of which it becomes 
my duty ta report to your Lordship. 

The Emperor, somewhat to my surprise, received me most graciously, 
saying that he was glad to see me, that he had felt sure 1 must wish to converse 
with him upon the late important events, and that, as I must be aware, he was 
always ready to receive me. 

I had expected that His Majesty would have opened the conversation, but 
instead of that he desired to hear what I thought of the events which had led to 
the rupture of the negotiation at Constantinople. 

In general terms I expressed my deep regret at any circumstances which 
threatened the good understanding which ought to exist among all Govern- 
ments, and peculany between those of England and Russia, when the Emperor 
asked me very pointedly whether he had not kept faith with me? at the same 
time alluding to passages in former conversations which I had held with His 
Majesty. 

L replied that of the wish entertained by the Emperor and his Government 
to keep faith with every one no doubt could be entertained, and therefore it was 
that [ was compelled to infer that some misapprehension (mésentendu) must 
exist with regard to the demands upon the Porte. 

His Majesty, | said, would perhaps be good enough to allow me to reca- 
pitulate events, 

When the dispute, I said, respecting the holy places took place, 1 was told 
that Russia required a satisfaction for the past and security forthe future. Later, 
this was explained to me more fully as meaning that the status of the Greek 
and Latin rights should be settled by a firman, and that this firman should be 
sanctioned by a Treaty or public Act, in short by an international engagement. 
It was further stated fo me, and this over and over again, that the precaution 
was required, as it was essential that Russia should possess an instrument of the 
same value as Capitulations often invoked by the French Government; but, I 
said, Sir, there never was to my knowledge any question of new rights to be con- 
ferred upon the Crown of Russia, and when your Majesty complains (as the 

Emperor had done) of English diplomacy in Turkey, it may well be conceived 
that an English diplomatist would give his support to those pretensions which 
had been made known and admitted to be just, whilst he your oppose those of 
which he had no knowledge. 

The Emperor replied that I was quite correct; that a confirmation of 
existing rights had been all that it was intended to ask for, and all that had been 
demanded by Prinee Menchikoff. 

l1is Majesty then spoke with some vivaeity of the conduct of the Queen's 


09 


Ambassador at Constantinople, saying that in strict right he should be justified 
in asking for explanations of Her Majesty for this conduct. This he should not 
do, but he had now an opportunity of judging of the feelings of the English 
Government towards him. Professions of goodwill and friendship had been 
made to him; if, as he hoped and believed, those professions were sincere, the 
conduct of Her Majesty’s Ambassador at Constantinople could not be approved of. 
___ [requested permission to observe, that. Lord Stratford's conduct was to be 
judged of by the circumstance to which I before alluded, that ts, by the fact 
whether or no the Treaty, or “Sened,” or note to be required from the Porte, 
confirmed old rights, or invested the Emperor with new ones. 

I hoped that His Majesty would excuse me if I remarked that I was not 
aware of any Treaty which gave to Russia the sort of protectorate now claimed ; 
and I said, Sir, so much is this the case that when Colonel Rose wrote word that 
it was conjectured that a protectorate was one of the points to be demanded of 
the Porte, I took upon myself to say that I believed the suspicion to be devoid 
of foundation. 

The Emperor insisting upon the ancient date of his rights, I ventured to 
ask by what Convention they were guaranteed ; and when His Majesty alluded 
to that of Kainardji, I took the liberty of replying, that having looked into the 
ear of 1774, I had been unable to discover anything of the kind. 

: added, that perhaps His Majesty would allow me to call upon the 
Chancellor in his name, and ask him to show me the Article or Articles 
referred to. The Emperor rejoined, with much good humour, that 1 was quite 
at liberty todo so; that I might, if I pleased, call for the originals of the 
Treaties, 

After this discussion had continued a little longer, 1 observed that | had 
now to make an appeal to the Emperor's goodwill and high feelings; that | 
had been informed that unless the breach recently made in the relations between 
Russia and Turkey should be speedily repaired, His Majesty intended to give 
orders for the occupation of the Principalities; that I would earnestly beg that 
no orders to this effect should be ‘raed until time were afforded for comnni- 
eation with Her Majesty's Government, 

The Emperor observed, that the demand was just, and that my wishes had 
been forestalled : that a courier would be dispatehed to-morrow (meaning the 31st, 
to-day) to Constantinople, to apprize the Turkish Government that eight days 
were allowed for reconsideration of the terms proposed; but that i at the 
expiration of the term, satisfaction were not affor ed, His Majesty, however 
unwillingly, must give orders for the advanee of his forces, 

Allow me, Sir, I said, as very important interests are at stake, to suggest 
that you should wait until I can have an answer to the reference which on the’ 
a of June eaipnes ave to make to Her Majesty's Government. ‘That, the 

mperor replied, is not necessary, as already a reference t ndon 
aes ne ag cae ry \ rence to London has been 

The precaution, Sir, I said in reply, was very commendable; but permit me 
to remark, that little attention would be paid by Her Majesty's Government to 
Prince Menchikoff’s statements, in comparison to what would be bestowed 
upon your Majesty's representations. Will it not, then, be better to awnit an 
answer to the words which your Majesty has just spoken, or to those which you 
may think proper to address to me ? 

Upon this point the Emperor was not to be moved. Sir Hamilton Seymour, 
he said, has had several conversations with the Emperor, who spoke to him with 
a total absence of reserve. Sir Hamilton Seymour must have written a report 
of these conversations. I have nothing to add to the information of which the 
English Government is in possession. 

We next spoke of eventualities, If hostilities broke out in the East, the 
event might, the Emperor feared, produce evil consequences for Her Majesty’s 
Government. TI replied, that I thought it highly probable that, in this event, 
the publie would not fail to reproach the Government with their extreme confi- 
dence in the intentions of the Emperor of Russia, which had led to the neglect of 
those precautions usually resorted to when the safety of Turkey was menaced. 
As regards myself, I said, Sir, 1 believe your Majesty knows my feelings ; 
nobody can be more indifferent than I am whether I retain or lose my: position, 
With regard to Her Majesty's Government, the question has a very different 
importance. It is probable that a change of Government, under existing 


360) 


circumstances, must have very disastrous effects—that is a point which I leave 
to your Majesty’s consideration. 

After a digression upon this subject, 1 returned to the former, and, as it 
appears to me, the real point of the whole question. Sir, I said, as your 
Majesty is good enough to listen with great patience to my observations, permit 
me to remark, that if your Majesty is correct in stating that no fresh rights are 
sought for the Imperial Government, the objections entertained towards the 
note presented for the Porte’s acceptance and signature must tum upon a 
matter of “rédaction:” allow me, then, to inquire whether there will be any 
objection to such an alteration m the terms of the note as shall remove all 
doubts—as shall leave a simple confirmation of old rights, and preclude the 
possibility of any new ones being claimed. 

No, the Emperor replied, certainly not. Every effort has been made to 
meet the views of the Turkish Government, or rather of the English Ambas- 
sador. ‘The note having been rejected shall now be accepted as it stands, 
without the alteration of a single word; and its acceptance shall be signified 
within eight days, or Turkey must abide by the consequences, 

The Emperor proceeding to speak as if England must necessarily be a 
party to any war which might break out in consequence of a refusal by the 
Sultan to accept the conditions offered by Prince Menchikoff, 1 said it is impos- 
sible, Sir, to take a more dispassionate view than I do of the state of Turkish 
affairs. Your strength and the weakness of the Ottoman Empire are so palpable 
that 1 do not question the power which you possess of overrunning the country 
when you please; only I would remark, as I was born in 1797, it is not probable 
that 1 should ever witness the conclusion of a war commenced under such 
circumstances, The fact is, I continued, Sir, that the repose of the world 
depends mainly upon the relations in which England and Russia stand to each 
other; a good understanding existing between the two countries, the peace of 
Europe is assured; two such colossal Powers disagreeing, the peace of the 
world is troubled, and the greatest mischief may be inflicted by each upon the 
other. 

There, the Emperor said, you are perfectly right. 1 am a year older than 
you are; family considerations, national interests, every motive the most 
powerful, induce me to wish for peace. We require peace for the consolidation 


of a young country. War, I well know, would paralyze commerce in the. 


North, and would lead to its utter destruction in the South; but you see what 
my position is. [ am the head of a people of the Greek religion; our 
co-religionists of Turkey look up to me as their natural protector; and these 
are claims which it is impossible for me to disregard. I have the conviction 
that good right is on my side: I should therefore begin a war, such as that 
which now impends, without compunction, and should be prepared to carry it 
on, as | have before remarked to you, as long as there should be a rouble in 
the Treasury, or 4 man in the country. 

The Emperor proceeded again to speak of Her Majesty's Ambassador at 
Constantinople, whom His Majesty regards (and as I assure him without any 
reason) as lis personal enemy; the position of affairs, His Majesty said, is a 
yery singular one, We had a dispute with France, who, finding that she was 
wrong, withdrew her Ambassador, and sent another in his place, when the 

uarrel is terminated without difficulty. At ite conclusion, however, the 
English Ambassador, who is understood to be instructed to support my claims, 
takes part against me; in the arrangement to be made with the Porte proves 
himself more Turkish than the Sultan’s own Ministers, and prevents the accept- 
ance of conditions which had been offered with full consideration for the 
Sultan's dignity and independence, whilst the French Ambassador takes no 
part against me. 

] will not conclude the report of my conversation with the Emperor with- 
out stating, that the patience which His Majesty bestowed to the various 
observations which I addressed to him, was the more remarkable as I happen 
to know that some strong and indiscreet expressions with regard to the bad faith 
of the Government, which had escaped me under the influence of fresh feelings, 
had been brought to His Majesty's knowledge. 

Tt was to these which His Majesty alluded in the first question which he 
addressed to ime. 

Upon quitting the palace, 1 ealled upon Count Nesselrode, to whom I 


361 


related my conversation with His Imperial master, laying particular stress upon 
the reference which I was empowered to make to his Excel ency. 

Count Nesselrode replied, that there could be no doubt of the fact being 
as it had been stated by the Emperor; but this was said, as appeared to me, 
with a want of assurance ; and I propose returning to the subject, and request- 
ing a reference to the Treaty by which any protectorate of the Turkish Greeks 
is secured to the Crown of Russia. 

_ Baron Meyendorff, who, | may remark, was to set off yesterday upon 
his return to Vienna, is equally positive as to the rights already possessed by 
Russia ; this, however, does not alter my opinion, and the clearer the right may 
be, the less will be the difficulty of establishing it by proof. 

At the same time I will not, on this occasion, mention Baron Meyendorff's 
name without stating, that the part which he has taken in this new crisis, is one 
which is infinitely to his credit. 

I have omitted many points of minor importance which were touched upon 
by the Emperor, but am willing to believe that these will find their place ina 
long report upon the Turkish difficulties which has been for the last two or three 
aah in preparation, and which, if completed and approved of by the Emperor, 
will be despatched by messenger this evening to Baron de Brunnow, 

I have, &c. 


(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

| RECEIVED on Sunday afternoon the 5th instant, by telegraph from 
Lord Bloomfield at Berlin, the communication which you requested him to 
forward to me that, “at the date of the 30th of May, the Emperor whom you had

Turkish Government of the projet de note which was delivered to them by Prince 
Menchikoff ;” and in consequence of your request that a reply might if possible 
be sent to you by telegraph, I sent a message to Lord Bloomfield in the course 
of Sunday night, by telegraph, directing him to “inform you that the form of 
a Treaty is alone objectionable. Russia can in other ways get anything she is 
entitled to claim.”

that not Lord Stratford de Redcliffe alone, but the Sultan and his Ministers

The Emperor cannot doubt the warm feelings of friendship towards himself 
entertained by our Gracious Sovereign, and His Imperial Majesty must be also 
aware that it is alike the duty and the desire of Her Majesty’s Government to 
maintain the most cordial relations with Russia, feeling how essential such 
relations are to the peace of Europe, and viewing as they do with alarm and 
abhorrence whatever may tend to the interruption of that peace. His Imperial 
Majesty may therefore be well assured that it is upon no light grounds that they 
differ from him as to the demands he now makes upon Turkey; and Her 
Majesty's Government will not bring themselves to think that these demands do 
not still admit of settlement in a manner entirely consistent with the dignity of 
His Imperial Majesty without having recourse to those measures of coercion 
which, onee undertaken, must soon have the most baneful effects throughout 
Europe, and which even now are looked to by the evil-minded with joyful 
expectation, while by every friend of order they are regarded with the deepest 
apprehension. 

Her Majesty's Government, I repeat, do not believe that Europe can be in 
danger of the terrible and overwhelming calamity of war from a question such as 
that which is now pending at Constantinople; they do not believe that the 
door will be finally closed against an arrangement which to them appears to be 
still practicable and they venture therefore to hope that the demands of Russia 
may be confined to the recapitulation of existing Treaties and their due fulfilment, 
but without seeking to extend that influence over the Greek subjects of the 
Porte that Russia must always and necessarily exercise. Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment are convinced that such a course would not be inconsistent with the dignity 
of the Emperor, and they are encouraged in the hope that it may still be adopted, 

with reference to the misunderstanding under which they have so long laboured 
with respect to the Emperor's intentions, with reference also to the most recent 
declaration of His Imperial Majesty of his own views as to the objects of Prince 
Menchikoff’s demands, but, more than all, with reference to that pacific policy 


which has invariably and with most signal success been maintained by the 
Emperor of Russia.

My Lord, Berlin, June 5, 1853. 

T HAVE the honour to forward herewith a copy of a despatch which I 
received this morning from Sir Hamilton Seymour, the substance of which will, 
I hope, have reached your Lordship in the course of to-day by telegraph, 

As the intelligence contained in this communication came by post, and was

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 
(No. 211.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, June 8, 1853. 

COUNT WALEWSKI has communicated to me a despatch from M. 
Drovyn de Lhuys stating that his Excellency’s despatch announcing that the 
British fleet under the command of Admiral Dundas was placed at the disposal 
of Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, had been laid before the Emperor, and that His 
Imperial Majesty rejoiced at the identity of views and action which existed 
between his own Government and that of Her Majesty, and hoped that the 
result would be to prevent the complications that might arise in the Kast, and 
seriously menace the general peace. 

The despatch further states the reasons which induced the Emperor to 
direct that authority should be given to M. dela Cour on the 22nd March last 
to send for the French fleet to the Dardanelles, and that Admiral de la Susse 
will now receive orders, at the same time as Admiral Dundas, to proceed towards 
the Dardanelles, and to anchor in Besika Bay. | 

M, Drouyn de Lhuys then, after adverting to the circumstances which 
would render it expedient to afford assistance to Turkey, and to the advice which 
should be tendered to the Sultan, concludes by saying that if similar views and 
intentions are entertained by Her Majesty’s Government, their answer will record 
the union of France and England for an object that can give no cause for alarm 
to other Powers, as the Governments which signed the Convention of the 13th 
of July, 1841, will be at liberty to associate themselves with us in the manner 
and according to the means that they may think proper to employ. 

Your Excellency is accordingly instructed to intorm M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
that his despatch has given much satisfaction to Her Majesty’s Government, 
who entirely concur in the views and intentions which it sets forth. 

It has hitherto been the carnest desire of Her Majesty's Government to 
avoid any demonstration that should wear the appearance of threat or even be 
thought to endanger an amicable settlement of the negotiations pending at Con- 
stantinople; but | have repeatedly informed the French Ambassador, and it has 
been announced in both ‘Wodses of Parliament, that a complete identity of 
opinion existed between the two Governments, and that both consequently were 
desirous to uphold the Turkish Empire. 

The time has however now arrived when an understanding as to unity of 
action becomes necessary, and Her Majesty’s Government cordially agree with 
the French Government that the main object of this must be to avoid complica- 
tions dangerous to the peace of the world, and to afford time to the friendly 
action of diplomacy to prevent a more complete rupture between the Cabinet of 
St. Petersburgh and the Ottoman Porte. 

They desire equally with the French Government to prove that they are 
animated by no hostile feeling towards Russia, by exerting their best efforts to 
reconcile the claims of that Power with the sovereign rights of the Porte, They 
intend, as does the French Government, scrupulously to observe the Treaty of 
1841, and to excite no alarm on the part of other Governments; and finally, 
they hope that the Representatives of England and France at Cansantinonle 
will, in the exercise of the great powers now confided to them, observe the 
utmost moderation and diseretion. 

In the belief that the above is oa faithful interpretation of the despatch of 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys, and with the desire that unreserved confidence should 
exist between the two Governments upon this important question, your Excel- 
lency is instructed to give to M. Drouyn de Lhuys a copy of this despatch, 
together with copies of my despatch to Lord Stratford placing the British fleet 
at his disposal, and of the instructions that have in consequence been sent to 
Admiral Dundas. . 

Tam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

ence of Turkey is still a recognized object of eatg tae and most especially

367 

of 1840, professes an unabated adherence to this principle. But the legalized 
introduction of a dominant foreign influence may prove as fatal to the independ- 
ence of a country as partial dismemberment or military occupation. Cireum- 
stances have brought this question to an issue. If the Porte be right in its 
apprehension and resistance, Her Majesty's Government will no doubt employ 
their available means for the purpose of rescuing it from an unmerited and 
imminent danger. Unsupported by such assistance, whetiver single or united, 
moral or material, the Turkish Empire will have to undergo either the risks of 
actual war with disproportioned means of defence, or a protracted state of tension 
and alarm, involving much expense, and liable to terminate at least in hostilities, 
orin a disastrous compromise. 

The solemn assurances repeatedly given by the Emperor of Russia, the 
total absence of any just cause of war, and the terms in which Prince Menchikoff 
declared his final resolution, would seem to forbid a recourse to immediate hosti- 
lities. But some expressions which have occasionally escaped from His Majesty's 
lips, the signal want of harmony between certain statements of Count Nesselrode 
and certain proceedings of Prince Menchikoff, the unexplained continuance in 
Bessarabia of w strong Russian foree occupying advanced positions, and the latest 
reports from Galatz and Trebizond, indicating preparations for a general move- 
ment, leave a painful doubt upon the mind. 

In reliance rather on principles than appearances, | have hitherto advised 
the Turkish Ministers, not indeed to suspend altogether the defensive preparations 
which they had commenced before my arrival, but to continue them with as little 
excitement and outward demonstration as the nature of the service would allow. 
This method of proceeding they have hitherto observed with scrupulous atten- 
tion, and nothing at all calculated cither to express defiance or to provoke 
resentment has appeared in their operations, Now that the threatened rupture 
has actually oceurred, more active and decided measures of preparation must. in 
their judgment be adopted; nor could I, with any shadow of fairness, or indeed 
with much prospect of success, attempt to dissuade them from putting them- 
selves without delay into a more effective posture of defence. 

It is not necessary for this PuEpoee to depart from the principle of a moral 
resistance, which, as your Lordships knows, | have recommended to the Porte, 
not only as the safest ground to occupy at present, but as the wisest with refer- 
ence to future results. The possibility of maintaining this position hereafter 
must, of course, depend on the conduct of Russia, and the Sultan meanwhile has 
to guard his responsibility towards the nation, no less than his Ministers have to 
provide for their own towards the Sovereign, 

On the supposition of its being found impossible to avoid hostilities, | need 
not suggest to your Lordship the probable issue of the struggle, if Turkey were 
left to sustain singlehanded all the weight and pressure of its formidable oppo- 
nent, In that case—a case which I am unwilling to anticipate—the sooner the 
Porte were apprized of its helpless condition the better. Placed at the mercy of 
Russia, the Sultan would have no choice but to accept the terms of pardon, 
which a triumphant enemy, anxious to save appearances towards Europe, and 
determined at the same time to accomplish his purpose, might be expected to 
grant. 

I would not willingly exaggerate the character and drift of that purpose; 
but, judging from what little knowledge | possess of Russian policy in this 
country, and not losing sight of the lessons derived from experience, | cannot 
disguise my conviction that it involves the establishment of a predominant 
influence over the counsels of the Porte, tending, in the interest of absolute 
power, to exclude all other influences, and to secure the means, if not of hasten- 
ing the downfall of this Empire, at least of obstructing its improvement, and 
settling its future destinies to the profit of Russia, whenever a propitious 
juncture shall arrive. Other and juster considerations—those in particular of 
religion and good neighbourhood—may have their place in the Emperor's 
mind; but the master-view is the one most likely to predominate under 


favourable circumstances, and thither, 1 humbly conceive, the forethought and 
energies of Western Europe cannot be too soon or too vigorously directed, 
There is little room for supposing, that even the tranquillity of Turkey 
would be promoted by a compliance with the demands of Russia. ‘The exercise 
of a protecting influence over the churches and clergy of the Greco-Russian 
religion, as it 18 omniously called by Russian statesmen, would ever be attended

the millions who profess the Greek religion in Purkey, by ho means exempt

to their tributary subjects in general, the full and free exercise of religious 
worship, together with the enjoyment of all that pertains to its maintenance 
and efficiency. The Turks: are not indifferent to this clam. Their fears of 
Russia and consequent need of European support increase their sense of it ; and 
the Porte is now going to proclaim with due formality a solemn confirmation 
and enforcement of all the religious privileges accorded of old or in later years 
to its Christian subjects, An additional pledge of sincerity 1s to be conveyed 
in this instance by the Sultan’s firmans, in virtue of their official Saami canon 
to the Representatives of the five Powers who concluded the Treaty of 1540. 

We are thus brought by a spontancous but necessary act of the Porte BED 
that ground where a lever may best be planted for exercising more actively than 
heretofore a joint European direction, in place of any single influence exciting 
too much jealousy to work with advantage. The meetings of the four Repre- 

sentatives lately held at my suggestion, and the collective communication 
addressed by them to Reshid Pasha, fall in with this idea; and it remains for 
Her Majesty's Government to follow up the principle, now recommended to 
their approval, by a confidential understanding with the Cabinets of I aries eee 
and Vienna, preparatory to a more complete agreement between the five

out the objects of soma soonsnn i tian manner as might prove most 
ient, and give least umbrage to the Forte, 
ee el denying that the general convenience of Europe calls for the 
preservation of this Empire, however deep and wide-spread may be the germs of 
decay in its bosom, At a period of frequent change arid rapid movement, the 
hour of its dissolution, if not retarded by adequate combinations, may atrike 
much sooner than is generally expected. We are taught by experience that the 
Tarks alone are not equal to the task of improvement on a sufficient scale. 

‘The separate exertions of friendly Governments have hitherto Scanner no 
more than some imperfect and insulated measures. They have sane vort 
of that suatained and pervading system of reform, without which it is idle to 
look for any real or durable return to 4 healthy condition, In the united 


369 


wisdom. of the five Great Powers of Christendom, the Porte might find an 
auxiliary capable of leading it with safety in the path of European civilization, 
and the same friendly union which halt render that important service would 
strengthen the bonds of peace, and afford no weak security against the impa- 
tience or ambition of any single State. 

But the field of improvement is a wide one. The obstructions are sented 
deep in religious prejudice, erroneous principles, and inveterate abuses. The 
views of the Five Powers, when applied to particular objects, would be ocea- 
sionally divergent, and it may be doubted whether all of them would enter with 
the same conviction and the same singleness of purpose upon a reconstructive 
policy. It would probably be found necessary to limit the suggestive action of 
the Conference, and to give it principally a preventive character, with the 
view of diverting the Porte from ill-advised enterprizes and unjustifiable evasiona, 
nor less of imposing on each of the Powers—together with a constant respect 
for the rights of the Porte as an independent State—that degree of forbearance 
in the prosecution of its claims which would be compensated by the support and 
effective cooperation, when needed, of the others, There is reason to hope that 
the dread of having to deal with this kind of European Confederacy would 
Ce ey on the policy of the Porte, and also on the conduct of its 
administration in matters of current interest. [t is evident at the same time 
that a collective interference must be reserved in practice for cases of magnitude 
and real importance. A want of attention to this rule would be productive of 
much embarrassment, if it did not finally defeat the main purpose of the Allies. 
The restraint upon each Power could hardly be viet to go beyond.a fair 
trial of their collective influence, and an engagement not to resort without due 
notice to separate means of coercion, 

With respect to suggestions of improvement in the internal conduct of the 
Porte’s affairs, a previous distinct understanding as to the more prominent 
objects of recommendation and to the course of procedure, both in urging and 
enforcing their adoption, would be indispensable. Guidance without dictation, 
compliance without restraint, constitute the ideul of such a plan; but perfection 
is rarely attainable in human contrivances, and suceess must ultimately be 
sought either in coercion or abandonment,—the former an inroad on national 
independence, the latter an invitation to single aggression and eventual 
dismemberment. 

Notwithstanding its difficulties, inconveniences, and hazards, the experiment 
is one that has many and powerful considerations to recommend it, All Europe 
professes the same creed with respect to Turkey. Its decline is iuawesnnned é 
its dissolution is deprecated; its vices and its resources are alike universally 
acknowledged ; its dangers, when left to itself, ure obvious to the meanest capacity. 
By what more promising or safe method than the one suggested can the evils 
implied in those opinions be either avoided or remedied ? ‘The interests of govern- 
ment, of commerce, of humanity, of morals and religion, are all more or less 
concerned in the rescue of this noble Empire from the degrading consequences of 
a vicious and oppressive Administration combined with a jealous and unexpansive 
policy. Such are the requirements of the age, and such the progress of events, 
that Turkey must either be brought, as a whole, into greater accordance with 
Europe, or be fractionally assimilated with neighbouring Empires by repeti- 
Soe of that process which hag already curtailed its extent to an ominous 
egree. 

If there be one Power among the five more interested than another in the 
support and improvement of Turkey, it is evidently Great Britain, which has 

everything to gain from the expansion of Turkish resources, and little, by com- 
parison, to seize in the scramble for Turkish spoils. How indeed can it be 
otherwise ? The Turkish Empire—still of vast extent—is rich in the elements, 
and poor in the means of production, It has need of British science, enterprize, 
skill, capital, and energy, to place the one upon a level with the other. To these 
auxiliaries an easier admission will naturally be given in proportion as more 
enlightened maxims prevail in its government, and with our peay but 
necessitous redundance in Popplenan, manufactures, and machinery, our defective 
supplies of grain, our dependence on foreign countries for raw materials, and our 


maritime ubiquity, we cannot fail of deriving exhaustless profits from the 
advancement of Turkey in all that constitutes the wealth and strength of an 
empire. Hitherto we have endeavoured, as your Lordship must be aware, to

realize those views by the exertion of British influence moving in the line 
pursued by Turkey itself, and occasionally in concert with other friendly Powers ; 
never secking any exclusive advantage, but acting on broad European principles 
for the benefit of all classes within the Empire, and of all commercial nations 
without. The language which I hold to the Sultan and his Ministers is still of 
the same character, and their assurances are sufficiently favourable to warrant 
the hope of some proficiency in a right course as soon as the present unusual 

ressure upon their attention shall have subsided. It remains with your 
oraship to consider the expediency of bringing a combination of influences to 
bear upon the same point. Meanwhile we have to deal with circumstances of 
greater urgency, and the Porte is compelled by them to employ a large portion 
af its energies in another direction. ce ibe and appearances, confirmed by some 
partial facts, and expressions dropped by Russian agents, concur to prepare us

Vice. Consul Cunningham to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


(Eixtract,) Galatz, May 16, 1853. 

FROM Ismail it is reported that besides the bridges to cross the Danube 
which are being got ready, certain portable bridges of great length are preparing, 
supposed to be for passing marshy ground. It is also said that after the arrival 
ofa steamer at Ismail from Odessa or Sevastopol, guns were immediately put 
into pontons. 

e learn also from Reni that all the waggons have been impressed to carry 
army stores forward to the frontiers of Moldavia, not only the waggons not 
otherwise employed, but even those loaded and engaged in transporting grain. 
These were stopped on the road and unloaded wherever found, and the contents 
left on the wayside, Merchants at Reni, therefore, refused to sell grain except- 
ing what they had already in warehouse. 

With regard to the number of troops in Bessarabia, nothing satisfactory can 
be learnt; but it appears that there are about Leovo and Sculeni, 1 polk of 
Cossacks, | polk of Hulans, and 4 polks of infantry, A polk, or regiment of

My Lord, Trebizond, May 16, 1853. 


1 HAVE the honour to inform your Lordship that some traders have

Russian force had arrived at that garrison from the Caucasus, They estimate

traders quitted Alexandropol about four weeks ago.

Inclosure in No, 382, 
Lord Stratford de Redelijffe to Sir G. H. Seymour. 


Sir, Constantinople, May 23, 1853, 

LONG before this letter can reach St. Petersburgh, you will probably have 
heard, from some other source, of Prince Menchikoft’s departure from Constanti- 
nople, and of the suspension of diplomatic relations between Russia and the 

Porte. I shall deem myself sufficiently fortunate if my letter arrives in time to 
five you a just notion of the causes of his failure, before any mistaken or hasty 
resolution be adopted by the Russian Cabinet in consequence of that disappoint- 
ment. Iam the more desirous of bringing the case to your knowledge in its 
true colours because it has come round to me that lam suspected of having 
mainly contributed to the Ambassador's discomfiture ; not that | would take the 
trouble to remove any error of that kind from personal considerations, but 
simply because a false impression of our policy at home may follow from the 
imputation, and diminish for a time your means of exercising a salutary influence 
in Eastern matters. 

When I left England, and indeed when I arrived here, afler passing through 
Paris and Vienna, it was generally supposed that the only important object of 
Prince Menchikoff’s embassy was to settle the question of the Holy Places, To 
all appearance no one, even at Vienna, dreamed of the far more important 
demands which Russia held in reserve, and which, when finally made known to 
the Turkish Ministers, were strictly confined to them, as matters not to be 
divulged with impunity to any third party. Though I was not long in obtain- 
ing access to the secret, | did not the less endeavour to promote an early and 
amicable adjustment of what belonged more particularly to the holy places ; 
and | had the good fortune to receive an acknowledgment of my friendly ottices 
from Prince Menchikoff himself, The confidential interview which took place 
between us afforded me in due time an opportunity, of which | availed myself, 
to apprize his Excellency of the difficulties which | foresaw that he would 
encounter whenever he entered upon the ground of the Russian protection and 
Greck privileges. 

1 must do him the justice to say that he listened to me with courtesy, and 
subsequently gave me to understand that he had partially moditied his demands 
with reference to the considerations which I had urged, Unfortunately 
the amendment was superficial; and when the Turkish Ministers, immediately 
upon the arrangement of the first question, were compelled by a peremptory 
requisition from the Prince to enter seriously into the remaining questions, 
they manifested a settled determination not to comply with that part of 
them which related to a guarantee in the shape of an engagement binding upon 
both parties with the force of a Treaty. 

From this resolution of theirs [ was not prepared to dissent, for the reasons 
which are stated in a confidential letter subsequently addressed by me to the 
Russian Ambassador, less with any hope of inducing him to alter his views,

UNE partaite entente sur quelques questions entre la Sublime Porte et la 
Cour de Russie n’ayant pas pu avoir lieu, les relations officielles entre les deux 
Gouvernements en sont venues 4 un point qu'elles ont été rompues. Nous 
espérons, toutefois de la faveur Divine, que l'affaire s'arrangera sans qu'il en 
résulte aucunes difficultés, 

Seulement, comme chacun donnera a cette circonstance, lorsqu’elle sera 
parvenue A la connaissance du public dans le pays ot vous étes, différentes 
interprétations, et se livrera A son penchant naturel; et si de mauvais procédés, 
tels que changer de maniére de traiter les négocians et les protégés de la Cour 
de Russie, ct molester les sujets de la Sublime Porte ont lieu, on en ressentira— 
Dieu nous en préserve!—les mauvaises consequences; c'est pourquoi il est 
devenu nécessaire de déyelopper ici le systéme que les autoritds de la Sublime 
Porte sont chargées et seront désormais obligées de suivre, 

Il faut done, en premier lieu, protéger, plus que jamais, les négocians et 
les sujets Russes ; avoir des égards pour eux faciliter leurs affaires ; avoir des 
attentions pour les Consuls et autres Agens de la Cour de Russie; et ticher 
d'éviter de leur donner, en quoi que ce soit, le moindre juste sujet de plainte. 
‘On mettra tous les soins possibles 4 protéger et défendre en chaque occasion 
tous les sujets de la Sublime Porte, et a éviter en méme temps de singérer 
en aucune manitre dans Vexercice de leur culte, en vertu des privileges

leur devoir d'étre trés-vigilans dans l’exercice de leurs fonctions et de les remplir 
avec beaucoup de prudence et de sagesse.

mépris ct vexés. Le principal objet en voe est que tout en traitant parfaite-

Inclosure 3 in No. 384. 
Consul Gardiner to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, 


My Lord, Jassy, May 19, 1853, 

_ | HAVE the honour to report to your Excellency that the public mind at 
Jassy is kept in constant alarm from the expected return of the Russian forces 
to occupy this and the neighbouring Principality ; for Vice-Consul Cunningham 
writes also from Galatz that there had been much perturbation and inquietude 
caused to the mercantile body, from the political news of their correspondents 
at Constantinople. ‘The presence of your Excellency is of itself sufficient. to 
dispel all doubts. I have the honour to report the circumstances, for they 
have certainly produced a general impression of doubt and dismay. 

The Hospodar had mentioned to me two or three days ago that several 
Kiussian Engineer officers had visited Sculeni, and had examined very par- 
ticularly the state and solidity of the bridge thrown over the Pruth at that 
place, which is the chief passage to and from Russia and the Principality. The 
chief merchandize from Russia comes also by this same bridge, which consequently 
requires to be kept in good repair. The Prince added, that the Russians had 
been collecting at Reni, a Russian port near Galatz, a quantity of materials as 
in 1848, but having waited on the Prince to-lay, he said that he had reccived no 
intelligence whatever to indicate any intention of the Russian forces to cross the 
Pruth, and [hope that the alarm is altogether unfounded. 

I have, &e. 


(Signed) SAMUEL GARDINER,

IS Shahan, 1269. (26 Mai, 1853.) 
LA question des Licux Saints, qui formait un des objets de la mission du 
Prince Menchikoff, Ambassadeur Extraordinire de Russic, a été résolue A la 
satisfaction des deux Parties, 

_ Quant aux propositions d'une portée extraordinaire, faites par le Prinve au 
sujet des priviléges de ln religion et du clergé Grees, il est de l'honneur du 
Gouvernement Impérial de préserver de toute atteinte tant a présent qu’a 
Vavenir les privildges religioux et les droits ct immunités accordés aux sujets 
Grecs de l’Empire Ottoman, a leur clergé, A lours éelises, & leurs monastéres, 
yar les illustres aneétres de Sa Majesté Impériale le Sultan, et confirimés par Sa 
fajesté elle-méme; et de méme qu'il n'existe aucune intention ni aucune 
pensée de porter atteinte i ces priviléges, de méme il n'y a aucun doute sur les 
intentions amicales et sineéres de Sa Majesté I'Empereur de Russie envers 
Empire Ottomane. 
outefois, comme il est éyident quest un Gouvernement prenait vis-A-vis 
d'un Gouvernement étranger, soit par Séned sous forme de Convention, soit par 
hote ou déclaration, un engagement qui aurait pour objct les droits, immunités, 
et priviléges accondés 4 une communauté religicuse constituant une partie consi- 
dérable de ses sujets, lors méme que ces priviléges seraient considérés sous le

point de vue purement religieux et clérical, un tel engagement porterait atteinte 
au droit d'indépendance et & Vautorité du Gouvernement qui le subirait; et 
comme de plus il est facile de démontrer qu'il n'y a aucune analogie entre une 
question de cette nature et quelques concessions stipulées dans les temps 
anciens, la Sublime Porte, en exposant d'une part au Prince Menchikoff le 
véritable état de choses dans un langage plein de sincérité et de loyauté, a

tte infiniment que le Prince Menchikoff en soit yenu au point de rompre

Loin d’étre animé d'un sentiment hostile envers le Cabinet du Russie, le

The Eurl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received June 8.) 


(No, 228.) 
My Lord, Vienna, June 4, 1855. 

AS Count Dimitri Nesselrode in passing through Vienna on his route from 
Constantinople to London had represented very generally and particularly to 
Count Buol, that the consent of the Turkish Government to the mitigated 
demands of Prince Menchikoff had been prevented by the interference of Lord 
Stratford de Redeliffe, I thought it advisable, towards counteracting any impres- 
sion which might be produced, to_ place ‘n the hands of Count Buol for bis 
perusal, the despatch of Lord Strat ‘ord addressed to Sir H. Seymour, and dated 
the 28rd ultimo, in which His Lordship’s conduct is 60 clearly and so ably 
described, | 

Count Buol stated his concurrence with the sentiments expressed in this 
despatch, and that he considered the proceedings of Lord Stratford as he had 
described them, and as M, de Klezl had also represented them, as entirely 
satisfactory.

My ae eet ees Paris, June 9, 1853. 

Prussian Ministe informed me confidentially that he ha: - 
nicated to M. Drouyn de Lhuys a despatch from his Garaanient, dated the 3rd 
instant, explanatory of the attitude which Prussia will take in regard to the 
Eastern question. As a similar despatch will no doubt have been communicated 
to your Lordship by M, von Bunsen, and as Lord Bloomfield has written amply

allude to it, were it not that M. Drouyn de Lhuys, in expressing the general 
satisfaction at the tone of the despatch, takes exception to the expression * free 
from all engagement,” of which the Prussian despatch makes use when speak- 
ing of the expectant attitude which the Prussian Cabinet has assumed. 

 M. Drouyn de Lhuys observed to Count Hatzfeldt, that he could not 
admit that any of the Great Powers who signed the Treaty of 1840 is free from 
all engagement, or at liberty to act on the present occasion as she may think 
that her own imterests dictate, At the same time he does not wish to press for 
any immediate expression of opinion, so long as there is any chance of an 
amicable arrangement of the differences which exist between Russia and Turkey 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys has addressed a despatch in the same sense, but in stil 
stronger terms, to M. de Bourqueney at Vienna. ,

That the Emperor and his Government are aware that the position which 
they have made for themselves is disadvantageous, and that they are desirous 
that the interposition of some foreign country, probably that of England, 
should afford them the means of extrication, That the Emperor would he 
reluctant to push matters to the last extremity, but still that if he did so, a 
better position as regards the Russians and the Greeks would be made than that 
which Russia would possess by a settlement of the question by an acceptance, 
however tardy, of Prince Menchikoff’s note. In the employment of violent 
measures against Turkey, General Castelbajac expresses his belief that the 
Emperor would carry with him the sympathy of the great mass. of his 
people, 

L collect from General Castelbajac’s correspondence and conversation thit 
he considers the pending question as one more interesting to England than to 
France ; and he observes: with truth that more bad faith has been exhibited 
towards the other Powers than to France, as with regard to her there have been 
fewer professions of acting with perfect openness, 

‘The French Minister remarked to me upon the little attentions (les petites 
cajoleries) already shown him by some of the Emperor's attendants, ancl 
expressed his contempt for the small artifices of a Court which thus endeavoured 
to recommend itself to different Foreign Missions. 

The Austrian Legation appears to have been as much taken by surprise 
by the pretentions of Prince Menchikoff as have been General Castelbajac and 
myself. 

Baron Lebzeltern acquaints me that, in consequence of apprehensions 
which had been felt at the Austrian Mission at Constantinople, Ihe had been 
instructed to wait upon the Chancellor and to request some information as to 
the demands which were about to be made upon the Porte. In reply to his 
inquiries the Chancellor acquainted Baron Lebzeltern, a fortnight or three weeks 
ugo, that the Russian demands were of avery simple nature. That they went 
only to the point of obtaining a solemn confirmation of the rights already in the 
possession of Russia. 

It would appear that, however at variance with previous declarations, and 
however unfounded in justice the objects now nverred by Russia may be, there 
exists a full intention of supporting them with energy. I know upon certain 
rrounds that the greatest activity is observed at the Etat Major, and that the 
heads of the departments are engaged day and night at their offices, 

It is with pain Tadd that the late conduct of the Emperor's Government 
has taught me not only that no confidence is to be placed in Russian assurances, 
but that words are to be taken ina sense the very opposite of that which use 
assigns to them. 

"When then [ am told that in the event of a rapture with Turkey the 
Emperor's first military operation will be to-oceupy the Principalities, it may 
possibly be that this announcement covers the purpose of making a sudden descent 
upon the very heart of the Sultan’s dominions; upon the bad fuith which begets 
this mistrust, | will not enlarge, 

L will only remark that if 1848 exhibited the excesses of democratic move- 
inents, the present year fas already afforded some remarkable instances of the 
waywarness and want of honesty of autocratic proceedings. 

I have, Xe. 
(Signed) G. H, SEYMOUR.

from the Porte but confirmation of old rights. Like me he is still assured by 
his Excellency that this purpose has never varied, and that Prince Menchikoft’s

of the Treaty of Kainardyi

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, June 4, 1853. 

IN the course of a conversation which J held yesterday with Count Nessel- 
rode, L remarked to him that I found myself in the painful position of having 
given to Her Majesty’s Government very incorrect information as to the object 
of the Russian Embassy to Constantinople, 

__ The Chancellor hoped that 1 would not deny that the demands made by 
Prince Menchikoff, and modified as they had been at last, were extremely 
moderate. ‘That, | observed, was a point upon which [ was not called upon to 
express an opinion, 1 would only keep in sieht the fact of the abject being 
pee een from that which had heen stated to me to be sought by the 
mperor’s Cabinet. 

In a later part of the conversation, after dwelling upon the most unac- 
ceptable part which had been assigned to myself in the late transaction, I 
observed to Count Nesselrode that whatever objections were entertained by Her 
Majesty's Government to the eoncesstons which it was attempted to extort: from 
the Porte, it could not be doubted that they were much increased by the con- 
ceilment which had been practised ; that many difficulties would have been 
avoided by a little moze frankness as to intentions. 

lt is indeed remarkable that whereas the Russian Government professed 
constantly to have the double intention of not asking for any extension of rights, 
but of placing old ones under the sanction of an international Act of at least the 
game value us that possessed by the Capitulations with France, both points 
are now seen to be lost sight of; privileges of which very slight mention is made 
in the Treaties of Kainardji and Adrianople are to be secured to the Crown of 
Russia, and (which is a new feature in diplomacy) the privileges supposed to be 
derived from existing Treaties are to receive the sanction of an official note. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) G, H. SEYMOUR.

because it affords a striking proof of the Porte’s conviction that the demands of 
Russia left no alternative but that of refusal with all its risks.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl af’ Clarendon.—( Received June 12.) 


(Na. 67.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, May 27, 1853. 

| THINK it my duty to record that the note verbale presented to the 
Porte by Prince Menchikoll on the yyth of March, and inclosed with Count 
Nesselrode’s dora to Baron Brunnow of the fy ultimo, was never commu- 
nicated to this Embassy. I have questioned M. Pisani on the subject, and he 
assures me that Rifaat Pasha would never be brought to admit its existence. 
That Minister, who is not remarkable for firmness, was probably restramed from 
disclosing it by the Russian Atubassador’s intimidating language. 

Your Lordship has too much discernment not to have noticed the deceptive 
manner in which the intended demand of a guarantee is vaguely associated with 
the Greeks at large, while limited in appearance to the Sanctuaries in Palestine. 
Jacob's voice and Esau’s hand were never more skilfully combined, 

‘The ‘Turkish Ministers are more apprehensive of a coup de main than of 

neral hostilities. They are consequently increasing their preparations for the 
the defence of the Bosphorus, and I believe it is their intention to make, if possible, 
a vigorous resistance. In whatever manner the present alarm may terminate, 
they have much to endure, and the expense of weparation alone will prove a 
serious burthen, to say nothing of the hands which will be withdrawn from the 
early harvest of this country, and the danger of insurrection among the Greek 
inhabitants of Bulgaria. 

I have, &e. | 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

Russian Government is still anxious to find, and ready to avail itself of, any 
loophole that may be devised for a safe and honourable retreat of the Emperor 
of Russia from the false position in which he has placed himself. 

{ have not failed, on my part, in all my conversations with M. Dronyn 
de Lhuys, and with those of his colleagues who have oftener access to the 
Emperor, to inculcate the duty which devolves upon the Great Powers of 
smoothing the way to 4 reconciliation between Russia and Turkey by all the 
honourable means at their disposal, a course which I feel no doubt your 
Lordship will approve. I have found the French Ministers in general ready 
to admit the necessity of so domg, though some among them, and especially 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys, appear to cntertain the conviction that to arrange the 
present quarrel is but ‘o put off the evil day, and that we shall, ere a very long 
period anaes: have to encounter Russia on the same eround, and probably 
under less favourable auspices, when she herself shall have chosen the moment 
and devised the eause of a fatal rupture with Turkey.

No, 405. 
Circular Addressed to Her Majesty's Ministers abroad: 


Sir, Foreign Office, June 13, 1553. 

THE vupture of the diplomatic relations between Russia and the Porte has 
been the cause of great regret to Her Majesty's Government. 

The repeated assurances of the Russian Government, given both to the 
Government of Her Majesty and to the French Government, that Prince Men- 
chikoff’s mission to Constantinople had reference solely to the Holy Places, had 
led Her Majesty’s Government confidently to hope that the satisfactory 
arrangement of that long-pending question would have removed all grounds of 
difference between Russia and the Porte. 

But, under the plea of confirming ancient ‘Treaties, further demands were put 
forward by the Russian Ambassador, involving a protectorate of the Greek 
Chureh in Turkey, not only as regards the spiritual, but also the civil rights and 
immunities of its members. antite, & 

Every concession which could be made was offered by the Turkish Govern- 
ment, who, throughout these trying negotiations, displayed a most moderate and 
conciliatory spirit; but it would have been impossible for them to have complied 
with these last demands without derogating from the sovereign rights of the 
Sultan, and virtually surrendering the independence of the Ottoman Empire ; 
and Her Majesty's Government have, therefore, entirely approved the advice 
ziven by Lord Stratford de Redelifie to the Porte. 
~ "In these views and opinions there is A complete agreement between Her 
Majesty's Government and the French Government; and the English and French 
fleets, which have been ordered to approach the Dardanelles, will act im concert 
under the orders of the respective Ambassadors of the two countries. 

Iu taking this step Her Majesty's Government are actuated solely by the 
desire to uphold the independence of the ‘Turkish Empire—an independence 
which the Great Powers are deeply interested in upholding, and which has been 
acknowledged by them as necessary to the balance of power in Europe. And 
although Her Majesty's Government cannot conceal from themselves the grave 
character of these occurrences, yet the moderation which has hitherto distin- 
guished the policy of the Emperor of Russia; the repeated declarations which 
His Imperial Majesty has made of his desire to respect and maintain the integrity 
and independence of the ‘Turkish Kimpire ; and the interest which all Europe 
possesses in preventing the disturbance of peace ; induce them still to hope that 
an amicable solution of these difficulties may be found. 

You will take every proper opportunity of urging the Government to which 
you are accredited to use all the influence they possess in favour of moderate and 
pacilic counsels. 

Tam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

My Lord, Paris, June 13, 1853. 
M. DE LHUYS has read to me a confidential despatch addressed by him 
to Count Walewski, and intended for communication to your Lordship, giving a 
summary of the conversation whieh he held two days ago with M. de Kisseleff 
and to which reference is made in my despatch No, 423 of yesterday's date. 
I observe that in this despatch M. de Lhuys states that the request for French 
ae i conker tee epee prour of the demands of Russia, came from 

. Kisseleff, and not, as 1 informed your Lordship yesterday I had | 

believe, from St. Petersburgh. : Rieti nctncae 
In the course of the eonversation which I had with M. de Lhuys, and which 
was in general a mere repetition of former conversations on the same subject, he 
said that France was quite willing to assist the Emperor of Russia to extricate 
himself with honour from the false position in which he had placed himself, and 
that he had stated as much to M. Kisseleff, adding that, in his opinion, nothing 
could be easier than to find means for so doing. One plan he indicated was that 
of consigning all the demands made by the Emperor in favour of Russian sub- 
jects to n Convention, and attirming all the rights of the Greck subjects of the 
Porte by a Firman, which might be rendered more solemn by a reference in it to 

previous Conventions which treat of the subjects between Russia and the Porte 
M. de Lhuys was much more moderate in his tone to-day than I have yet 
heard him when speaking on this subject. |

No, 408, 
The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Bloomfield. 


se Foreign Office, June 14, 1853. 
; seed vali vho called upon me yesterday 
VE expressed to the Chevalier Bunsen, who ca nm 7 
at Pr beds the satisfaction of Her Majesty's Government at learning Be 
Lordship’s despatches that their views upon the Eastern question were n 
perfect harmony with those of the Prussian Government, 


405 


Tn answer to an inquiry from me, the Chevalier Bunsen said that he had 
received no instructions from Baron Mantenffel beyond those by which he was 
directed to communicate to me a few days ago certain despatches from the 
Prussian Minister at Constantinople. 

I requested the Chevalier Bunsen to convey the thanks of Her Majesty's 
Government to Baron Manteuttel for this friendly communication, and to state 
that they saw with pleasure that Baron Wildenbruch shared the opinions and 
justified the conduct of Lord Stratford, who has been charged by Prince Men- 
chikoff with having, through motives of hostility to Russia, induced, or rather 
compelled, the Turkish Government to reject the proposals of Russia, to which, 
but for the intervention of Lord Stratford, they would have been prepared to 
accede. 

I then held to the Chevalier Bunsen precisely the same language as I used 
in a conversation, on the preceding day, with Count Colloredo, and which you 
will find recorded in my despatch No, 150 to Lord Westmorland, herewith in- 
closed. I impressed upon him that the policy of Her Majesty's Government 
was essentially pacific; that they desired that an honourable issue should be found 
for Russia from the embarrassing position in which she was now placed, and 
which was so full of danger to Europe ; and that they did not think such an issue 
should be despaired of, if good faith and good will were manifested by Russia, 
and that she would really be contented with the status quo in Turkey, and the 
fulfilment of existing Treaties, without seeking to acquire more extended influ- 
ence over the subjects of the Porte. : 

In furtherance of this object, I said that Her Majesty's Government were 
anxious to learn the opinions of the Prussian Government, and to cooperate 
with them in any course of proceeding that may be considered practicable, I 
also expressed to the Chevalier Bunsen the wish of Her Majesty’s Government 
that he might have permission to attend any conference that may hereafter be 
held here, with a view of bringing the question again within the pale of negotia- 
tion, and solving it in a manner that should be satisfactory to the Emperor of 
Russia, without infringing on the sovereign rights of the Sultan. 


Your Lordship is instructed to read this despatch and the inclosure to Baron 
Manteuttel. 


Tam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

Memorandum.—(Communicated to the Earl of Clarendon by the Chevalier 
Bunsen, June 15.) 


LE premier axiome pour le traitement politique de la question Orientale 
doit étre celui-ci: La Turquie est une nécessité Européenne, Mais pour qu'elle 
continue d’exister, ce qui est indispensable, il faut que les cing Grandes Puis- 
sances s'unissent solidairement et fermement & eet effet. Ce nest quune 
pareille union qui puisse rendre possible et garantir cette existence. Cependant la 
simple promesse, le simple désir de cette union, ne suffisent pas 4 la réaliser, et 
encore moins 4 la rendre efficace. II s’agit plitot de donner foree et autorité a 
une telle entente, Et cela ne peut se faire qu’'en organisant des: éléments anta- 
gonistiques pour une action commune, et en créant des formes qui donnent une 
garantie pour la durée de l'union. L’Empire Ture n'est ni un Etat Chrétien nian 
Etat social: sous ces deux points de vue il n'a aucun titre a la sollicitude des 
Etats Chrétiens civilisés. 1! doit son importance ainsi que lombre de force vitale 
qui lui est resté, uniquement A la politique et A l'intérét genéral de Véquilibre 
Européen. De nos jours il n'est qu'un zéro politique artificiel dans le grand 
calcul Européen, lequel, par conséquent, ne peut Ctre soutenu que politiquement 
et artificiellement, savoir par le moyen d'une union spéciale de toutes les cing 
Grandes Puissances. Une pareille union doit avoir comme premiére base et 
comme base immuable, la conservation de la Turquie dans son actuel état 
territorial. Mais ne nous trompons pas! Cette conservation est impossible 
i moins que, des & présent, lentitre indépendance de la Porte dans ses 
relations exterieures et son autonomie compléte 4 lintérieur ne lui soient 
earanties vis-d-vis de chacune des Grandes Puissances, Si lon ne veut pas 
accélérer la choite de la Porte, et Vaececélérer d'une maniére violente, il est néces- 
saire que les violences et les empictements que certiines Puissances ont exercées 
individuellement contre elle, cessent désormais. A lavenir il ne devrait étre 
porté par aucune Puissance le moindre prejudice aux droits de souveraineté du 
Sultan. Si cependant ces droits et cette autonomic devaient ¢tre amoindris, il 
faudrait que cela se ne fic qu'au profit du culte Chrétien et de la civilisation 
Chrétienne en général, et dans l'intérét de toutes les Purssances Chrétiennes, 
C'est ce principe qui devra former la seconde base de union mentionnée et qui 
lui donnera le cachet de la solidarité durable et de son ulilité Européenne. II est 
vrai que les cireonstances imposent aux Gouvernements Chrétiens le devoir de 

ménager et de soutenir un Etat non-Chretien et corrompu: mais ils sont tenus 
4 ne lui porter secours pareeque l'Europe ne peut pas permettre que cet Empire 
eesse d'exister intempestivement et au profit d'une seule ou de plusieurs des 
Grandes Puissances. De plus les Gouvernements Chrétiens, en aidant ia Turquie, 
doivent reconnaitre Vubligation de protéger de toute maniére les éléments d'une 
civilisation Chrétienne qui s'y trouvent, en les plagant sous la sauvegarde
