No. 421. 
The Earl of Clarendon to Sir G, H, Seymour. 


(No. 108.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, June 15, 1853. 
THE Russian Government have constantly professed that they sought no 
increase of influence or power over the subjects of the Porte professing the Greek 
religion, and that the fulfilment of existing Treaties, and the maintenance of the 
stalus quo in religious matters, were the sole objects of the demands made by 
Prince Menchikoff. 
But it appears from the despatch of Count Nesselrode to Baron Brnnnow 
of ©, which has been communicated to me, that in the event of these 


V4 Ly a Le i ' * a q 
demands being again rejected by the Porte, a Russian force will immediately 


occupy the Principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia ; and as this will be not 
alone a violation of the Turkish territory, but may also lead to a general revolt 
among the Christian subjects of the Porte, and to events of a character far more 
deplorable, the subject assumes an European importance, upon which, before a 
decided opinion is pronounced by Her Majesty’s Government, it is essential that 
no misunderstanding should exist, 

It must be quite unnecessary for me to observe that Her Majesty’s Govern- 
ment pretend not to interfere with any just claim of Russia upon the Porte, nor 
to dispute her right rigidly to enforce the fulfilment of Treaties; but they desire 
that the independence of Turkey should be maintained, and that a right unduly 
to interfere in her internal affairs should not be conveyed by the Sultan to any 
other Power. 

The Treaties relied upon by Russia, in justification of Prince Menchikoff’s 
demands, are those of Kainardji and Adrianople ; and it is with respect to them, 
and for the purpose of doing no injustice to the Russian Government, that Her 
Majesty's Government will feel themselves indebted to Count Nesselrade for 
such explanations as he may be disposed to afford to you. 

By the ‘Treaty of Kainard) the Christian religion and churches are pro- 
tected, and some privileges and immunities are granted; but I look in vain for 
any sanction afforded by that Treaty to the demand of Prince Menchikoff that 
the orthodox churches and clergy throughout the Sultan's dominions are to be 
seeured in the possession of all the rights, privileges, and immunities which 
they have enjoyed ab antiquo. 

The term ab antique must of course refer to @ period far antecedent to 
that of 1774, the date of the Treaty of Kainardji; but under this vague form 
of expression, Russia would acquire an unquestionable right to claim privileges 
granted in the earliest periods of the Mahometan rule—privileges which, con- 

jerring vast secular os well ag spiritual pores upon the Greek clergy, have, by 
the process of time and administrative changes, long since become obsolete, but 
which, being revived by Russia, with the right to enforee them, would enable 
her to exercise supreme control over fourteen millions of subjects of the Porte, 
and to render the Sultan a mere vassal of the Emperor. 

Nor let it be supposed that this ia % forced or unfounded construction of 


417 


Prince Menchikoff’s demand, for he himeelf, in his note, dated the 21st of May, 
which has caused a profound impression throughout Europe, has proclaimed 
that religious objects ulone have not been aimed at by him: and can the refusal 
of the Sultan to part with lis sovereign rights, be imputed to him as an 
offence? Can it be held to justify the forcible occupation of his territory ? Can 
it be possible that for such a cause Europe shou d now stand exposed to the 
horrors of war by the Emperor of Russia, who throughout ewes reign, has 
laboured so gloriously for the maintenance of peace? Tia 

But I repeat what T have on a former oceasion written to you. Her 
Majesty's Government rely too firmly upon the justice and moderation of the 
Emperor, to believe in the possibility of war ; and they are convinced, that if 
such should be the will of His Imperial Majesty, a solution of this embarrassing 
question might be found perfectly consistent with the dignity of the Emperor 
and the security of the Greek church, without infringing upon the rights of the 
Sultan, whose very weakness should be his protection, even if the maintenance of 
the Turkish Empire were not a fundamental principle of European policy. 

I cannot conclude this despatch without expressing the regret with which 
Her Majesty’s Government have learnt that to the different Courts of Europe, the 
Russian Government has addressed unmeasured complaints of Lord Stratford 
de Redclitte, and have attributed to him-alone the failure of Prince Menchikoff's 
mission; but you will ask Count Nesselrode calmly to consider whether if the 
views taken by His Majesty's Government of Prince Menchikoft’s demands be 
eorrect, it required the intervention or adyice of Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to 
secure their rejection; and if, on the other hand, these demands were as insigni- 
feant in themselves, and as acceptable to the Porte, as they are said to be 
whether the British Ambassador would have influence enough, even if there had 
been uny conceivable object in his so doing, to control the Sultan, the Divan, and 
the Ministers, and induce them, against their own opinions, to brave the menaces 
of Prince Menchikoff, and to bring down upon themselves the consequences of 
an act which they must have considered to be uncalled for and impolitic. 

You are instructed to read this despatch to Count Nesselrode. 

Lam, &e. 
(Signed) ) CLARENDON,

Consul Yeames to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Odessa, May 24, 1853 

| HAD the honour of writing to your Excellency on the 11th ultimo. 

The steamer “ Gromonosetz,” with Prince Menchikoff and his suite on board, 
arrived at this port yesterday morning at 9 o'clock, and though no public 
communication was made, it soon transpired that the negotiations had 
terminated unsatisfactorily, Great consternation has in consequence spread 
through all classes in this city: At 11 o'clock the Prince had a conference in 
quarantine with General Liiders, the Commander of the 5th Corps d' Armée, 
the Acting Governor-General, and the Governor of the town. The great intimacy 
between our families enabled me to have a conversation with the General on his 
way back from the quarantine, and he informed me that all diplomatic relations 
with the Porte had ceased, and that the steamer “ Bessarabia” was to leave the 
Bosphorus three days alter the “ Gromonosetz” with M, Ozéroff and the rest 
of the Russian Mission; he said that concession to the ultimatum had been 
refused, and that the resistance ia ‘avec amertume” attributed to your Excel- 
lency's influence, Tasked if it was war; ihat, it was replied, depends upon the 
will of the Emperor. No such alternative, therefore, has been predetermined, 

can again state, and with assurance, that a war with Turkey is far from 
being desired in the army, further than that it may suit the needy, when by the 
occupation of the two Danubian Principalities, they will be entitled to double 


id All the troops, if not now countermanded, are to go into camp on the 27th 
instant, The artillery has not been yet brought forward, as I have erroneously 
stated, ‘The 4th Corps d’Arméc, according to previous orders, was put into 
motion on the Gth instant for concentration on the Dniester, ‘The reserves are 
still far in the rear. 

| observe this morning that the “ Gromonosetz” is in free communication 
with the shore; and the Prince, therefore, is probably in the town. I have not 
heard anything said of his future motions. 

T have, &e. 
(Signed) JAMES YEAMES. 


No. 426. 
The Karl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon. —(Received June 15.) 


(No. 207.) 

My Lord, Vienna, June 11, 1853, 
THE communications from St. Petersburgh which Baron Meyendorff 

expected, have arrived, and have been brave it before Count Buol, who still feels 

that he cannot approve the line taken by the Russian Cabinet in the affairs of 


42] 


Turkey. He much regrets that the Emperor Nicholas should have claimed the 
adoption by the Sultan, without any modification, of the last proposition of 
Prince Menchikoff, and that the Russian Government should have accompanied 
the demand with the threat of the immediate occupation of the Principalities by 
a Russian force, in case of refusal. In the hope of averting the calamities which 
must arise from such a measure, Count Buol has written to Petersburgh to 
represent in the strongest manner the hostile feelings which such a step would 
occasion, and to urge at least delay till the other Powers, parties to the Treaty of 
1841, should have an opportunity of using their good offices with the Porte to 
obtain some arrangement which might be satisfactory to the Emperor, and avoid 
the dangers to which all Europe would be exposed by war. Count Buol has also 
written to Constantinople, pointing out to the Turkish Government how desirable 
it would be that they should seek by every means consistent with the honour 
and independence of the Sultan to meet the requisitions of the Emperor, and 
he expresses a hope that the last note which was proposed to Prince Menchikoff, 
and refused by him, may, by trifling alterations, be adapted to the exigency of the 
moment, Ccunt Buol also recommends the Turkish Government to accept, for 
the moment, the Emperor's declaration, that he does not consider the occupation 
of the Principalities os the commencement of war, and that he will take no 
further measures of hostility, but await in that attitude the mediation of the 
friendly Powers. Count Buol strongly recommends that if the Russian troops 
eross the Pruth, the Turkish Government should not attack them: he advises 
this conduct, not upon any principle of right, but to avert a calamity; for not 
only does he dread the misfortunes which must be entailed by the commencement 
of hostilities, but he is persuaded the Turkish army is not in a state to cope with 
the Russian forees in the Principalities. He likewise believes that if general 
hostilities took place, the Christian population in many of the provinces would 
rise. The intelligence he has from Greece, as well as from other parts where 
the Greck population is numerous, leads him to this impression. 

Count Buol earnestly hopes that, notwithstanding the present threatening 
aspect of affairs, a peaceable solution will be obtained ; but if war was to be the 
eonsequence of what may take place, the policy of Austria would be to acknow- 
ledge the right of each of the Four Powers to act according to its own convic- 
tions; the Austrian Government will take no engagement either with Turkey to 
support her, or with Russia not to oppose her ; it will remain free to act according 
to its own judgment. 

Count Buol has not concealed from Baron Meyendorff the unfavourable 
Impression which the Emperor's conduct has made upon all His Majesty's 
friends; and he hopes the Baron may, by representing it, assist in bringing about 
a more favourable decision. Count Buol has received despatches from Count 
Colloredo of the 7th instant, giving an account of his conversation, with your 
Lordship and Lord Aberdeen upon the affairs of ‘Turkey, and he ts very much 
pleased with the moderation and desire of conciliation which were evinced in 
those conversations. He is particularly pleased with an assurance that the fleet 
would not for the present, in TR aaauths the Dardanelles, violate any treaty. 
An expression, also, that it was possible the Principalities might be occupied 
and yet no state of war be declared by Turkey, was remarked upon by him as 
being satisfactory ; for he thinks this essential, and will strongly recommend to 
England and the other Powers, that if Turkey does not declare the occupation 
of the Principalities an act of war, the other Powers should equally refrain from 
doing so. I have, &c. 

(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

My Lord, Paris, June 14, 1853. 
COUNT HATZFELDT has received from his Government a despatch dated 
the 10th instant, which is identical with that addressed on the same day to 
M. Bunsen, and communicated by the latter to your Lordship. . 
312 


422 


Count Hatzfeldt saw M. de Lhuys yesterday, and read to him the despateh 
in question. The following have been confidentially reported to me as the 
remarks made by the French Minister on the occasion : | 

«The present despatch is not 80 satisfactory as that communicated to me 
from the same quarter some days ago. M. de Manteuffel appears to have 
changed his point of view. He now seems to look for peace only, and to set 
the preservation of the Ottoman Empire on one side. If that 1s the case, 
England and France cannot agree in the policy of Prussia, for they prize the 

cservation of the Ottoman Empire even beyond the preservation of peace, 
ie however, the Prussian Governinent means and will declare that the two can 
go hand in hand, and that their object is to ensure the continued existence of 
the Turkish Empire by pacific means, England and Trance can and will unite 
their adviee with that of Prussia and of Austria (if she 1s willing) to obtain the 
desired result.” | 

So much for the general question. Upon certain points of the despatch 
M. de Lhuys observed to the Prussian Government: Ist, That he could not 
admit, as M. de Manteutfel appeared to argue, that the acceptation by the Porte 
of Prince Menchikoff’s last propositions would deprive them of that bilateral, 
and consequently that obligatory form which a Treaty or Convention would give 
to them, because Prince Menchikoff had taken care to insert In the note whieh 
he proposed the Porte should sign, words signifying that it had an obligatory 
power. | 

2nd. The French Minister remarked that he could not allow that the ex- 
ceptional position of the Principalities established by Freaty gave the Hussians 
any right to enter them ou the present occasion. Such an entry would, in his 

opinion, be an act of aggression, although the Turks might not necessarily con- 
sider it-an act of war. But it would make France more anxious than ever that 
the Porte should persist in its refusal to accept Prince Menchikoff’s propositions, 
heeause if Russia claimed the right of occupying the Principalities under Treaty 
now, what would she do when her powers of interference with the internal 
affairs of the Ottoman Empire should be so greatly augmented t 

rd, M. de Lhuys pointed out to the Prussian Minister that although there 
was no intention to irritate or provoke in sending the fleets to the Dardanelles, 
and that there was still every disposition to negotiate, yet the two Governments 
of England and France had not adopted this measure solely as a means of sup- 
yorting their diplomatic representations, but were quite prepared to give the 
Porte the material assistance which those fleets coul atlord, should the Sultan 
call upon them to do so for the preservation of his domimons. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon. —( Received June 17.) 
(No. 439.) 
My Lord, Paris, June 16, 1853. 
M. DROUYN DE LHUYS has beet good enough to read me & despatch 
which he received this morning from the French Minister at Munich, who gives 
an account of a conversation which he had had with M. Van den Pfordten, on 


423 


the present aspect of affairs. This despatch will be communicated to your Lord- 
ship by Count Walewski, but it is of sufficient importance to induce me to give 
you in a few words the summary of it. 

M. Van den Pfordten is informed by the French Minister of the reasons 
which have induced the English and French Governments to send their fleets to 
the Dardanelles, and of the intimate union which exists between the two Cabinets 
in their policy on the Oriental question. In his answer he not. only admits the 
legitimacy of the cause which the two Governments defend, but he declares his 
satisfaction at secing them united to curb the ambition of Russia. [He expresses 
the hope that the other great Governments of Europe will join England and 
France, and that every State will adopt means for letting the Emperor of Russia 
know their opinion of his present conduct, M, Vanden Pfordten represents 
Germany as having been too long under the thraldom of Russia, and he accuses 
the Emperor of being the cause of many of the evils under which Germany still 
labours ; and he says that itis but a just retribution that he who so long has 
dictated to others should now be dictated to himself. 

Whatever may be the paramount cause of this language, it is of importance 
at this present moment ; for the opinions of the smaller Courts of Germany must 
have some influence on those of the greater. 

I have. &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

My Lord, Paris, June 16, 1853. 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS has read to me two very important despatches 
which he has addressed to the French Ministers at Berlin and St. Peters- 
burgh in answer to the communications which my previous despatches will have 
informed your Lordship have been made to him on the parts of the Cabinets ot 
Prussia ond Russia relative to the Oriental question, 

The first of these is very much in substance what T had the honour to 
report to your Lordship yesterday had been M. Drouyn de Lhnys’ language to 
the Prussian Minister; but the opportunity is taken to make the Prussian 
Government clearly understand the identity of feeling which unites the English 
and French Cabinets on this question; and while it declares in the meoneey 
terms that whatever may be the policy pursued at Berlin and Vienna, England 
and France will remain true to the cause of the integrity and independence of the 
Turkish Empire it expresses the sincere wish of the French Government to see 
the other parties to the Treaty of July 1841 join with them in defenee of ‘Treaty 
engagements, and the desire for a pacific solution of existing dillerences. At the 
same time France claims the right of being informed how far in all eventualities 
she can count on the support of Prussia. 

The despatch to General Castelbajac contains an explanation of the reasons 
which have induced the Governments of Great Britain and France to send their 
fleets to the Dardanelles. It is stated to be a measure of precaution rendered 
necessary by existing circumstances. France counts upon the Emperor's 
vious conduct and character not to push his quarrel with the Porte to extremities, 
assures the Russian Cabinet of her desire to cooperate for the just settlement of 
any fair claims Russia may have upon the Porte, points out the danger to which 
Europe would be exposed by war, and repels the insinuation which Count 
Nesselrode appears to have made, that the responsibility of war would rest with 
those who encouraged the Porte in her resistance to the demands of Russia, 

As copies of those despatches will be communicated to your Lordship by 
Count. Walewski, | need not add more, They do honour to the policy of the 
Government which sanctioned and to the pen which wrote them, and I feel sure 
that your abate will be satistied with them, 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys informed me further that he should in the courscof 
the day address an appeal to the Austrian Government in the same sense as that 
addressed to Berlin. Lhave, &c. 


(Signed) COWLEY.

No. 432. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon—(Received June 17.) 
(No, 270, Confidential.) 


My Lord, St, Petersburgh, June 7, 1853, 

WITH reference to your Lordship's confidential despatch marked No. 83, 
Tam anxious to observe to your Lordship that amongst the many new features 
which distinguish the policy at present pursued by Russia towards the Porte, 
and that which is announced, is that of an anomaly which, although being unlike 
peace, is still maintained by the Emperor not to be regarded as war, 

His Imperial Majesty, whilst announcing his intention of occupying the 
Principalities, if at the end of the week given for fresh consideration Prince 
Menchikoff’s note be not accepted by the Porte, states that he shall not make 
war upon Turkey: that he is desirous of being able to refrain from the use of 
violence ; and that he is anxious as before to respect the independence of the 
Sultan and his dominions. 

It is wholly out of my power to reconcile the first of these intentions with 
the professions by which it is accompanied, and | imagine that the explanation 
would be sought in vain in any Treatise upon the Law of Nations. I feel it my 
duty, however, to notice the discrepancy, because it occurs to me that should 
the occupation of the Danubian Provinces take place, and should it be followed 
by the entry of Her Majesty's fleet into the waters of Constantinople, the 
Emperor, under the strange view which he is seen to take of public rights, will 
be apt to consider himself as the party having a right to complain of aggression, 

| have, &e. . 


(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

would be quite justified in regarding it as an act of war, notwithstanding the 
announcement of the Emperor of Russia that war is not intended, 

Her Majesty’s Government are however of opinion that the Sultan should 
be strongly advised to refrain from acting upon his undoubted right, and 
declaring war against Russia ; not alone because Turkey is unprepared for war, 
and that her nayal and military and financial resources are feeble as compared 
with those of Russia, but because it is of the utmost importance to prove to the 
world that where such vast social interests are concerned, no step has been 
taken in haste; that every measure which a conciliatory spirit ean devise has 


been exhausted; and that upon Russia alone will devolve the fearful responsi- j 


bility of involving Turkey, and possibly Europe, in a war which no man will 
be found to justify, and the duration and disastrous consequences of which 1t 1s 
impossible to calculate. 

In the event, then, of no éther steps being taken than the occupation of the 
Principalities, Her Majesty's Government would recommend that a solemn 
protest be addressed to the Russian Government against such an invasion of the 
Turkish territory, which is rendered more unjustifiable by the reasons assigned 
in its defence by Count Nesselrode in his note to Reshid Pasha, 

The Porte should then, in language more definite and intelligible than has 
hitherto been used, explain the real character and practical operation of the 
Russian demands. the extent to which a compliance with them would confer 
upon the Emperor of Russia new influence over the Greek subjects of the Porte, 
and the consequent impossibility that the Sultan should consent to such an 
infringement of his sovereign rights—the Sultan being at a loss to conceive how 
this should cause the resentment of Russian, or be made matter of complaint 
against the Porte, because the justice and moderation of the Emperor's cha- 
racter forbid the idea that he would knowingly advance a claim unsupported 
by reason or right, and beeause both to the Sultan himself and to the different 
Powers of Europe, the Emperor has recently given assurances of his desire to 
respect the dignity of the Sultan, and to maintain the independence of the 
Turkish Empire. 

It might moreover be stated that the Sultan has given proofs of Ins earnest 
desire to meet every just claim on the part of Russia, and to redress any just 
grievance under which his Greck subjects may labour; that reparation has been 
made with respect to the holy places, and the question settled to the entire 
satisfaction of Russia; and that the Porte is now prepared to give more explicit 
assurances in order to confirm that settlement. 

The Russian Government should further be informed that the Porte hus 
issued a firman which confers upon its Greek subjects the most complete 
téleration, and secures to them the fullest enjoyment of their religious rights, 
immunities, and privileges; and in connection with this firman it appears to Her 
Majesty’s Government that an explanatory Act might be offered by the Porte 
in the words of the Treaty of Kainardji, or with such change of that form of 
words as the Turkish Government may consider safe and consistent with the 
dignity of the Sultan,

1 HAVE been asked by Reshid Pasha, in the name of his Government, 
whether L advise that resistance should be offered to a Russian army crossing 
the Danube and invading Turkey. 1 have replied, that in my opinion it is 
desirable to avoid collision as long as possible, that the line which cannot be 
passed by an enemy without danger to the capital, is the one where forbearance 
must necessarily cease, and that a professional opiion ean alone with propriety 
decide that question, which must partly be solved with reference to the available 
means of resistance, 

I am informed by M. Pisani that the Porte adopts the principle thus offered

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received June 20.) 
(No, 268.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, June 5, 1853. 

I UNDERSTAND upon good authority that the Emperor, upon being 
informed of the conversations which have taken place in Parliament respecting 
Prince Menchikoff’s demands upon the Porte, remarked upon the “ éternelle 
méfiance” exhibited upon these occasions in the intentions of Russia towards the 
Sultan | 

His Majesty, in allusion to the declaration stated to have been made by 
Government as to their intention, in conjunction with France, of upholding the 
upholding the independence of the Turkish Empire, further observed that in this 
respect the purpose of the two Governments agreed entirely with his own. 

On the same day this observation was made to me, as coming from himeelf, 
by the Chancellor. 

The unity of purpose upon a given point, however, evidently does not inter- 
fere with the Emperor's intention of being prepared for any differences which 
may arise with regard to others; | understand that extensive orders have been 
given for collecting the supplies of food which would be required fora large army 
upon entering a oo country, and, as Lam positively assured, a fresh park of 
artillery stationed at Moscow has been despatched to the South. 

The Russian funds, which are perhaps less subject to fluctuation than any 
others, have fallen 4d. in the silver rouble at Odessa, and 4d. at St. Petersburgh, 
in consequence of the intelligence from Constantinople, and of the still more and 
evidently unfounded reports which are in circulation; whilst the general anxiety 
and want of confidence which prevail here have had the effect of paralyzing com- 
merce at the very moment when it ought to be putting forth its greatest activity.

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, June 6, 1853, 

THE French Minister has read to me the minutes of a conversation which 
he had the honour of holding with the Emperor on the 4th instant. 

His Majesty received General Castelbajac in the most gracious manner, and 
alter expressing his regret at secing him so seldom and desiring him to ask for 
an audience whenever he pleased, proceeded to speak of the affairs of the East. 

His Majesty began by recapitulating the various circumstances connected 
with the disputes of the Gis and Latins at Jerusalem, and observed (which 
had not before appeared) that his wish to have the question settled at Constan- 
tinople had proceeded trom his desire of keeping clear of any altercation with the 
French Government. 

In speaking of the late diplomatic rupture and its possible consequences, 
the Emperor appears to have been more explicit with General Castelbajac than 
he was with me; partly, | presume, because the subject is now more familiar to 
him than it was when 1 was last at the Palace, partly because His Majesty's 
feelings could be better expressed to any diplomatic agent than to a servant of 
the English Government. 

His Majesty laid the chief blame of the rejection of Prince Menchikoft's 
note upon Her Majesty's Embassy, and as usual spoke in strong terms of disap- 
probation ofall those who called in question the moderation of which the Russian 
Government had given proof upon this occasion.

‘ No. 448. 


Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received June 20.) 


(No. 272.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, June 9, 1853. 

THE Chancellor has had the kindness to send me, this morning, Baron 
Brunnow's memorandum of the 44th ultimo. 

I regret not being able to copy this document, which I am requested to 
take back to his Excellency in two hours’ time, as it is one which requires 
attentive consideration. 

It appears to me that Baron Brunnow's arguments in favour of the justness 
of the demands made by Russia upon the Porte are conclusive or inconclusive, 
according to the starting point of the discussion. 

If the Russian Cabinet require only that the settlement of the Greek and 
Latin dispute at Jerusalem should be made permanent and binding, by means 
af an Act of as stringent a nature as the Capitulations between France and the 
Porte, | am bound in honesty to state that the demand corresponds closely 
with the intentions which had been repeatedly made known to me. 

If, on the contrary, the whole relations of the Greek Church in Turkey 
towards the Sultan are to be changed, I can only say that the idea is not only 
new to me, but that itis opposed lo the repeated explanations and assurances 
which | have received from the Chancellor. 

But, remarks Baron Brunnow, if England had undertaken to procure the 
aeceptance of the Russian demands, she would have had a right to ask for the 
detail of propositions. 

She did not; and she remained “ libre de ses conseils, comme la Russie, a 
son tour, est restée libre de son action.” 

This passage suggests two observations. It may be that Russia (supposing 
her at least not to be bound by Treaty to respect the independence of the 
Sultan) would have been at liberty to follow ae own free action towards 
Turkey, and to withhold a knowledge of her intentions from Her Majesty's 
Government; but she did not use that right. Explanations very full—assur- 
ances very tranquillizing, were voluntarily given; and the question now is, does 
the course of action pursued by the Russian Cabinet correspond with those, in 
fact, engagements ? 

Again, Baron Brunnow speaks of “propositions ;"" but did the communi- 
cations made by Prince Menchikoff to the Sultan's Government, contain 
propositions, or were they demands under menace in case of refusal ? 

In a subsequent passage of his memorandum, Baron Brunnow quotes the 
following passage of a despatch of Prince Menchikoff's, as explanatory of the 
Russian views : * 

‘Nous ne demandons pas le droit de protéger des Chrétiens du rit ortho- 
doxe, sujets de la Porte, mais le maintien du statu que religieux de ce rit,’ 

If this is so, assuredly there can be no incompatibility between that which 
the Emperor has a claim to ask, and that which the Sultan would do well to 
grant—the demand for a confirmation of old rights, not the grant uf new ones. 

Further on, and speaking in the name of His Imperial Majesty, Baron 
Brunnow says: “ [la tenu uniquement en vue de sauvegarder 'Eglise Orthodoxe 
en Turquie contre les empittements et les lésions dont elle venait d'éprouver 
linjuste et flagrante atteinte.” 

With this view, continues M. de Brunnow, [is Majesty insists upon 
obtaining from the Porte “un Acte formel, un Acte explicatif.” ‘Cet Acte 
dans la pensée de Sa Majesté ne doit servir qua confirmer |'Eglise Orthodoxe 
dans la possession des droits dont elle jouit en Orient; 'Empereur ne demande 
ni plus ni moins.” 

“Un Acte formel, un Acte explicatif,” appears, however, to have been that 
which it would have been in Prince Menchikoff's power to obtain at Constanti- 
nople, but that which he did not consider worthy of aceeptance. 

At the close of his memorandum, Baron Brunnow lays down what is the 
greatest proof of respect for an independent Sovereign, “It is," he says, ‘‘ that 
of not preventing him from fulfilling his engagements towards a friendly and

honour to the Emperor, and without danger either to the independence ol 
Turkey or to the peace of Europe.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received June 20.) 


(No, 273. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, June 9, 1853. 

IF there were no other reason for holding fast to truth, there would be 
this very adequate one, that a single departure from it constantly involves 
many others. 

This remark is suggested by the flagrant contradiction which is to: be 
observed between the declarations made to your Lordship and to myself, as to 
the Russian intentions with regard to Turkey, and the course of threats and 
probable violence which has been commenced under the auspices of Prince 
Vienchikoff. 

That a gross deception has been practised upon Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment, of which, to my eternal regret, | have been made a princi yal instrument, 
ig not to be denied; the only question appears to me to be, to what extent that 
deceit was premeditated, and at what period it commenced. 

It is very possible that it may have been so from the outset, and that the 
Emperor discovered in the dispute which arose respecting the holy places, an 
opportunity which might be turned to the purpose of carrying through a scheme 
of ambition: but it is likewise not improbable that the deception may be of a 
more recent date, and that it originated in the perception of a quiet confirmation 
of the Emperor's rights at Jerusalem, being a conclusion which by no means 
responded to the expectations raised among Greeks and Russians by the 
Emperor's armed diplomacy and the extent of his military preparations. 

As regards Baron Brunnow, the part assigned to him has been, if I do not 
err, similar to that which I have been called to play in the transaction, 

Having had several opportunities of reading his private letters, a8 well as 
his public despatches, | conjecture him to have been the better qualitied to mis- 
lead Her Majesty’s Government from having been himself misled and deceived 
as to the Emperor's real objects. 

However this muy be, the system of disregarding truth being once 
establighed, there appears to be little feaitntion as to its adoption. 

The Emperor, as [ have had the honour of stating to your Excellency, 
acquainted General Castelbajac on the 4th instant, that the Austrian and 
Prussian Cabinets approved of the proceedings of the Russian Embassy at 
Constantinople, and, as | have since ascertained, declarations to the same effect 
had been made by the Chancellor to the Grecian and Swedish Envoys. 

As I am compelled to speak in terms which are painful to apply to a 
Sovereign whom | have every wish to be able to respect, it may be but justice 
to offer perhaps the only excuse which is to be ae for a portion of his late 
conduct. 

Supposing, as it may appear there is good reason for believing, that His 
Majesty imagines himself tobe possessed of much more extensive rights, as the 
dejender of the Greek religion, than any ‘Treaty ever assigned to. him, and if it

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, June 10, 1853, 


1 HAVE held a second conversation with General Castelbajac, at which 
he observed that he was now able to give me more ample particulars of what 

sed between the Emperor and him on the 4th instant. 

The two points which I think it right to notice to your Lordship, are the 
following : 

His Imperial Majesty having observed that he was convinced that the 
good faith for which the Emperor Napoleon was so remarkable, would lead him 
to take a very favourable view of the demands upon the Porte by Prince 
Menchikoff: to this the Marquis de Castelbajac represents himself to have 
replied, that certainly the rectitude of his Imperial Master had been manifested 
upon three remarkable oceasions. It had been shown in the manner in which 
he had accepted the mode of recognition by some of the great Powers—it had 
been shown by his eagerness to see good relations re-established between Austria 
and Prussia—it had again been shown by his willingness to accept the settlement 
of the Holy Places Question upon terms which, although not quite agreeable to 
his feelings, were such as he had thought it right to accede to, out of regard 
to the general interests of Europe. 

The other point is of much greater importance. Having requested General 
Castelbajac, now that he bad time to make his report, to inform me precisely 
what the Emperor had said respecting his intentions, he stated, that His Majesty's 
declaration was as follows : 

Que si les Tures ne se décidaient point & accepter la note qui leur avait 
été remise par le Prince Menchikoff, il se verrait dans obligation d'occuper la 
Valachie ct la Moldavie. Que dans ce cas il espérait que la France et 
l’'Angleterre ne donneront point & leurs flottes les ordres de franchir les Darda- 
nelles, que si celles-ci devaient y arriver ce ne serait par sur lui que pesernit la 
responsabilité de ce qui pourrait sen suivre: Qu’il se garderait bien (?) [or 
some similar expression which General Castelbajac could not call to mind, but

My Lord, St. Petershurgh, June 10, 1852, 

[ HAVE had the honour of receiving your Lordship’s despatch No. 81, 
upon which I am desirous of offering some observations before stating that the 
orders which it contains have been acted upon. 

[t has been, I can assure your Lordship, a great relief to me to learn that 
if my reports have been the means of misleading Her Majesty's Government 
with regard to the intentions of the Imperial Cabinet towards Turkey, the fault 
— if it is one—is not to be ascribed to the incorrectness of my statements. J might 
indeed have misapprehended Count Nessclrode’s expN OnE and assurances 
if only once given, but it can hardly be imagined that [ can have misunderstood 
their meaning when repeated over and over again, and the hypothesis of misap- 
prehension becomes wholly inadmissible when it is seen that the successive 
statements of the Russian Cabinet to the English Envoy have been re-echoed 
seriatim to Her Majesty's Principal Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs by the 
Emperor's Minister in London. I am, however, desirous of acknowledging to 
your Lordship, that such blame as may attach to a complete belief in solemn 
assurances, very justly belongs to me, and that it has been my misfortune, as | 
thought it my duty, to express to Her Majesty’s Government the confidence 
with which those assurances inspired me. As matters of fact, | have often been 
called upon, it is true, to notice to your Lordship cireumstances which appeared 
to be in contradiction with the moderate and conciliatory intentions professed by 
the Imperial Cabinet ; but I could not prevail upon myself to allow appearances, 
however suspicious, to outweigh distinct explanations and assurances equally 
explicit. 

‘ I may now be permitted to state to your Lordship that the explanations 
which I have been ordered to seek of the Russian Government have been in 
some measure forestalled by the communications made to Her Majesty’s Govern- 
ment, through the Russian Mission in London, and by my own despatches. 

Before this despatch can leave St, Petersburgh, your Lordship will have 
learned that, instead of explaining former declarations, the Russian Cabinet is

Lordship’s despatch, and with this view U waited upon his Excellency yesterday,

The conversation which ensued was as little satisfactory as possible, and 

the Chancellor himself appeared in low spirits, and perhaps more distant than 
usual in manner. 

Her Majesty's Government, he said, had expressed a desire to receive 
explanations from the Emperor's Cabinet. By this time they must be received : 
they would be found in the account of my audience of the Emperor, and in 
the long “ travail” which had been addressed to Baron Brunnow. 

Some discussion ensued as to the striking difference observable between the 
explanations given to your Lordship and to myself by Baron Brunnow and 
Count Nesselrode; when it was soon to be seen that it would be impossible 
to come to an understanding as to facts, 

I begged leave to pass co a more practical part of the question—to sugvest 
that it would be most desirable that time should be given for reflection and 
deliberation, and that resolutions which might lead to the most serious*conse- 
quences, should not be acted upon hastily. 

The Chancellor said the period for deliberation was known to me; that ifat 
the end of eight days Prince Menchikoff’s note should not be accepted by the 
Porte, orders would be given for the immediate occupation of the Principalities. 

When I remarked that another eight days would intervene before the news 
of a refusal could reach St. Petersburgh, Count Nesselrode stated that this was 
not to be counted upon; that on the intelligence he referred to aITiving at 
Odessa, orders for the advance of the troops would be given by the General in 
command there. 

_ A fresh discussion then arose, in which I stated that although I could not 
give my word of honour that such was the case, a distinct impression had 
been upon my mind of twenty-four days being the probable term assigned—eight 
for the messenger’s journey to Constantinople, eight days for his return, and an 
intermediate eight days for deliberation. That I had made this statement to 
Baron Meyendortf, who was just setting off for Vienna, some minutes after leaving 
the Emperor's presence. The Chancellor thought that His Imperial Majesty 
would hardly be brought to accord this delay. 

I then spoke of some middle course which it would not be dificult to 
suggest for an adjustment of differences. ‘The Chancellor had thought upon the 
point, but could not see any could be devised. ‘ You have known me,” he 
said, “two years; you have seen that J am nat disposed to violent measures (i 
casser les vitres), Well, I declare to you that I could not advise the Emperor to 
recede; his dignity would be lowered, his position would be compromised—it 
would be a triumph for the Turks and a humiliation for Russia. ‘The inevitable 
result would be a war with Turkey. The insolence of the Turks would become 
such, that friendly relations with them would become impossible.” 

I replied that assuredly nothing could be further from my wish than to 
lower the Emperor's position, but that I desired that all jarties concerned should be 
spared humiliation, and that if necording to his notion, Governments friendly 
to Turkey, and bound by Treaty to respect her independence, were to counsel 
her to accede to a demand which was held to involye the sacrifice of that inde- 
pendence, his Excellency must see that they would be called upon to act a 
part unworthy of their dignity. 

The Chancellor would not admit that there was any compromise of inde- 
pendence in the assent to be given by Turkey to the demands made upon her 
At least, I said, it may be taken to be the opinion of all impartial men whohave 
given their attention to the subject. | 

Count Nesselrode then, with a warmth of manner which appeared to me to 
be assumed for the occasion, remarked upon the unfair and rejudicial manner 
in which the claims and the grievances of Russia were a ways received by 
Foreign Cabinets ; on these occasions the cternal jealousy of Russia came to 
light. [france had intended to bombard Tripoli,—not a word of blame was to 
be heard ; Russia sought temperately for redress of a serious gricvanee, and 
exceptions were instantly raised—instantly Russia was charged with a Wish to

My Lord, Foreign Offce, June 21, 1853. 

THE Chevalier Bunsen, on the 4th instant, showed me a despatch from 
Baron Manteuffel, stating that he had learnt with sincere pleasure the moderate 
views entertained by Her Majesty's Government upon the Eastern question, and 
authorizing the Chevalier Bunsen to attend any conference here to which he 
might be invited, having for its object a peaceful solution of the matters in 
dispute between Russia and the Porte, with the understanding, however, that 
any distinct proposal should be received by the Chevalier Bunsen subject to the 
approval of his Government. 

I requested the Chevalier Bunsen, as your Lordship is also instructed, to 
express to Baron Manteuffel the satisfaction of Her Majesty's Government at 
this fresh proof of the confidence and identity of views that exist between the 
two Governments.

No. 462. 


The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 
(No. 174.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, June 21, 1853, 

ON the 19th instant, Count Colloredo read to me a despatch from Count 
Buol stating that the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh had asked for the good offices 
of the Austrian Government with the Porte, und that the Internuncio had 
accordingly been instructed to point out to the Turkish Minister for Foreign 
Affaires that as Prince Menchikoff, in his last project of note, had abandoned the 
bilateral form which was considered objectionable, there ought no longer to be 
the same difficulty in acceding to the proposals of Russia. 

It was not expected, however, that this advice, even if it should arrive 
within the eight days allowed to the Porte for decision, would have any effect ; 
and, in contemplation of its failure, the Internuncio was to request Reshid Pasha 
to consider what difference existed between Prince Menchikoif's last project and 
the note from the Porte which he declined to receive on the ground that official 
relations between the two countries had ceased ; and that if this difference could 
be reconciled, and a new proposal were offered by the Porte, Count Buol 
engaged to make it known at St. Petersburgh. 

Count Buol then asks for the cooperation of Her Majesty's Government 
with the Turkish Government, and the intimation of our confidence in the 
Emperor of Russia, whose assurances, that by the occupation of the Princi- 
palities he does not intend war nor territorial aggrandisement, but simply their 
retention until he obtains satisfaction from the Porte, should be received by 


——oo = 


Europe as an unmistakeable pledge (gage non équivoque) of his peaceful 
sentiments. 

Count Buol expresses an earnest hope that the Powers will abstain from all 
demonstrations that might unduly excite the hopes of the Porte, and still farther 
embarrass the Emperor of Russia with reference to the national and religious 
feelings of his people. 

Rut he adds that he should deplore that the Emperor gave immediate 
effect to his intention of oceupying the Principalities ; that the Austrian Govern- 
ment have frankly expressed themselves ‘n that sense, and hope to obtain a 
delay if [ pour peu que ”] the Sultan shows any apirit of conciliation ; and, with 
that object, they have engaged the Porte not to give to the occupation of the 
Principalities a character of “' flagrant hostility.” 

I told Count Colloredo that although L fully agreed with some portions of 
the despatch, yet I could not help saying that it would be more satisfactory if 
+ were less one-sided, and if the concessions urged upon the Porte had likewise 
been recommended to Russia. 

| told him, aleo, that confidence was not an act of volition, but depended 
on reason or experience, and, after all that had passed, we could feel no conti- 
dence that the violent and unjustifiable occupation of the Principalities would 
not be followed by a further invasion of the Turkish raied & in which event 
Her Majesty’s Government reserved to itself an entire freedom of action, im 
conjunction with France, for the protection of Turkey, 

Count Colloredo, I said, must be well aware from his previous commu- 
nications with me, that Her Majesty’s Government were anxious to cooperate 
with Austria im bringing this question to an amicable settlement; and I had the 
catisfaction to inform him that the instructions to the Internuncio did not 
materially differ from those sent to Lord Stratford, who, I was sure, would 
gladly favour any proposal acceptable to the Emperor of Russia that did not 
compromise the independence of the Sultan; but that, if any such proposal 
were made, Austria, whose good offices had been asked by Russia, would have a 
right to insist upon its being received in a peacelul and conciliatory spirit. 


lam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

No. 465. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received June 22.) 


(No, 287. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, June 14, 1853. 

THE explanatory circular published in the St. Petersburgh Journal of 
the 12th instant, and forwarded to your Lordship by post in my despatch, 
No. 285, is a paper well deserving of attention. f 

It is speciously written ; it 1s calculated to produce a considerable effect 
upon those who have no knowledge of the subject; but its assertions are open, 
not only to so much observation, but to so much positive contradiction, that 
little more is proved than the great wish entertained by its compilers to mislead 
public opinion. . 

I request your Lordship’s consideration of the following passages, which I 
indicate by their first words ; 

« Je crois superflu de yous dire qu'il n'y a pas un mot de vrai dans la pré- 
tention que les journaux nous ont prétee de réclamer, &c. 

“ Soit toute autre protection religieuse tendant 4 depasser celui que nous 
exercons traditionellement de fait et de droit en Turquie en vertu de nos Traités 
antéricurs.” 

Prince Menchikoff is seen to have broken off diplomatic relations with the 
Porte, and Turkey to be menaced with a war, because the grant of a right of 
protectorate, which no Treaty ever gave to Russia, is demurred to by the Sultan. 

“ Vous connaissez assez la politique de l'Empereur,” Sc. What is here 
stated respecting His Imperial Majesty's views is, it is to be hoped, correct : but 
if so, the policy followed towards Turkey is singularly at variance with its pro- 
fessed object; Turkey, like every other feeble State, being of course unable to 
resist a course of constant interference and encroachment. 

“ Nous n'avons pas besoin pour en eurveiller d'autres droits que ceux que 
nous assurent nos ‘Traités,” &e. 

Tt follows that the demands upon the Porte have been made unnecessarily. 

“ La mission du Prince Menchikoff n'a jamais eu d’autre objet que Varrange- 
ment de l'affaire des Lieux Saints.” aa 

Such, indeed, was the statement constantly made to me; its incorrectness 
is proved by the fact of the arrangement Se pies the Holy Places being the 
mere prelude to requisitions affecting the whole religious, and therefore political 
relations of the Greek subjects of the Porte towards their legitimate master. 

The object of Prince Menchikotf’s mission is subsequently stated to have 
been in part to “corroborer cet arrangement [respecting the Moly Places) par un 
Acte authentique.” : 

Again 1 would remark that this was the repentedly avowed intention of 
the Russian Cabinet, It is, however, doubtful whether, in the opinion of any 
impartial person, an authentic Act relating to the state of rights at Jerusalem 
can be held as having shadowed out, or as now corresponding with, a Russuin 
protectorate throughout the Sultan's dominions, 

Cette garantie [that of a Convention conhrming the new arrangements) 
Empereur y attachait d’autant plus d importance quelle constituait au fone 
la seule et unique réparation qu'il demandait.” ; a 

The Chancellor appears to have forgotten that, directly or indirectly, the 


453 


dismissal of Fuad Effendi, who was considered the Minister by whom offence 
had been given to Russia, was required by Prince Menchikoff, His Excellency 
has. likewise lost sight of the fact of his having declared to me that Fuad's 
withdrawal was actually regarded by the Emperor's Government in the light of 
a reparatory act. 

With regard to Prince Menchikoff’s diplomatic proceedings, it is stated, 
“ De Traité proprement dit il n’en a jamais été question.” 

In this passage it is seen that the Chancellor's memory has again served 
him il. 

Upon the withdrawal of the Embassy from Constantinople, Count Nessel- 
rode stated to me that the conciliatory conduct of Prince Menchikoff had been 
fully evinced by his having demanded, first, a Treaty, then a‘ Sened,”’ and having 
finally professed his readiness to accept a note. 

«En principe une Convention, ou meme un Traité pareil, n’auraient rine 
d'insolite, et nous ne comprenons pas en quoi ils seraient plus attentatoires aux 
droit d’autonomie souveraine de Sultan que les Capitulations ou autres Actes que 
posstdent déji en Turquie la France et l’Autriche. 

As regards France, itis at least questionable whether her protecting rights 
are claimed on behalf of any Roman Catholic subjects of the Sultan; but the 
object of this and other passages of the circular is to prove that the question of 
principle involyes one of numbers; that it follows as a matter of course, that if 
the Emperor of Austria can be permitted to protect a few thousands of Catholics, 
there is no ground for refusing to the Emperor of Russia a right of protectorate 
over twelve or fourteen millions of Greeks. 

But this is one of the many cases in which principle is less to be considered 
than its application. 

That the Kings of France, for instance, were of opinion that there was 
nothing derogatory in the employment of foreign troops, is proved by the exist- 
ence of a Scotch, and later of a Swiss body-guard ; a principle, therefore, was 
admitted: but these Sovereigns would probably have thought their independence 
alittle compromised, and their security somewhat endangered, if the foreign 
soldiers in their pay had been four times more numerous than the national army. 

1 will not occupy your Lordship’s time by offering, as I might do, the 
refutation of several others of the statements to be found in the Russian 
Circular, There are few parts of it indeed with which T agree, except with that 
which gives it to be understood that no arrangement which could be made would 
much affect the overpowering influence which the Emperor exercises de facto in 
Turkey. ‘The influence, however, being real, and even avowed, it might have 
been hoped that the respect so constantly proclaimed by His Imperial Majesty 
for the rights of independent Sovereigns, would have led him to have been 
unwilling to have inflicted a particular humiliation upon the Sultan by the 
demands now brought forward. There remain two reflections which I am 
desirous of submitting to your Lordship. The right possessed by Russia to 
make what is termed, in M, de Brunnow’s late memorandum, a proposition to 
the Porte cannot be contested; but it may well be doubted whether, in the 
opinion of any of those Cabinets to whose verdict Russia now appeals, the 
courteous refusal of the Sultan to comply with what he considers an unsafe 
proposition, ean be considered as justifying the breaking off of diplomatic 
relations, and a recourse to measures of coercion. The precedent thus esta- 
blished is a dangerous one. Further I would observe, and this in some measure 
apologetieally, that the difficulty of learning the nature even of the declared 
intentions of the Russian Cabinet may be judged of from that of reconciling 
their account of actual events with the existence of known facts, and with the 
simple evidence of the senses, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon —(Received June 23.) 
(No. 933.) 
My Lord, 


Constantinople, June 7, 1853. 
THE Ottoman Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs sent yesterday to 
consult me as to the expediency of writing in the name of the Porte to direet 
the Princes of Moldavia and Wallachia to retire from their respective Governments 
in the event of the Principalities being occupied by a Russian force, 

I replied in the following words : 

If the Princes of Moldavia and Wallachia were to leave their respective 
Governments in consequence of a Russian occupation, their retirement would 
afford to Russia a pretext for appointing other Princes from among its own 
creatures, and perhaps even making some new institutional arrangement fivour- 
able to its views against Turkey, 

I think it would be better for the Princes to retain the reins of Government 
as long as their communications with the Porte are free, and they are allowed to 
administer the affairs of the Principalities according to the existing institutions. 

Should they be restrained in those respects, the Porte might then recall 
them with the advantage of throwing the odium of that measure on the Russians, 
and contrasting the Porte's forbearance with their illegality and violence. 

It is to be hoped that the supposed contingency will not occur; but as the 
Porte appears to have adopted my advice, I should be glad to learn that it meets 
with your Lordship’s approbation, 

I have, Ke.

that province on their way to Wallachia, 

Now the mere passage of the Danube by the Russian troops and their 
subsequent march through a portion of Bulgaria, not leaving any post nor 
keeping up a line of communication in Bulgaria, would be one thing ; while the 
passage of the Danube, followed by the retention of posts and the establishment 
of 4 line of communication in Biitcerin, would be another; und Her Majesty's 
Government consider that the Porte would do well to reserve to itself, instead of 
leaving to Omar Pasha, to decide upon the important distinction between the 
two cuses. nak

No. 475. 
The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


(No. 100.) 
My Lord, Foreign Ojfice, June 24, 1853. 

HER Majesty's Government consider that every fair advantage should be 
taken of the present position of the Turkish Empire to press upon the Sultan 
and his Ministers the importance of removing all civil distinctions between the 
Christian and Mahomedan subjects of the Sultan, and of giving the former an 
equal degree of assurance with the latter as to the impartial administration of 
justice by the Turkish tribunals. 

Your Excellency has long and zealously laboured to obtain for the 
Christians in Turkey that their evidence should be received in the courts of 
justice with the same consideration and respect as that of their Mussulman 
fellow-subjects, and that the barbarous distinction which fanaticism has long 
interposed between Turks and Rayahs in this respect should no longer be 
allowed to prevail, 

The firman which in 1850 your Excellency obtained from the Porte for 
reculating the mixed jurisdiction in Egypt, gave a limited sanction to the 
principle for which Her Majesty's Government have so earnestly contended, 
that the oath of a Christian witness should be regarded in the same light as that 
of a Mahomedan witness; and that a Mussulman should no longer enjoy 
impunity for crime on the ground that Christian testimony, frequently the only 
one that could be adduced, was inadmissible against a Mussulman, 

Your Excellency is. instructed to state to the Porte that it is the deliberate 
opinion of Her Majesty's Government that the only real security for the con- 
tinued existence of Turkey as an independent Power, is to be sought by enlisting 
the feelings of its Christian subjects in its preservation; that, although Turkey 
may get over her present difficulties by the aid of her allies, she must not reckon 
upon external assistance asa permanent resource ; but that she must create for 
herselfa surer defence in the affections of the most intelligent, active, and enter- 
prising class of her subjects; and that it is impossible to suppose that any true 
sympathy for their rulers will be felt by the Christians, so long as they are made to 
experience in all their daily transactions, the inferiority of their position as com- 
pared with that of their Mussulman fellow-subjects ; so long-as they are aware 
that they will seek in vain for justice for wrongs done either to their persons 
or their properties, because they are deemed a degraded race unworthy to 
be put into comparison with the followers of Mahomet. 

Your Excellency will plainly and authoritatively state to the Porte that 
this state of things cannot be longer tolerated by Christian Powers. The Porte 
must decile between the maintenance of an erroneous religious principle, and 
the loss of the sympathy and support of its allies. You will point out to the 
Porte the immense importance of the election which it has to make; and Her 
Majesty's Government conceive that very little reflection will suffice to satisfy 
the Turkish Ministers that the Porte can no longer reckon upon its Mussulman 
subjects alone as a safeguard against external danger, and that without the 
hearty assistance of its Christan dependents, and the powerful sympathy 
and support of its Christian allies, the Turkish Empire must soon cease to 
exist, 

fam, &c. 


(Signed) | CLARENDON.

1 dwelt upon this subject in my reports as lightly as possible; firstly,

reproaches so confidently made, should be (as they have proved to be) utterly

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe’s correspondence having satisfied me that his 
Excellency had been most unjustly accused, I was glad to have an opportunity 
of addressing to the Chancellor the letter of which a copy was submitted to 
your Lordship by my despatch No, 284 of the 11th instant, 

In writing that letter [ had another object. 1 had learned by experience 
that promises and assurances are not considered very binding by the Russian 
Government. I saw from the amount of naval and military preparations going 
forward, that there was considerable appearance of a pursuit, which began in 
duplicity, being carried on by violence, and I reflected that the only remainin 
hold upon the Emperor's mind, might be that love of personal reputation which 
he has always been supposed to cherish. 

Independently, therefore, of my wish that tardy justice should be done to 
the able and important exertions of Lord Stratford de Redcliffe towards recon- 
ciling conflicting interests, | was not sorry to direct the attention of the Chan- 
cellor to an approaching publicity as to late diplomatic proceedings from which 
Her Majesty’s Government has certainly nothing to fear, but which may be 
extremely fatal to that high character which has been enjoyed hitherto by the 
Emperor Nicholas. 

In further justification (however little required) of Lord Stratford de 
Redclifie, [have thought right to place in the Chancellor's bands. and. to give 
some diplomatic publicity here to the paper signed by the Ambassador of 
France, the Minister of Prussia, the Austrian Chargé d'Affaires as well as by 
Her Majesty’s Ambassador, and which was transmitted toa your Lordship 
in Lord Stratford's No. 55, of the 2nd ultimo.

at a fixed purpose on the part of the Russian Cabinet to mislead Her Majesty's 
Government. There is one cireumstance of another character which I think it 
right to recall to your Lordship’s recollection, 

L allude to the fact of the Emperor having discouraged my idea of proceed-

my post, but itis difficult to reconcile the Emperor's wish to detain me here with 
a purpose of acting in a manner contrary to the inteutions expressed to myself.

Count Nesselrode then indulged in a good deal of abuse of the French

Nesselrode what an unfortunate policy that must be which suddenly places the

with observing that, as regards Her Majesty's Government, there was no wish 
to raise a crusade against Russia; that, as 1 had said before, all that was desired 
was, Whilst making allowance for the position taken up by the Emperor, to 
provide for the security and independence (de sauvegarder) of Turkey.

become feeble allies ; that less intimate friends are now all but open opponents ; 
that the opinion of all Europe is against them, and that in prudence they would 
do well to settle, by the less striking means of diplomatic discussion, questions

further misapprehensions that, with a view to showing that my language was 
the expression of the feelings and views of Her Majesty's Government, I would 
read to his Mxeelleney (although I was perhaps not authorized in doing so), 
your Lordship’s two despatches No. 93 and No. 96. 

The Chancellor immediately took note of the words, “and to obtain such 
guarantees as should effectually guard against all future differences on the 
question,” which are to be found in the first of these papers ; and said, that in 
the construction to be placed upon this sentence lay the whole quetsion pending 
between the two Governments. 


The remark gave rise to a fresh argument, with which it is not necessary to 
trouble your Lordship, 

At its conclusion the Chancellor observed, that the protectorate exercised 
in Turkey by the Emperor of Russia being a matter of fact and notoriety, it 
appeared to him ineredible that the Governments interested in the existence of 
the Ottoman Empire should hesitate in advising her to subscribe to terms 
which evidently in no way changed the condition of things, 

I begged to remark that this assumption was not borne out by fact; that, 
as it had been seen, not one of the Representatives of the Four Powers at Con- 
stantinople would take upon himself to counsel the adoption of conditions which 
were considered dangerous to Turkey; and M. le Comte, I continued, permit 
me to remark, you alone are of your opinion; Russia, accustomed to majorities 
—Russia, in the habit of guiding other Governments, now finds that the 
opinions of the Four Great Powers are opposed to hers; surely this gives matter 
for reflection, 

The Chancellor said, this might or might not be so; that he was grieved 
that any difference of opinion should prevailed among Allhed Powers; and at a 
later period of the conversation, acquainted me that pressing instructions had 
been sent from Vienna, urging the Turks to accept the note. But, the 
Chancellor said, the point of view from which the question is to be regarded, is 
this: you are interested in the continued existence of the Turkish Empire, and 
certainly you are not more so than we are ourselves; no Power is interested in 
this object in the same degree as Russia; but you must see that the force of 
Turkey is wasting away, and that one fillip (chiquenaude) from Russia causes it 
to fall altogether, Surely then, in See prudence, you should offer advice

which, without producing any change in the real state of affairs, removes all 
danger from the Sultan’s dominions. 

Allow. me, I returned, M. le Comte, to put the question differently. 
Interested as you ought to be, and as now, having lived some time in 
Russia, I believe you to be, in the preservation of Turkey, ought you not to 
refrain from placing her in the dilemma either of accepting a measure which the 
majority of friends consider destructive of her independence, or, by a refusal, of 
incurring a war which implies her destruction ? 

The Chancellor could not allow the question to be so put; for Russia it 
was-a matter of necessity that her influence should be very great (very great 
or paramount, for I cannot state which), and this influence is destroyed, if the 
Turks are not driven to necepl the terms which have been proposed to them. 

Count Nesselrode then enlarged upon the horrors of war, the unbounded 
injury which it would entail upon his own country and upon England, and com- 
mented upon the disproportion of the object as stated, with the sacrifices which 
would be made forits attainment. Hethought war in such acause could hardly 
be undertaken by the Government of a country professing such peaceable inten- 
tions, and so manilestly interested in the cultivation of peace, as England. 

L observed that no Government and no people could he more disinclined to 
zo to war than those of England ; but that nothing could better prove the force 
of feeling in England, than that war should be coolly considered, when interests 
dear to all English feelings were considered in danger. 

‘After some hesitation, Count Nesselrode begged to know whether I had 
any proposition to make to him. I replied, M. le Comte, the only thing | have 
to suggest is, that you should be good enough to take into consideration the 
words of Lord Clarendon’s despatch to which you just now pointed, and that 
you should endeavour to strike out some course by which you may “ obtain such 
guarantees as shall effectually guard against all future differences on the ques- 
tion (of the Holy Places), without seeking the guarantee in a measure of wiliieh 
the Allies in general, as you are aware, think very unfavourably.” 

The Chancellor having with some reluctance undertaken to speak to the 
Emperor upon the subject, and having expressed a wish of being allowed to read 
to His Majesty your Lordship’s two despatches Nos, 93 and 96, I made up my 
mind to leaving them in his Excelleney’s hands,

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 
(No. 256, Confidential.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, June 25, 1853. 

| INCLOSE to your Excellency the draft of a despatch to Viscount Stratford 
de Redeliffe, conveying a recommendation to the Porte, which Her Majesty’s 
Government hope may afford a solution of its difficulties with Russia. 

The recommendation is to unite together in one Act the stipulations im 
favour of Christians and of the Christian religion that are to be found in the 
Treaties of Kainardji and Adrianople, as well as other matters contained therein 
which more especially concern Russia, and to send this proposed Convention 
by an Ambassador to St. Petersburgh, who should have power to sign it, but 
not to assent to alterations without reference to the Porte, 

Before taking any step in the matter, however, Her Majesty's Government 
are anxious to have the concurrence of the French Government; and your 
Excellency 1 therelois batracad to communicate to M, Drouyn de Lhuys the 

espateh, together with the form of Conventi re thi i a 
f be hy toge ion that we think might be adopted 

_ Your Excellency will lose no time in informing me of the opinion ~ 
tained by M, Drouyn de Lhuys; and if, as Her Majeaty’s Gouentaaat Rent 
should he favourable, the despatch and Project of Convention shall fromediately 
he sent to Constantinople, and copies to Berlin and Vienna for the purpose of 
securing, if possible, the support of the Prussian and Austrian Governments 
both at Constantinople and at St, Petersburgh, of a project which has been 
sanctioned by the Governments of France and England. | 

It appears to Her Majesty’s Government that this may be a mode of uniting 
the Four Powers together for a practical purpose, and of bringing the whole 
weight of their moral influence to bear upon the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh. | 

I am, &c. | 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

HER Majesty's Government expect shortly to learn from your ry 
that the ultimatum of Count Nesselrode, addressed to Reshid Pasha, has ets 
rejected by the Porte; and they see no reason to doubt that the Eroperee af 
Russia will, in consequence, execute his threat of occupying the St Sa tice 

Against this act Her Majesty's Government have, by my despatch f oy 3 
of the 18th instant to your Excellency, recommended the Porte to protest im 
strong terms. 

it +; an act of violence and injustice; it rests upon no right, and can a 
defended on no principle; it is dangerous as a precedent, and as an abuse a 
power that every civilized community 18 interested in denouncing. ne Ene 
State is tacitly permitted to make inadmissible demands upon a wea ae pee 
on their rejection, to invade and to hold a portion of its territory, professing 
that it is not an act of war, but avowedly for the purpose of coereing it inte @ 
surrender of its rights and independence, international law ceases to exist, anc 
the mutual obligations upon which society depends are grossly violated. 

After mature deliberation, however, Her Majesty's Government saw Tcason 
to advise the Sultan not to exercise his unquestionable right of declaring war 
avainst Russia upon the occupation of the Principalities ; but if Russian aggression 
were to be carried further, and if any other portion of Turkish territory were to 
be invaded, active operations on the part of Furkey would seem to be inevitable, 
and eventually the English and French fleets might be called upon to protect 
Constantinople, ; 

af Enaland and France might thus find themselves opposed to Russia ; and if 
war should ensue, Europe might be convulsed from one end to the other; for 
we cannot shut our eyes ta the fact that this would become & wat of Ho ordinary 
character, and soon cease to be within the control of those by whom it was 
originally undertaken, It would be a war of opinion, and the atruggle ol 
nations against their rulers; the disaffected everywhere would seize * SEO: 
tunity to avenge their real or imaginary wrongs, and revolution would shake the 
social fabric of Europe to its foundation, a 

It is the duty of Her Majesty’s Government to guard against such a contin- 
gency, anc its dieaatsoue results, by every means at their CORI: ee 
policy of France upon the Eastern question is happily identified with teed 
England; and her cordial cooperation towards the maintenance of peace ma wit : 
confidence relied upon by Her Majesty's Government, Both Powers are bout 
by the same obligations towards ‘Turkey, and by both they will faitht y be 
fulfilled; but upon a question involving such momentous interests, no false step 

must be made; freedom of action must not be unnecessarily fettered ; and it 18 
essential therefore, that upon the precise nature of these obligations no mtscon- 
ception should be permitted to exist. First, then, as to the Treaty at et 
which was signed by the Five Powers, in the persuasion * that their union and 
agreement offer to Europe the most certam ledge for the preservation of 
general peace—the constant object of their solicitude ; and their said Majesties, 
desiring to attest this agreement by giving to His Highness the Sultan a mam 
fest proof of the respect they entertain for the ey of his aa 
rights, as well as of their sincere desire to see consolidated the repose of his 
p bee. 7 a4 he, p ; 

mae the principles thus laid down, Her Majesty s Government eneely 
adhere; the same spirit which dictated this preamble animates them now ; but 
it ia the Articles of the Treaty alone that have a binding foree, und to which 
the Five Powers are compelled to adhere; and Her Majesty S Sarena: 
consider, therefore, that eal eould not rely upon this ‘Treaty in demanding

‘ame to her assistance, f | 
oA TS cube intentions, however, that are recorded in the preamble, the 
frequent declarations of policy respecting Turkey made by Great Britain, our 
commercial interests and the balance of power in Europe furnish abundant 
motives for desiring the integrity of the Turkish Empire, and for resisting the 


471 


encroachments upon it of any other Power, whatever be the form that those 
encroachments may assume. 

But I repeat again, that before the time for adopting a policy of resistance 
shall arrive, it is alike our duty and our interest to exert our utmost efforts, in 
conjunction with Her Majesty’s allies, to preserve peace on terms that shall be 
safe and honourable to the Sultan, and entirely satisfy every claim that Russia 
ean with justice put forward. 

The Emperor of Russia, throughout these painful negotiations, has declared, 
and he has recently renewed the declaration, that he seeks no increase of power 
or influence over the Greek subjects of the Porte, and desires only the main- 
tenance of the stadus quo in religious matters, and the fulfilment of existing 
Treaties. Her Majesty's Government would therefore recommend the Turkish 
Government to take this declaration as the basis of a new agreement, and to 
embody in one separate Convention every stipulation in the Treaties of 
Kainardji and Adrianople by which Turkey ts now ei to Russia. 

It appears to Her Majesty’s Government that, from Articles VIT, VIL, 
XIV, XVI, XVU, and XXUI, of the Treaty of Kainardji, and Article V of the 
Treaty of Adrianople, a Convention new in its form, but in its substance contain- 
ing no extension of rights, might be framed, which the Sultan, without loss of 
power, might propose, and the Emperor might, without loss of dignity, accept. 

Her Majesty's Government would further recommend that this Convention 
should be sent to St. Petersburgh by a special Ambassador, who should have 
power to sign, but not to alter it without reference to the Porte. He should 
lay before the Emperor the recent firman in favour of the Greek Church, by 
itself, as evidence of the good faith with which, even by anticipation, the terms 
of the Convention will be carried out by the Sultan. 

He should also lay before the Emperor the firmans respecting the holy 
places, and be empowered to give a written assurance as to their fulfilment, 
taking care, however, that such assurance in no way infringes upon the rights 
acquired by the Latin Church, or militates against a similar guarantee being 
given to the French Government and to other Powers; and Instly, the Ambas- 
sador should, by Convention or note, assign to the Russians at Jerusalem a 
hospital, and such other buildings as may be required, 

If the Porte should think proper to act upon this advice, and if a proposal 
so fair and complete be rejected, Her Majesty’s Government will consider that 
it will be manifest to the world that the claim of religious rights covers ulterior 
desigus on the part of Russia, hostile to the independence of Turkey; and the 
Sultan may then justly claim the sympathy and support of every Government 
in Kurope. 


I am, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS received this morning despatches from 
St, Petersburgh (he could not tell me the exact date, but they have not been 
above six or even days on the road) in which General Castelbajac states that in 
a conversation which he had had with Count Nesselrede, the latter had said 
that if the answers from London and Paris to the communication lately made 
from St. Petersburgh on the Eastern question were satisfactory it was still 
possible that the Russian troops might not cross the Pruth, 

L asked if any explanation was given of the meanin attached by Count 
Nesselrode to the word “‘satisfactory.” It might mean that Russia would be 
contented with the pacific assurances of the two Cubinets, and of their desire to 
aeo an arrangement honourable to both Parties concluded between Russia and 
the Porte; or it might mean that Russia expected that England ond France were 
to bow to her arguments, and disown their Ambassadors at Constantinople. 
General Castelbajac does not seem to have given any indication of the sense im 
which Count Negsselrode’s words were uttered.
