Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.— (Received June 27.) 


(No. 96.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, June 10, 1853. 

A LETTER from Count Nesselrode to Reshid Pasha, dated St. Peters- 
burgh, May 19, I presume old style, was received yesterday by a Russian war- 
steamer under merchant colours, and delivered to the Pasha by M. Argyropulo, 
the Russian interpreter. Its purport is, that the Emperor entirely approves of 
Prince Menchikoft’s conduct, and that, without actually making war, his army 
will in a few weeks cross the frontier to obtain a “material” guarantee from the 
Porte, until the “ moral’? one demanded by his Ambassador shall be obtained. 
Count Nesselrode ends by advising Reshid Pasha to sign the project of a note 
delivered to him by Prince Menchikoff before his departure from Constantinople, 
and to send it without the slightest alteration—“ sans variation” —to that Ambas- 
sador at Odessa within eight days at latest. ‘The rest of the letter is a 
mixture, as usual, of reproach, friendly assuranees, and menace, conve fed in no 
flattering form, 

Rechid Pasha lost no time in sending me a copy of the letter. He gave M. 
Pisani to understand that the Porte would not accept the overture, which is, in 
fact, the same identical proposal which has been already rejected. 

Since writing what precedes, I have seen Reshid Pasha, the French 
Ambassador, the Prussian Envoy, and the Austrian Charge d’Affaires, to whom 
copies of Count Nesselrode’s letter had been sent. They all hold the same 
language with respect to that communication. It offers, in truth, no alternative 
but a simple acceptance of the terms before refused as inadmissible, or an armed 
invasion of the Turkish territory, with the view of obtaining by force what the 
Porte will not spontaneously accord. The Sultan has taken cognizance of the 
letter, which will also be submitted to the Council. 

The present occasion does not admit of my saying more, My impression 
is, that the Porte will persist in ie rete of the Russian demands, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received June 27.) 
(No, 251.) 
My Lord, Berlin, June 24, 1853. 


WITH reference to my despatch No. 244 of the 21st instant I have the 
honour to inform your Lordship that the late communication of the French 
Minister at this Court to Baron Manteuffel has produced a further instruction 
to Count Hatzfeldt, which announces the policy of Prussia to be still more in 
harmony with that of England and France, on the Turkish Question, than it 
appeared to be some time ago. 

The-attitude of Prussia is one of pacific remonstrance, in which she will 
endeavour to exert a beneficial influence at St, Petersburgh. 

Mention is made in this despatch of the Treaty of July 1841, the import- 
ance of which Baron Manteuffel fully recognizes, stating that he has not yet 
thought it advisable to appeal to it in his official communications, but he admits 
its full force, and announces his readiness to invoke its provisions, if circum- 
stances should hereafter occur which may render this course advantageous. 

Baron Manteuffel read this despatch to me hastily, yesterday, and it is 
useless for me to allude further to the subject, as his Iexcellency will send a 
copy of it to Chevalier Bunsen for communication to hae Lordship. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved June 27.) 


(No. 254. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, June 24, 1853. 


WITH reference to your Lordship’s despatch No. 131 of the 21st instant, 
I have the honour to state that I had some conversation this evening with Baron 
Manteuftel as to the policy of Austria with respect to the affairs of Turkey, and 
told his Excellency that Her Majesty’s Government hoped he would exert all 
his influence at Vienna to engage the Austrian Government to enter as cordially 
as possible into our views ; for it was of the greatest importance that an agree- 
ment of opinion between the Four Powers should be manifested, and that no 
approval of Russian demands should take place. 

I said that | felt called upon to make this statement to him in consequence 
of the different impressions which the policy of Austria had made here and in 
London; that I had already reported to your Lordship, in my despatch No, 243, 
of the 2lst instant, that a more favourable account had been reccived at Berlin 
than that which | had forwarded last week, and that I was desirous to learn from 
him whether the opinions he then stated had undergone any change. 

His Excellency replied that he had heard from Chevalier Bunsen that Her 
Majesty’s Government was in possession of reports from Vienna which differed 
certainly from those which had reached him, and that he was willing to believe 
that he might have been unfavourably impressed as to the intentions of Austria ; 
that he grounded his opinions on the only communications which he had as yet 
received from the Imperial Government, which were instructions to Baron Bruck, 
and that none other had been made, 

He added that he had to-day received a despatch from Baron Canitz, the 
Prussian Chargé d'Affaires at Vienna, which was more satisfactory ; and that he 
should certainly do all in his power to encourage the Austrian Government to 
maintain their independence in treating the Eastern Question with the Russian 
Government; and he assured me, further, that no exertions should be wanting 
on his part to carry out the policy which Prussia desired to follow, and which it 
would give him the most sincere pleasure to see asl i by Austria. 

| have, &c. 


(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

My Lord, Berlin, June 24, 1852. 

THE impression made on Baron Manteuffel by the last despatches which 
have reached him from St, Petersburgh, is as unfavourable as ever, and he does 
not understand that there is the least disposition on the part of the Russian 
Government to modify their demands on the Porte. 

His Excellency mentioned to me in confirmation of this opinion, that he had 
directed the Prussian Chargé d’Affaires to represent to Count Nesselrode the 
advantage in the interests of peace, of the Emperor receiving a Turkish Ambas- 
sador with new proposals for an arrangement of the points in discussion between 
the two Governments, and that the Chancellor had replied that the question 
could not be entertained until the note was signed.

No, 499. 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon,—( Received June 27.) 
(No. 247.) 
My Lord, Mienna, June 21, 1853. 


I READ to Count Buol your Lordship’s despatch No. 161, in which you 
state that Her Majesty’s Government have learnt the opinion of that Minister 
on the present aspect of Turkish aflairs, as reported in my despatch No, 237, 
with great satisfaction, 

Count Buol was gratified by this statement of the sentiments of Her 
Majesty’s Government; and as I afterwards read to him your Lordship's 
despatch No. 150, in which your conversation with Count Colloredo is detailed, 
he begzed me to assure you that he entirely coincided with the policy of Her 
Majesty's Government therein described, and that it was the greatest satisfaction 
to him to observe that, upon the important questions now pending in the East 
of Europe, there was no difference in the sentiments entertained in regard to 
them by either of the two Governments of England and of Austria, 

Count Buol said that he had already received from Count Colloredo a report 
of the conversation now described by your Lordship, with which he had been 
highly satisfied, but it had not entered into so many details as those given by 
your Lordship, which had rendered the expression of your sentiments still more 
valuable to him. 

There was one point alone which was mentioned by your Lordship upon 
which he wished to make a remark, and which referred to the desire you 
expressed that Count Colloredo might be instructed to take part in any confer- 
ence that it might be considered useful to hold in London, huving for its object 
a solution of the existing difficulties in a manner both safe and honourable for 
Russia and for Turkey. Upon this proposal Count Buol desired to state that, 
however willing he should be to allow Count Colloredo to take part in bringing 
about the objects so described, yet he thought that, for the moment, while the 
decisions both of the Governments of Russia and of the Porte had not yet been 
declared, it would be premature to form a conference which might have the 
appearance of arranging itself in opposition to Russia, and of imposing terms 
upon her Government. Moved by this sentiment alone he recommended that, 
for the present, no measure should be taken towards the assembly or preparation 
of this conference, although he fully admitted the force of all the stipulations of 
the ‘Treaty of 1841, and the obligations they imposed upon the Five Powers 
parties to it; and in case of the complications arising between Russia and 
Turkey, which at present there was too much reason to dread, he looked upon 
the stipulations of that Treaty as the groundwork upon which the peace of 
Europe could best be re-established, and to which the Austrian Government 
would lend its most cordial assistance, 

Count Buol stated that he had Sane a communication as to a conference 

3Q2 


of the Five Powers from the French Government (of which I had already been 
informed by M. de Bourqueney) which was of a similar character to the one 
made by your Lordship. The despatch of M, Drouyn de Lhuys, which treated 
of this subject, and which had been read to him, was dated the 12th instant, and 
referred to the stipulations of the Treaty of 1841, by which the Five Powers 
were “garans de Vintégrité de la Turquie,” and therefore the French Government 
ealled upon the Five Powers to meet in conference, to take into consideration 
the questions at present in dispute with the Porte before they should be resolved 
by one of those Five Powers by the force of arms. 

Count Buol stated that the despatch of M. Drouyn de Lhuys was extremely 
well written (an opinion with which I was able to coincide, as it had been read 
to me by M. de Bourqueney), but that he had replied to it in the same manner 
in which he had answered the Boge from your Lordship. He had, however, 
taken the opportunity of stating istinctly that he recognized all the obligations 
of the Treaty of 1841, and he looked to them, in case of more serious complica. 
tions, as the hope and security for the future maintenance of the integrity and 
independence of the Turkish Empire. 3

My Lord, Paris, June 26, 1883. 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS read to me this afternoon a despatch from

aceount ofa short conversation which he had just had with Count Buol on 
Fastern affairs. Count Buol had asked, in a tone of disquictude, what was to 
be done if Russia persisted in her aggressive intrusions. ‘ You have nothing 
for it,” replied M. de Bourqueney, “but to establish a Conference. A Con- 
ference will be the only remaining chance of safety for Turkey.” * That will be 
the second phase of the question,” rejoined M. de Buol, without contesting the 
truth of M. de Bourqueney's assertion ; “it will then become Turopean, 
But, from the indications I have, it 1s not probable that Russia will consent.” 

M. de Bourqueney adds that Count Buol avoids all discussion of the 
astern Question with Baron Meyendorff.

No, 505. 


The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Bloomfield, 


(No, 145.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, June 28, 1853. 

THE Chevalier Bunsen has communicated to me the project of a Conven- 
tion, a copy of which is inclosed herewith, to be signed by the Five Powers, for 
the future regulation of the religious rights and immunities enjoyed by the 
Christian subjects of the Porte, and stipulating that in the event of any measures 
becoming necessary with reference to the above objects against the Porte on the 
part of one of the Contracting Powers, such measures shall only be taken in 
concert between all the Powers, and after due deliberation at a conference to be 
held at London. 

Your Lordship is instructed to convey to Baron Manteuffel the thanks of 
Her Majesty's Government for the communication, and to state that they concur 
in its spirit, and will be happy to cooperate with the Prussian Government 
towards the object sought to be attained by the Convention whenever the time 
for bringing the question forward shall arrive; but Her Majesty's Government 
apprehend that it would be premature to do so at present. 

I am, &c. 


(Signed) | CLARENDON.

Church alone.

unaccepted answer, which he had put together, and sent to Count Walewski, for 
communication to your Lordship. He did not, hywever, he added, hold in any

Church should be solemnly recognized by the Sublime Porte, so that no doubt 
or uncertainty should exist as to the right of the members of that Church fully 
to participate in the privileges, immunities, and other advantages which by

the 42 July, 1774, and by the further Treaty between the same Powers con- 
cluded at Adrianople on the y4y September, 1829, were stated generally to belong 
to the Christian religion in the said dominions; and His Highness the Sultan

This shows that the Russians have not forgotten the lesson which was

ing the peace of the world in their pursuit of a selfish and inadequate object. 
I will only observe that the effect of His Imperial Majesty's late diplomacy has 
been already to place him in contradiction with those principles which for the 
last quarter of a century it has been his buast to uphold; to reunite the two 
Governments which it was his wish to keep asunder; to procure @ pre-eminent 
lace at the Council Board of Sovereigns for the illegitimate possessor of a throne 
he co much desired to keep in the back ground; and to commit to revolutionary 
France that defence of Conservative principles, and that upholding of inter- 
national engagements, which he suddenly abandons.

No, 512. 
Sir G. H, Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received June 29.) 


(No. 305, Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, June 21, 1853. 

ACCORDING to information received by the Imperial Government the 
state of Turkey is deplorable: several of the provinces are so overrun by 
brigands, that not only villages but towns are attacked by them; the dissensions 
between Turks and their fellow Greek subjects are so great that at any moment 
scenes of violence may be expected; the Councils of the Sultan are torn by 
uncertainty and apprehension, and the military resources of the Empire are so 
inadequate that Omar Pasha has only been able to collect 12,000 men with 
which he was hastening to ocoupy Shuma. 

Lam very far from asserting that these statements are correct, but 1 think 
it right to state to your Lordship what information is sent in by the Russian 
agents, as by this the decisions of the Government are likely to be influenced, 

The reports which have reached me as to the state of the Russian army in 
the South is, T must remark, as little flattering as those which are made to the 
Imperial Cabinet with regard to Turkey. 

A large number of men are upon the sick list; the officers of the different 
corps give a very indifferent account of the mens’ clothing and accoutrements, 
and the want of boots and shoes is severely felt even before any invasion of an 
enemy's, or as IT should more properly say a friendly country has been under- 
taken. 

No one here appears to consider it possible that with an army so ill- 
provided as that now assembled, a campaign in Turkey can be attempted at 
this advanced period of the season, but a very general belief prevails that 
50,000 men wil be marched into the Principalities, 

Some uneasiness is felt by the British merchants here at the critical aspect 
of affairs; but -as far as 1 have an opportunity of judging, the best possible spirit 
prevails amongst them, . ; 

They desire that ever reasonable effort should be made to avoid war, they 
ave no wish that peace should be prolonged by means of dishonourable con- 
cessions, and they feel as they have every right to do that in a war between 


489 


England and Russia, the great balance of loss must be borne: by the latter 
Power. 

On some future occasion, I shall have the honour of addressing your 
Lordship in more detail upon this subject; in the mean time I will only remark 
that the Russians, who for years have been only in the habit of measuring 
their strength against Persians, Turks, Tartars, and other uncivilized nations 
and tribes, are prone to form an incorrect estimate of their resources. Unless! 
much err, a war between Russia and the west of Europe could not be carried on 
for two years without producing such o crisis as would render the condition of 
this country as preeariousas that of Turkey is represented as being. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received June 29.) 


(No. 306. Secret.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, June 21, 1853. 

WITH reference to my despatch No. 302, I have the honour of inclosing 
to your Lordship the copy of the answer which has been returned by the 
Chancellor to my letter of the 18th instant, 

In my rejoinder, a copy of which I have likewise the honour to transmil, 
[ have taken note of the objects professed to be sought at Constantinople by the 
Russian Chancellerie, and which, if words bore the same sense in this country 
which is affixed to them in all others, might I think be obtained for the Emperor 
without danger to the Sultan's authority, I have further attempted to reconcile 
the Russian Minister to the idea of the differences with the Porte being sub- 
mitted to negotiation. 

‘As regards the insinuations thrown out in Count Nesselrode’s letter against 
a most valuable servant of the Crown, it is really unworthy of the man by 
whom it is made, and the Sovereign whose prejudices he 1s seen to adopt. 
Your Lordship will, I trust, not disapprove of the manner in which I have met 
an indirect accusation. 

The explanation of this maliciousness is very simple. Prince Menchikoff 
has compromised such reputation as he possessed at Constantinople, where he 
proved himself an awkward diplomatist, and when after failing to make an 
advantageous Treaty, he failed again i his endeavour to get up an intelligbile 

uarrel, 
3 lt became necessary to account for failure, and the ready method was before 
him—he had only to charge his English colleague with having intrigued 
against him. 

That Prince Menchikoff should have acted this part is no matter of surprise; 
that his calumnies should have been adopted by the Emperor and his ancient 
servant must, like many late p in Russian history, be painful to those who 
take an interest in the character of public men. 


T have, &e. 
(Signed) G, H. SEYMOUR,

No. 614. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received June 30.) 


(No. 100.) : 
My Lord, Therapia, June 15, 1853. 


I HAVE seen Reshid Pasha this morning. No change appears to have 
taken place in the counsels of the Porte respecting Russia, His Highness’s 
answer to Count Nesselrode’s letter will be delivered to-morrow for transmission 
to St. Petersburgh. I have seen the draft of it, which will probably undergo 
some further amendment. Count Nesselrode is given to understand that his 
advice cannot be followed in the present instance, but a readiness is expressed 
on the part of the Sultan's Government to send an Ambassador to St. Peters- 
burgh for the purpose of resuming the dropped negotiation, provided there be no 
further question of an engagement inconsistent with the Sovereign rights and 
independence of the Porte. . 

Judging from the language of the Russian Embassy when it was here, | 
cannot venture to augur any pood result from this overture. But I have not 
hesitated to recommend its adoption to Reshid Pasha, now that the Porte has 
taken up a ground acknowledged as right and necessary by the general voice of 
Europe, and that the Emperor of Russia may possibly be thereby disposed to 
better counsels, notwithstanding the embarrassing position im which he has 
Naced himself. 

Iam just informed, though not on official authority, that Admiral Dundas 
has brought up his fleet to Besika Bay. The French Admiral will probably 
reach the same station to-day or to-morrow. 
I have, &e. : 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE

No, 517. 


Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received June 30.) 


(No, 102.) 


My Lord, Therapia, June 16, 1855. 

I HASTEN to transmit herewith a copy of Reshid Pasha's answer to Count 
Nesselrode’s letter, of which both the substance and a copy have been succes- 
sively forwarded to your Lordship. 

The Porte, as you will perceive, my Lord, has in no respect receded from 
the position which it occupied at the time of Prince Menchikoff’s departure. 
Appropriate remarks have been made on all the salient points of Count Nessel- 
rode’s letter. The menace of sending the Russian forces across the frontiers, at 
the same time that the intention of making war against the Sultan is discarded, 
has been noticed in becoming, though moderate, terms. ‘The last proof of an 
unpretending and conciliatory spirit is given by the expression of the Porte’s 
readiness to send an Ambassador to St, Petersburgh, and there to resume the 
negotiations upon a distinct understanding that the Russian Government will 
no longer urge the pretension which at present forms the essential matter of 
difference between that Power and the Porte. 

It may well be feared that the prospect of success in making this overture 
is extremely slender, but in the hope of averting so great a calamity as war, I 
feel that no chance should be neglected. 

TL have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

No. 418. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received June 30.) 


(No. 103.) 
My Lord, Therapia, June 16, 1853. 

I HAD an audience of the Sultan this morning and presented Her Majesty's 
letter announcing the birth of a Prince. His Majesty received the communication 
with much interest, and desired me to assure the Queen that any incident 
calculated to augment Her Majesty's domestic happiness was a cause of real 
gratification to himself. . 

I took advantage of the opportunity to offer Her Majesty’s condolence on 
the severe affliction which the Sultan had recently experienced by the loss of his 
mother, the late Validé Sultana. 

I next referred to the arrival of Admiral Dundas with the squadron under 
his command in Besika Bay, and explained to His Imperial Majesty with what 
friendly sentiments and eventual intentions so powerful a force had been placed 
at my disposal. I gave him distinctly to understand that peace was the great 
object of British policy, as it was no doubt that of His Majesty's, and, con- 
sequently, that the services of the British squadron could only be called into 
more decided action for the purpose of averting an immediate and otherwise 
unavoidable danger from the Ottoman Empire, and the independence of His 
Majesty's authority when menaced by foreign aggression. 

The Sultan acquiesced in this dectaration of the views of Her Majesty's 
Government, and expressed a deep feeling of gratitude for the unequivocal marks 
of sympathy and cordial support afforded to him and his empire under the 
critical circumstances in which he is now placed. 

He was, moreover, pleased to express his satisfaction with the counsels 
which T had occasionally given him during the late negotiations. 

Before leaving His Majesty's presence I reminded him of what I had 
frequently stated before with respect to the importance, and indeed necessity, of 
no louger deferring those additional acts of benevolence towards his Christian 
subjects, and those comprehensive measures of administrative improvement, 
which are so imperiously required for this empire by the general voice of Europe 
and the necessities of the time. IT expressed my unwillingness to trespass at any 
length upon his Majesty's indulgence during the period of religious seclusion 
now in progress, but I solicited his permission to enter more particularly upon the 
subject with one or more of his confidential servants, in order to prepare a 
distinct plan for His Majesty's consideration hereafter. The Sultan condescended 
to declare his approbation of this suggestion ; and I hope that with the assistance 
of Reshid Pusha, and the employment of other means, | may be abie finally to 
realise ‘a portion at least of the hones which I have made it my duty to cherish 
in spite of frequent disappointment, 

I have, &c., 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE. 


No. 519, 


Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received June 30.) 


(No. 104. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Therap, June 17, 1854, 
THE Sultan's Minister for Foreign Affairs, on receiving Count Nesselrode’s 
letter of the $7 May, requested that I would draw up the reply to it. Although 
in the present state of things I conceived that it would be more prudent not to 
comply with his wish, I cheerfully undertook to suggest any amendments that 
might occur to me in his Highness’s draft of the letter. Thus far I have taken 
part in the composition, and that passage in particular which takes notice of 
Count Nesselrode’s declaration as to the Russian armies passing the frontier was 
introduced at mv suggestion, I thought that the silence of Reshid Pasha on ¢o 
offensive an intimation would be liable to misconstruction, but I took care ta

word the animadyersion in such manner as not to engage the Porte to more 
than a moral resistance. 

The idea of an eventual Embassy to St. Petersburgh originated with my 
French colleague, or rather perhaps with M. de Klezl, who several weeks ago 
warmly recommended the adoption of that expedient to the Turkish Minister. 
I have thought from the first that the measure would in all likelihood prove as 
fruitless in the experiment as it was obvious in conception. It was not to be 
expected that the Emperor of Russia, who fancied that he had found no small 
amount of double dealing in the conduct of the last Turkish Ambassador 
accredited to his Court, and who complained that the Sultan’s assurances, though 
addressed directly to himself, were never realized, would be satisfied or even 
otherwise than irritated by a fresh attempt to soften him with autograph letters 
and extraordinary Embassies. My impressions on this subject were confirmed 
shortly after the departure of Prince Menchikoff by a member of the Russian 
Embassy, who assured me that the Sultan’s Ambassador, if an appointment of 
the kind were to take place, would not be received at St. Petersburgh, and that 
the case had been provided for in the instructions given to his chief. 

I have nevertheless acquiesced in the present overture, for reasons which I 
hope will be found satisfactory by Her Majesty’s Government. Before it can 
reach the Emperor of Russia, His Majesty will have learnt how completely the 
opinion of Europe has shown itself adverse to his pretensions, and with what 
difficulties he will have to contend in proceeding to give effect to an aggressive 
policy against Turkey. It is reasonable to hope that under such circumstances 
the Russian Government may be inclined to catch at anything which may offer a 
chance of relieving it with honour from the embarrassment of a false position, 
To these considerations may be added the hypothetical nature of the present 
overture which shelters the Sultan from the humiliation of having his Ambas- 
sador rejected, while it affords an additional evidence of the Porte’s conciliatory 
and peaceable spirit within the limits prescribed by a due regard for its indepen- 
dence and sovereign authority. Such are the principal motives which have 
prevailed with me to acquiesce in M, de la Cour's experiment, and most sincerely 
do I hope that the result may be such as every friend of peace must desire. 1 
have taken care that there should be no mistake as to the Porte’s consistency on 
the main point of difference, and if the Emperor Nicholas were after all to accept 
the proposal, it is understood that Her Majesty's Embassy will have a voice in 
the selection of the Ambassador and a control over the draft of his instructions. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

No, 524, 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received June 30.) 


(No. 251, Confidential.) 


My Lord, Vienna, June 27, 1853. 

IN obedience to. the instructions contained in your Lordship’s despatch 
No, 168, I waited upon Count Buol for the purpose of ascertaining whether the 
views of Austria in the affairs of Turkey were such as [ had expressed them in 
my despatch No. 237 and other recent despatches to your Lordship, or whether 
they were more accurately represented by the impressions which, from the docu- 
ments transmitted to me by your Lordship, Baron Manteuffel appears to 
entertain with regard to Austrian subserviency to Russia. I am happy to be able 
to inform your Lordship that the correctness of my statements in the above- 
mentioned despatch, and subsequently, as to the line of policy adopted by Count 
Buol, is completely corroborated not only by his own verbal assertions, but also 
the correspondence with his own diplomatic agents in London and St. Peters- 
burgh, as well as by his communications with Baron de Bourqueney, In the 
execution of your Lordship’s directions I felt that the only mode of dealin 
fairly with Count Buol in my endeavour to obtain the information you wishe 
for, was to state to him without reserve the representation which had been made 
eondemnatory of his policy, and confidentially I read to him a précis of those 
representations. Count Buol immediately sent for his correspondence with 
London and St. Petersburgh, and he read to me his despatches to Count 
Colloredo of the 14th and 41st instant. He read also a private letter to Count 
Colloredo of the 14th instant, as well as the despatches to Baron Lebzeltern, 
the Austrian Chargé d’ Affaires at St. Petersburgh, and his replies ; also the last 
despatch of the 18th which he had addressed to that gentleman, 

The result of this recapitulation of Count Buol’s correspondence proved 
that he had blamed the manner and form of Prince Menchikoff’s negotiations ; 
that he objected to the Convention and the Sened he had proposed; that he 
also objected to some of the terms of the last note presented by him; but with

The conclusion of the conversation was more satisfactory than some preé- 
ceding parts of it had been. The Chancellor said that in spite of all that was 
said and done, he still clung to the expectation of the present crisis being sur- 
mounted without an interruption of peace. 

I must not, however, conceal from your Lordship my belief that the 
eceupation of the Principalities is resolved upon; and that it is only at that 
stage of the proceedings that the Russian Cabinet looks to an amicable adjust- 
ment (however brought about) of the differences which now exist between the 
allied Cabinets. 

According to my views, a Russian occupation will serve only to render 
composition more difficult; hut, as | before stated, the impression which my 
various conversations with the Chancellor have left upon my mind is, that the 
measure is decided upon. 

I ought, perhaps, to have stated that, in the course of my interview the 
Chancellor having remarked upon the unreasonableness of expecting that the 
Emperor should be called upon to recede from his position, and to modify terms 
already so modified, 1 begged leave to observe that nothing could have been 
more impartial and consistent than the conduct of Her Majesty’s Government ; 
that when France had unluckily disturbed a slumbering question, the language 
of Her Majesty’s Government had been: “ You have been the first to trouble the 
repose which prevailed ; you are bound to take the first steps towards the settle- 
ment of the differences to which your conduct has given rise.” Now, T went 
on to say, Her Majesty's Government does not even go so far. Their language 
is: “It is now Russia who, by her demands, puts the peace of Europe in 
danger, Let us settle the difficulty by negotiation, and let Russia meet us only 
half way.”

No. 529. 


Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received July 1.) 
(No. 314.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, June 24, 1853, 
- ‘THERE are some particulars of the conversation which: I held’ with the 
Chancellor on the 22nd which I reserve for a confidential despatch. 

Upon my asking for explanation as to’ the stipulations of the Treaty of 
Kainardji, and the Greek rights enjoyed ab antiquo, the Chancellor replied that 
they could be best given by Baron Brunnow; that he himself knew little of the 
matter, while Baron Brunnow was well versed in Oriental questions. 

I then suggested the idea of a memorandum, and I did so partly because I 
have learnt how important it is that explanations should be given in a recorded 
shape, and partly because the mystification which has been resorted to upon 
some late occasions is such, that I am persuaded that many of these ex planalions 
do but render an obscure and doubtful point still more obscure and involved. 

A portion of the Chancellor's conversation, | would further remark, led me 
to believe that he has been grossly misled as to the feeling which prevails in 
England, and as the error might be dangerous, I cleared it up. 

The Chancellor dwelt upon the horrors of war, and was certain, from what 
he learnt, that those who clamoured the most for violent measures, would be the 
first to recoil if there was the slightest appearance of a war with Russia ; that no 
one in England desired it. 

I intreated of his Excellency pot to foster such illusians ; were he more 
correetly informed he would find that as usual the Government were web meme 


seu 


504 


pacific than the people; tnat the difficulty was not as to going to war, but’as to 
keeping the country back from war; and that if my words were not credited, I 
would only request that the newspapers representing every shade of political 
opinion in England might be consulted. Upon this point, and upon one or two 
others, | found it necessary to speak more plainly to the Chancellor than 1 am 
in the habit of doing. His new practice of representing Lord Stratford de 
Redcliffe as a sort of incarnation of opposition to the Emperor's views, I thought 
extremely objectionable. 

It was Lord Stratford alone who had taken so exaggerated a view of the 
Russian demands. He had alone prevented their acceptance. It was now asked 
that the Emperor should give way; but really, when it became a personal 
question between a Sovereign and an Ambassador, in his opinion it was for Lord 
Stratford, and not for the Emperor, to recede. 

To this, and further reproach and inuendo of the same description, I simply 
answered that it was time to give up addressing to an individual roaches 
which, if deserved at all, should be addressed to a Government; that Lord 
Stratford’s conduct had been most proper and judicious, and as such had been 
entirely approved of; that his Lordship had given able and welcome support to 
Prince Menchikoff’s demands as far as they had been explained to him and 
approved of by him; and that, if he had not followed the Prince in his sudden 
and more distant flight, it was simply because he thought that what was proposed. 
was full of danger for Turkey—an opinion in which her Majesty’s Government 
completely concurred, . 

The explanation which the Chancellor has given to various persons as to 
the present policy of the Western Governments is this: England has adopted it 
in deference to the prejudices of her Ambassador at Constantinople. Brine 
(who has not the remotest interest in Turkey) has likewise taken it up, with a 
view to forming an alliance with England. 

I have, &e. 


(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.
